We’ve introduced a series of legislative reforms, including particularly CAIL. CAIL is, as the member will be well aware, the Criminal Activity Intervention Legislation Act. This is a piece of legislation that has been seen to be critically important for the police and, indeed, it was something that they have been relying on in a range of different circumstances. Our job as governors is to continue to build on that programme, and the announcements that we made yesterday, and indeed today, continue to address the issues in law and order that we continue to see.

explanation: The question asks how priorities are determined given an apparent disagreement between the PM and Deputy PM. She denies the disagreement and says Cabinet has made decisions, but never reaches the "how" — the mechanism asked about goes unanswered.
question: How does the Government determine its priorities in justice when the Prime Minister says there’s been an explosion in crime, but the Deputy Prime Minister says of crime in Auckland, “Oh, I wouldn’t say it’s bad at all.”? How can a Government determine priorities when there’s no agreement on the scale of the problem that it’s trying to fix?
statement: Oh, there’s a very clear agreement. Cabinet has made a raft of decisions in the law and order space and will continue to do so.

explanation: Asked to resolve an either/or (trend down vs 40% increase), she engages both halves squarely: acknowledges the increase, says it peaked in August, and says numbers have come down since. That is a real answer to "which is it". Slight padding about commitment keeps it off the top, but the core is addressed.
question: So which is it: the trend is down or ram raids have increased by 40 percent in the last year?
statement: They remain too high and that’s why we’re taking further actions to bring them down. I do acknowledge there has been an increase in ram raids, which peaked in August of last year. I remain committed to tackling the problem. While we have seen those numbers come down since August, I do not believe any ram raid is acceptable.

explanation: Asked WHY ram raids increased on her watch. She offers no cause at all — she restates the August peak and pivots to what the Government is funding, then attacks the previous Government's record. The causal question is never reached.
question: Why have ram raids increased since she became the Minister?
statement: We have seen, as I have said, a peak in August of last year, but that is exactly why this Government is taking action to fund our front-line police, to make sure we have the resources there to prosecute, and to make sure that those young repeat offenders are brought to account. That is resourcing our front line, unlike that member’s previous Government that cut front-line resources.

explanation: Asked why NZ was safer under National. She does implicitly contest the premise by setting Labour's record against National's, which is engagement with the comparison at the heart of the question — but she never says she rejects the premise, and never addresses the 'why' as put. Gestures at the question without landing on it.
question: Well, why was New Zealand safer under a National Government than it is under a Labour Government?
statement: Did that member say that he feels that all New Zealand—the track record for Labour is that we have delivered 1,800 extra police, we have put $35 million into retail crime prevention, we have enabled Operation Cobalt with 40,000 charges brought against gang members, we have rolled out the tactical response model right across to keep our cops safer, and we have introduced legislation that enables new warrant powers for intra-gang conflict. I put that up against the track record of the previous National Government, which closed over 30 police stations, which froze the police budget, which let police numbers fall, and cut victims’ funding.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements were made; she names the announcement ($26m for police prosecutions) and what it covers. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made about the pursuit of criminal offending?
statement: I was pleased to announce yesterday an additional $26 million for police prosecutions to help clear the case backlog in the District Court. This is a significant investment in police resources, which will lead to a strengthened prosecution service, and it means that police can take stronger cases against criminals that cause harm to our communities. Overall, police will get more resources devoted to their work, to improve the quality and the preparation for their in-court work. I have heard firsthand from our communities that they want the Government to go further in breaking the cycle of crime but also to hold accountable those repeat offenders. That is exactly why this Government is doing that by giving police the tools they need to get the results.

explanation: Asked what practical impacts the funding will have; the answer is entirely about the impacts (44 in-court staff, 41 support roles, file quality, fewer adjournments). Squarely on the question.
question: What practical impacts will this additional funding have?
statement: The police prosecution staff do a fantastic job, but they have been under considerable demand over the past few years. This is a significant investment that will help ease that pressure and help them to focus on greater outcomes for our communities. An additional 44 staff focused on in-court work will be funded by the initiative and a further 41 positions will be funded for key support roles to enable prosecutors to focus on in-court activities. There will also be a focus on the consistency of file preparation, and an increased use of digital files means the file quality will improve. This will allow disclosure of information in a more timely way and also reduce the number of adjournments due to disclosure delays.

explanation: Asked what other improvements will be made; she lists further improvements (case progression, deployment, fewer repeat appearances). Open-ended question, engaged directly.
question: What other improvements will be made?
statement: An investment in case progression and resolution will involve improved processes and supporting how prosecution staff are deployed in each case and in each court. This investment will also mean more meaningful court appearances when the cases do arrive at court. Cases won’t need to go back time and time again, meaning fewer appearances in court. This will help with some of the demand pressures on the police front line, and they won’t need to repeatedly attend court. All these improvements will mean quicker progress for victims and provide a greater sense of justice as cases are resolved through the courts. We’ve heard from the community and are strengthening police to better represent and support victims through funding this increase.

explanation: Asked how this frees up the front line; she gives the mechanism — support staff absorb admin, fewer adjournments mean less time in court, more time in communities. Answers the 'how' as asked.
question: How will this free up the police front line?
statement: These changes are about raising accountability for those who commit crimes by ensuring that we have dedicated police resources that will be focused on working to prosecute offenders. Dedicated support staff will help our front line completing key administrative tasks. Our front-line staff will spend less time in court giving evidence as a result of having those decreased adjournments. All of these changes mean our front-line officers can spend more time in their communities rather than sitting at a desk dealing with administration. That’s a win for our police and a win for our communities.

explanation: A yes/no question answered "Yes." One word, complete, no dodge.
question: Does she stand by all of her actions and policies?
statement: Yes.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether the spend was good value; "Yes" answers it completely. The absence of justification is a lack of detail, not a dodge — that belongs to Specificity, not here.
question: Does she believe that spending $1 million on an attendance awareness campaign was good value for money when it was “not expected to have a direct quantifiable impact on attendance rates”?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Two-part question: value for money, and — if so — how the Te Tiriti framing teaches 7-year-olds numeracy. "Yes" answers the first part and, by answering it affirmatively, triggers the second part, which is left entirely unaddressed. Half the question engaged.
question: Does she believe spending $1.3 million on a new maths and statistics curriculum was good value for money; and, if so, how will “expressing the centrality of Te Tiriti o Waitangi and its principles” teach 7-year-olds basic numeracy skills?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Same two-part structure, but the unanswered half is a narrow factual one — how many attendance officers have been recruited. "Yes" resolves the value-for-money half and leaves the number completely unsupplied; a dodged specific factual ask weighs heavier than a dodged open one.
question: Does she believe that spending $74 million for 82 new school attendance officer roles is good value for money; and, if so, how many attendance officers have been recruited to date?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked how the public can have confidence in her given the alleged wasteful spending. She disputes the premise by asserting the initiatives are working, which is some engagement, but the question — the basis for public confidence — is never addressed. Contesting the premise without reaching the question.
question: How can the public have confidence in her when she prioritises wasteful spending on vanity projects over basic things like making sure the next generation of New Zealanders knows how to read and write?
statement: All of those aspects and initiatives that the member has talked about are making a big difference to this country and to our young people. They are wonderful initiatives; wonderful programmes.

explanation: Two-part question: actions since 2017, and will legislation be introduced this Parliament. Both parts are met head-on — 'no policy decisions have been made... no changes will be introduced before the House rises' answers the second squarely, and the consultation/Law Commission review history answers the first. Length and detail are not what earn the score; the fact that neither half is left hanging is.
question: What actions has the Government taken based on the consultations and reviews of the Burial and Cremation Act 1964 since 2017, and will she introduce legislation on this subject in this Parliament?
statement: Talofa lava, Mr Speaker. In response to the last question, I am open to amending the Act, but no policy decisions have been made to do so. No changes will be introduced before the House rises next month. In response to the first part of the question, the Ministry of Health – Manatū Hauora ran a public consultation process on possible options to modernise the legislation in late 2019. That consultation followed a review by the Law Commission, which concluded that the Burial and Cremation Act 1964 is outdated and should be repealed and replaced with new legislation. The ministry’s public consultation process identified further areas that needed consideration. Since then, health officials have been engaging further with individuals and community groups who have an interest in this area of reform. One issue being actively considered is whether a broader range of factors needed to be considered, the impact of non-regulatory changes such as implementing online death certification, and updating guidance for practitioners.

explanation: Asked (a) whether Ngā Pou Herenga, a named group, was consulted, and (b) whether tangata whenua acting as funeral guides were specifically consulted. The named group is never mentioned at all — that half is simply not answered. The tangata whenua half is answered only at a general level (iwi/hapū contacted, marae and trust submissions listed) without reaching the 'funeral guides' specificity asked for. Half the question engaged, half avoided.
question: So with the consultation the Minister has undertaken, has that included with community sector groups such as Ngā Pou Herenga—the Funeral Guides Collective—and, if so, was there specific consultation with tangata whenua, who act as funeral guides on marae and in their communities?
statement: I’m advised that Manatū Hauora officials undertook public consultation in 2019 and 2020 on potential options to modernise the Burial and Cremation Act 1964 in relation to legislation. The group Death Without Debt provided a public submission and met with officials in August last year to discuss the burial and cremation work programme and policy proposals. Health officials contacted a number of Māori providers based on iwi and hapū listed in Te Kāhui Māngai—the directory of iwi and Māori organisations—as well as other groups such as the New Zealand Māori Council. Manatū Hauora asked these groups and organisations to submit on the consultation document and to disseminate it amongst their members. There were a total of 196 submissions on the consultation. This included submissions from Ngāi Tahu Māori Law Centre; Ngāheke, Waiwhetu Marae; Te Korowai o Ngāruahine Trust; and Tūwharetoa Māori Trust Board. In addition, there were 14 individual submitters who identified as Māori.

explanation: Asked what affordable options outside the private funeral industry have been considered. The answer effectively says none yet — 'officials are continuing to work on options... that advice has not yet been received' — which is a direct, if unhelpful, response to a 'what have you considered' question. Marked down only because the closing pivot to MSD/ACC grants substitutes an adjacent topic for the one asked about, blunting the core of it.
question: What affordable options for whānau has the Minister considered, if any, outside of the private funeral industry, that currently enjoys a captive market for pre - cremation and burial paperwork in almost all after-death care?
statement: I’m very aware of the costs for whānau in the private funeral industry. Health officials are continuing to work on options in this area. That advice has not yet been received. In other portfolios, there are a number of Government initiatives to support whānau who might be struggling with the costs associated with funerals. For example, depending on the circumstances, grants may be available from agencies including the Ministry of Social Development, ACC, and a range of charitable organisations.

explanation: The question has a soft frame ('what does the Minister say to') but a hard core: the group's call to extend the health and disability code so doctors complete pre-cremation and burial paperwork. The response addresses the group — acknowledges and empathises with them — but never engages the proposal itself, deferring to 'still considering... further advice in the next few months'. Responds to the questioner's framing while stepping around the substantive ask.
question: What does the Minister say to advocacy group Death Without Debt—who are in the gallery today—who are concerned about funeral-driven poverty, in her call for extending the health and disability code to include after-death care so doctors complete pre - cremation and burial paperwork and the public is not forced to depend on the private funeral industry to do so?
statement: I am aware of and empathise with Death Without Debt’s concerns. I acknowledge the work they do and their members’ advocacy. Manatū Hauora is still considering work in this space and expects to provide further advice in the next few months.

explanation: Asked whether she had considered the impact of severe weather on tangihanga. 'I have not received any advice on this issue' is a plain no — a refusal-shaped answer that nonetheless answers completely. The follow-on about local authority responsibility explains rather than deflects. That the answer is unsatisfying to the questioner is a matter for other attributes.
question: Has the Minister considered the impact that severe weather events have on tangihanga and funerals in areas such as Te Tairāwhiti, where we must cremate our loved ones, such as we did two weeks ago with my uncle Kahu Smiler, because the high water table will preclude burials, potentially, for months?
statement: First of all, my condolences to the member for her whānau’s loss. I have not received any advice on this issue. However, the management of cemeteries and burial grounds is the responsibility of local authorities, and those decisions sit with local authorities.

explanation: A narrow two-part factual question — current budget, and comparison to 2015-18 — met with both figures ($2.8 billion vs $1.7 billion) and the comparison stated outright. The opening and closing talking-point framing surrounds the answer but does not replace it; the numbers asked for are given.
question: What is the current State highway maintenance budget for 2021-24, and how does this compare to 2015-18?
statement: The Government is spending more on road maintenance, including on pothole repairs, than any previous Government. The current State highway maintenance budget is $2.8 billion for the period 2021-24, a 65 percent increase on the $1.7 billion from 2015-18. With the increased frequency of severe weather events, increasing the resilience of our roading networks is critical to our economy. Maintenance spending on all roads, including local roads, has increased by 54 percent since this Government took office. This has meant we have been able to fund huge increases in pothole repairs and road resurfacing.

explanation: A precise number was requested and a precise number was given (60,989), and the 'is this an increase' half is answered explicitly. The chosen comparison baseline (2013-14 rather than the prior year) is a question of whether the comparison is apt, which belongs to Rigor, not to whether the question was engaged.
question: How many potholes did Waka Kotahi repair in 2022-23, and is this an increase?
statement: Well, in 2022-23, Waka Kotahi repaired 60,989 potholes. This compares with just 12,739 pothole repairs in 2013-14. That’s an almost 500 percent increase in pothole repairs.

explanation: Both parts answered directly: the required resurfacing rate is given as a figure ('around 9 percent or 2,000 kilometres'), and recent trends are supplied. The preamble explaining why resurfacing matters is padding around, not instead of, the answer.
question: What percentage of the network needs to be resurfaced each year to maintain the State highway network, and what recent trends in resurfacing is he aware of?
statement: Resurfacing, of course, is absolutely critical, because if you don’t resurface the road, when the road gets dished with heavy trucks and cracks, the rain gets in, and you get potholes. So what is needed to prevent that, according to Waka Kotahi, is around 9 percent or 2,000 kilometres of the State highways need to be resurfaced each year. Other than during the first wave of COVID, this Government has delivered more than 2,000 kilometres of road resurfacing every full year we’ve been in Government. In contrast, between 2013-14 and 2015-16, road resurfacing halved to 4.5 percent—half of the 9 percent required.

explanation: A yes/no question — is he satisfied with the current level of road maintenance — answered by narrowing the object of satisfaction: satisfied 'that we have been catching up', which is not the same claim. He then concedes 'there's still a lot of work to do', which points toward no without ever saying it. Engages the subject and hedges around the core rather than dodging outright.
question: Is he satisfied with the current level of road maintenance in New Zealand?
statement: Well, I’m satisfied that we have been catching up on a lot of road maintenance. I’m also aware that the severe weather events that we’ve had this year, particularly in the upper half of the North Island, are absolutely unprecedented. So there’s still a lot of work to do, and this Government is committed to doing that work—committing to funding it, committing to doing it properly, and committing to funding it properly.

explanation: Asked directly whether the Government intends to defund police highway work. No statement of intent is ever given. The reply describes the funding of ~1,000 traffic police and argues there is little money to be saved there — an oblique implication of 'no' that leaves the question formally unanswered. The topic is engaged; the question is not.
question: Does the Government intend to defund police work on our main highways?
statement: Well, the major component of the cost of safety measures that are funded by the Government is the approximately 1,000 police dedicated to traffic duties that the Government funds. It’s really important work, and there’s actually not a lot of money to be saved there that could be spent on potholes.

explanation: 'Does she stand by her statement; if so, why?' — she says she stands by it and then supplies reasons, so both halves are covered. Slight discount because she restores a longer version of the quote than the one put to her, subtly shifting what is being stood behind, but she does not evade the yes.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “It is my view that New Zealanders feel safer”; if so, why?
statement: I stand by my full statement at the time it was given: “It is my view that New Zealanders feel safer with a Government on track to deliver 1,800 extra police.” I stand by that statement given the recent announcement the Government has made to empower police to crack down on youth offending, as well as gang offending—this includes introducing an aggravating factor that would apply whenever adults aid, abet, or incite a person under the age of 18 to carry out an offence. It would also make it an aggravating factor when posting offending behaviour online for both adults and also for young people. It includes introducing great accountability for youth offending by bringing youth justice tools and approaches into the Family Court. And, finally, I’m pleased to see a funding boost of $26 million for the Police Prosecution Service.

explanation: A narrow, checkable factual question — is the 40 percent increase figure correct — and the figure is never confirmed, denied, or corrected. The reply opens on talking points about unacceptable offending and Government action, and the one gesture at data ('the trend is down from a high in August, in 2022') answers a different question about direction of travel rather than the stated figure. A specific factual question squarely avoided.
question: Is it correct that ram raids have increased by 40 percent in the last year?
statement: The current level of offending is entirely unacceptable, and that is why this Government is taking further action to break the cycle of offending and to hold those repeat offenders to account. The trend is down from a high in August, in 2022, but we have got a lot more work to do and we remain committed to doing that.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all Government statements and actions; he opens with "Yes" — a complete answer to a yes/no question — before elaborating on ram-raid policy. The elaboration is unrelated padding, but the question itself was squarely answered.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, particularly my decision to wish the member a very happy birthday! But I particularly stand by the Government’s decision to introduce a new offence to prosecute ram raids: a new Youth Court pathway enabling 12- to 13-year-olds to be brought before the Youth Court for ram-raiding. We’re also extending the successful circuit breaker intervention programme, which has worked for nearly 75 percent of the young people referred to it. The measures introduced to date to combat youth offending have been working for most kids, but we recognise that we need more tools in the tool box to respond to the worst repeat offenders. Nobody wants to see any child or young person locked up, and that’s why these changes are part of a continuum of work focused on prevention, protection, and accountability that breaks the cycle.

explanation: Asked when he expects inflation to return to 3 percent; he names a timeframe — the second half of next year, per Government agency forecasts. Direct and complete.
question: When does he expect inflation to return to 3 percent, like in the US and Canada?
statement: There are a range of forecasts, but if you look at the Government agencies, most of them would be forecasting that in the second half of next year.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees his spending has contributed to inflation; he never says yes or no, but does contest the spending premise on its own terms (spending as a share of GDP is falling, latest numbers are down). Engages the core factual dispute while side-stepping the inflation link.
question: Does he agree his rampant spending of an extra billion dollars of spending each and every week has contributed to inflation in New Zealand now being higher than all the major Asia-Pacific economies, including the US, Canada, Australia, Singapore, China, and Japan?
statement: Actually, if the member looks at the current Government’s spending and the spending over the forecast period, Government spending as a proportion of GDP is declining—and, actually, the most recent Government spending numbers indicate that Government spending is down.

explanation: Asked whether three named items were good value or wasteful spending; he takes only one of the three, does not say whether it was good value, and turns it into a point about National's own positions. It grazes the question without reaching it.
question: Does he think spending $200 million on a light rail business case, $1.7 billion on consultants, or $51 million on a cancelled bike bridge are actually good value for money, or are they just more examples of wasteful spending driving up inflation?
statement: Well, if we just take one of those figures—the spending on consultants that the member has just mentioned—I would note that those consultants work on a range of different projects, many of which the National Party are arguing we should do more of.

explanation: Asked why he spent months on a wealth tax instead of a growth plan; he asserts a growth plan exists and lists trade achievements, never addressing the wealth-tax work the question was about. Answers a different question than the one asked.
question: Why, with the country in a recession and inflation at record highs, did he waste months designing a wealth tax when he should have been designing an economic growth plan?
statement: The Government has an economic growth plan. I note, for example, the work that we have done to increase our international trade, including one of the most successful track records of any New Zealand Government in entering trade agreements around the world. Unlike the members opposite, we don’t just talk a big game on trade; we actually deliver results.

explanation: Asked why the growth plan has left NZ the only country in the region in recession; he offers no cause, instead disputing the framing by citing cumulative post-COVID growth. Contests the premise rather than answering the "why".
question: Why has this fantastic economic growth plan led to New Zealand being the only country in a recession in the Asia-Pacific region?
statement: The economy is 6 percent bigger than it was before the global pandemic. Members can take quarter-by-quarter figures if they want to, but, if you look at the totality of the period since COVID-19, our economic performance rates pretty well compared to the other economies that we would typically compare ourselves to.

explanation: Asked again why NZ alone is in recession; this time he gives a specific cause — the cyclone's effect on the quarterly figures, without which there would be no recession. Squarely answers the question put.
question: Why are we the only country in the Asia-Pacific region in a recession, then?
statement: If you look at the most recent quarterly figures for economic growth, it factors in the severe effects of the cyclone. Without the cyclone, we would not be in recession.

explanation: Asked whether the wealth-tax resource would have been better spent on cutting waste; he gives no answer either way, redirecting to what drove spending growth and then to National's fiscal plan and Nicola Willis. The core of the question is never reached.
question: Wouldn’t it have been better, instead of spending millions of dollars and thousands of hours in the bureaucracy developing a wealth tax, for that resource to actually have been focused on stopping wasteful spending so that Kiwis can get to keep more of what they earn?
statement: I note once again that, when the member talks about wasteful spending, he fails to acknowledge what the increase in Government spending has been driven by—by population growth; by increased wages for our teachers, our doctors, and our nurses; and by the introduction of programmes that New Zealanders rely on. And I note that he still isn’t indicating how the National Party is going to make its promises add up. They keep promising to spend more money and cut money at the same time. It’s no wonder Nicola Willis fails to produce an alternative fiscal plan—because she simply can’t make it add up.

explanation: Asked what announcements she has made on support for those hit by extreme weather; she names the announcement and its terms (start date, weekly payment, rate set at average regional rent). Directly responsive.
question: What announcements has she made about supporting people impacted by the extreme weather events?
statement: This morning, I was pleased to announce that the Government is providing support to displaced homeowners impacted by recent extreme weather events. The interim payment will be available from 4 September 2023, made weekly and directly to homeowners, and set at 100 percent of the average rent declared by accommodation supplement recipients in the recipient’s region. Having visited a few of the impacted areas and met informally with residents, I’m hopeful that this is the security and certainty they both need and deserve as they continue to plan and recover from the extreme weather events.

explanation: Asked how much homeowners will receive; she gives the scaling basis and a concrete worked figure of up to $610 per week. Answers the amount question asked.
question: How much support will homeowners receive?
statement: The amount will be scaled according to the homeowner’s location and household make-up. For example, a two-parent family with three children in Auckland could receive up to $610 per week through this programme. We based the settings for this support on the Canterbury Temporary Accommodation Assistance put in place following the earthquakes, but are making sure that we continue to work on an enduring solution, building on the experience in Canterbury.

explanation: Asked what further announcements she has made beyond the accommodation package; she names the social sector recovery plan and what it funds. Directly on point.
question: What further announcements has the Minister made in addition to the Temporary Accommodation Assistance package?
statement: Yesterday, in Thames-Coromandel, I announced the social sector recovery plan. The plan helps to ensure people’s needs will continue to be met over the next two years through a suite of tangible actions. Some examples of where the funding is going to include personalised support and referral services for people impacted by land-zoning change; support for students who have missed school, so they can catch up on lost learning; education and training for providers to support whānau, rangatahi, and tamariki with anxiety and mental wellbeing; and support for volunteers and community workers suffering burnout.

explanation: Asked how else the Government is supporting affected regions; she names a further specific measure — $200,000 for Coromandel tourism promotion. Answers the question asked.
question: How else is the Government supporting regions impacted by the weather events?
statement: Whilst in Thames-Coromandel yesterday, I announced a boost in support for local tourism and businesses. Government have committed $200,000 to support promotion efforts to help bring visitors back into a part of the country which was badly affected by Cyclone Gabrielle. We’re working alongside the council and local businesses to make sure New Zealanders know that the Coromandel is open for business over the coming summer.

explanation: Asked (a) does he stand by his dated answer about when the PM ruled out a wealth tax, and (b) has the PM asked him to develop income tax reduction proposals since 11 April. Answered both parts explicitly — yes, then no. Terse and undetailed, but every part of the question is squarely engaged.
question: Does he stand by his answer to my question yesterday, asking on which date the Prime Minister informed him he would rule out the introduction of a wealth tax, that “In the lead-up to the final Budget paper going to Cabinet, which I believe was on 11 April”; if so, has the Prime Minister asked him to develop any proposals for delivering income tax reduction since 11 April 2023?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes. In answer to the second part of the question, no.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the quoted statement, and what economic conditions would justify introducing a wealth tax. Only the first part is answered ("yes"); the substantive second part — the core of what was being probed — is left entirely unaddressed.
question: Does he stand by his statement last week that ultimately the decision was made not to go ahead with a wealth tax “given the significance of the change in difficult and highly uncertain economic conditions”, and, if so, what are the economic conditions in which he believes New Zealand should introduce a wealth tax?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes.

explanation: Asked directly what economic conditions would make a wealth tax appropriate. He declines by labelling it hypothetical and then pivots to attacking the Opposition's unfunded tax cuts. The dismissal is not a plain refusal to answer so much as a redirection to talking points about a different question.
question: What are the economic conditions in which he believes New Zealand should introduce a wealth tax?
statement: That is a hypothetical question. What I do know is that the economic conditions that New Zealand is in right now are not the ones where a programme of unfunded tax cuts that would proportionately benefit the wealthiest New Zealanders are a good thing to do, as the member would propose.

explanation: Asked whether a wealth tax remains on the table pending convenient conditions. Answered with a flat "No" plus the ground for it (ruled out by the PM). It engages the yes/no core directly; it ignores the rhetorical tail about advisers' warnings, which was not the question.
question: Isn’t it the case that a wealth tax remains firmly on his table, he’s just waiting for the economic conditions which will provide him a handy excuse—and this despite the pages and pages of warnings from taxpayer-funded advisers that introducing a wealth tax would completely undermine the innovation and entrepreneurship needed for a strong economy?
statement: No, that has been ruled out by the Prime Minister.

explanation: Asked what support the Government gave to hosting the FIFA Women's World Cup. Answered with the support given — $55m total, broken into facilities, legacy programme and NZ Football funding. Directly and completely on the question asked.
question: What support has the Government given to the hosting of the FIFA Women’s World Cup?
statement: The Government has invested $55 million to ensure a successful co-hosting of the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2023 alongside Australia. Of this, around $25 million has been provided to support upgrades at sporting facilities across Aotearoa New Zealand. A further $10 million has been set aside to support a leverage and legacy programme, which includes around 50 activities and projects across the country. New Zealand Football has also received funding to help capitalise on the increase of interest in football off the back of the tournament to grow the game here in Aotearoa New Zealand.

explanation: Asked how the funding supported venue facility upgrades. Answered exactly that: 30 facilities, and the kinds of upgrades made. No drift off the question.
question: How has the funding supported the upgrades of facilities at event venues and trading grounds?
statement: Well, the upgrades have happened in 30 sporting facilities across the country. They include pitch, lighting, and facility enhancements; unisex changing spaces; and event infrastructure. These upgrades are critical to ensure the success of the tournament, but will also benefit local communities, football clubs, and many different sporting codes that use these facilities for years to come.

explanation: Asked what support was provided to build a long-term legacy from the event. After a short framing preamble about the wider strategy, he answers with the $10m leverage and legacy programme, its domains and a concrete example. The core is reached, slightly late.
question: What support has been provided to leverage the event to create a long-term legacy for New Zealand?
statement: Well, the decision to invest in this event aligns with the overall Government’s Strategy for Women and Girls in Sport and Active Recreation, which aims to grow female participation, create new female leaders, and raise the visibility of women’s sport. The $10 million leverage and legacy programme I mentioned is critical to supporting these outcomes. It includes a broad range of projects that drive benefits for Aotearoa New Zealand in education, sport, tourism, international relations, community development, business, health, culture, and conservation. Just one example is the GirlBoss programme, which is a collaboration between GirlBoss New Zealand and the Ministry of Education to use sport and the event as a platform to encourage young women to explore career pathways in psychology, sports science, advanced medicine, surgery, and other related fields.

explanation: Asked how the World Cup support aligns with the women and girls in sport strategy. He states the strategy's three themes and how hosting such events advances them, which is the alignment asked about, though he wanders into unrelated pride and a match plug at the end.
question: How does the Government’s support for the FIFA World Cup align with the Government’s women and girls sport strategy?
statement: In 2018, the Government launched New Zealand’s first ever women and girls in sport strategy, with three themes of participation, leadership, and valuing and visibility. I am proud of the strides that we’ve made in promoting women’s sport across New Zealand in the world. The FIFA Women’s World Cup in 2023 is the third of three World Cups that we have hosted for women—the ICC Cricket World Cup and the Rugby World Cup—along with the International Working Group World Conference on Women in Sport. By creating a platform such as this, we encourage and inspire women and girls to be involved in sport, and these types of events will play a key role in advancing the outcomes of the strategy. I’m looking forward to watching the Football Ferns take on Norway in the opening match at Eden Park tomorrow night, and I’m sure all members in the House will join me in wishing the team all the best.

explanation: Asked whether it is acceptable that the Public Works Act still permits compulsory acquisition of Māori land (with a conditional follow-up if not). Answered "yes" outright, which disposes of the conditional, and then explained the position. Direct on the question put.
question: Does he think it is acceptable that the Public Works Act continues to allow compulsory acquisition of Māori land; if not, when will Māori land be fully protected?
statement: To the first part of the question: yes. However, I would note to the member that compulsory acquisition of land under the Public Works Act is only ever the final step in a lengthy acquisition process. For Māori land specifically, the Crown recognises the special significance of Māori freehold land and always looks to employ methods other than compulsory acquisition. Compulsory acquisition is a tool to be used when the situation requires it, and without compulsory acquisition significant infrastructure like roads, railways, and schools simply would not happen.

explanation: Asked what work LINZ has done on preventing compulsory acquisition of Māori land. The reply asserts "considerable work under way" and that they are "aware" and "working through it carefully" without identifying any work at all, then repeats an earlier justification. It gestures at the question rather than reaching it.
question: What work, if any, has LINZ done on preventing compulsory acquisition on Māori land?
statement: There’s been considerable work under way to consider the issues of Māori land, the views of Māori landowners, and to ensure that acquisition of Māori land does not occur when it is not necessary. We are aware of the issue, we’re working through it very carefully. But I’ll remind the member again: it only ever occurs if a greater good of a public asset is required for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked how much Māori land has been compulsorily acquired since 1981. He does not supply the figure, but says plainly that he does not have it and offers to answer in writing — a candid engagement with the question rather than a pivot, short of the complete answer sought.
question: How much Māori land has been compulsorily acquired since the Public Works Act was passed in 1981?
statement: I’m afraid I don’t have that total area. I’m quite happy to answer that question, if you’d like to send it to me in written form.

explanation: Asked why no central records exist. He engages head-on by disputing the premise ("I'm sure there are") rather than pivoting, but then declines the substance with "I don't have the information with me" — the "why" is never reached. Contesting the premise is real engagement, so this sits mid-scale rather than at the bottom; incompleteness, not vagueness, is what caps it.
question: Why are there no central records of Māori land taken through compulsory acquisition?
statement: I’m sure there are. It’s just that I don’t have the information with me here now.

explanation: A yes/no question about directing LINZ to pick up a specific work programme. The response reports cross-agency discussion, a general government concern about Māori landowner rights, and a justification for acquisitions — but never says whether he will direct LINZ. The core of a narrow question is left untouched.
question: Will he direct LINZ to pick up the work programme signalled by Minister Mahuta in late 2019 to address issues with public works acquisitions of Māori land?
statement: I know there’s been a lot of cross-agency discussion on this issue and I know that that work that was undertaken has progressed. At this stage, the one thing that Government has been concerned about is to ensure that the rights of Māori land owners is not overruled. But, at the end of the day, should acquisition of any of that land occur, it’s only for significant public assets and infrastructure that we all need to exist as a country.

explanation: Asked whether he has confidence in the offer-back process. He states he considers it robust, open and transparent and has "no reason to believe there are any injustices" — that is an affirmative answer to a confidence question, even without the word "yes". Whether the confidence is warranted is Veracity, not this.
question: Does he have confidence that all surplus land previously taken for public works is being returned to Māori land owners without financial disadvantage under current processes?
statement: I am aware that the offer-back process is a very robust, open, and transparent one. I have no doubt that everyone is doing their very best to ensure the rights of all landowners, particularly Māori, are upheld through that process. It’s complex, sometimes lengthy, but I have no reason to believe that there are any injustices being imposed upon any Māori land owners.

explanation: Asked what responsibility he takes for above-target inflation. He answers it: responsibility for the target range sits with the Reserve Bank, and he accepts responsibility for the Government's fiscal decisions. The trailing economic-record material is padding, but the question was squarely addressed before it.
question: What responsibility, if any, does he take for inflation having been above the Reserve Bank’s 3 percent target every quarter since June 2021?
statement: Just as in the period from the December 2017 quarter to the March 2021 quarter, when inflation sat within the Reserve Bank’s 1 to 3 percent target range, I accept that responsibility for managing that target range sits with the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. I also accept responsibility for the Government’s fiscal decisions throughout the largest shock to the New Zealand economy since World War II. This has seen our economy at least 6 percent larger than it was before COVID, unemployment at record lows, and debt lower than many other countries we compare ourselves to. I would note that today’s inflation data reflects a continuation of the downward trend which has seen the annual inflation rate fall over successive quarters from its peak of 7.3 percent in June 2022.

explanation: Asked how he explains the tradeable/non-tradeable gap. He offers exactly that — two explanations (construction inputs being largely imported, and weather events on food prices) — and even contests the question's framing directly rather than sliding past it. Whether the explanation holds up is Veracity.
question: How does the Minister explain to New Zealanders that tradeable inflation—things bought and sold overseas—is 5.2 percent, but non-tradeable inflation—buying and selling things within New Zealand—remains at 6.6 percent, the same as it was a year ago?
statement: Two things that I would explain that with. The first of those is that while I know the member wants to conflate non-tradeables with domestic, it doesn’t always exactly work. For example, the biggest increase we’ve seen in this particular quarter of data is in the construction sector. In the construction sector, 90 percent of the goods used in house-building are either imported or made from imported goods. Secondly, the weather events in the country have undoubtedly led to increases, particularly in food prices.

explanation: Two-part question: is he aware of the figure, and is his construction explanation therefore false. He answers the awareness part directly and meets the challenge with "I stand by my answer", which is a response rather than a dodge, but he does not engage the specific ex-housing figure that was the point of the question.
question: Is the Minister aware that non-tradeable inflation, excluding the purchase of new housing and, therefore, construction goods, is 6.3 percent higher than overall inflation, and, therefore, his excuse he’s trotted out so many times that non-tradeables are high because of construction goods simply ain’t true?
statement: I am aware of the definition, as the member is. I stand by my answer and I’d also continue to point out to the member that the period of time that we are dealing with here is one in which the weather events in New Zealand have had a significant impact across the economy, and I note that I’m not the only one saying that—as the member and I have previously discussed—but it’s also the planet on which Sharon Zollner lives.

explanation: Asked whether $121bn of borrowing might have contributed to local inflation, and if not, why not. Neither branch is answered — he restates that he stands by the fiscal decisions, notes others called for spending, and jabs at the questioner. A direct causal question left unaddressed.
question: Does the finance Minister believe that him borrowing and spending a net $121 billion of extra debt in the six years he’s been finance Minister might have just contributed a bit to local inflation, and, if not, why not?
statement: As I said in my primary answer, I stand by the financial and fiscal decisions the Government has made in the face of the biggest shock to the New Zealand economy since World War II. In this House, consistently over the last few years, members from all sides have called for there to be more spending to support New Zealanders through what has been a very, very challenging time. I’m sure the member will enjoy his role as a professor of hindsight economics; we don’t get to live in that role.

explanation: Asked what he would say to a struggling family. He says what he would say to them — acknowledgement plus the specific supports offered. The closing swipe at ACT is a Focus/Civility matter and does not reduce forthrightness; the question's form was answered in its own terms.
question: What would the finance Minister say to a family of four who are paying $110 a week more for groceries than they were when he became the Minister of Finance, and who are getting a little bit tired of his smart-arse remarks and excuses blaming everyone else?
statement: What I would say to that family is that I recognise that for them, and many New Zealanders, these are incredibly difficult times. That is the reason why this Government has stepped up consistently to support families through lifting the family tax credit, through lifting childcare assistance rates, through lifting benefits, and through supporting New Zealanders through this period of time. What I’d also say to that family is that the alternative in an ACT Party - led economic policy would see them much, much worse off.

explanation: Asked whether he really believes the family would be worse off. "Absolutely, I do believe that" — an unambiguous yes, followed by his reason. The Roger Douglas quotation is colour, not evasion.
question: Does he really believe that if that family had two people on the average wage with them being $4,400 a year better off thanks to paying less tax while not a single front-line service is reduced is worse off—really?
statement: Absolutely, I do believe that because they would be entering into an era where, unfortunately, as the member’s former idol would say, there would be a political party in charge that “represents only the wealthy” and has been captured by a “small libertarian element who did not want public super or public healthcare at all”. I can hardly believe I’m quoting Roger Douglas in the House, but that’s what he said.

explanation: Asked what recent trade announcements he has made. He names one directly — the signing of the EU-NZ FTA — with its scope and expected effect. A friendly question, but the scoring is the same: it was answered.
question: What recent announcements has he made about prospects for New Zealand’s trade?
statement: It was my privilege to travel to Brussels with the Prime Minister last week to officially sign New Zealand’s free-trade agreement with the European Union. This is a groundbreaking free-trade agreement that delivers our exporters unprecedented access to a market of 450 million people and an economy worth around $27 trillion. We expect that the European Union - New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (EU-NZ FTA) will increase our exports to the EU by up to $1.8 billion per year by 2035. I’d also like to take this opportunity to thank the negotiating team, and all the officials who worked so hard to help us secure this fantastic deal for New Zealand.

explanation: Asked how the FTA will benefit New Zealand business; the response is about exactly that — duty-free coverage, phase-in, immediate tariff savings. Squarely on the question asked.
question: How will the EU-NZ FTA benefit New Zealand business?
statement: I’ll try and summarise it briefly: once the FTA enters into force, 91 percent of New Zealand’s goods exports to the EU will be duty free, and that rises to 97 percent after just seven years. From day one, Kiwi exporters will save $100 million in tariff reductions, the highest immediate tariff savings ever delivered by a New Zealand free-trade agreement. This Government understands that trade is key to our economy and we’re committed to securing high-quality agreements like the EU-NZ FTA, which will cut costs for exporters, boost opportunities for small businesses, and create and protect jobs for Kiwi families.

explanation: Asked how the FTA supports the primary sector; the response works through horticulture, seafood, honey, dairy and red meat. The question is answered on its own terms. The detail level is Specificity and does not lift this score above other direct answers.
question: How does the EU-NZ FTA support New Zealand’s primary sector?
statement: Well, the EU-NZ FTA brings new opportunities and huge benefits for our world-leading primary sector exporters. Our horticultural sector will see $46 million in tariffs slashed from day one; our fish and seafood producers will see immediate removal of $20 million in tariffs; major honey exporting regions like Northland, Hawke’s Bay, and Coromandel will benefit from the phased removal of 17 percent tariff on honey over three years, and for mānuka honey that will be eliminated from day one. Our dairy and red meat sectors will see the opportunity for over $600 million in additional export revenue to the EU per year, once fully implemented, with quotas, that, if filled, could see New Zealand provide 60 percent of the EU’s butter imports, and 96 percent of the EU’s sheep meat imports. This Government understands the role that export earnings play in the success of our primary industries, and the EU-NZ FTA delivers new opportunities for our primary producers.

explanation: Asked how the EU-NZ FTA supports the Trade Recovery Strategy. The answer stays on the strategy in general (trade matters, opening doors, a list of seven FTAs) and is cut off before it ever connects the EU deal to the strategy. It gestures at the question without reaching it.
question: How does the EU-NZ FTA support the Government’s Trade Recovery Strategy?
statement: This Government recognises that trade is crucial to our economic success, and we know that one in four New Zealanders’ jobs depend upon trade. That’s why, as part of our Trade Recovery Strategy, we’re committed to opening as many doors as possible for Kiwi exporters. Since 2017, since this Government came in, this Government has secured seven new or upgraded free-trade agreements: Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership—

explanation: Two-part question: explain the 'two or three reports away' statement, and did ED wait times rise or fall. Both parts are engaged — the statement is placed as being about admissions data rather than wait times, and a direction of change is given for the published quarter, with the current quarter flagged as not yet validated.
question: How does she explain Health NZ statements that emergency department wait-time data could be “two or three [quarterly] reports away”, and have emergency department wait times increased or decreased this year to date?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, the statement from Dr Richard Sullivan, interim national medical lead for Te Whatu Ora, was that the publication of emergency department (ED) admissions data will be delayed—not emergency department wait times. To answer the second part of this question about emergency department wait times, Te Whatu Ora recently published its clinical performance metrics for the reporting period January to March 2023. Overall, the proportion of emergency department stays under six hours decreased by 9 percent for the period from January to March 2022, to January to March 2023. ED presentations also increased by 9 percent during the same period. Te Whatu Ora does not yet have validated data available for the April to June 2023 quarter.

explanation: Asked whether all 12 indicators will be reported and, if not, which. Answered directly — all 12 will be — with the ED admissions delay noted. The yes/no core is squarely met.
question: Will all 12 of the health performance indicators be reported going forward, and, if not, which will not be reported?
statement: Indeed, the approach outlined following the publication of the report into these matters is that all 12 will be. However, there is a delay in the data for ED admissions because there is variation—as is gone into in great length in that report—in the way in which the admissions are coded.

explanation: Asked whether the delay covers ED admissions and ED wait times. The reply is a jab at the questioner but it does carry the answer: wait-times data has already been published, so the delay is not in that. Rudeness is not scored here; the question was engaged, though the answer is left to be inferred rather than stated.
question: Is the delay in ED admissions and ED wait times?
statement: If the member had read the last quarterly report, he would be aware that data on the shorter stays in ED figure—commonly called the ED wait times—has been published.

explanation: Asked whether she or her office had any involvement in preventing publication, and what involvement. The reply pivots to how important the data is and backing the team — no yes, no no, and no account of any involvement. A narrow factual question left untouched.
question: Has she or her office had any involvement in preventing ED wait times from being publicly reported, and, if so, what involvement?
statement: Throughout this discussion about the importance of this data, I have maintained that it is incredibly important that this data is available and that this report was undertaken in order to make sure that high-quality data is available, and I back the team to make sure they have the right data before it is published.

explanation: Same question put again. This time the reply does reach the second half — her office's role was to request that Te Whatu Ora publish the correct data — but never squarely answers whether there was involvement in preventing publication. Partial engagement; the disfluency itself is not penalised.
question: Certainly. Has she or her office had any involvement in preventing ED wait times from being publicly reported, and, if so, what involvement?
statement: I have, at the time that—no—at the reports that—the role of my office has to be—has been to request that Te Whatu Ora publish the correct data.

explanation: Asked whether she instructed officials to withhold the data, and when. The reply describes the instruction she did give (publish the correct data), which addresses the subject matter and implies a denial, but the yes/no is never given and the 'when' is unaddressed.
question: Has she issued any instructions to officials to withhold ED wait time data, and, if so, when?
statement: The member raised concerns publicly about errors in emergency department data. I asked Te Whatu Ora to ensure they publish the correct data.

explanation: Asked whether she ever instructed her office to withhold reporting, and when. The reply speaks to the position she maintained — that the correct data should be released — which bears on the question and implies no, but does not answer about instructions to her office or give a time.
question: Has she at any time offered instructions to her office to withhold the public reporting of ED wait time data, and, if so, when?
statement: There was a protracted period of time where there were concerns about the accuracy of ED data that Te Whatu Ora held, and consistently throughout that, I maintained a position that the correct data should not be released—sorry, the correct data should be released.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements had been made about increased international tourism capacity. The announcement is named directly — new China–New Zealand direct airline connections. The trailing promotional line does not displace the answer.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made about increased capacity for international tourism in Aotearoa New Zealand?
statement: Great news: I was recently in China where, alongside the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins, we announced new China to New Zealand direct airline connections, which will significantly increase the capacity of incoming tourists every month. We’re actively working to attract visitors globally, including from China, that match our tourism objectives and who will positively contribute to New Zealand’s economic recovery.

explanation: Asked which new air routes had been announced. The routes are named — Guangzhou–Christchurch reinstated and three extra Guangzhou–Auckland services. Complete.
question: What new air routes have been announced?
statement: The new China Southern Airlines itinerary includes the reinstatement of the Guangzhou-Christchurch connection and the introduction of three additional services between Guangzhou and Auckland. The increased capacity will bring approximately 7,000 seats per month. These additional routes add to the direct air connections between our two countries, which are expected to grow to at least 80 percent of pre-COVID levels by September 2023.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions. 'Yes' is given up front; the 'in the context in which they were made' rider is a mild qualification, not an evasion.
question: Does she stand by all of her statements and actions?
statement: Yes; in the context in which they were made and undertaken.

explanation: Asked to explain why she told the House Cabinet had agreed a new offence when it had agreed an aggravating factor. An explanation is offered — she was referring to Cabinet's consideration of both options — so the core is engaged, though the reply then moves to the Prime Minister's responsibility and restates the policy rather than staying on her own account. Whether the explanation is convincing is a Veracity/Rigor matter, not this one.
question: Can she explain why she told Parliament yesterday that Cabinet agreed to make a new offence for using a young person to commit a crime, punishable by 10 years in prison, when that was the same mistake the Prime Minister made on Monday, which he had to correct 90 minutes later, since Cabinet actually agreed to make it an aggravating factor for sentencing?
statement: I was referring to Cabinet’s consideration of the two options as part of the package that we considered on Monday. To the latter point, ultimately, the Prime Minister has accepted responsibility and acknowledged the mistake that was made with respect to the announcement of those materials. The fact remains we’re creating a new aggravating factor that would apply when an adult, whether or not connected to an organised crime group, commissions a person under 18 to carry out an offence.

explanation: Asked why the Government is muddled on justice policy. "We're not" rejects the premise head-on rather than sliding past it — a two-word contradiction is still a direct engagement with the core proposition. It stops short of 1.0 only because the interrogative "why" is left unaddressed even conditionally; but there is no pivot, no talking point, no counter-attack. Brevity and unhelpfulness are not evasion.
question: Why is the Government so muddled about its justice policies three months before an election?
statement: We’re not.

explanation: Two-part question: (a) do you stand by the tweet, (b) if so, how did it inform today's tougher-consequences announcement. Part (a) is answered squarely and immediately ("Yes, I do stand by that tweet"). Part (b) — the actual point of the question, the apparent tension between the tweet and the announcement — is never reached; the response instead re-emphasises a different component of the tweet about National's policy. Half the pair answered, and the half avoided is the load-bearing half.
question: Does she still stand by her tweet on 18 June: “locking people up and throwing away the key is exactly what gangs want. They want NZers to pay for their university of crime.”; if so, how did it inform her announcement today that certain crimes need tougher consequences?
statement: Yes, I do stand by that tweet and, in particular, in the full context it was made. I particularly stand by the component that says that the National Party’s law and order policy lacks any evidential foundation.

explanation: Asked what reports have been seen about how Matariki 2023 was marked. The response is entirely about how it was marked — events by marae, hapū and iwi, council gatherings, the hautapu at Mount Ngongotahā, the national broadcast. It engages the question as asked throughout, with no pivot. Marked slightly below the top because it recounts personal observation rather than reports as such, but that is the ordinary form of this question type and the substance requested is delivered.
question: What reports has she seen about how Kiwis around Aotearoa marked Te Rā Aro ki a Matariki 2023?
statement: Te Rā Aro ki a Matariki 2023, the first distinctly New Zealand public holiday, was celebrated last Friday for the second time, and it was exciting to see how people of all backgrounds embraced it and got involved with their local community. This year’s theme was “Matariki Kāinga Hokia - Matariki calls you home”, and this could be clearly seen from the events organised by local marae, hapū, and iwi, family fun gatherings organised by councils, and individual whānau and family coming together. As the Minister, I was honoured to attend the live nationally broadcasted traditional hautapu ceremony at Mount Ngongotahā in Rotorua alongside my colleague the Hon Peeni Henare. The broadcast also featured pre-recorded events from around the country showcasing other tribal variations, such as puanga. I was hugely appreciative of the efforts of Ngāti Whakauē made to host us for the hautapu. They shared their aroha for Matariki with all New Zealanders and helped to increase awareness and education on its significance. As I said on Friday, when I think about Matariki, it’s not necessarily about following rules or regimented traditions but rather about embracing the values and principles of Matariki: remembrance, celebrating the present, and looking to the future. Those values can be as simple and universal as aroha and te taiao, appreciating the people, and respecting our environment.

explanation: Asked about the success of the Matariki Ahunga Nui Fund. The response is about exactly that: $3 million distributed, 120 successful applicants, 321 applications, oversubscription offered as the measure of success. Squarely on the question from first sentence to last. (Its detail level is a Specificity matter and did not move this score.)
question: What reports has she seen about the success of the Matariki Ahunga Nui Fund for 2023?
statement: Celebrations across Aotearoa have been significantly enhanced through over $3 million of the Matariki Ahunga Nui Fund, which saw 120 successful applicants receive funding to host events and wānanga in 2023. The fund is inclusive of all unique iwi variations of Matariki that exist, such as puanga, and is inclusive of different iwi having distinct approaches to calculating and acknowledging the timing of the Māori New Year. For 2023, the contestable funding was designed to support Māori communities in leading and delivering Te Kāhui o Matariki - focused initiatives that regenerate mātauranga Matariki in line with the celebration of the public holiday. I have been advised that there were many thoughtful and high-quality applications which demonstrated the deep aroha for Matariki, and so much so that the fund was heavily oversubscribed—receiving a total of 321 applications. This is a real sign of the widespread desire to continue to tautoko and celebrate the public holiday.

explanation: Asked for evidence of positive impact of the public holiday. Evidence is what is supplied — an estimated $160 million domestic tourism benefit, matariki.com page views up from 6,621 to 10,375, 15,000 additional site visits year on year. Directly responsive to the specific thing asked for; whether those figures are accurate is a Veracity question, not this one.
question: What evidence has she seen of positive impact of Te Rā Aro ki a Matariki as a public holiday for Aotearoa?
statement: While many of us already have Matariki traditions through Te Rā Aro ki a Matariki, this has been shared and embraced right across the country. In 2022, it is estimated that the benefit of Matariki to domestic tourism was up to $160 million, and we anticipate it being similar in 2023. As Kiwis, we’re out and about across the motu, visiting whānau and friends and visiting other rohe—certainly what I saw in Rotorua. The indications from initial social media monitoring are that people were keen to find out about Matariki events near them, with the event pages on matariki.com increasing in views from 6,621 in 2022 to 10,375 in 2023 for the same period, and there were over 15,000 more overall visits or clicks to the website in June and July compared to the same period last year.

explanation: Asked how the Government is supporting Matariki in the years ahead. Answered with the forward commitment: $18 million over four years from Budget 2023. The surrounding material about cultural identity is padding rather than deflection — the core of the question is reached explicitly and early.
question: How is the Government supporting Matariki in the years ahead?
statement: As part of Budget 2023, this Government announced a further investment of $18 million over four years to build on the initial momentum from the inaugural public holiday and to see expanded public awareness and understanding of Matariki. We know that cultural identity has benefits for all New Zealanders as a way of coming together, celebrating our rich history, culture, language, practices, and ceremonies, and as noted by Dr Rangi Mātāmua, Chief Adviser - Mātauranga Matariki, traditions don’t just happen; they need commitment and participation to thrive. I’m proud to be part of a Government that is demonstrating that necessary commitment and is always looking to create new ways to uplift and enhance wellbeing for all. Mānawatia a Matariki!

explanation: "Does she stand by all of her statements and actions?" — answered "Yes," which is complete. The qualifier "in the context that they were given and taken" hedges the edges slightly rather than withholding the answer, so it lands just below the unqualified "Yes" case.
question: Does she stand by all of her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context that they were given and taken.

explanation: A compound challenge: how could omitting the three sciences from the draft curriculum be a good idea, and why no intervention over months of ministry work. The response contests the premise directly — "The member is wrong", the final curriculum will include chemistry, physics and biology — which is genuine engagement with the factual heart of the attack, not a pivot. But it answers about the final curriculum where the question was about the draft, and the ministerial-oversight limb is left entirely untouched. Partial engagement, core only glancingly hit.
question: How could she possibly believe that leaving chemistry, physics, and biology out of the draft science curriculum was a good idea, leaving the ministry to work on this curriculum for months without her intervention when teachers are now saying it’s embarrassing and will lead to an “appalling” decline in student achievement?
statement: The member is wrong. The final curriculum will include chemistry, physics, biology, and other core science topics. That is not in question.

explanation: A narrow, closed factual question — name any other country whose science curriculum omits those three words. "I refer the member to my first answer" names no country, and the answer referred back to did not name one either. The cross-reference functions as a refusal to engage rather than a refusal to comply (which would have scored high, e.g. "No, I can't name one"). Narrow question, core entirely avoided.
question: Can she name any other country that doesn’t mention the words “chemistry”, “biology”, and “physics” in their science curriculum?
statement: I refer the member to my first answer.

explanation: Asked what recent reports have been seen on the New Zealand economy. Answered with a named source and figures — Stats NZ migration data, net gain of 77,810, arrivals of 181,100. That is a report on the economy, so the question is engaged. The closing turn to "our immigration reset is working" is advocacy, and the migration focus is a narrow slice of a broad question, but nothing here dodges what was asked.
question: What recent reports has he seen on the New Zealand economy?
statement: This is a tough period for New Zealand and for the global economy. However, there are signs of the resilience of the New Zealand economy as we navigate a pathway through a difficult and uncertain environment. Stats NZ reported earlier this month that there was a net gain of 77,810 people arriving in the year to May. The number of arrivals stood at 181,100, the second-highest on record for an annual period since the March 2020 year. That more than offset the departures of 103,300. Of the 181,100 who arrived, 85 percent were non - New Zealand citizens. Our immigration reset is working, and it is attracting overseas workers with the skills that businesses require to rebuild the economy.

explanation: Asked about reports on tourism and its economic impact. The response is tourism arrivals data and the FIFA Women's World Cup visitor and travel estimates throughout — both limbs of the question (tourism, and its economic impact) are addressed. No pivot at any point.
question: What reports has he seen on tourism and its impact on the economy?
statement: Stats NZ also reported that overseas visitor arrivals were 160,300 in the month of May, up 87,600 from the same month a year earlier. That level was around 73 percent of the pre-COVID number in May 2019. On an annual basis, overseas visitor arrivals rose to 2.45 million. With the FIFA Women’s World Cup now under way, the tournament is providing a boost to the tourism and hospitality industries during July and August, which are traditionally quieter months for the sectors. We expect to welcome more than 25,500 international visitors to New Zealand for the games being held here, with two-thirds of visitors coming from the United States. In addition to this, FIFA is estimating that around 70,000 New Zealanders are traveling around the country to attend matches.

explanation: Asked for other reports on the economy. Supplied one — the BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index at 50.1, with sales, new orders and employment movements. Directly on the question. The closing sentence returns to a prior theme but only after the question has been answered.
question: What other reports has he seen on the economy?
statement: Activity in the services sector expanded modestly in June, with the BNZ - BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index at 50.1—a reading above 50 indicating that the sector is generally expanding, while below 50 that it is declining. Sales and new orders expanded slightly, though employment declined for the first time since December 2022. As I said in my earlier answer, this is a tough period for many New Zealanders, but our economy is resilient, and we are building for the long term to deliver higher-wage jobs while also lowering emissions.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on exports and their economic impact. He names the source (Stats NZ, yesterday) and reports its content — monthly and annual export figures, breakdown by trading partner — which is squarely what was asked. The closing third drifts into general fiscal talking points, but the question had already been reached. Padding after an answer is not a dodge.
question: What reports has he seen on the export sector and its impact on the New Zealand economy?
statement: Stats NZ reported yesterday that exports rose 1.3 percent, to $6.3 billion in June, led by dairy products. On an annual basis, exports rose 8.2 percent, to $72.8 billion. Looking at New Zealand’s key trading partners, exports rose by 11.3 percent annually to Australia, 11.7 percent to the US, and 2.9 percent to China. As I have said previously, 2023 is a difficult year for the global economy. However, there are reasons to be optimistic, including unemployment being at record lows, inflation heading in the right direction, and public debt levels well below those of the countries with which we compare ourselves. We will continue to carefully and responsibly prioritise our spending without unnecessarily adding to inflation, taking a balanced approach that gives New Zealanders choices and flexibility to respond through these testing times.

explanation: A yes/no question — does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions. Answer opens with "Yes", which is complete. The subsequent Fonterra material is volunteered elaboration, not a substitute for the answer.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, particularly the partnership with Fonterra to co-fund a range of projects to cut coal use at its dairy factories. This partnership will result in halving Fonterra’s manufacturing emissions by 2030, equivalent to taking 120,000 cars off the road, and it will leverage up to $790 million worth of investment. This partnership sits within a backdrop of recent Stats New Zealand data showing New Zealand’s emissions decreasing for a third successive year under this Government. I heard firsthand during my recent trade missions that New Zealand’s climate credentials are crucial to our exports. This Government is committed to reaching our emissions reductions budgets, both for the sake of the environment but also because it benefits our exporters.

explanation: Two parts. The first (was Treasury right) is answered outright: "Yes, in answer to the first part". The second (will he index brackets to inflation) gets a clear negative in substance — now is not the right time — though he reframes it as "tax cuts" rather than bracket indexation and never says the word no. Both halves engaged, the second slightly off-centre.
question: Was Treasury right that inflation has pushed tens of thousands of Kiwis into higher tax brackets over the last six years, and, if so, will he adjust tax brackets for inflation to let Kiwis keep more of what they earn?
statement: Yes, in answer to the first part of the question. I’ve been very clear that I don’t think now is the right time for tax cuts in this—the magnitude of tax cuts proposed by the National Party would ultimately result in higher inflation for longer.

explanation: Asked whether the Revenue Minister's resignation amounts to a vote of no confidence in his tax policies. The response never touches his own Minister or his own policies at all; it turns immediately on the questioner's party and their tax plan. A complete pivot to attack — the core is untouched.
