Lists concrete things done: the women's health strategy, breast-screening access work, abortion safe areas, surgical mesh and birth injury action, maternity and cervical screening work. Broad question, broadly but squarely answered.
question: What has this Government done to improve women’s healthcare and services so that they feel listened to and are enabled to live longer in good health, with increased wellbeing and quality of life?
statement: This Government is proud of the work we have undertaken for women, and I am excited about the ongoing mahi. Last month, we launched the first women’s health strategy, which sets the direction for improving the health and wellbeing of women over the next 10 years. Right now, to achieve that overall vision, our Government is acting to improve women’s health. We know that breast cancer screening saves women’s lives, and we are working hard on improving access to our breast-screening programme, so that all the women who are already eligible for free mammograms get one. We’ve brought in abortion safe areas, which mean that people who wish to access abortion health services should be able to do so safely and without fear of harassment or intimidation. We’ve taken action on surgicalmesh harm and injuries during childbirth. We also have important work under way on integrating maternity and child services on maternal mental health and on cervical cancer screening.

explanation: Asked how breast cancer screening was strengthened and how equity for all women was improved. The strengthening half is answered squarely (new IT register, workforce plan, opt-out model, Saturday and after-hours clinics). The equity half is only reached obliquely via access measures for overdue and unscreened women, never addressed as equity in its own right.
question: How has the Government strengthened breast cancer screening services and worked to ensure we improve equity for all women?
statement: This Labour Government has made substantial efforts to improve the national breast cancer screening programme. We have invested in a new IT register because our current register in no longer fit for purpose to provide a modern breast cancer screening service, and to support any future programme changes like extending the age range. However, once implemented, the new system will enhance and support women’s participation in breast cancer screening, with an opt-out screening model based on the population register. To get the staff we need for breast screening, our health workforce plan and breast-screening Aotearoa workforce development strategy focuses on recruitment and retention of the medical imaging technologists and radiologists. We need to enable more women to be able to be screened. We are also working hard to make sure that all women who are currently eligible for a mammogram get one. That is why providers of the breast-screening Aotearoa programme are offering Saturday and after-hours screening clinics and visits, and working with primary health organisations to identify overdue or unscreened women.

explanation: Asked how the Government has demonstrated improvement in listening to women. Answers with cases framed as responses to what women raised — surgical mesh credentialing and pause, the pelvic mesh service, birth injury legislation and ACC claim numbers. Engages the "listening" framing rather than pivoting away from it.
question: How has the Government demonstrated improvements in the health system when it comes to listening to women?
statement: In response to women’s struggle for the treatment of birth injuries and for the restorative justice process on surgical mesh, we have acted. Our work to address the harm that surgical mesh can cause has seen six surgeons credentialed to remove it, educational materials for primary-care providers rolled out across the country, and a specialist female pelvic mesh service established to support and care for women. To date, this service has already received at least 109 referrals. Last week, the Director-General of Health supported a pause on surgical mesh to treat stress urinary incontinence, while we take further steps to minimise harm linked to the procedure. We are well under way to achieving the conditions to lift this pause, including progress towards establishing a register, and providing structured, informed consent with a patientdecision aid. We’ve also listened to women who have experienced a birth injury. We amended legislation so that women with listed birth injuries can access more timely surgeries and pelvic physiotherapy. Data from ACC shows that women are accessing this important support, with 4,470 claims accepted between 1 October 2022 and 2 August 2023.

explanation: Asked what further initiatives and investment are coming. Answers forward-looking: Kahu Taurima, investment in 40 hauora Māori and five Pasifika providers, educational tools, a national bereavement care pathway, the new HPV screening programme. Some of it is already-done work rather than further work, which slightly blunts the fit to "further".
question: What further initiatives and investment will the Government be making in women’s healthcare services?
statement: Through Kahu Taurima, we have begun an ambitious transformation programme for all women and whānau welcoming and raising babies, through to their fifth birthday. Already, we’ve invested in 40 hauora Māori and five Pasifika providers so that they can implement wraparound services that put women and whānau at the centre of their maternity and early-years journey. We are also developing educational tools for health professionals to support pregnant people with disabilities to have a better-quality experience as they navigate the health system. And we are developing a national bereavement care pathway to make sure that all bereaved women and their whānau are provided with high-quality, individualised, safe, and culturally responsive care across Aotearoa. Last, but definitely not least, in September, we launched our brand new HPV screening programme. This Labour Government has invested in not only a new register but also an entire new screening system for cervical cancer. We are using the latest innovation in screening to provide a test that women and people with a cervix can do themselves.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: is he confident in all the actions and processes of Oranga Tamariki. The reply substitutes a narrower claim — confidence that OT has made significant progress — and closes conceding more work is needed on its practices, without ever saying whether he is confident in all of it. Not a pivot to talking points or an attack, so it engages the topic, but the absolute the question turned on is left unanswered.
question: Is he confident in all the actions and processes of Oranga Tamariki?
statement: I’m confident that Oranga Tamariki has made significant progress across a range of topics in the children space, including through our work to move to transfer resources and decision making to iwi and communities through the enabling communities work under the future direction plan. So far, nine prototypes have been launched with iwi and communities across the country, moving decision making and resources closer to tamariki and their whānau. We are already seeing how Oranga Tamariki’s change in approach is working, with uplifts down 70 percent since 2018, and we now have the lowest number of children in care since 2010. However, there is more work to do to improve Oranga Tamariki’s practices.

explanation: Asked to confirm the review would be delivered by end of August. He engages the timing question head-on: he has received no drafts, it is still being worked on, and he plainly says he does not know when it will be released. Saying "I don't know, and here's why" answers the question rather than dodging it; the closing sentence about expectations is padding but does not displace the answer.
question: Can he confirm that the review led by Mike Bush into serious misconduct by staff at Oranga Tamariki youth justice residences will be completed and presented to the Oranga Tamariki chief executive by the end of August, as was reported on 10 July 2023?
statement: Neither myself nor the office have received any version of the drafts of the report. I am advised that the report is still being worked on by Mike and his team. At this stage, I do not know when the report will be released, as it is being produced independently. I expect the review to comprehensively identify concerns and areas for improvement and provide a plan to address the findings.

explanation: Asked whether he can understand why care-experienced youth are protesting about unkept promises. He neither says yes nor no, opens with a jab at the questioner for not listening, and re-states the report's independence — an answer to the previous question, not this one. Only marginally above zero because the independence point is a faint implicit rebuttal of the premise.
question: In light of that answer, can the Minister then understand why youth care - experienced youth stood outside Parliament today and said, “Keep your promises.”, because they are sick of promises being made and not being accomplished?
statement: If the member had listened, it is a report that’s being produced independently. If I was to interfere, I would be accused of trying to influence the report in my favour.

explanation: Asked to explain why four staff have been on paid suspension for over two years. He does give a reason — it is an employment process he cannot intervene in — which is genuine engagement, but he never touches the part of the question that carries the sting, the two-year duration. Partial answer around the core.
question: Can he explain why four Oranga Tamariki staff members continue to be on paid suspension for over two years?
statement: I think we’ve covered this in the House before. That is an employment process, and, of course, I can’t intervene in an employment process. We have to let it run its course.

explanation: Two-part question. The first part gets an unambiguous "No, I don't think it's acceptable." The second part ("what are we doing about it") is answered obliquely — he explains why motels are used and that stays are short and supervised, rather than naming remedial action. Direct on the main clause, glancing on the follow-on.
question: Does he think it’s acceptable for 30 young people each month to be housed in motels by Oranga Tamariki due to lack of suitable alternative options, and, if not, what are we doing about it?
statement: No, I don’t think it’s acceptable, but there are times when accommodation can’t be found with the young person’s whānau, or even non-members of the community, so we have to keep them safe somehow. Usually, they’re in a motel for only one to three nights, and they are supervised.

explanation: A narrow two-part factual question, answered with both numbers: six nights since 1 July with no resident medical officers, and three unfilled nights in October (none in September), with the roster horizon stated. The mitigation commentary afterwards is surplus, not evasion.
question: How many nights since 1 July 2023 have there been no junior doctors available to cover overnight ED shifts at Palmerston North Hospital, and how many similar roster gaps are there through to the end of October?
statement: I am advised that since 1 July 2023, there have been six nights with no resident medical officers, where two senior medical officers covered the night duty in the emergency department (ED). The current roster goes to 15 October. There are no roster gaps in September, and three nights currently in October with gaps yet to be filled. MidCentral is making every effort to mitigate roster gaps, and recently the senior medical officer team has reviewed current vacancies and stepped in to provide additional support. I am grateful to them for their contributions. Despite these challenges, I can confirm MidCentral is on track to meet planned care targets.

explanation: Asked what responsibility she takes for the 24-hour waits. "We do not like to see those sorts of waits" concedes the fact but not the responsibility, and the answer immediately pivots to funding and demand measures. The question's core — accountability — is never reached, though the pivot is at least on the same subject rather than an attack.
question: What responsibility does she take for a recent weekend at Palmerston North ED, where 14 patients spent more than 24 hours sitting in chairs waiting to be admitted?
statement: We do not like to see those sorts of waits. That is why we have funded that hospital to develop additional space, including the recently opened 12-bed emergency department observation unit. In addition, Palmerston North is one of the hot spots with a number of measures in place to address acute demand.

explanation: "What does she say to the wife" invites a response to that person, and she gives one: she calls it extremely distressing and offers to have the case followed up if details are shared. That is a real answer to what was asked, not a dodge; short of full marks only because it deflects the individual case into a process request.
question: What does she say to the wife of an elderly man taken to Palmerston North one evening who, hearing nothing, turned up at ED the next morning to be told he still hadn’t been seen and “there was my poor old husband stooped over in the chair, asleep, confused, incontinent, and freezing”?
statement: That is an extremely distressing story to hear, and if that member wants to share details of it, we will make sure that it is followed up on.

explanation: Asked what Health New Zealand's response was to the clinical director's warning. She describes an institutional response at length — roster steps under way, and a new external rapid review team with Palmerston North first in line — so the question is substantially engaged, but she never says what was actually said back to that clinician. Answers a near-neighbour of the question asked.
question: What was Health New Zealand’s response to the clinical director of Palmerston North ED, who stated that his hospital “is at serious risk of being unable to provide an emergency medicine service”?
statement: That is a very serious concern, and I understand—as I outlined in my primary answer—a number of steps are under way to make sure that roster gaps are addressed. But I have a wider concern when clinicians express that they cannot resolve their concerns through regular processes. That is why Te Whatu Ora is developing an external rapid review team to assess and address these types of situations. It will draw on national and international best practice to improve performance and learn and adapt across our hospital system. Palmerston North will be the first hospital to have the opportunity to use this model, but this team will be available to assess events in other hospitals, as needed, over the coming months. This new rapid review team will support clinicians and other hospital workers to tell their side of things to an expert reviewer so that rapid solutions can be found. This process does not replace existing line management, health and safety, or quality assurance processes, which are of course the first port of call.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether she is shutting clinicians down, answered "No" in the first word, with a one-clause rationale. Complete and unambiguous.
question: Further to that answer, is she shutting down clinicians from going into the public domain when they feel they are getting no relief or remedy from the Minister and her office?
statement: No, we are taking their concerns seriously and providing a forum in which they can be heard.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has seen on the ASEAN FTA; he names the specific announcement (signing the upgrade in Semarang) and its context. A friendly question, but engagement is what is being measured and it is answered squarely.
question: What recent announcements has he seen regarding the ASEAN–Australia-New Zealand Free Trade Area?
statement: On Monday last week, I was fortunate to travel to Indonesia to sign an upgrade to New Zealand’s free-trade agreement (FTA) with the Association of South-east Asian Nations—ASEAN—and Australia in the margins of the ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting in Semarang. The upgrade was welcomed by ASEAN as the FTA is viewed as ASEAN’s highest-quality free-trade agreement. The agreement has been in force since 2010 and is a central pillar of our relationship with ASEAN. The 10 countries have a population of over 700 million and, as a bloc, are New Zealand’s third-largest trading partner, with our exports totalling over $9.6 billion in 2022.

explanation: "What does this upgrade do?" is answered with what it does: alignment with RCEP-era agreements, a first-of-its-kind sustainable trade framework, and entry into force in 2024. Directly on the question.
question: What does this upgrade do?
statement: The upgrade brings elements of the original agreement into line with more recent free-trade agreements such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), and, in a first for any ASEAN agreement, the upgrade introduces a framework for cooperation on sustainable trade issues, including the environment, labour standards, and women’s economic empowerment. This upgrade will come into force in 2024.

explanation: Asked how the upgrade benefits New Zealanders; the response enumerates benefits — investor and service-provider conditions, fee transparency, supply commitments, customs and e-commerce rules. Answers the question asked, with the usual soft framing but no evasion.
question: How does this upgrade benefit Kiwis?
statement: This upgrade further boosts our already strong economic and trading ties with ASEAN and helps further cut red tape and costs on Kiwi businesses. The benefits include improved conditions for investors and service providers, greater transparency of fees and charges, commitments to support the flow of essential goods in times of crisis, and streamlined customs procedures. Recognising the huge increase in digital trade, the upgrade also introduces stronger e-commerce rules that aim to increase consumer protection and support the expanded use of e-invoicing in cross-border trade.

explanation: Asked how the upgrade advances trade priorities. The answer names the mechanism directly — it advances the Trade for All agenda, strengthens existing FTAs, and adds a sustainable-trade cooperation framework — before padding with FTA statistics. The core 'how' is engaged, not dodged.
question: How does this advance the Government’s trade priorities?
statement: The upgrade advances the Government’s Trade for All agenda, strengthening our trade relationships and the FTAs that underpin them. Importantly, the upgrade introduces a framework for cooperation on sustainable trade issues. These FTAs have not only created new opportunities for Kiwi businesses; they also reflect New Zealand’s international leadership on sustainable and inclusive trade. Over the past five years, we’ve concluded four FTAs, with the UK, EU, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, and RCEP, along with three FTA upgrades with China, Singapore, and now with the ASEAN - Australia - New Zealand FTA. Right now, almost three-quarters of our exports are with trading partners with whom we have an FTA. Six years ago, in 2017, this figure was around 50 percent. As a Government, we’re supporting Kiwi exporters to succeed and expand their international trade.

explanation: A yes/no 'does he stand by' question, answered 'Yes, I do' at the outset. Complete and immediate; the elaboration afterwards does not detract.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “We also want to see steps made towards a ceasefire”?
statement: Yes, I do, and like everyone in this House, I am absolutely appalled by the human tragedy that has unfolded in Israel and Gaza since 7 October. I just think the images on our TV screens are incredibly distressing and confronting for all of us as New Zealanders to watch, and I especially regret that the parties have not been able to agree a further extension to the recent pause in fighting.

explanation: Asked whether the Government supports calls for an immediate and permanent ceasefire, and if not, why not. The reply says 'we would like to see a ceasefire, but...' and lists conditions, never stating support or non-support for the specific call. The 'why not' is gestured at through the conditions, so it is a partial answer rather than a pure pivot.
question: Does the Government support calls for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in the war in Gaza; if not, why not?
statement: Well, we would like to see a ceasefire, but in order to achieve a sustainable ceasefire, as the member well knows, both sides actually need to be able to do so, and that means that they both have to agree to be able to put down their arms, they both have to actually agree to cease fighting across the whole area of the conflict in Gaza and in Israel, both parties actually need to commit to a political process and a peace process to resolve their differences, and both sides need to take those steps in order to get those conditions in place.

explanation: A yes/no about the Government's position, answered with an explicit 'No' followed by a restatement of the position. The rest is repetition, but the question itself is squarely answered.
question: So is it the Government’s position that New Zealand should only call for a ceasefire once it’s already happened?
statement: No, I’ve been very clear: we would like to see a ceasefire, but it requires both parties to actually make that a sustainable action and ceasefire.

explanation: 'Yes, we do.' A two-word complete answer to a closed question. Brevity is not evasion.
question: Does the Government support an “immediate, durable and sustained humanitarian truce”, as called for in UN Resolution 2712?
statement: Yes, we do.

explanation: A narrow, precise question — what is the difference between the two formulations — met with a restatement of the prior answer. The distinction asked about is never addressed at all. Dodging a question this specific is the worst case.
question: What’s the difference between that and an immediate ceasefire?
statement: As I said, we want to see a ceasefire that takes place. It requires conditions on both sides to be adhered to, as I’ve outlined.

explanation: The same definitional question, put again in full. The reply again restates the preference for a sustainable ceasefire and the both-parties condition, and never contrasts the two terms. Repeating a non-answer to a re-put question is a clear dodge.
question: What is the difference between an immediate, durable, and sustained humanitarian truce and an immediate, permanent ceasefire?
statement: Look, as I’ve said before, we would like to see an enduring, sustainable ceasefire. Yeah, we would all like to see that in this country, but the reality is, for a sustainable ceasefire to take place, you need both parties to agree to it.

explanation: Asked why the Government won't call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire. The reply does supply a rationale — the conditions each side must meet for a ceasefire to be sustainable — which addresses the 'why' obliquely, but never confronts the refusal to make the call itself. Partial engagement.
question: Why won’t the New Zealand Government call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire when more than 16,000 people have died, the great majority of them civilians, and that is continuing as we speak?
statement: As I’ve said, we would all like to see a sustainable ceasefire, but it actually requires all parties to actually make the conditions to make that happen, and for that to happen, for hostilities to cease, Hamas needs to actually cease its attacks on Israel, needs to stop exploiting civilian infrastructure and using civilians as shields, and it needs to locate and release all the remaining hostages. On the other hand, we actually need to see Israel respecting the laws of humanitarian law and war, we need to make sure that they’re actually ensuring that innocent civilians are being protected, they need to make sure that their civilians have access to food and fuel and resources and medical supplies, and we also need to make sure that the loss of life that we saw in the North doesn’t take place in the South. So there are responsibilities on both sides of this equation. There are responsibilities on both parties to make sure we get an enduring, sustainable ceasefire.

explanation: 'Does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions?' — answered 'Yes, I do' immediately, then elaborated. Complete answer to the question asked.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, I do, and particularly my statement yesterday that New Zealand is under new management and that we are here because we are the parties that can get things done for New Zealanders. We are focused on three things: rebuilding the economy, restoring law and order, and delivering better outcomes for New Zealanders.

explanation: A compound question: stand by the commitment, and if so agree with the Commissioner that cost-benefit analysis should precede legislation. 'Yes, I do' affirms the first part and, read plainly, the second, but leaves which is being affirmed slightly ambiguous. It engages both limbs rather than pivoting away, so it lands above partial. Terseness alone does not reduce the score.
question: Does he stand by his commitment to remove the ban on new offshore oil and gas permits, and if so, does he agree with the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment that a thorough analysis of the costs and benefits of removing the ban should be undertaken before any legislation is introduced?
statement: Yes, I do.

explanation: Two limbs: commitment to rigorous cost-benefit analysis, and acceptance of the IEA's advice against new oil, gas and coal investment. Only the first — the uncontroversial one — is answered; the IEA limb, which was the point of the question, is left untouched. Answers a narrower question than the one asked.
question: Is he committed to the principles in his coalition agreements of rigorous cost-benefit analysis and basing decisions on data and evidence, and, if so, does he accept the advice of the International Energy Agency from 2021 that if Governments are serious about the climate crisis, there can be no new investments in oil, gas, and coal from now?
statement: Yes, we do support rigorous cost-benefit analysis.

explanation: Asked whether the IEA's analysis is wrong — a yes/no question about a specific body of analysis. The answer never engages with the IEA at all; it asserts that NZ needs transitional energy and that gas serves that role. That is a pivot to the government's position rather than a verdict on the analysis. Not penalised for brevity or for being contestable — it simply never reaches the question.
question: Is the International Energy Agency’s expert scientific and technical analysis wrong?
statement: It’s very obvious to us that New Zealand needs transitionary energy sources, and gas is a good part to doing that.

explanation: Asked what he would say to Vanuatu's climate minister, who argued no new fossil fuels are compatible with 1.5 degrees. The reply does offer something addressed to that objection — a commitment to climate goals plus the claim gas is better than coal — so it engages the substance of the challenge. But it never responds to Regenvanu specifically or to the 'no new fossil fuels' point that was quoted, so it partly covers a sprawling question rather than meeting it.
question: What would he say to Vanuatu’s climate change Minister, Ralph Regenvanu, who said, in relation to his Government’s plan to reopen oil and gas drilling, “We call on them not to do it. To be in line with Paris, the 1.5 degree target, the science says you cannot do new fossil fuels.”?
statement: We’re deeply committed to delivering on our climate change goals and commitments, but we believe that gas is better than coal.

explanation: A two-part question: does he agree with his own past quote about social licence, and does he accept that reopening drilling would fail Pacific neighbours. The answer is a joke about Christopher Luxon being a smart man. Neither part is addressed; the wit deflects rather than engages.
question: Does he agree with Christopher Luxon, former CEO of Air New Zealand, that “We risk losing our social licence to operate if we do not genuinely address climate change.”, and, if so, does he accept that reopening oil and gas drilling would mean failing our Pacific neighbours and our mokopuna?
statement: I agree Christopher Luxon is a very smart man.

explanation: Two parts: will the package be self-funding, and what specific revenue measures will fund it. The first is answered with a flat 'Yes' — direct and complete. The second is not answered, though she says plainly that advice is still coming and details are unfinalised, which is closer to a stated refusal-for-now than a dodge. Half the question squarely met, half deferred.
question: Will the tax cut package promised by the Government in the Speech from the Throne be “self-funding”; if so, what specific revenue measures will be used to fund it?
statement: Yes. I continue to seek advice from officials on the implementation of tax changes as part of the Budget process. I am still receiving advice on tax policies, and the details of any specific revenue measures the Government may choose to pursue are yet to be finalised.

explanation: Asked to confirm an earlier statement she had already made — a question about the record, not about future decisions. The reply retreats to 'still receiving advice' and 'won't get ahead of decisions', which answers a different question (what will be decided) than the one asked (what did you say). It is at least a plain deflection rather than an attack, but the core is avoided.
question: Can the Minister confirm her earlier statement that revenue from rolling back the previous Government’s smoke-free policies will be used to fund the tax cut package?
statement: As I say, I am still receiving advice on tax policies and I do not intend to get ahead of final Government decisions.

explanation: Asked to confirm a media statement or say her position had changed. The answer quotes Robertson's own past words back at him and accuses him of hiding a wealth tax. The questioner is attacked; neither confirmation nor change of position is ever given. Scored low for the dodge, not for the rudeness.
question: Can the Minister confirm her statement made to the media that revenue derived from rolling back smoke-free changes will be used to fund tax cuts, or has her position on that changed?
statement: “We consider a range of issues around tax on an ongoing basis, and information about those will be released at an appropriate time.”, said one Grant Robertson on 2 May 2023. The difference between my approach and the previous Minister’s approach is I’m not hiding a sneaky wealth tax or capital gains tax when I answer these questions.

explanation: Asked whether she regrets the smoke-free funding statement. 'I regret very little' is a quip, but it does convey an answer — no. It engages by implication rather than squarely addressing the specific statement in question, so it lands mid-scale: not a pivot to talking points, not a direct response either.
question: Is she now regretting saying that the Government’s tax cut policies would be paid for by rolling back the smoke-free law changes?
statement: To quote a member of this House I admire very much, one Judith Collins, “I regret very little”.

explanation: A narrow factual question: on what date will New Zealanders know. 'In due course' is a non-date, and the rest is a jibe at the questioner. It touches the topic of timing without supplying anything that answers 'what date'. A dodged narrow question is a worse failure than a partly-covered broad one.
question: That was actually Édith Piaf, if I remember correctly. On what date will New Zealanders know how she is paying for the tax cuts that she has promised them?
statement: They will know in due course, and I’m sorry to say it, but I doubt that the member will be the first to know.

explanation: Asked to confirm she knows neither how the cuts are funded nor when she will say. She contests the premise by re-asserting that the package is self-funding, which engages the first half, then turns to an attack on the questioner's economic record. The 'when' half is never addressed. Partial engagement; the attack itself is a Civility/Focus matter and did not move this score.
question: So can she confirm that she is telling the House she doesn’t know how she’s paying for her tax cuts and she doesn’t know when she’s going to be able to tell New Zealanders what kind of tax cuts they will get or how they will be paid for?
statement: As I said in answer to the primary question, which the member may not have listened to, yes, the tax reduction package promised by the Government in the Speech from the Throne will be self-funding. I’ll tell you what else it’ll do: it’ll put real cash into the bank accounts of working people—bank accounts that have been eroded by a cost of living crisis presided over by that member, who over-taxed them, spent their money badly, and left the economy in tatters.

explanation: Standard 'does he stand by all statements and policies' — answered 'Yes, I do' before adding an unprompted cellphone-policy flourish. The question is answered directly and completely; the padding neither adds nor detracts here.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and policies?
statement: Yes, I do, and particularly our commitment to lifting educational achievement by removing distractions like cellphone use in the classroom to ensure that young people receive the quality education they deserve and lets them live the life that they ultimately want.

explanation: Asked what government policy on Fair Pay Agreements is. The answer states it plainly: both parties oppose FPAs, campaigned to repeal within 100 days, and the government will remove the law before any agreement is finalised. Whether the surrounding justification is sound or partisan is Rigor and Focus; as a response, it is direct and complete.
question: What is Government policy on Fair Pay Agreements?
statement: ACT and National are both strongly opposed to fair pay agreements. When the law was introduced, both parties opposed it, and both campaigned to repeal it in the first 100 days of this Government. As a Government, we are committed to acting quickly to remove this law before any fair pay agreements are finalised and the negative impacts are felt by the labour market. Fair pay agreements would reduce choice in workplaces and undermine the flexible labour market which has underpinned New Zealand’s economic success for the past three decades. Our Government believes the best way to introduce the wages of workers is to improve productivity and reduce regulations so businesses have more money to pay staff more.

explanation: Asked what economic impacts she expects if the Act is not repealed. She names them: increased costs to businesses, higher consumer prices, possible closures, fewer hires and reduced hours. It is a friendly patsy question and the claims are contestable, but the question asked for expected impacts and expected impacts were given.
question: What economic impacts does she expect if the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 is not repealed?
statement: If any fair pay agreements were finalised, the increased costs would have greatly affected a range of businesses up and down the country, regardless of whether they could have afforded them. This would have increased prices for consumers and could cause business closures, which is worse for employees. I don’t consider that a blunt tool will help our labour markets for either employers or employees. Workers could have been negatively impacted, for example, if employers chose to hire fewer people or reduce hours of work due to higher costs that they face.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on the impact of fair pay agreements on business. She names two — Horticulture NZ and Federated Farmers — and quotes both. It is a friendly question with an easy answer, but the answer is squarely on the question asked.
question: What reports, if any, has she seen on the impact of fair pay agreements on businesses?
statement: Many businesses submitted on the introduction of fair pay agreements, concerned about the impacts they would have. I have a few examples. Horticulture New Zealand said, “This will be a burden on the Government to administer and compliance check yet another regulatory instrument being imposed on business. Most businesses will likely have to employ additional resource to administer the regime—where their margins are already very stretched.” The Federated Farmers of New Zealand said, “Employers are facing an ever-increasing range of compliance and the accompanying costs, following the difficult period of the impact of COVID-19 and the likelihood of an approaching recession. We are concerned that as employers face ever increasing administrative complexities and costs, some business owners will be forced to downsize or simplify their business to avoid employing people or some close the doors entirely.” There are many more.

explanation: Two-part question: why delegate to Costello, and why no delegations to Doocey and Seymour. He answers the first squarely (to give effect to the NZ First coalition agreement) and addresses the second only obliquely — 'the remaining delegations will be finalised shortly' explains that they are pending rather than why none has been made. Half the question is engaged.
question: Why did he delegate responsibilities for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act 1990 to the Associate Minister of Health Hon Casey Costello, and why has he not made any delegations to the other associate Ministers of Health, Hon Matt Doocey and Hon David Seymour?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The current delegations I have given to the Associate Minister of Health, the Hon Costello, give effect to the coalition agreement with New Zealand First. I can assure the honourable member that the remaining delegations will be finalised shortly.

explanation: Asked to confirm whether he set an expectation that the Associate Minister repeal the 2022 amendments, and if not, why not. 'The Minister expressed an interest in the delegation, and I agreed' answers neither branch — it describes who wanted the delegation, not what expectation was set. The core of a narrow confirm/deny question is left untouched.
question: Can the Minister confirm that when setting the delegation to the Associate Minister the Hon Casey Costello, he set an expectation that she repeal the 2022 amendments to the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act 1990 either directly or by reference to the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement, and, if not, why not?
statement: The Minister expressed an interest in the delegation, and I agreed.

explanation: Asked whether it is his expectation that the Associate Minister will repeal the 2022 amendments. 'It is my expectation that the Minister will fulfil her duties under the delegation' is circular — it restates the question's premise without disclosing the content of the expectation. A yes/no was available and not given.
question: Is it the Minister’s expectation of the delegation that the Associate Minister will repeal the 2022 amendments to the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act and, therefore, cost, as per the regulatory impact statement and evidence at select committee, over 8,000 lives, losses to Māori life expectancy, and billions in healthcare costs?
statement: It is my expectation that the Minister will fulfil her duties under the delegation.

explanation: Asked whether he considered his Framework Convention obligations before making the delegation. 'I considered all the required responsibilities when I made the delegation' functionally answers yes, by inclusion rather than by name. The lack of detail about the Convention is a Specificity matter, not a dodge; the yes/no core is reached.
question: Did he consider his obligations under the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control to keep tobacco industry influence out of Government before making the delegation to the Hon Casey Costello, who has previously chaired the Taxpayers’ Union, an organisation reported to receive funding from tobacco companies?
statement: I considered all the required responsibilities when I made the delegation, and I have full confidence in the Minister.

explanation: Asked whether he delegated the Act to avoid answering to a list of health organisations. 'No' answers it directly and completely. The trailing expression of confidence is padding, but the question was a yes/no and he gave the no.
question: Did the Minister delegate responsibility for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act because he doesn’t want to answer to the Cancer Society, the Stroke Foundation, the New Zealand Nurses Organisation, the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency, the Secondary Principals’ Council of New Zealand, and his own professional college, the College of General Practitioners, not to mention hundreds of other organisations that have condemned his actions?
statement: No, I have full confidence in the Minister.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on Lake Onslow. He states the announcement — the scheme has been axed — and dates it to this week. Direct.
question: What recent announcements has he made on the Lake Onslow Pumped Hydro scheme?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. This week, I announced that the coalition Government had axed the former Government’s hugely wasteful $16 billion Lake Onslow scheme This decision fulfils another commitment under our coalition Government’s 100-day plan.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on the scheme. He identifies one, from Contact Energy's chairperson, and summarises its warning. Answers what was asked.
question: What reports has he seen on the Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme?
statement: I’ve seen a number of reports on the pumped hydro Lake Onslow scheme, including from Contact Energy chairperson Rob McDonald, who warned that this scheme would have a chilling effect on a robust renewables investment pipeline in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether he has seen any other reports on the cancellation. 'Yes,' followed by the report he has seen. Complete.
question: Has the Minister seen any other reports on the cancellation of the Lake Onslow scheme?
statement: Yes. I have also seen a report in The Press today where Labour’s energy spokesperson, and the former Minister for Energy and Resources, has said that Labour is rethinking its policy on this scheme.

explanation: Asked what the Government's next steps are to ensure energy security. He opens by re-litigating the Onslow cancellation but then does state next steps: cutting red tape, doubling renewable energy by 2050, and gas as a transition fuel. The question is reached, with a preamble.
question: What are the Government’s next steps to ensure energy security?
statement: Well, the first priority was to scrap this Lake Onslow scheme within our first hundred days. Our next steps are to cut the red tape and to recognise the nature of the energy problem facing our country so that we can double renewable energy by 2050. Axing the Lake Onslow scheme and our coalition Government’s commitments to allow natural gas to function as a transition fuel will give our energy sector much greater confidence to invest in the dry year solution and keep the lights on.

explanation: Asked whether he is committed to the goal of 1 million te reo speakers by 2040. He restates a commitment to encouraging as many speakers as possible — conspicuously substituting an unbounded aspiration for the specific target and date he was asked to endorse. The yes/no is avoided.
question: Is he committed to the goal of achieving 1 million speakers of te reo Māori by 2040?
statement: I’m committed to encouraging as many people as possible to learn and speak te reo Māori—te reo rangatira.

explanation: Asked what reports had been received on student achievement. Names a specific report (PISA 2022) and states its finding. Directly and completely answered.
question: What reports has she received on student achievement?
statement: The 2022 Programme for International Student Assessment results released this week show a decline in the performance of 15-year-old students in maths compared to 2018 and confirm the long-term trend of declining achievement in core subjects.

explanation: Asked what the results show. States what they show — continued declining outcomes — before adding a line about the Government's plan. The core is reached; the tack-on doesn't displace it.
question: What do these results show?
statement: These results show us that our education system has continued to deliver declining outcomes for learners, but our Government has a plan to turn this around.

explanation: Asked whether the Government has plans to change this. Answers 'We certainly do' and then names plans. A direct yes with substance behind it.
question: Does the Government have plans to change this?
statement: We certainly do. In our first hundred days, the coalition Government is moving with urgency. We are removing distractions from classrooms by banning cellphone use during the school day in order to lift engagement, achievement, and, importantly, wellbeing. We also will ensure students at primary school receive at least one hour of reading, writing, and maths throughout every day.

explanation: Asked what else the Government is doing. Names further items (the 'Teaching the basics brilliantly' policy, knowledge-rich curriculum, consistent progress measures, structured literacy). Squarely on the question asked.
question: What else is the Government doing to turn around the declining levels of achievement?
statement: This is just the very start. Our “Teaching the basics brilliantly” policy builds an important foundation to ensure young people receive the high-quality education they deserve, that allows them to live the life that they want. Our Government will ensure that we have a knowledge-rich curriculum, consistent measures of student progress, and structured literacy in every primary classroom.

explanation: Asked whether the Government will join the call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire, and if not, why not. Never says yes or no to joining that call, but does give the Government's position and a reason ('simply calling for a ceasefire does not make one a reality'). The 'why not' limb is engaged; the yes/no is not.
question: Will he lead the Government to join the United Nations Secretary General, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and the majority of New Zealanders according to a recent poll to call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza; and if not, why not?
statement: In the eight weeks since Hamas unleashed its shocking terror on the people of Israel, targeting civilians including young children, we have witnessed a devastating level of human suffering and loss of life. As in today’s motion, we can all agree that a ceasefire—a permanent cessation of armed hostilities—would be the ultimate outcome we all seek. No one in this House wants this conflict in the Middle East, but for a durable ceasefire to be viable, the parties must take urgent steps towards establishing a ceasefire. We recognise, again, that that point is not straightforward. Simply calling for a ceasefire does not make one a reality. That’s why we are calling on all parties and all countries with influence in the region to take urgent steps towards establishing a ceasefire now, permanently.

explanation: Asked to acknowledge a death toll and that disproportionate targeting of civilians can never be self-defence. Neither limb is acknowledged or denied — both are deferred to a competent judicial body. That is a stated position rather than pure evasion, but it hedges around the acknowledgment that was asked for.
question: Does he acknowledge the deaths of over 16,000 Palestinians, more than 7,000 of whom are children, and that the disproportionate targeting of civilians can never constitute an exercise of the right to self-defence?
statement: We are concerned about such reports. They raise serious questions about whether international humanitarian law is being fully observed. Accountability for breaches of international humanitarian law is crucial. Whether these have been committed requires a decision from a competent judicial body such as the International Criminal Court. It is not for me to comment on specific cases without the facts and evidence. We support the gathering of evidence of possible war crimes for an International Criminal Court process.

explanation: Asked to acknowledge the targeting of journalists, medics and civilian areas. Answers 'Of course we acknowledge that' — an explicit yes — before pivoting to 7 October. The pivot follows the answer instead of replacing it.
question: Does he acknowledge the verified targeting of journalists, doctors, nurses, medical facilities, and entire civilian neighbourhoods, and that this can never constitute an exercise of the lawful right to self-defence?
statement: Of course we acknowledge that, but we also wonder why there’s such an absence of the mass assault and massacre on 7 October this year. “Why are we hearing just one side of the story?”, is what a lot of people with balance and fairness want to know.

explanation: Asked to acknowledge the restriction of aid corridors and that cutting off humanitarian aid can never be self-defence. Neither the factual acknowledgment nor the legal proposition is addressed; the response is a lecture to the questioner about legal training, from which only an implicit 'I won't judge' can be extracted.
question: Does he acknowledge the restriction by Israel of aid corridors into Gaza, which has left over 2 million people without adequate access to water, food, and life-saving medicine, and that cutting off of humanitarian aid to civilians is considered a war crime and therefore can never constitute the right to self-defence?
statement: For a trained lawyer, coming to a conclusion on a case before you’ve heard the evidence laid out for you is not a sound way of behaving. That’s what a legal training means. You first hear the evidence and then, against the principles of precedent, we then make a decision. We’re not going to make a judgment without any facts before we come to that judgment.

explanation: Asked when New Zealand will take a strong international position. Gives a conditional answer to the 'when' — once international bodies reach conclusions, not before — then trails into a general plea for balance. The core is reached, loosely.
question: When will Aotearoa take a strong international position calling for the prevention of genocide, as is our obligation pursuant to the genocide convention; to protect the rights of children, as is our obligation pursuant to the UN convention on the rights of children; and to act in the interests of global peace and security where war crimes are alleged?
statement: As in the previous answers, when we have seen international bodies charged with the conclusions that might arise from such an investigation, coming to those conclusions and not beforehand by making allegations without, again, laying out the factual evidence or the balance of 7 October this year, when out of left field, with no information or forewarning at all, so many hundreds and hundreds of people have lost their lives, and then people were made hostages. Again, we want to see balance and fairness when we approach these international issues, and not just one side of the story.

explanation: Asked what plans exist to support the Reserve Bank in achieving low and stable inflation. Names the plan: legislation, to be introduced that evening, returning the bank to a single inflation focus. Directly answered.
question: What plans does the Government have for supporting the Reserve Bank to achieve low and stable inflation?
statement: Inflation has been out of the Reserve Bank’s target range now for 2½ long years, and New Zealanders are doing it tough in a cost of living crisis. The public knows that this Government’s commitment to beating inflation is rock-solid, which is why, later this evening, the Government will introduce legislation returning the Reserve Bank to a single focus on inflation. After 30 years of an extremely successful inflation-targeting regime, where the Reserve Bank largely managed to control inflation, the previous Government muddied the waters by introducing a secondary objective to focus on employment as well as inflation. Now, as the Reserve Bank wrestles with trying to bring inflation back under control, our Government will clarify the bank’s objectives and support public confidence that inflation can and will be returned below 3 percent.

explanation: Asked what support had been received from the Reserve Bank. States that the governor wrote back offering support and quotes the reply. Direct and complete.
question: What support has she had from the Reserve Bank in returning the bank to a single focus on inflation?
statement: I wrote to the Reserve Bank outlining proposed changes to the monetary policy remit last week and the governor wrote back offering the Reserve Bank’s support for the changes, noting that “Giving the inflation objective priority will assist the credibility of the inflation target.” I want to thank the Reserve Bank for their support in recent days as we move back to a single focus on inflation. I know the Government and the bank are in lockstep in our shared goal of getting inflation back under control.

explanation: Asked what OTHER plans the Government has for achieving low and stable inflation. Restates the Reserve Bank Act change as one step and then turns entirely to the previous Government's spending record. No other plan is ever named.
question: What other plans does the Government have for achieving low and stable inflation?
statement: Amending the Reserve Bank Act is an important step but just one step in our plan to beat inflation. The governor was right when he said monetary policy needs mates, but the mates have been few and far between for the last few years. For years, the last Government’s only response to inflation was more spending. Instead of just delivering income tax relief, they experimented with broken policies like the cost of living payment and, during their term in office, managed to increase Government spending by 80 percent. And yet, which New Zealander can point to a central government service that is 80 percent better?

explanation: Asked what other plans the Government has for achieving low and stable inflation. Willis names concrete plans — reducing business costs, and 100-day plan items (ending the ute tax, RMA reform repeal, labour market flexibility, cancelling fuel tax hikes). A friendly question, but the question asked for plans and plans were given.
question: What other plans does the Government have for achieving low and stable inflation?
statement: The Government recognises that inflation has many influences. We are also committed to reducing costs on business which end up being passed on to New Zealanders, and this will help reduce inflationary pressure in the economy. We’re already taking actions through our 100-day plan, including ending the ute tax, abolishing the Government’s broken Resource Management Act reforms, restoring flexibility in the labour market, and cancelling Labour’s plans for fuel tax hikes next year.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all the Government's statements and policies. Peters says yes, qualified to the evidence available at the time, and states he would revise on new evidence. That is a direct answer with a stated limit. The insult attached to it is a Civility matter and does not reduce the score.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and policies?
statement: With regard to evidence and information at the time of those statements, yes. But, of course, where new information or evidence emerges, we acknowledge that and don’t just carry on like a bigoted lefty shill.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Peters' 2018 statement that the oil and gas ban 'makes sense'. He never says whether he agrees. He pivots to the Government's 'settings on the future' and to the circumstances of 2018, then turns a question back on the member. The core of the question — agree or not — is left untouched.
question: Does he agree with the statement made by then Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters in 2018 that the oil and gas ban “makes sense” and that introducing the ban was the change that New Zealanders wanted?
statement: Can I just say that the Prime Minister and this Government have its settings on the future, and if the Prime Minister and that member with the question were to go back and examine the time and the place when that statement was made, there was a ban on at the time. Does that member not remember that?

explanation: Asked whether reopening the coast to oil and gas contradicts the Climate Change Minister's COP28 call to phase out fossil fuels. The answer describes what is happening at COP28 and praises the representatives, but never addresses whether the two positions contradict each other. A narrow yes/no was avoided entirely.
question: Is reopening the New Zealand coast to oil and gas exploration a contradiction to the Minister of Climate Change’s call for a global agreement to phase out fossil fuels at COP28?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister: right now at COP 28, they are wrestling with that very issue, and they’ll be probably working days longer than that because they haven’t come to an agreement. And the two representatives at that time—the previous member and Minister in charge of it and the present Minister—are doing a fine job to ensure that New Zealand’s commitments remain the same going forward.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made on setting speed limits. Brown states the announcement directly: amending the speed limit rules, removing deadlines for speed management plans, allowing authorities to stop blanket reductions. Answers exactly what was asked.
question: What announcements has he made on setting speed limits in New Zealand?
statement: Today, I announced that the coalition Government is amending speed limit rules as part of our commitment to stop blanket speed limit reductions across the country. Kiwis have been faced with blanket speed limit reductions due to the previous Government’s speed limits rule, which fails to prioritise the economic impacts of slowing New Zealanders down and the views of road users and local communities alongside safety. Changes that I have announced today will remove deadlines for speed management plans and allow road-controlling authorities to stop blanket speed limit reductions on our roads while we write a new rule.

explanation: Asked why the changes were made. Brown gives the reasons — removing the previous Government's mandatory blanket reductions, prioritising productivity and travel times, avoiding wasted spend on plans about to be superseded. The dig at the Opposition is a Focus/Civility matter; the 'why' was answered.
question: Why have these changes been made?
statement: These changes have been made to remove mandatory requirements set by the previous Government for road-controlling authorities to implement blanket speed limit reductions across the country. This coalition Government wants to see a transport system that boosts productivity and economic growth and allows New Zealanders to get where they want to go quickly and safely. Given our coalition Government has begun work on a new rule, I wanted to ensure road-controlling authorities avoid wasting public money—something the Opposition doesn’t care about—on finalising speed management plans only to have to revisit these plans under a new rule.

explanation: Asked what the next steps are for ending blanket speed limit reductions. He states the next step: writing a new rule accounting for economic impacts, travel times, community views and safety. Directly responsive.
question: What are the next steps for ending blanket speed limit reductions?
statement: Very good question. The next step is to write a new rule that takes into consideration a wide range of factors including economic impacts, including travel times, and the views of road users and local communities alongside safety when setting speed limits. The National-ACT coalition agreement is committed to reversing blanket speed limit reductions where it is safe to do so, and this will come as welcome news to Kiwis around the country who have been faced with unnecessary blanket speed limit reductions under the previous Government. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what requirements he will set for speed limits outside schools. He states the requirement: variable speed limits on roads approaching schools during pick-up and drop-off times, in contrast to blanket 30 km/h urban limits. Answers the specific question asked.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. What requirements will the Minister set for speed limits outside of schools?
statement: This new rule that I will develop next year will require road-controlling authorities to implement variable speed limits on roads approaching schools during pick-up and drop-off times. This differs to the previous Government’s rule which resulted in blanket speed limit reductions to 30 kilometres per hour on many urban roads. Our coalition Government’s new rule will keep young New Zealanders safe while allowing Kiwis to get where they want to go quickly and safely.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by Willis' statement about the smokefree legislation's ~$1 billion effect on the books. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, and complete — the question was a yes/no and it got one.
question: Does she stand by Nicola Willis’ statement, “Coming back to those extra source of revenue and other savings areas that will help us to fund the tax reduction, we have to remember that the changes to the smoke free legislation had a significant impact on the Government’s books—with about $1 billion there.”; if not, why not?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether she had sought official advice on minimum employment standards (plus a rhetorical 'is it because of ideology' tail). She answers the factual limb flatly and immediately — 'I have not asked for any advice on alternative models' — and then gives her actual reason (the 100-day repeal commitment), which addresses the second limb too. Blunt and unaccommodating, but nothing is dodged.
question: Has she sought advice from officials on their preferred option of minimum employment standards to ensure there is no race to the bottom for low-wage workers, and, if not, is that because she is more interested in disproven right-wing ideology than in lifting wages?
statement: I have not asked for any advice on alternative models. I am focused on delivering on this Government’s 100-day commitment to repeal the fair pay agreements. I look forward to working with the member, over the next three years, in this portfolio. Clearly, he’s interested in where we get to.

explanation: Asked the standard 'does he stand by all his Government's statements and policies?' — a yes/no. The reply cross-references answers given to other questions rather than saying yes or no. It points at where an answer might be found instead of giving one; a listener cannot extract the position from the response itself.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and policies?
statement: In the same way as we answered for questions two and three, and again in question eight.

explanation: Asked how he can stand by using urgency to push through the legislation given the cost of living. He engages by rejecting the question's premises as untrue and offers a partial reason (the economic 'inheritance', urgency before Christmas), then slides into attacking the questioner's ideology before being cut off. Half an answer: the premise rejection and the inheritance point are responsive, but the 'why urgency' core is only grazed.
question: How can he stand by his decision to use parliamentary urgency to push through legislation that will increase unemployment and insecure working conditions, while reducing wages, when people are trying to survive a cost of living crisis and put more kai on the table for Christmas?
statement: Because none of those statements in that so-called question are true. But they are relevant to the inheritance that this Government is, sadly, having to deal with now, and desperately before Christmas. And so if they’d paid more attention to the economy, rather than their woke, idiotic, left ideals—

explanation: Asked for his justification for repealing fair pay agreements given the leaked Cabinet paper. He spends most of the answer on his own credentials and who set the threshold, but does reach a justification at the end — productivity as the basis for pay — before being cut off. A real reason surfaces, but late and around a large detour; the leaked Cabinet paper is never touched.
question: Yes, I do. Thank you. What is his justification for repealing fair pay agreements and reducing the wages and conditions of Māori, Pasifika, young people, and women, as highlighted by his own Government’s leaked Cabinet paper?
statement: Well, first of all, the integrity of the person answering this question on the subject of incomes and wages is that that threshold was set in the previous Government, not by Labour or the Greens but by New Zealand First. We want the working class of this country to get fairly paid, but we want a thing called productivity, and we know it’s only based on—

explanation: Asked why the Government is reinstating 90-day trials given the 2016 Treasury research. He gives a direct rationale (a willing business plus a willing worker is what drives employment, so the trial length is not the operative factor) and directly rebuts the predicted harm ('those consequences simply will not happen'). Whether that reasoning is sound is a Rigor question; as an answer, it addresses the 'why' squarely.
question: Why is this Government planning to bring back 90-day trials, which will disproportionately punish tangata whenua, particularly rangatahi trying to get their foot in the door of the job market, when the research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms’ overall hiring but instead just make it easier for firms to sack people without cause and with fewer dismissal costs?
statement: The fact is—if anyone understands economics—a willing business and a willing worker are critical to employment. So whether it’s one month, two months, or three months, the fact of the matter is that the sound connection of those two will work. However, it is our intention as the Government, the moment someone is no longer able to work, to be on their case to get them back into work. So the consequences that that member’s talking about simply will not happen.

explanation: A narrow two-part factual question: how many FTEs must be trained annually to hold the 1:480 ratio, and is the 500 additional to that. He answers neither — no number, no yes/no — and instead disputes that the ratio was ever finalised or funded. Attacking the premise of the metric leaves both limbs of a precise question untouched.
question: How many Constabulary Full Time Equivalents does Police expect to need to train each year for the next two years in order to maintain the 1 to 480 ratio, and will the Government’s commitment for “no fewer than 500 new frontline police within the first two years” be in addition to that?
statement: I’m advised that the 1:480 ratio was never finalised, nor was it funded adequately by the previous Government.

explanation: Asked a clean yes/no: will constabulary FTE numbers be 500 higher in two years' time. He restates the commitment to 'an additional 500', which is adjacent to the answer, but never confirms the net headcount in two years — precisely the distinction the question was probing. Partial: the core is hedged around rather than reached.
question: Will the number of constabulary fulltime-equivalents be 500 higher in two years’ time?
statement: Well, in the police, numbers matter, and we’re committed to the coalition agreement that we have with New Zealand First. They delivered 1,800 additional police officers, and they’re now committed to an additional 500.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware 500 will not cover attrition, and whether he is comfortable overseeing a reduction. He engages the attrition subject honestly (recruiting pressure, Australian poaching, retirements) but answers neither limb: no acknowledgment of the shortfall as such, and no answer on whether he is comfortable with a reduction — he closes by reasserting the 500 instead.
question: Is he aware that 500 additional police officers over two years is not enough to even replace attrition, and is he comfortable overseeing a reduction in front-line numbers?
statement: Well, the 500 is additional police officers. The challenge that we’ve got as an incoming Government is that it’s become very apparent to us that the police have got big challenges around recruiting. The recruiting pipeline, there’s pressure on that; we’ve got the Australians here recruiting our police officers; we’ve got a lot of officers coming up to retirement age. So she should understand that there’s challenges there, but the good news is the police remain committed to delivering an additional 500 police officers.

explanation: Asked how the public can have confidence in him given an expected decrease in front-line numbers. It was an open 'how' question and he supplies a responsive form of answer — they can, because the Government takes public safety seriously. The reason is a slogan, but thinness is Specificity, not evasion; he does state a ground for confidence rather than changing the subject.
question: How can the New Zealand public have confidence in him if he expects to oversee an overall decrease in constabulary front-line numbers?
statement: Well, they can have confidence in me and this Government because we take public safety seriously.

explanation: Asked whether New Zealanders will feel safer with fewer police, and if not, what he will do. He denies the premise head-on as his first move — 'there's not going to be fewer police on the streets' — which is a definite, contestable answer to the question actually asked. The following talking points add nothing, but the core was met, not avoided.
question: Does he expect New Zealanders to feel safer with fewer police on our streets, and, if not, what is he going to do about it?
statement: Well, there’s not going to be fewer police on the streets, number one. Number two, police officers are actually going to be on the front line serving the communities that they work in, and, number three, you’ve got a serious Government now that actually takes public safety seriously, and the country’s going to be safer.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on recent policing. He names a specific operation and recounts what it produced. Whatever this is as a question (a friendly one), the response lands directly on what was asked.
question: What reports has he seen on policing in recent weeks?
statement: Very good question. Police have done some outstanding work recently. This has included Operation Shadow in Hamilton City and the wider Waikato region, targeting illegal street racing offenders. Police have made 12 arrests, issued 220 infringement notices, and suspended three licences in response to road users blocking roads and exhibiting unsafe driving behaviours. There were seven arrests made for excessive breath alcohol, two for disorder, one for driving while suspended, one for a breach of home detention, and another had an existing warrant for arrest. I know and the police know that our communities are fed up with this behaviour, and I congratulate police for their outstanding work. Police said—and I quote—“We want to send a message to anyone involved in this type of behaviour that Police will work incredibly hard to hold you to account for any illegal activity”.

explanation: Asked what reports he has received on the policing of gangs. He describes the police handling of the Foxton gang tangi and the monitoring around it — squarely on the subject asked about, with no pivot.
question: What reports has he received from police on the policing of gangs?
statement: I was very impressed by how police staff handled the recent gang tangi in Foxton. Police monitored the movements of gang members across the North Island roads and made it clear they had a strong presence and that law and order would be maintained. They made sure members of the public were able to go about their business freely and safely. I want to thank police for ensuring there were minimal disruptions to the public and that they were kept safe.

explanation: Asked for the SOURCE of her billion-dollar figure. She answers 'the source was my answer to the question' — circular — then pivots to Budget sensitivity and to a timing technicality (the statement predated her swearing-in). No source is ever named. The timing point is a sliver of engagement, so not a floor score, but the core of a narrow question is avoided.
question: What is the source of her statement that there is a billion dollars a year impact on the Government’s books from undoing the smoke-free changes?
statement: The source was my answer to the question, and I continue to seek advice from officials on the spending and revenue implications of coalition commitments. Many of those details are Budget sensitive and I will make announcements about them in due course. As the member well knows, the statement he is referring to was made before I was sworn in as the Minister of Finance.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: has she been advised of a billions-per-year impact? The response is a verbatim repeat of the previous non-answer — 'continue to seek advice', 'Budget sensitive', 'in due course'. Never yes, never no. 'Continue to seek' faintly implies not-yet-advised, which is all that keeps it off zero.
question: Has she been advised that there is a billions of dollars a year impact on the Government’s books from undoing the smoke-free changes?
statement: As I say, I continue to seek advice from officials on the spending and revenue implications of coalition commitments. Many of those details are Budget sensitive and I will make announcements about them in due course.

explanation: Asked to rule out using smoke-free revenue for tax cuts. She neither rules it out nor declines to; instead 'multiple sources of revenue and multiple spending commitments' (an implicit fungibility argument) followed by a pivot to Robertson's own tobacco tax take. The implicit non-ruling-out is real but is never stated as an answer.
question: Is she ruling out using the revenue from winding back smoke-free initiatives to fund tax cuts?
statement: As the member knows, the Government has multiple sources of revenue and multiple spending commitments. It is this Government’s expectation that, just as was the case with his outgoing Government, tobacco will continue to be regulated and taxed. I note that during his time as finance Minister, he collected hundreds of millions of dollars in tobacco tax revenue, which was used for a wide range of purposes, including health and education services and Working for Families payments.

explanation: The rule-out question re-put, sharpened with the 'immoral' quote. Same generic revenue-goes-to-everything formulation, then a turn onto the questioner ('Opposition does appear to suit him'). Scored low for never giving the rule-out, not for the jibe — incivility is a separate attribute.
question: That’s very philosophical, Mr Speaker. Will she today rule out using the revenue gained from stopping the smoke-free changes for tax cuts in light of Sir Collin Tukuitonga describing doing so as “immoral”?
statement: Just as was the case with his Government, tax revenue from a range of sources will be used to support the activities of Government, including delivery of health services through to transfer payments and paying down debt. The member may not like the answers to my questions, but in Opposition he’s going to have to get used to it. And if I may say to the member, Opposition does appear to suit him.

explanation: Asked for the Government's sentencing position and why. Both halves are delivered: the position (a tougher approach, limiting sentencing discounts) and the reason (public safety, victims, real consequences for serious offenders). Direct and essentially complete.
question: What is the Government’s position on sentencing, and why?
statement: The coalition Government will take a tougher approach to sentencing law so serious offenders face real consequences for their crime as part of our plan to restore law and order. The coalition Government will prioritise public safety and victims through a series of measures we have agreed to implement. These include limiting massive discounts that weaken offenders’ final sentencing.

explanation: Asked what recent estimates he has seen. He states them outright — officials' estimate of 4,600 to 7,800 serious and violent offenders receiving discounts above 40 percent in 2021–22. Exactly the question asked, fully answered.
question: What recent estimates has he seen about sentencing discounts?
statement: I’ve been advised by officials that, for serious and violent offenders who pleaded guilty in 2021–22, their best estimate is that between 4,600 and 7,800 offenders were issued with a sentencing discount of greater than 40 percent.

explanation: Asked why the Government is concerned about large discounts. He gives the reason: public feedback on violent crime and the denunciatory role of sentencing. Whether that reasoning is sound is a Rigor matter; as a response it lands squarely on the question.
question: Why is the Government concerned about large sentencing discounts?
statement: The strong feedback we’ve received across the country this year is that many New Zealanders are concerned with increased violent crime and want to see tougher consequences for serious violent and sexual offenders. Part of the role of sentencing is to denounce the criminal act and to recognise the harm caused to victims.

explanation: Asked what PROGRESS he has made implementing the plan. He opens with a swipe at the previous Government and mostly reports intentions — 'prioritising its plan', 'we have committed to limiting total sentence discounts to 40 percent'. The 100-day plan reference and the 40 percent commitment are concrete enough to count as partial engagement, but commitments are offered where progress was asked for.
question: What progress has he made on implementing the Government’s plan to take a tougher approach to sentencing?
statement: I’m pleased to inform the House that the coalition Government is prioritising its plan to restore law and order after six years of a Government being focused on reducing prison numbers without reducing crime.
