As well as the measures listed in our 100-day plan, we have committed to limiting total sentence discounts to 40 percent. This will ensure that serious offenders face real consequences for their crime.

explanation: Asked whether she accepts Treasury advice on disproportionate impacts. 'I have not received any advice from Treasury, nor would I expect to' is blunt, complete, and squarely addresses the question's premise — the forthright-refusal case, not a dodge. Held below 0.9 only because the substantive 'if not, why not' is left implicit rather than answered.
question: Does she accept the Treasury’s advice that the removal of fair pay agreements would disproportionately affect women, young people, Māori, and Pasifika; if not, why not?
statement: I have not received any advice from Treasury, nor would I expect to.

explanation: Two parts: does she acknowledge Christmas stress for low-wage workers, and why remove workplace rights first. She reframes the first into a general cost-of-living acknowledgment rather than conceding the specific point, but does answer the second head-on — nobody is worse off because no fair pay agreement was ever finalised. Half squarely met, half slid past.
question: Does she acknowledge that Christmas is a particularly stressful time for low-wage workers, and if so, why is her first action as Minister to remove workplace rights instead of improve them?
statement: I acknowledge that many Kiwis are struggling with a cost of living crisis, and that’s why this Government is focused on improving productivity, reducing regulation, and getting rid of inflation so that Kiwis have more money for them and their families. But I want to acknowledge, when it comes to the fair pay agreements, nobody will be worse off with the removal of the fair pay agreements, because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised.

explanation: A narrow factual question — how many WORKERS are in sectors that instigated bargaining. She supplies the number of agreements (six) and 'many New Zealanders', which answers a different, easier question, then returns to the nothing-was-finalised talking point. She engages the topic but substitutes her own count for the one requested.
question: Does she know how many workers are in sectors that have already instigated bargaining under the fair pay agreements framework, and, if not, why hasn’t she asked?
statement: There have been six fair pay agreements that are currently in a bargaining process. There are many New Zealanders who are being represented during that process. But, of course, I want to stress that not a single member involved in that process has a fair pay agreement, because not a single fair pay agreement has been finalised or signed. So no Kiwis are worse off.

explanation: 'Workers in Australia, across industries, are better off' concedes the awareness half directly rather than contesting it — genuine engagement. The 'why should New Zealanders settle for less' half gets a generic productivity/flexible-labour-market answer, which does reach the question (we shouldn't; this is our route) even though it never touches sector bargaining. Vagueness here is a Specificity issue, not a dodge.
question: Is she aware that bus drivers, cleaners, and early childhood education teachers earn at least 30 percent more pay in Australia, where sector-based bargaining is in place, and, if so, why should New Zealanders settle for less?
statement: Workers in Australia, across industries, are better off. But that’s why this Government is focusing on making sure that we have a flexible labour market where we increase productivity, where we have businesses able to invest in their workers and invest in their businesses so workers and business are better off in our economy. That is the focus of our Government—to have a thriving economy where businesses have more money to pay their staff more.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with a specific Climate Change Commission statement. He never says agree or disagree; instead he denies the premise ("we're not weakening our actions"). That denial does engage the substance of the quoted claim, so it is not a pure pivot, but the agree/disagree core is left unanswered. Partial.
question: Does he agree with the Climate Change Commission that “Weakening action on climate policy during times of adverse economic conditions—which climate change is only likely to exacerbate—is not sustainable and will greatly compromise [Aotearoa New Zealand’s] ability to meet [emissions budgets and the 2050 target].”?
statement: We’re not weakening our actions on climate change; we’re just going about it a different way.

explanation: A sharp binary question — will he or will he not instruct all Ministers to implement the commission's advice. The answer is commitment language ("committed to delivering on climate change", Ministers working "through their respective portfolios") that never says will or won't. A narrow yes/no dodged in favour of talking points.
question: Will he or will he not instruct all Ministers to implement the commission’s advice in their work programmes?
statement: Our Government’s committed to delivering on climate change, and our Ministers are making sure that they can do that through their respective portfolios.

explanation: "Does he stand by all of his Government's statements and actions?" answered "Yes" in the first word — direct and complete. The subsequent 100-day-plan promotion and swipe at the previous Government are padding, but padding after an answer is not evasion (and its partisanship is Focus/Civility, not this attribute).
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and particularly the Government’s statement that we will be a Government that gets things done for New Zealand. That starts with our 100-day plan, which includes a number of changes to make it easier for Kiwis to be able to get ahead, make our communities safer, and deliver better health and education for our young people. This is a Government that’s got a mandate for change, and its focus is on delivery for New Zealanders, unlike the previous Government.

explanation: Asked what reports she has received on inflation; she names them and their content — inflation at 5.6 percent, the Reserve Bank's most recent Monetary Policy Statement on non-tradable inflation easing gradually. The question is squarely engaged. The added reassurance and single-mandate legislation are extra, not a substitute.
question: What reports has she received on the challenge of inflation in New Zealand?
statement: The reports I have received confirm that inflation remains a major challenge in New Zealand, at a rate of 5.6 percent, even while inflation falls rapidly overseas. The Reserve Bank has said in their most recent Monetary Policy Statement that non-tradable inflation is easing only gradually, highlighting the challenge facing the Government and the Reserve Bank as we look to win the fight on inflation in coming months. I want to reassure New Zealanders who are struggling with the cost of living that beating inflation is this Government’s top priority. Our first act in Parliament was to introduce and progress legislation returning the Reserve Bank to a single mandate, ensuring New Zealanders can have confidence that our commitment to beating inflation is rock solid.

explanation: Asked how NZ inflation compares to overseas; gives the comparison directly — 5.6 percent at home against 3.1 percent in the United States. Exactly the question asked, answered on its own terms.
question: How does inflation in New Zealand compare to other countries overseas?
statement: Well, while inflation remains very high at home, at 5.6 percent, other countries offshore are already making significant progress. Inflation in the United States fell to just 3.1 percent overnight.

explanation: Asked what factors kept domestic inflation high; she supplies factors — over-reliance on monetary policy and the fiscal deficit, citing the OECD, plus the forecast $11.4 billion deficit. Blaming the previous Government is a partisan framing, but factors were genuinely named, so the question was engaged rather than sidestepped.
question: What factors have led domestic inflation to remain so high?
statement: According to the OECD’s latest economic outlook, “Up until late 2023, too much weight has been put on monetary policy to reduce inflation, requiring higher interest rates”, and that “The fiscal deficit is contributing to this imbalance.” The incoming Government will not be able to fix in one Budget an imbalance of spending that has built up over six years. However, the outgoing Government has left us with a forecast deficit this year of $11.4 billion—and that’s in the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update. But we are already taking early action, as part of the 100-day plan, to end wasteful spending, and I look forward to giving many speeches on that.

explanation: Asked what next steps the Government is taking on the cost of living; she names one — fiscally neutral tax relief next year — plus reducing wasteful spending. A long list of the previous Government's projects pads it out, but a concrete next step was given before the padding started.
question: What next steps is the Government taking to support New Zealanders with the cost of living crisis?
statement: We know that New Zealanders are struggling, which is why the Government is committed to delivering fiscally neutral tax relief next year. After years of watching their money squandered on wasteful projects like Lake Onslow, light rail, the Auckland bike bridge project that cost millions and went nowhere, like the TVNZ-RNZ merger, the jobs tax, the income insurance scheme, and all of the other items in the policy bonfire, our Government is committed to reducing wasteful spending and delivering income tax relief for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked for updates on regional development investments; he provides one — the Snowy River goldmine investment repaid in full at $15 million, 50 employed with 140 more expected. Whether that is a representative or verifiable update belongs to Veracity/Specificity; as a response it delivers what was requested.
question: What updates can he provide of any regional development investments?
statement: It’s my pleasure to announce to the House that as a consequence of a far-sighted politician six years ago making an investment, on behalf of the Government, in the Snowy River goldmine, the entirety of the $15 million has been paid back. This goldmine in Te Tai Poutini, the West Coast, enjoyed the upside of employing 50 people. Another 140 are on the way as they seek to raise $100 million—a great example of central government collaborating with industry in regional New Zealand.

explanation: Asked if he is confident seabed mining will feature in regional development; answers "Yes" outright and adds that it has a legitimate place. The disparaging aside about hapū in Taranaki is a Civility matter and does not displace the answer, which came first and was unambiguous.
question: Is he confident that seabed mining will feature in regional development investments?
statement: Yes. Seabed mining has a legitimate place in New Zealand’s regional economy. Sadly, a number of pixie-like hapū in Taranaki have sought to undermine this legitimate industry. I can assure you, though, that the Environmental Protection Authority legislation, if it needs to be changed to give certainty to investors—and we will not have tikanga Māori mangled and distorted 37 kilometres off the coast of Taranaki.

explanation: Asked how oil and gas will feature in regional development. He does answer — a key role in security of supply, with legislative change to give investors certainty — but wraps it in digression about the 2030 renewables aspiration and "the grown-ups". Vagueness is Specificity's concern; the question itself was reached, if loosely.
question: How will oil and gas investments located in regional New Zealand feature in regional development?
statement: I brought this document here with me today, which contains an assertion, aspirational in nature, that, by 2030, all sources of energy to maintain security of supply in regional New Zealand will be renewable. Oil and gas will play a key role, and when that legislation is changed in regional New Zealand, it will offer certainty to the investment community. And then the grown-ups will ensure that there is security and manageable risk in our energy sector, unlike what we hear from the other side of the House. I look forward to providing that educational service to other members of Parliament.

explanation: A narrow factual question — the total cost of the coalition tax relief. She does not give a figure, but she does address the ask head-on and states the reason (the advice is Budget sensitive), promising details later. That is more than a pivot yet less than the blunt refusal the rubric scores high: "in due course" defers rather than answering or declining outright.
question: What is the total cost to the Government of the “tax relief” outlined in the Policy Programme of the Government as expressed in the coalition agreements?
statement: The Government stands by the commitments set out in our coalition agreements. The advice I have received on the potential fiscal impact of tax relief is obviously Budget sensitive, and I look forward to updating the House on details in due course.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned by any recent policing report he has seen. He says yes, names the specific report and quotes its finding. The core (concerned? which report?) is engaged directly and completely; the closing partisan jab is a Focus/Civility matter and does not move this score.
question: Given his focus on public safety, is he concerned by any recent reports that he has seen on policing?
statement: Yes, I’m very concerned about a report that was released last week. The report was released by the Committee for Auckland with Deloitte and Auckland Unlimited. It says—and I quote—“Auckland ranks only 124th in safety, marking a three-year decline and positioning it among the lowest-performing peer cities on safety and [the] bottom within Australasia.” I am incredibly concerned that our biggest city and our economic centre is now one of the lowest ranked cities in the world for public safety. It is a stain on our nation and a terrible indictment on the record of the previous Government. This Government is committed to turning that around, supporting police, and improving public safety.

explanation: Asked what changes are proposed to the Oranga Tamariki legislation. She names the change — repealing section 7AA — and explains why. Squarely answers what was asked.
question: What changes, if any, is the Government proposing to the legislation that governs Oranga Tamariki?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The coalition agreement between National and ACT commits to repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act. Section 7AA was introduced as a way for Oranga Tamariki to honour the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. While it might’ve been well intentioned, the law has had some serious unintended consequences. That’s because section 7AA creates a fundamental conflict between protecting the best interests of children on one hand and honouring the Treaty in the other.

explanation: Asked what impact the change will have on services and supports for Māori children. Opens with a direct claim of impact — 'nothing about this change will affect the support services and programmes' — then supports it. Direct answer to the question posed; whether it is true is Veracity, not this.
question: What impact will this change have on the services and supports Oranga Tamariki provides to Māori children and young people?
statement: Nothing about this change will affect the support services and programmes that Oranga Tamariki provides for Māori. Repealing section 7AA is about ensuring the safety and wellbeing and the best interests of children and young people so that it’s the paramount consideration of Oranga Tamariki. The Oranga Tamariki Act already has provisions which protect the rights of whānau, hapū, and iwi, and I have also already made it very clear to officials that they should continue working with iwi and Māori organisations where this is achieving positive outcomes for young people.

explanation: A 'does she stand by' question, answered 'Yes' with the specific comments she stands by. Complete.
question: Does she stand by her recent statements in relation to fair pay agreements?
statement: Yes, especially regarding my comments that fair pay agreements (FPAs) would reduce flexibility, choice, and agility in workplaces; also, that to lift productivity and drive economic growth there needs to be flexible workplaces where employers and employees can agree on terms that suit their unique situations.

explanation: Asked whether she accepts she received MBIE advice that removal would disproportionately affect women, young people, Māori and Pasifika. She answers a narrower adjacent question — she did not *ask* for cost-benefit advice — and describes what she did receive (the RIS cover sheet), but never says whether she accepts receiving advice with that content. Partial engagement, core sidestepped.
question: In response to an earlier question, she stated that she hadn’t received any advice from the Treasury. Does she accept that she received advice from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) that the removal of fair pay agreements would disproportionately affect women, young people, Māori, and Pasifika?
statement: I have not asked for advice on the costs and benefits of repealing the fair pay agreements from MBIE. What I have received is a cover sheet to MBIE’s 2021 regulatory impact statement (RIS), which updates the sections of that RIS to reflect the proposal which is to return the fair pay agreement system to the status quo. To be clear, the regulatory impact statement from MBIE from 2021 recommended against introducing a fair pay agreement system.

explanation: Asked a narrow factual question: does she accept the cover sheet states X? She replies about what she does accept — that the statement has been taken out of context — which implicitly concedes the statement is there but never gives the yes/no asked for, and closes on a different point (no FPAs finalised). Partial.
question: Does she accept that the regulatory impact statement cover sheet that she received from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment on 28 November 2023 states that the removal of fair pay agreements would disproportionately affect women, young people, Māori, and Pasifika?
statement: What I accept is that the statement within the cover sheet to the regulatory impact statement has been taken out of a wider context where it suggests that the benefits of the fair pay agreements that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment mentioned only apply to employees within the scope of a fair pay agreement. To be clear, there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised, so no one is worse off.

explanation: Same narrow document question about paragraph 13. She repeats the 'out of context' reframe without confirming or denying what the paragraph states, then pivots to general talking points about productivity and reducing regulation. A specific factual question left unanswered with a drift into stump material.
question: Does the Minister accept that on paragraph 13 of that RIS, it clearly states that depending on the sector and occupations where FPAs are concluded, they could disproportionately benefit some population groups covered, including women, young people, Māori, and Pacific peoples?
statement: What I acknowledge is that that statement has been taken out of the wider context, which is that this cover sheet is an update to the regulatory impact statement which was against the fair pay agreement. What the statement suggests is that we’re taking away the fair pay agreement bargaining process. There have not been any fair pay agreements signed, and so therefore anybody who was worse off is only in theory worse off, because there have not been any fair pay agreements signed. What this Government is committed to doing is making sure that we have a Government that benefits business and benefits workers. The best way to improve the conditions of all Kiwi workers is to make sure that we have high productivity. We reduce regulation—

explanation: Asked whether she accepts FPAs would in theory benefit those groups. Answers 'No,' and gives her reason (disemployment effects). A blunt, contestable answer, but it engages the question head-on.
question: Does she accept, then, that if the fair pay agreements legislation which she intends to repeal was not repealed, in theory it would benefit Māori, Pacific, young people, poorer workers?
statement: No, because this Government believes that the fair pay agreement system would have made vulnerable workers worse off. This is because of disemployment effects where businesses who could not stomach the added cost to their businesses lay off workers or close up entirely or don’t offer any more jobs. The best way to help vulnerable workers is to have a flexible labour market that works for all New Zealanders, where every business has the opportunity to employ more staff and have more money to pay their staff more.

explanation: A two-pronged either/or question. He takes both prongs explicitly: yes, he stands by his statement, and yes, he also stands by the Minister's, with a reconciliation of the apparent conflict. Whether that reconciliation holds up is Rigor/Veracity; as an answer it addresses what was asked.
question: Does he stand by his statement in relation to the Paris Agreement 2030 emissions reduction targets, “We are going to meet our commitments and obligations”, or does he agree with his Minister for Resources, who said yesterday that “We are not going to meet the 2030 dreamy, fairy-tale, aspirational figures”?
statement: Yes, I stand by my statement. The Government is going to meet its obligations and commitments that it’s made on climate change, and I also stand by the statement from the Minister of Resources as well, because he was clearly talking about the previous Government’s 100 percent renewable electricity target, which is, actually, a fairy tale and is counter-productive.

explanation: Asked whether the Government has any targets or policies to reduce fossil fuel use across energy AND transport to replace the dropped 2030 target, and if not why not. He offers one electricity-side policy (doubling renewables) and never says whether replacement targets exist, nor touches transport or the 'if not, why not' limb. Gestures at the question without reaching it.
question: Does his Government have any targets or policies to reduce fossil fuel use across the energy and transport industry to replace the 2030 renewable electricity target, and, if not, why not?
statement: Yeah, we’re going to actually electrify New Zealand by doubling the amount of renewable electricity that’s in New Zealand so we can make the transition well and make our sectors move to clean, green energy.

explanation: Asked if he is concerned about the contradiction. 'Absolutely not' is a direct, complete answer to the question actually put, followed by his reasoning. He does not rebut the specific examples cited, but the question's core was whether he is concerned, and that was answered.
question: Is he concerned about the growing contradiction, under this Government, between New Zealand’s international and climate commitments and domestic plans which undermine efforts to reduce emissions, such as reopening oil and gas drilling and cancelling the Clean Car Discount?
statement: Absolutely not. We are deeply committed to delivering on our climate goals and commitments. The way we go about doing that may be different from the previous Government, but don’t misunderstand our commitment to the targets and goals.

explanation: Two prongs: does he stand by his 'climate deniers' statement, and is he embarrassed by the Minister's 'great lie' remark. 'Climate change is a crisis' engages the underlying dispute and implies he stands by his position, but he never says so, and the embarrassment limb is left entirely untouched. Terse is fine here — incomplete is what costs it.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “There is no reason for climate deniers and climate minimalists in the 21st century”, and, if so, is he embarrassed by the statements of the Minister of Resources that “One of the great lies about climate change is that, yes, apparently, it’s a crisis.”?
statement: Climate change is a crisis.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her earlier answers that she does not know which revenue initiatives will fund the tax relief. She neither confirms nor denies; she disputes that the quote is fairly represented and asks to see it in context. That is engagement with the premise rather than an answer to the yes/no question, and no refusal is stated either.
question: Does she stand by the answers she’s given in this House that she does not know what specific revenue initiatives will fund the tax relief programme?
statement: I would have to see that comment in context to believe it is being fairly represented in the House.

explanation: Asked how she can promise fiscally neutral tax relief without knowing the cost. She answers the core squarely: she does know the cost, and she is declining to share it because it is Budget-sensitive. A stated refusal to disclose is a direct response, not a dodge. The trailing attack on the questioner is a Civility/Focus matter and does not lower the score; a small deduction only because the fiscal-neutrality half is left implicit.
question: How can she say that she will deliver fiscally neutral tax relief, when she doesn’t know how much it’s going to cost?
statement: Because I do know how much it’s going to cost, but I am not sharing with that member the information when it is Budget sensitive. I can also be confident about delivering tax relief, because, unlike the member opposite, I actually believe New Zealanders deserve to keep more of what they earn, and they deserve a Government that won’t waste their hard-earned wages on boondoggles, like he did.

explanation: Asked why she changed her position on the app tax. The reply gives no reason; it disclaims responsibility for manifesto commitments. That addresses the question's scope rather than its content — closer to "not mine to answer" than to an explicit refusal — so it partly engages but never reaches the why.
question: Why has the member changed her position on the app tax?
statement: I am not responsible for commitments made in party manifestos.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with her own past statement that the app tax was an outrage and should be reversed. She opens with a direct "I do agree with Nicola Willis," which answers it, then runs into talking points about tax relief and the previous Government. The core yes is delivered before the padding; slight deduction because the "should be reversed" half is not separately confirmed.
question: Does she agree with Nicola Willis, the National Party finance spokesperson, who said that the app tax was an outrage and should be reversed?
statement: I do agree with Nicola Willis. And what I also agree with Nicola Willis on is that it is time for a Government that stops tax grabbing and should start by prioritising income tax relief for working people. We have been left with fiscal constraints, by the previous Government, that are extreme, and, in that context, our priority must be letting New Zealanders keep more of what they earn with personal income tax relief.

explanation: Asked how she can remain Minister of Finance in a Government imposing a tax she called outrageous. She engages the tension — she agreed in the context given, and as Minister she is responsible for the Government's collective decisions — which implies an answer (collective responsibility) without ever stating it. Partial: the core is approached but not squarely resolved.
question: In light of that answer, that she agrees that the app tax was outrageous and should be reversed—she agrees with Nicola Willis on that—how can she continue to be the Minister of Finance in a Government that is now imposing the app tax?
statement: I agreed with the statements of Nicola Willis in the context in which they were given. As the Minister of Finance, I am responsible for the policy commitments of our Government and its decisions.

explanation: Asked what actions he is taking to repeal the Clean Car Discount by 31 December. He names the action taken (legislation introduced yesterday) and the effective cut-off. Direct and complete.
question: What actions is he taking to repeal the Clean Car Discount scheme by 31 December?
statement: Our coalition Government committed to axing the ute tax and Clean Car Discount scheme by 31 December, providing assurance to hard-working New Zealanders that they can purchase the vehicles that they need without being unfairly penalised; and ending what is a fiscally unsustainable scheme. Yesterday, I introduced legislation to the House to axe the ute tax by 31 December and deliver on this commitment. This means that charges will end for vehicles after 11.59 p.m. on 31 December 2023, and buyers of low-emitting vehicles will no longer be able to apply for rebates.

explanation: Asked why the actions are being taken. He gives the reason — the scheme's deficit against its promised fiscal neutrality. Directly responsive; whether the figures are accurate is a Veracity question and does not bear on this score.
question: Why are these actions being taken?
statement: A very good question. The previous Government promised the scheme would be “fiscally neutral”, but, as at 30 November, $579 million has been paid out in rebates and $13.5 million has been spent on administration costs, while only $290 million has been received in charges. This has left taxpayers footing the bill for an eye-watering $302.5 million deficit.

explanation: Asked what subsidies have been paid out under the scheme. He answers with subsidies to high-end vehicles and a $122 million figure. Squarely on the question, though it addresses one slice of the subsidies rather than the whole; a total is never given.
question: What subsidies have been paid out under the scheme with this $302.5 million deficit?
statement: Well, the $302.5 million deficit hitting taxpayers’ pockets has contributed to thousands of subsidies to high-end vehicles costing $70,000 or more. In the last 18 months alone, over $122 million has been paid out to those buying high-end vehicles under this scheme. Our Government does not believe that taxpayers should be subsidising those who can already afford to purchase these vehicles.

explanation: Asked what advice he has seen on the scheme's financial sustainability. He states what the advice says — the scheme will not survive past mid-2024 without listed changes. Direct and complete.
question: What advice has he seen on the financial sustainability of the scheme?
statement: Well, advice I have received shows the Clean Car Discount scheme will not survive past mid-2024 without substantial changes to how it operates. Continuing the scheme would likely require a combination of lowering and restricting rebates to electric vehicles; increasing charges and applying them to all petrol, diesel, and some hybrids; or providing more Crown funding. This will only worsen equity issues and could result in taxpayers footing an even bigger bill.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions. "Yes." One word, complete, no evasion.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked what the conflict created by section 7AA is. She identifies it: the meaning of honouring the Treaty is not clear, so decisions vary with interpretation. That is the question answered. Whether the reasoning holds up is Rigor and does not move this score.
question: The Minister said that section 7AA creates a fundamental conflict between protecting the best interests of children, on the one hand, and honouring the Treaty, on the other; what is the conflict?
statement: From what I’ve been hearing from community organisations and groups, and also hearing from news articles around the issues with section 7AA, the intent behind honouring what the Treaty means is not clear. It depends on how someone interprets what honouring the Treaty means. And so that creates a conflict, because, when decisions are being made, the decisions may vary on the interpretation of what honouring the Treaty means.

explanation: Asked whether she still maintains a conflict exists given section 4A's paramountcy clause. She never says yes or no; she pivots to what the change is about (clarity for social workers) and refers the member to other sections. The specific challenge put to her is left untouched.
question: Does she still maintain there is a conflict, when section 4A says, “In all matters relating to the administration or application of this Act (other than Parts 4 and 5 and sections 351 to 360), the well-being and best interests of the child or young person are the first and paramount consideration, having regard to the principles set out in sections 5 and 13”?
statement: This change is about helping provide clarity of focus to social workers to any decisions they make around removals and placements, and there are already provisions in the Act that provide rights to whānau, hapū and iwi. I refer this member to sections 4, 5, and 13 of the Oranga Tamariki Act.

explanation: Asked for confirmation she will meet the listed Māori partners before the bill's introduction. She engages the subject but converts a yes/no commitment into a double conditional — she has 'asked for advice' and will meet 'if my calendar has the space'. The core (will you, before introduction?) is left unanswered while circling it.
question: Can the Minister confirm that before the introduction of the bill, she will meet with the strategic Māori partners: Eastern Bay of Plenty Iwi Provider Alliance, Māori Women’s Welfare League partnership, Ngāti Kahungunu partnership, Ngāi Tahu partnership, Waikato-Tainui partnership, Tūhoe partnership, Ngāpuhi partnership, Ngāti Toa Rangatira and Te Āti Awa partnership, and Te Kahu Oranga partnership?
statement: I have asked for advice on how I can organise to meet with these groups that have committed partnership agreements, and if my calendar has the space to do this, I will do so.

explanation: Asked how she can feel proud given the claimed effect on tamariki. She answers the 'why proud' part directly (proud to be Minister, putting things in place for children) and explicitly rejects the question's embedded premise, which is engagement rather than evasion. She does not address the alienation-from-whakapapa charge on its own terms, so it is partial.
question: In light of her response to question No. 4, that she is proud, how can she possibly feel proud to condemn future generations of Māori tamariki to be alienated from their whakapapa, language, and culture?
statement: I am very proud to stand here and be the Minister for Children and to make sure that I am putting things in place to make the lives of children in New Zealand better. Nothing I have ever said or done implies that I want to destroy Māori heritage, whakapapa, or anything to do with Māori ethnicity.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing to improve literacy and numeracy. Names the specific action — the hour-a-day policy notified in the Education Bulletin, an average hour a day of reading, writing and maths for years 0-8. Squarely on the question.
question: What is the Government doing to improve literacy and numeracy achievement in New Zealand?
statement: Yesterday, the Education Bulletin was sent out to the education sector, indicating the Government’s intention to implement the hour a day policy into New Zealand schools. Improving outcomes in reading, writing, and maths is a priority for this Government, so I have asked schools with students in years 0 to 8 to spend an average of an hour a day teaching reading, writing, and maths.

explanation: Asked why an hour a day on each subject matters. Gives the reason (fundamental skills that unlock the curriculum) plus the Royal Society finding on variation and its recommendation. Drifts into a swipe at the previous Government at the end, but the 'why' is reached first.
question: Why is it important that children spend an hour a day on each of these subjects?
statement: Reading, writing, and maths are fundamental skills that unlock the rest of the curriculum. In a 2021 report into the teaching of mathematics in New Zealand, the Royal Society found significant variation amongst schools in terms of the amount of time devoted to teaching maths, with some teachers scheduling maths for as much as seven hours a week, while others teach it for fewer than three. It was their recommendation, in that report, to introduce an hour a day of mathematics. The previous Government ignored those recommendations. But this Government will be introducing an hour a day to see all children, across New Zealand, getting consistent, high-quality education that they deserve, and this is just the first step.

explanation: Asked what results indicate the change is necessary. Cites 2022 PISA maths decline and the national monitoring study's 41.5 percent of year 8s at curriculum. The requested evidence is supplied directly.
question: What results has the Minister seen to indicate that this change is necessary?
statement: The 2022 Programme for International Student Assessment results show a significant decline in the performance of 15-year-old students in maths, compared to 2018, and confirms the long-term trend of declining achievement in core subjects since 2000. The 2022 national monitoring study showed that only 41.5 percent of our year 8s were at curriculum for maths after eight years of schooling. These results show us that our education system has continued to deliver poor outcomes for learners. But our Government has a plan to turn this around. Our Teaching the Basics Brilliantly policy, which includes an hour a day, builds an important foundation to ensure young people receive the high-quality education they deserve and allows them to live the life that they want.

explanation: Asked what an hour a day looks like in practice in the classroom. She does describe practice — across the school day and curriculum, explicit teaching, collaborative learning, activities, games — so the question is engaged, but much of the answer restates intent and expectation rather than the classroom picture asked for.
question: What will an hour a day look like in practice in the classroom?
statement: As I said in the Education Bulletin that went out this week, we know that many schools already do an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths. But it is our intention to ensure that this great practice is happening consistently across the sector in New Zealand. We expect that these hours take place across the entire school day and throughout the curriculum. This will include explicit teaching, collaborative learning, activities, games, and all the other best-practice techniques teachers use to engage and develop young people’s skills. But, rest assured, it is our expectation that our young people are getting access to an hour of reading, writing, and mathematics every day, across the whole country, in every classroom.

explanation: Asked what communication he has had with the Ministry and NZTA about transport's role in reducing emissions. He answers with what the incoming-Minister briefings covered, which touches the topic but describes documents sent to him rather than the communication he had. Half the question is met.
question: What communication, if any, has he had with the Ministry of Transport and Waka Kotahi NZ Transport Agency regarding the role transport will play in reducing climate emissions?
statement: The Ministry of Transport and the New Zealand Transport Agency’s briefings to the incoming Minister covered key transport issues, including the role transport can play in the reduction of emissions.

explanation: Asked whether he instructed officials that transport will have little to no role in emissions reduction. No yes or no is given; he substitutes a different instruction (stopping the VKT work programme) which is relevant and implies an answer, then pivots to a reports-versus-infrastructure line. Circles the core without stating it.
question: Has he instructed the leadership of Waka Kotahi and the Ministry of Transport that transport will have little to no role in emissions reduction this term?
statement: I have written to the New Zealand Transport Agency to ask them to stop work on the prior Government’s vehicle kilometres travelled reduction work programme, which was simply writing reports rather than actually delivering infrastructure. Our approach will be actually delivering infrastructure, while the last Government was all about writing reports.

explanation: Two-part question: committed to the transport emissions targets, and how. 'Yes' answers the first part completely and directly. The 'how' gets only a note that advice says the first budget period is expected to be met, which is not a method. One half answered squarely, one half not.
question: Is he committed to achieving the transport emissions reductions targets, and, if so, how does he intend to achieve them?
statement: Yes, and I have received advice that transport is expected to achieve the first emissions budget period, 2022-2025.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts the Climate Change Commission's advice that immediate decisive action is needed, and if not why not. Neither accepts nor rejects it — says he has asked for advice on the report, then pivots to infrastructure-versus-reports talking points. The operative yes/no is never reached.
question: Does he accept the advice from the Climate Change Commission on transport emissions that the need for decisive Government action is immediate, and, if not, why not?
statement: I’ve asked for advice in relation to the climate report which was released yesterday, but I would say that our Government’s approach will be actually on building infrastructure rather than wasting hundreds of millions of dollars on endless reports, business cases, and actually not delivering anything, which was the past Government’s approach.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts the advice on upfront-cost barriers and whether he will implement a price incentive to replace the Clean Car Discount. 'No' answers the operative half unambiguously and he states what he will do instead. Blunt and dismissive, but a direct refusal is not a dodge; only the 'do you accept the advice' half is left implicit.
question: Does he accept the advice from the Climate Change Commission, released yesterday, in relation to low-emissions and zero-emissions vehicles, that “Supports to address the upfront cost barrier are especially important.”, and, if so, will he implement a price incentive for zero-emissions vehicles to replace the Clean Car Discount?
statement: No, we’re not going to continue to waste hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayers’ money to subsidise wealthy New Zealanders to be able to buy electric vehicles they can already purchase. Instead, we will invest in supercharging the electric vehicle charging network, which is a priority under this Government.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on jobseeker support. Reports the November MSD numbers — 182,340 recipients, up over 11,000 this year. The partisan comparison at the end is Focus, not evasion; the question was answered.
question: What reports has she seen on the jobseeker support benefit?
statement: According to the latest benefit numbers released by the Ministry of Social Development in November, there are currently 182,340 people on jobseeker support. This is an increase of over 11,000 people this year alone. In total, there were 61,614 more people receiving the jobseeker support benefit during Labour’s time in Government.

explanation: Asked for the total emissions reductions resulting from doubling renewable energy. He never gives a figure for that policy; he offers investment certainty, NPS work, an admission that the advice is still being obtained, and an unrelated BCG figure for economy-wide electrification in 2050. The concession that the advice is yet to come is a partial engagement, but the number asked for is not reached.
question: What are the total emissions reductions that will result from the doubling of renewable energy that was promised by the Prime Minister?
statement: Our commitment to doubling renewable energy will provide businesses with the investment certainty they need to make the switch to renewable energy, which will ensure emissions reductions. We have started work on updating the national policy statement for renewable electricity generation to make it easier to consent renewable energy. Part of that work will include getting that advice. I note that the Boston Consulting Group study The Future is Electric found that electrification could reduce annual carbon emissions by 22 million tonnes in 2050.

explanation: Asked what percentage of NZ greenhouse gas emissions come from the energy sector. Despite garbled phrasing, he supplies a figure — 'about 50 percent' — which squarely responds to the question. Whether the number is accurate is a Veracity matter, not a dodge.
question: What percentage of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions come from the energy sector?
statement: Now, what percentage of our energies is about 50 percent.

explanation: Asked to confirm two specific percentages (5.7% electricity generation, 40.6% energy sector). He effectively confirms — 'those are very good statistics and I'm sure she's correct' — which is a yes, though delivered at one remove rather than as his own confirmation, so slightly short of complete.
question: Can he confirm that the percentage of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions that come from the electricity generation is 5.7 percent, whereas the percentage of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions that come from the energy sector is 40.6 percent?
statement: Well, as the member rightly knows, those are very good statistics and I’m sure she’s correct.

explanation: Asked what OTHER policies address the 40.6% of emissions from the energy sector beyond electricity generation. He restates the same renewable-electricity NPS policy and argues it extends to transport and industry. That is an attempt to bridge to the question's premise rather than a naming of other policies, so the core of the question is largely sidestepped.
question: What other policies, then, does the Government have to reduce the 40.6 percent of New Zealand’s emissions that come from the energy sector, given that the Minister’s own officials advise that only 5.7 percent of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions come from electricity generation and the Climate Commission advised complementary measures to the emissions trading scheme (ETS) are required to shift industrial and process heat from carbon sources?
statement: Well, as the member will know—being a former Minister for energy—the electrification of our economy is going to require a significant amount of more electricity to be generated. That is why we have a policy of updating the national policy statement for renewable electricity generation to double renewable energy in New Zealand. And it’s not just for electricity supply now, but for all of the other activities that it’s going to be required—in transport and industry and energy, all of those other factors—and I thought the member might know that.

explanation: Asked what policies would shift industrial and process heat from fossil fuels to electrification. He names one — the emissions trading scheme — and identifies it as the key tool. A named instrument is a real answer; the attack on the previous government is padding, and the absence of detail is a Specificity matter, not evasion.
question: OK. What policies does the Government have to move industrial and process heat coming from fossil fuel sources to electrification?
statement: Well, this Government will use the emissions trading scheme, which is a critically important tool—and a critically important market-based tool—to help move New Zealand and bend the curve of emissions down. That Government over there wanted to subsidise wealthy businesses with profitable businesses using taxpayers’ money. We’ll use the emissions training scheme as the key tool.

explanation: A two-part narrow question: confirm the ETS price would need to exceed $200/tonne, and say what that does to electricity and petrol bills. He confirms nothing about the price, says nothing about bills, and pivots to doubling renewables and withdrawing subsidies. Both halves are avoided.
question: Can he confirm that for the ETS alone to shift industrial process heat to electrification, the price needs to be in excess of $200 a tonne, and can he advise New Zealanders what it will do to their electricity and petrol bills at that price?
statement: What I can confirm is this Government is going to have the tools and the policies to double renewable energy in New Zealand so we can electrify our economy. What I will say, though, to the businesses—the profitable businesses—which were receiving subsidies under that Government, they will not be receiving them under this Government. They should be making those investments themselves. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what recent reports he has seen on infrastructure investment decision-making. He names the Auditor-General's report on the shovel-ready and NZ Upgrade programmes and states its findings. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent reports has he seen on decision-making processes for Government infrastructure investments?
statement: I’ve seen a deeply concerning report from the Auditor-General into the shovel-ready and New Zealand Upgrade programmes. The Auditor-General found that Ministers did not have enough information to be sure that decisions supported value for money, and that the Government carried out due diligence after announcements were made. He also has reported to Parliament that as part of putting together the report, some of the so-called shovel-ready projects were not actually shovel-ready at all. Like many who have read this report, I was shocked to learn of these findings and see how badly the schemes were managed.

explanation: Asked whether Ministers were given advice raising concerns about the proposed plans. He answers 'Yes, they were indeed' and specifies the value-for-money, cost-overrun and Ministry of Health warnings. Direct and complete.
question: Were Ministers provided advice which raised concerns about their proposed plans for these Government infrastructure investments?
statement: Yes, they were indeed. The Auditor-General found that at several points, officials advised Ministers of risks to value for money for both the Upgrade programme and the shovel-ready programme. What’s more, Ministers were explicitly advised there was a real risk of cost overruns as well as delays. The Ministry of Health advised a number of health projects were not ready to be announced, yet despite all these warnings, Ministers pushed on with the announcements anyway.

explanation: Asked whether the Auditor-General raised additional concerns about ministerial decision-making. He answers 'Unfortunately, he did' and enumerates them (unscoped projects, missing business cases, Auckland Transport). Direct and complete.
question: Did the Auditor-General raise any additional concerns about ministerial decision-making?
statement: Unfortunately, he did. He found that Ministers made their decision to progress some of these projects despite the projects not being fully scoped or even planned. Business cases were not always available or up to date. In the case of Auckland Transport, announcements were made about Auckland Transport projects and Auckland Transport were not even asked for the business cases or for information about the projects they were responsible for. It is clear Ministers were too worried about hitting “send” on press releases rather than ensuring value for money for taxpayers.

explanation: Asked whether the Auditor-General raised specific concerns about transparency and integrity. He answers 'Yes, he did' and quotes the relevant passages. Direct and complete.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Did the Auditor-General raise any specific concerns about transparency and integrity as part of these infrastructure investments?
statement: Yes, he did, and this is very worrying—the House should listen to this. The Auditor-General stated, and I quote, “A lack of transparency in documentation about how and why decision-makers made significant decisions can … create the perception that processes lack integrity.” To quote the report itself, “During the process of longlisting, shortlisting, and Ministers making final decisions … many changes were made to the list of projects under consideration. There were frequent discussions between Ministers’ offices and officials during this time, and some projects were added from outside of the Infrastructure Reference Group process … My staff found it difficult to determine how or why these changes were made.”

explanation: Asked whether stakeholders were well consulted. He gives an explicit 'the answer is no' and supports it with the Infrastructure Commission and Auckland Transport learning via media. The closing coalition-government material is surplus but the question itself is squarely answered.
question: Were the stakeholders to these impacted projects well consulted as part of this process?
statement: Well, it won’t surprise the House to learn that the answer is no. In one of the most surprising findings of this deeply troubling report, key stakeholders like the Infrastructure Commission and Auckland Transport had to find out about the New Zealand Upgrade programme through media coverage—and if that isn’t reflective of the priorities of the last Government, I’m not sure what is. We are a coalition Government who knows that high-quality infrastructure boosts our economy and benefits all New Zealanders. We are committed to multi-generational infrastructure up and down this country, but we also know that proper process and respect for taxpayer money should be at the forefront of our decisions, and it will be under this coalition Government.

explanation: Two-part question: what the 4 December Cabinet advice estimated the emissions impact of discontinuing the clean car discount to be, and whether it was inconsistent with other Ministry of Transport analysis. The second part is answered flatly ('consistent with all the advice'); the first — the estimated impact — is replaced with a claim that the sector remains on target, which is not the estimate sought.
question: What did the official advice provided to Cabinet on 4 December estimate would be the impact of discontinuation of the clean car discount on New Zealand’s carbon dioxide emissions, and were there any inconsistencies between this advice and other analysis provided by the Ministry of Transport?
statement: The advice to Cabinet noted that the transport sector remains on target to achieve its contribution to the first emissions reduction plan. Advice provided to Cabinet is consistent with all the advice provided to me by the Ministry of Transport.

explanation: Asked what labour market conditions have been over two years. Upston states them directly — 'one of the tightest in recent memory, with employers everywhere crying out for staff' — then adds blame and a jobseeker figure. The question's core is engaged and answered; the partisan add-on is a Focus matter, not a dodge.
question: What have the labour market conditions been over the past two years?
statement: Over the past two years, the employment market has been one of the tightest in recent memory, with employers everywhere crying out for staff. However, this opportunity was squandered by the previous Government, and, unfortunately, this has led to an increase of over 60,000 people on the jobseeker benefit.

explanation: Asked when jobseeker support is expected to peak. Answer names the date ('keep rising until January 2025') and the forecast level (197,400). Squarely on the question and complete.
question: When is the jobseeker support benefit expected to peak?
statement: The tough economic conditions that our Government has inherited mean that the number of people on the jobseeker benefit is expected to keep rising until January 2025. The latest figures, released in the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, forecast the number will increase to 197,400 New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Opens with 'Yes' and then elaborates. The elaboration is campaign material, but the question was a yes/no and it got an unambiguous yes.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially the very strong actions the Government has taken to ensure that we’re focused on improving the lives of New Zealanders by rebuilding the economy, and particularly with news out this morning that the previous Government’s economic mismanagement saw the economy shrink in three of the past four quarters—three of the past four quarters. In particular, I stand by our action to stop the significant risk posed to taxpayers by cost escalations on KiwiRail’s ferry project; also our action to focus the Reserve Bank on fighting inflation, which is, of course, pain and suffering to all New Zealanders; of course, our action to actually change the speed limit rules to allow New Zealanders to get to where they need to go faster and safer. I have to tell you this is a Government that is elected with a mandate for change and an unashamed and unflinching focus on cleaning up the mess left by that member’s Government to get our country back on track and realise all the great potential that sits in this country.

explanation: Two legs: does he stand by suspending regulatory impact statements, and does he think suspending advice is based on data and evidence. The first leg is answered plainly ('very comfortable'); the second is only glanced at via the 'won't add value' rationale rather than addressed as a question about evidence-based decision-making. Partial.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s decision to suspend regulatory impact statements for proposals in his 100-day plan, and does he feel that suspending advice on the impact of his decisions is based on data and evidence?
statement: We are very comfortable with suspending regulatory impact statements because we don’t think they’ll add value for decisions that we’re repealing legislation on.

explanation: Two legs: does he agree with his own quote about being straight with New Zealanders, and if so, what's changed. 'Very much' answers the first leg directly. The 'what's changed' leg — the point of the question — is never reached; he pivots to GDP and the New Zealand Upgrade Programme. Half the question engaged, the substantive half avoided.
question: Does he agree with the National Party leader, Christopher Luxon, that “I can tell you we’re going to be straight with the New Zealand people, tell it as it is—the good, the bad and the ugly”; if so, what’s changed?
statement: Very much—we’re going to be very straight up with the New Zealand people, and what they have heard today is that that was a previous Government that led three of the last four quarters’ declining economic growth. What they’ve heard today, and we’ve been straight up with the New Zealand people about, is a $15 billion New Zealand Upgrade project with an Auditor-General’s report that says it was appallingly managed—appallingly managed. What you’re going to see is a Government that is very focused on making sure taxpayers are not treated like bottomless ATM machines, that we get return for their money.

explanation: A narrow factual question with a binary answer: before or after the leak. The response says nothing about timing or the leak at all, switching to why repealing fair pay agreements is good policy. A specific question with a checkable answer, entirely sidestepped — the worst kind of dodge.
question: Did he suspend regulatory impact statements before or after the regulatory impact statement for repealing fair pay agreements was leaked?
statement: We are determined to make sure, through repealing the fair pay awards legislation, that we can actually make it easier for people to hire workers, not harder.

explanation: A disjunctive question: does he stand by the urgency process, or does he agree with Bishop's 'disgraceful way to make important law'. He explicitly picks and answers the first leg — 'In answer to the first leg of the question, yes' — which resolves the disjunction, though he pointedly leaves the Bishop quote untouched. Terse and unhelpful, but it engages rather than evades.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s decision to repeal fair pay agreements, the Reserve Bank dual mandate, and the Clean Car Discount under urgency with no select committee process or regulatory impact statement, or does he agree with Chris Bishop that “This is a disgraceful way to make important law.”?
statement: In answer to the first leg of the question, yes.

explanation: Loaded and multi-choice, but it asks a real question with a real core: why were regulatory impact statements suspended. The answer gives an electoral mandate for the policies, not a reason for suspending the advice, and declines to touch any of the four options. Talking points where a reason was asked for.
question: Has he suspended receiving regulatory impact statements because (a) he doesn’t like what they say, (b) he’s going to ignore them anyway, (c) he knows they’ll leak, or (d) all of the above?
statement: We went to an election, we had a campaign, we made very clear what we were going to do, and we’re going to do it.

explanation: Asked what reports she has received on the state of the economy. She names them — the Statistics New Zealand GDP release, the confirmed recession — and engages the question head-on. The swipe at the member for Remutaka is a Civility/Focus matter and does not displace the answer.
question: What reports has she received on the state of the New Zealand economy?
statement: New Zealand is experiencing difficult economic conditions. Statistics New Zealand confirmed today that GDP declined in the third quarter of this year, a third decline in just the last year. It’s also been confirmed that New Zealand did experience a recession at the end of the last year and the beginning of this year. I’ve also seen reports from the member for Remutaka, who claimed last week that we “inherited an economy that is growing faster than many economists had predicted” and that the economy was “never in recession”, but I have seen no evidence to confirm those reports.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on the outlook from here. The answer is mostly about the inherited position (deficits, an economy in decline) rather than the forward view; the only outlook content is 'won't be achieved overnight' and 'a massive task'. It brushes the question without landing on it.
question: What reports has she seen on the outlook from here?
statement: After six years of economic mismanagement, turning the New Zealand economy around won’t be achieved overnight. Our Government has inherited big fiscal deficits, a large current account deficit, an economy in decline, and a labour market on the skids. Rebuilding the economy will be a massive task, which is why we are moving fast and getting quick wins as part of our 100-day plan.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on GDP per capita. The answer is exactly that: the day's figures, no growth since early 2021, four consecutive backwards quarters, plus a comparison to the GFC. Direct and complete.
question: What reports has she seen on GDP per capita?
statement: Today’s GDP per capita figures show on a per person basis the New Zealand economy has gone nowhere since the start of 2021 and has gone backwards four quarters in a row. The last time GDP per capita continued to slide for at least that long was during the global financial crisis. Kiwis knew they were going backwards under Labour. Today’s data is just a confirmation of the challenge they face.

explanation: Asked what steps the Government is taking. Four are named — backing the Reserve Bank on inflation, eliminating wasteful spending, clearing blockages, reducing business costs. They are broad rather than itemised, but vagueness is Specificity; as a response to 'what steps', it addresses the question asked.
question: What steps is the Government taking to turn economic conditions around?
statement: The Government is taking urgent steps to rebuild the economy in the interests of all New Zealanders. We’re supporting the Reserve Bank in their fight to beat inflation, because after years of rampant spending, this Government understands that monetary policy needs mates. We’re eliminating wasteful spending, ensuring taxpayers’ money is spent well, and we’re clearing out the blockages in the economy and reducing costs on business so we can chart a course back to growth, investment, and opportunity.

explanation: Asked two things: will he attend Waitangi 2024, and what preparations have begun. He answers the first explicitly ("ana" — yes) and engages the second (planning under way across Government, calendar finalised shortly). The second half is thin on detail, but thinness is Specificity; both limbs of the question were reached.
question: Te Arawhiti: Is he planning on attending Waitangi 2024; if so, what preparations, if any, has started on behalf of the Government?
statement: E te Māngai o te Whare. In response to the first pātai, and in my Wanganui dialect, ana. In response to the second pātai, planning is well under way across Government, and the calendar will be finalised shortly.

explanation: Asked whether a named list of repeals will enhance the Māori-Crown relationship, and whether he and the PM will front up at Waitangi. He never says yes or no on the relationship — the core of the question — and pivots to anticipating a warm welcome. Only the attendance limb is glancingly implied, so a small amount of credit, not none.
question: Does the Minister think that repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, disestablishing the Māori Health Authority, repealing smoke-free legislation, removing Māori names of Government departments, repealing fair pay agreements, and introducing a Treaty Principles Bill will enhance the Māori-Crown relationship, and, if so, will he and the Prime Minister be prepared to front up and discuss this at Waitangi 2024?
statement: We look forward to a warm and cordial welcome by our Tai Tokerau whanaunga, where we will discuss many important—of national significance.

explanation: Asked whether he will ensure the PM attends. He responds that the PM's office and officials are making arrangements to come, but that the decision rests with the PM and their office. That is a direct answer to whether he can guarantee it — an honest "not mine to ensure, but it is being arranged" rather than a dodge.
question: Will the Minister ensure that the Prime Minister will be there?
statement: E mārama ana au e whaiwhai haere ana te tari o te Pirīmia me ōna āpiha kia whakarite mai te haere ki Waitangi, heoi anō, kei te Pirīmia me tōna tari te mana whiriwhiri.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with his own earlier statement about sharing power with Māori, and whether he will commit to discussing it at Waitangi. He answers neither limb, substituting a general claim about National-led Governments engaging with Māori and the Waikato River settlement. Neither agreement nor commitment is ever stated.
question: Does the Minister agree with the statement of a young Tama Potaka when he said central government and local government need to consider sharing power with Māori instead of hoping that Māori entitlements and demands will be satisfied with policies that, effectively, mainstream Māori into Pākehā society; if so, will he commit to discussing this at Waitangi 2024?
statement: National-led Governments have linked in and engaged with many Māori over time, including in Waikato, with the Waikato River settlement. That is a great reflection of working together.

explanation: Put as a statement rather than a question ("The Minister did not address whether he agreed..."), but it functions as a re-ask of the previous supplementary and draws a substantive reply rather than a Speaker's ruling, so I scored it rather than omitting it. The reply — pride in the number of Māori Cabinet ministers — does not touch the question of agreement at all.
question: The Minister did not address whether he agreed with the young Tama Potaka.
statement: I’m absolutely proud of there being the highest number of Māori members in the Cabinet that there ever has been.

explanation: Asked what steps she has taken to improve labour market flexibility. She names one directly: her bill repealing the fair pay agreements system passed its third reading today. The framing is promotional, but a specific step taken is squarely supplied.
question: What steps has she taken to improve flexibility in the labour market?
statement: Today I am pleased to announce that my bill to repeal the fair pay agreements system has passed its third reading in Parliament. By achieving this milestone, we are in the final stages of bringing about real change for businesses and workers that helps New Zealanders get ahead.

explanation: Asked how repealing fair pay agreements will benefit workers. She gives an actual causal answer — certainty for business, investment and growth, more and better jobs, productivity raising wages. It is contestable and heavy on talking points, but the question of mechanism was engaged, and whether the reasoning holds up is Rigor, not this attribute.
question: How will repealing fair pay agreements and improving labour market flexibility benefit workers?
statement: This Government wants to see higher wages and better conditions for workers, especially during a cost of living crisis. Repealing the fair pay agreements legislation gives businesses the certainty they need to invest and grow, creating more and better jobs. By repealing the fair pay agreements, we will have improved labour market flexibility, which has been a pillar for New Zealand’s economic success for the past three decades. This Government has removed these one-size-fits-all agreements, which have no place in an economy where innovation is key. The best and most sustainable way to increase the wages of workers and to achieve lower prices for consumers is to improve productivity and to reduce the regulations that hold businesses back.

explanation: Asked what message she has for those who opposed the repeal. The answer is that message: that the opposition was scaremongering, and that no worker (including the named groups) can be worse off because no agreement was ever finalised. Directly responsive to what was asked.
question: What message would the Minister have for those who opposed the repeal of fair pay agreements?
statement: There has been a lot of scaremongering around the repeal of the fair pay agreements. I do wish to clarify a few points. First, I want to make it clear that no worker will have their wages cut or be worse off, because no fair pay agreements were finalised. Secondly, Māori, Pasifika, young people, and women will not be harmed or made worse off by the repeal of the fair pay agreements, because no fair pay agreement was finalised. The minimum standards in employment law remain, including the minimum wage, health and safety law, and leave entitlements.

explanation: Asked what other plans she has to increase labour market flexibility. She names the next one precisely: a bill next week expanding access to 90-day trials to all employers. Direct and complete.
question: What other plans does the Minister have to increase flexibility in the labour market?
statement: Next week, I will be introducing a bill to the House to expand access to 90-day trials to employers. Whether a business has two or 200 employees, bringing on any new employee costs time, it costs money, and it is in the best interests of any business to find the right fit. Expanding access to 90-day trials will give workers access to new opportunities they would otherwise not have. They allow employers to employ someone who might not tick all the boxes, but a person who might have the right attitude. By delivering on this Government’s commitment to extend the availability of 90-day trials, this Government will give all businesses greater confidence to employ more Kiwis.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on primary sector export revenue forecasts. He names the report (Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries, released today) and its forecast — $57.7b falling to $54.3b to June 2024. Fully responsive.
question: What reports has he seen on the export revenue forecasts for the primary sector?
statement: The Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries report released today shows a forecast dip in export revenue. Exports hit a high of $57.7 billion this year but are forecast to drop to $54.3 billion in the year to June 2024. It’s been a tough few years for New Zealand’s food and fibre businesses. However, it’s still a strong result against a backdrop of very challenging times. The Government will be working with the primary sector to ensure they are productive and remain world’s best-practice food and fibre producers.

explanation: Asked what else the Government is doing to help farmers. He supplies concrete lines of action: targeting a doubling of export value over 10 years and work on non-tariff barriers costing ~$8b a year. Some padding, but the question is answered.
question: What else is this coalition Government doing to help farmers?
statement: We will be supporting our primary sector businesses through targeting a doubling of the value of exports over 10 years. We think we should measure ourselves more on how much we export and sell overseas by value, not just by volume. Non-tariff barriers cost New Zealand agriculture around $8 billion each year. We’re committed to working to resolve barriers that are preventing New Zealand’s world-class primary industry sectors from doing business with the world. We understand that part of growing value is getting more return for what we already export, and I’m delighted to work closely with the sector to see what else we should do to supercharge the support to businesses. We’re determined to the break down barriers that are such a drag on their product productivity and growth.

explanation: Asked what benefit the primary sector can expect from that work. Most of the answer recites the sector's existing contribution (export share, GDP, employment) rather than expected benefits, and closes on an attack on the previous Government. Partial credit only because "costs down, better rules not more regulations" does gesture at a prospective benefit; the core of the question is largely stepped around.
question: What benefit can our primary sector expect to see from this work?
statement: The Government is going to champion the significant achievements the primary sector has made at home and abroad. The sector accounts are 81.9 percent of New Zealand’s goods exports to the year June 2023. Food and fibre export revenue growth has exceeded the non-primary industries for seven of the last 10 years. Adding indirect effects, we estimate that the food and fibre sector contributions to GDP increased by 16 percent. They’re responsible for 13 percent of employment. When rural New Zealand does well, all of New Zealand does well, and when the rural economy is strong, New Zealand’s economy is strong. The coalition Government trusts farmers. We’ll be working to get costs down; better rules, not more regulations; supercharge the rural economy so farmers can be proud of what they do. We have stopped Labour’s war against farmers.

explanation: Asked WHY he won't release the draft RIS. "It was a draft document" is terse and unhelpful, but it is a reason, and it is squarely a response to the 'why' — the draft status is the ground for withholding. Engaged, not dodged; marked down only because the core is answered so thinly it barely closes the loop. Its lack of detail is Specificity, not Forthrightness.
question: Why won’t he release the draft regulatory impact statement that was prepared by the Ministry of Transport on the impacts of carbon emissions before we vote on the legislation today?
statement: It was a draft document.

explanation: Same 'why won't you release it' question. Gives the reason (draft) AND states what is being done about release — proactive release has been requested of officials. That addresses both the withholding and, implicitly, the timing. Short of 1.0 because the question specified 'before we vote today' and he never says whether release will come before the vote.
question: Why won’t he release the draft document so we can see what the draft advice was before we vote on the legislation?
statement: It was a draft document. I’ve asked Ministry of Transport officials to prepare the proactive release of this Cabinet paper and regulatory impact statement.

explanation: Asked WHY he won't release the emissions advice before today's vote. He instead reports the CONTENT of the advice (transport sector on target). That answers a different question than the one asked; the 'as I've said' gestures back at the earlier draft reason, which is the only thing keeping this above zero. Whether the on-target claim is true is Veracity and does not move this.
question: Why won’t the Minister release the advice produced by the Ministry of Transport telling us what the impacts of the repeal of this legislation will be on New Zealand’s carbon dioxide emissions before we vote on the legislation in the House today?
statement: Well, as I’ve said, the advice to Cabinet noted that the transport sector remains on target to achieve its contribution to the first emissions budget.

explanation: Asked whether the withheld official advice CONCURS with the Concept Consulting findings. He disputes the member's assertion — a partial engagement with the underlying claim — but never says anything about what the advice contains, then pivots to Ford's EV pricing. The core (does the advice agree?) is left untouched.
question: Does the official advice that the Minister is refusing to release before we vote on the legislation concur with the report released by Concept Consulting for Drive Electric that the reduced uptake of electric vehicles, because of the repeal of the Clean Car Discount, will see New Zealand spending over a billion more on imported oil from overseas and mean that we will import 100,000 fewer electric vehicles in the period from now to 2030, thereby increasing carbon emissions relative to if the scheme stayed in place?
