In one case, a caregiver had paid for counselling that was desperately needed for a child—they paid for it themselves so they didn’t have to wait months and months—only to be told that this would have to stop as it had not been approved by Oranga Tamariki. I am also focused on cracking down on serious youth offending and on deterring young people from a life of crime and equipping them with the tools they need to turn their lives around.

explanation: Asked what feedback the sector has given on her priorities. She does answer — 'overwhelmingly positive', and iwi and Māori strategic partners responded positively — but opens with a list of places visited and detours into a swipe at the media and the Opposition before reaching it.
question: What feedback has the Minister received from the sector about these priorities?
statement: I have been travelling all around the country visiting Oranga Tamariki site offices and residences and meeting with strategic partners, including Auckland, Lower Hutt, Hawke’s Bay, Christchurch, Whangārei, Kaitāia, and Palmerston North. The feedback I have received about my vision and priorities for Oranga Tamariki has been overwhelmingly positive. When people have heard about this Government’s plans beyond what they may get from the media or from some members on the other side of the House, people appreciate and understand that Oranga Tamariki needs to get back to its core purpose of keeping young people safe and making sure they are cared and loved for. Iwi and Māori strategic partners have also responded positively when I have met with them and talked about continuing to work in partnership with Oranga Tamariki. This matches with my vision to devolve decision making and accountability back to the communities who are best placed to know what their young people need to live a safe, fulfilling life.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has received from children. Gives a specific instance: a young person at a youth justice residence enthusiastic about the military academies. On point, answering about children rather than substituting the sector feedback from the prior question.
question: What feedback has the Minister received from children about her priorities?
statement: Just last week, I visited a youth justice residence. I had received feedback about a young person there who had heard about our plans to establish military academies. He was very excited about this and said he would be very excited to take part in something like this. This is just one example of the positive feedback I’ve received, not just from social workers and iwi and Māori partners but also from children and young people. They are the ultimate reason I am here, in this privileged position: to be able to make their lives better so they can not just survive but thrive.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen about the cellphone policy. Cites multiple media reports and quotes one — a Wellington student on concentrating better. Squarely what was asked for.
question: What reports has she seen about the introduction of the policy to remove the distraction of cellphones from school?
statement: There have now been multiple media reports of the positive changes seen in schools since this policy was introduced. A Wellington student was quoted as saying that by having her phone off and in her bag, she was already paying more attention to school notices and concentrating better in lessons without her phone distracting her. This is exactly why this Government has removed the distraction of phones from schools.

explanation: Asked what feedback she had seen from principals; she reports two principals' feedback (Otago, Central Hawke's Bay). Directly and completely on the question asked. That it is a friendly question and the feedback is one-sided goes to Focus/Veracity, not here.
question: What feedback has the Minister seen from principals about the policy to remove the distraction of cellphones from schools?
statement: An Otago principal said that their teachers support the ban, as the removal of phones helps students engage better with their learning. And a principal from Central Hawke’s Bay also reported that students have responded well to the change in policy and are engaging and interacting more face to face.

explanation: Asked for public feedback; she gives public correspondence and a quoted parent from The Northern Advocate. Squarely the thing asked for.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. What feedback has the Minister seen from the public about the cellphone policy?
statement: I have received multiple correspondence from the public supporting the policy, saying that it’s about time and it’s a no-brainer, and, in an interview with The Northern Advocate, a Kaitāia mother said, “They’re there to learn. As a parent, I think it’s really good. They’ve actually got to interact more.”

explanation: Asked for other feedback; she supplies a Wellington dean's observations before adding a summing-up line of advocacy. The question is fully answered first; the closing pitch does not displace it.
question: What other feedback has the Minister received about the cellphone policy?
statement: A Wellington year 9 dean said she has seen no cellphones in class at all or walking around during school on duty. She noticed students engaging in game playing, like cards, and said that the librarians have been thrilled with the number of books students are taking out and have noticed students are reading in the library much more than last year. We are pleased with the implementation of the Government’s policy, and it’s been warmly welcomed by principals and teachers and is having a positive impact on students.

explanation: A closed confidence question answered 'Yes.' One word, complete, no evasion. Unhelpfulness is not a dodge.
question: Does he have confidence that the proposed approach to fast-track consenting will protect due process for the consideration of environmental effects?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked to rule something out; answers 'No.' A blunt refusal to rule it out is a direct, complete answer to the question put.
question: Will he rule out including any projects that have already been considered and declined on environmental grounds, such as the Hananui open ocean salmon farm?
statement: No.

explanation: The question was whether he was aware of the panel's finding; he answers it plainly ('I haven't read the decision') and then pivots to a general defence of conditions on projects. Core engaged, then talked past — partial credit for the pivot, not for vagueness.
question: Is he aware that when the panel declined the Hananui salmon farm, they found that there was a risk that even a small change in their population could have “irreversible and catastrophic effects” on the survival of critically endangered hoiho / yellow-eyed penguin in the area?
statement: I haven’t read the decision of the panel in relation to that particular project, but what I would say in a more general sense is that it is possible to have environmental conditions proposed on projects that mitigate and remedy the environmental effects of a variety of projects, including, for example, renewable energy projects that will help decarbonise the economy and grow the economy at the same time, and I would have thought the member would be in favour of such projects.

explanation: Asked whether he would take responsibility in a specified scenario; he labels it hypothetical and moves to process and timetable for the bill. He never says yes or no, and the 'hypothetical' framing is a brush-off rather than a plain refusal to answer.
question: If a project that has been previously declined on environmental grounds by an independent panel is authorised by this legislation and then leads to the functional extinction of a species like the hoiho / yellow-eyed penguin, will that Minister take responsibility?
statement: Well, the member is asking hypothetical questions. I just haven’t ruled out the premise of his original question. Decisions around the precise pathway for projects that will be referred are the subject of discussions right now, as we work through the process of getting the bill ready for introduction within the hundred days. And once the bill is ready to go and it’s gone through Cabinet and presented to the House, he’ll have a good chance to have a look at it, as will a select committee.

explanation: Asked to confirm a quoted remark; he says 'Yes, in the sense that...' and explains the two referral pathways. Confirmed with a qualification that is itself responsive; the added COVID-legislation comparison is surplus, not a dodge.
question: Can he confirm the Hon Shane Jones’ comments to an energy breakfast this morning that under the new regime, “Permits will be granted by politicians,”?
statement: Yes, in the sense that Ministers will be able to refer projects. There will be two pathways. One will be there will be a range of projects listed in the legislation, and then the second pathway will be, upon application to the Government, Ministers will be able to refer projects to an expert consenting panel. This is not new, by the way, because the COVID fast-track legislation also listed projects in the legislation and also set up a process for Ministers to refer projects to an expert consenting panel. So this is not particularly new; this is the existing law. So, in that sense, Ministers will be able to refer projects to panels who will then set the conditions upon which those projects will take place.

explanation: Two asks — seek assurances on conflict-of-interest disclosure, and commit that no listed project is tied to donors. Neither is answered: responsibility is shifted to the Prime Minister and the donor commitment is not addressed at all.
question: Will he now seek assurances that all Ministers are fully meeting their conflict of interest disclosure obligations under the Cabinet Manual, as he described yesterday in relation to decision making on potential projects; and, if so, will he also commit to ensuring that no listed projects are connected to people or companies that have made substantial donations to coalition parties?
statement: Well, matters for the Cabinet Manual, as the member well knows, are matters for the Prime Minister, but I think I would be right in saying that the Prime Minister expects all Ministers to uphold the principles and the text of the Cabinet Manual.

explanation: 'Does he stand by his statement?' answered 'I do stand by my statement', with elaboration after. Direct and complete; the added policy material does not dilute the answer given.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “What we’re really focused on is delivering outcomes and working with communities—Iwi communities, Māori communities and others—to make the changes to the inequalities we see on a daily basis”?
statement: Āna, I do stand by my statement, and our Government deeply cares about inequalities of opportunity that many communities in New Zealand are facing, particularly Māori communities, around housing, health, and education. That’s why our view is that the devolution of resources is generally better, to achieve equalities of opportunity such as the recent funding announcement by the superlative Minita Matua tākuta Shane Reti to help with child immunisation rates.

explanation: Asked what he is doing for whānau and whenua Māori owners in those regions; he names ministerial visits and mainstream plus kaupapa Māori funding. The question is engaged and actions are named, though it stops short of what is being done for whenua Māori specifically. Its thinness is a Specificity matter; the partial score is for not fully reaching the region-and-whenua core.
question: What is the Minister doing to support whānau and owners of whenua Māori in Tairāwhiti and Kahungunu one year after Cyclone Gabrielle?
statement: Over the last couple of months, Ministers including myself have visited Te Tairāwhiti and throughout Te Matau-a-Māui to understand some of the challenges that those whānau are facing. There’s also some provision of funding, both in mainstream and kaupapa Māori pathway funding, to assist with those communities, and we continue to look at how we can use that.

explanation: A narrow two-part factual question — was he advised beforehand, and did he relay concern. He answers neither, offering only that Ministers are in regular communication. A precise question avoided this squarely is a serious failure.
question: Was he advised prior to the recent $63 million boost funding for Hawke’s Bay and Tairāwhiti announced by Minister Mitchell, and if so, did he relay any concern regarding the lack of any support for Māori and whenua Māori?
statement: Ministers including myself are in regular communications with one another about the efforts made to try and help those people who have gone through difficult weather events over the last year or so. As a result, I continue to work with and engage with those Ministers responsible for the kaupapa Māori pathway to support Māori land that has been—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on building costs. He names the source (Stats NZ inflation data) and gives its content (41 percent rise since 2019). Squarely answered.
question: What reports has he seen on the cost of building in New Zealand?
statement: I thank the member for the question. The latest inflation data from Stats New Zealand shows that the price of building a new house has increased by 41 percent as compared with 2019 prices. This massive increase in the cost of building over the last four years has made housing even more unaffordable for Kiwi families.

explanation: Asked whether building costs are higher or lower than other countries. He states plainly that they are generally higher and gives the Australian comparison. The sentence is garbled about which country the 50 percent applies to, but that is clarity/rigour, not evasion — the question was answered.
question: Are building costs higher or lower in New Zealand than other countries?
statement: Analysis shows that building costs are generally higher in New Zealand than in comparable overseas jurisdictions. In Australia, for example, the cost of building a stand-alone house is some 50—five-zero—percent higher in New Zealand. Clearly, this is not good enough, and we’re working to resolve that problem.

explanation: Asked what impact high construction costs have on New Zealanders. After a self-congratulatory aside, he lists impacts: harder first-home purchase, higher mortgage repayments, higher rents, more social housing demand. Directly on the question.
question: What impact do high construction costs have on New Zealanders?
statement: Another great question—I couldn’t have written it better myself. Not only do high building costs make it harder for families trying to purchase their first home but they also have far-reaching economic and social consequences, such as higher mortgage repayment costs, higher rents, and increased demand for social housing.

explanation: Asked whether the Government has plans to change this. Answers "Yes" explicitly and then names two: the granny-flat amendment to the Building Act and exploring a consent opt-out with long-term insurance. Complete.
question: Does the Government have any plans to change this?
statement: Yes, we certainly do—we certainly do. I’m pleased to inform all members that we most certainly do have plans in this regard. For example, our coalition agreement with our New Zealand First friends sets out that this Government will amend the Building Act to make it easier to build granny flats—smaller structures, up to 60 square metres—and, in addition, our coalition agreement with the ACT Party also states that the Government will explore allowing builders to opt out of needing a building consent, provided they have long-term insurance for the building work. So, again, we will explore that.

explanation: Asked what else the Government is doing. He answers with a further action — approving more building products to increase competition and lower material costs. Broad question, on-point response.
question: What else is the Government doing?
statement: Another good question. The Government is focused on slowing the rise of construction costs so that we can make it more affordable to build a home. Kiwis pay too much for building materials, for example, and ensuring more high-quality building products are approved for use in building sites across the country will increase competition, lower building material costs, and support our resilience in the event of supply chain disruption.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the statement, and what actions has he taken. He answers "yes" to the first with the fuller quote, and to the second names creating the mental health Minister role with responsibility for the ring-fenced funding. Both parts engaged; the second is thin as an action but is offered as one, and thinness is Specificity.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “under this Government, mental health will be a priority”; if so, what actions, if any, has he taken to make mental health a priority?
statement: In answer to the first part of the member’s question, yes, in the context of the full quote of establishing a mental health strategy within the Pae Ora legislation for the first time, where I said, “Why not have a strategy on X or Y or Z? Yeah, I agree … it comes down to priorities, and under this Government, mental health will be a priority—that’s why we’re legislating it as one of the strategies under the Pae Ora health reforms.” In answer to the second part: establishing the role of New Zealand’s first mental health Minister, which now includes the responsibility of the almost $2.5 billion of ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding.

explanation: Asked to confirm that supporting a former member's bill is the only real action in 80 days. He neither confirms nor denies; he cites workforce work with professional bodies and promises announcements "in due course". That implicitly contests the word "only", so it is not a pure pivot, but the yes/no is never reached.
question: Is the Minister’s answer that in 80 days, the only real action he has taken as the Minister for Mental Health is to support his former member’s bill?
statement: I’ve enjoyed working with mental health professional bodies to grow the pipeline of mental health professionals, and I look forward to making announcements about this in due course.

explanation: Asked two narrow things: has he set a wait-time target, and can he give lower South Islanders an assurance. He answers neither, refusing to "be lectured" and attacking the previous government's record via the Auditor-General report. A clean dodge of a specific question.
question: Has he set a target to reduce mental health specialist wait times, and can he assure lower South Islanders they won’t have to wait longer for mental health specialist services than those elsewhere?
statement: Well, I won’t be lectured by that member when, today, we published a report in the House from the Auditor-General that says more young people are waiting longer for specialist services when they came into Government—shame on them.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his advocacy statement and what projects he has advocated for in the first hundred days. He ignores the stand-by part and, where projects were asked for, offers only an ongoing cross-Government process with announcements "in due course" — gestures at the area without naming anything advocated.
question: Does he stand by his statement that being Minister for Mental Health is “also a role of advocacy where I can go to those Ministers and say, you know, ‘What are we doing in this space and can we do better?’ ”, and, if so, what projects has he advocated for in the Government’s first hundred days?
statement: I’ve been working with other Government departments to develop a cross-Government approach to mental health, and I look forward to making announcements about that cross-Government approach in due course.

explanation: Two parts: reports on the link between mental health and financial stress, and whether he asked the social development Minister to reverse the benefit indexation decision. He answers with a report on mental health services that is not about the financial-stress link — responsive in form, off the actual subject — and the benefit question is not touched at all.
question: What recent reports has he seen on the link between mental health and financial stress, and has he asked the Minister for social development to reverse her decision to index benefits in line with inflation, which will push more New Zealanders into poverty?
statement: Well, yeah, the report I have seen, sadly, is the one published today in the House at 2 o’clock from the Auditor-General, after I wrote to him in April 2022 because of the promised funding the last Government announced yet it made no material difference. The report findings are clear: things have got worse, there’s no workforce plan, and, basically, they failed in mental health.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on the fiscal response to COVID-19. She identifies the report (Secretary to the Treasury's Economics Forum speech) and quotes its findings. Directly answered.
question: What recent reports has she seen on New Zealand’s economic and fiscal response to the COVID-19 pandemic?
statement: I’ve seen a report delivered to the New Zealand Economics Forum by the Secretary to the Treasury in which she highlighted that effective fiscal stimulus in response to crises should be “temporary, targeted and timely”. She goes on to note in the speech that the bigger concern is the trajectory of spending and that, in New Zealand, operating expenditure has continued to exceed revenue on an ongoing basis, stating, “This was the case even through a period in which the economy was overheating and unemployment was at generational lows—normally a time when we expect fiscal policy to be at its tightest.”

explanation: Asked what impact fiscal policy has had on interest rates. She answers the causal question head-on, quoting Treasury's assessment that fiscal policy contributed to higher rates. The follow-on about mortgages and small businesses is colour, not a pivot.
question: What impact has Government fiscal policy had on interest rates?
statement: Well, the same speech goes on to note that fiscal policy has had an impact on inflation, with the Secretary to the Treasury noting, “Our assessment is that fiscal policy has contributed to interest rates being higher than otherwise.” And, of course, that has an impact on every single family with a mortgage, every person with a credit card debt, every small business trying to repay a loan. High interest rates hurt, and what we know is that loose fiscal policy has contributed to them being higher than they might otherwise have been.

explanation: Asked why structural deficits should concern New Zealanders. Gives three direct reasons (cost-shifting to future generations, reduced capacity for public services, debt-servicing costs) plus a figure. Squarely answers the question asked.
question: Why should New Zealanders be concerned about structural fiscal deficits facing the Government?
statement: Well, structural deficits ultimately have a fiscal impact, which means that they shift costs to future generations, they ultimately reduce Government’s ability to provide public services, and they add considerably to debt-servicing costs. This year, the Government is forecast to spend $8.8 billion just servicing New Zealand’s debt. That sum is more than the Government spent combined on secondary schools, police, and early childhood education last year.

explanation: Asked what action the Government is taking on spending. Names the fiscal sustainability programme and the baseline savings exercise targeting ~$1.5b p.a. The closing aside about a cartoon is off-topic but comes after the question has already been answered.
question: What action is the Government taking to bring spending back under control?
statement: The coalition Government has started an ongoing fiscal sustainability programme to embed a culture of responsible spending across Government. The first step of this programme is an initial baseline savings exercise for Government agencies, designed to find about $1.5 billion per annum in savings to deliver on our policy commitments and to fund critical cost pressures. This situation brings to mind a cartoon that the Hon Grant Robertson once shared with me in question time; I would like to congratulate him on his foresight and wish him all the best for his future.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the Government's statements and policies. "Yes, in the context they were given" is a direct affirmative with a qualifier — answered, not dodged.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and policies?
statement: Yes, in the context they were given.

explanation: Asked what he will do to protect the takatāpui community from discrimination. He rejects the premise about the trans-athlete policy (legitimate engagement with part of the question) but never addresses what, if anything, he will do to protect the community; "balance fairness and inclusion" restates a position rather than answering.
question: What will he do to protect the takatāpui community from increased discrimination as a result of his Government’s policies, such as their policy to ban transgender athletes from competing in publicly funded sports?
statement: That is not our policy. What we want to make sure is that sports balance fairness and inclusion.

explanation: Asked what will replace the Māori Health Authority to address health inequities. He does name a mechanism — working with local iwi to design solutions, in place of a central agency — so the question is engaged, but the core "what solutions" is answered only at the level of approach. Partial.
question: What solutions will be put in place to address Māori health inequities after his Government dismantles the Māori Health Authority?
statement: Well, we want to work hard to improve Māori health outcomes. We’re going to work with local iwi, in the spirit of localism and devolution, to design solutions to improve outcomes locally. We just don’t believe that the way to go about that is building a massive health central bureaucracy here in Wellington.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government is taking to push for a ceasefire. States one specific action (calling for a cessation of hostilities since October). Brief, but it is a responsive answer to what was asked.
question: What actions is his Government taking to push for a sustainable ceasefire in Palestine?
statement: We’ve been calling for a cessation of hostilities since October last year.

explanation: Asked how bad things must get before the Government cuts ties and sanctions Israel. He rejects the premise and says plainly that sanctions/cutting ties are not something the Government is interested in — a direct refusal of the proposed course, which answers the operative question rather than evading it.
question: How bad is the Prime Minister willing to allow things to get before his Government cuts diplomatic ties and sanctions Israel for war crimes against Palestinian civilians?
statement: I reject the assertion in that question. That is not something we’re interested in.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. "Yes, I do," followed by elaboration. Complete and direct.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, I do. In particular, I stand by my statement from the weekend where I said, “I haven’t met a single young Kiwi whose ambition, creativity, and spark would be best served by a life on a benefit.” That is why I’m very proud to stand by this Government’s actions to address the legacy of welfare dependency that the previous Labour Government was all too happy to grow. And, before I take any more questions, can I just acknowledge Grant Robertson’s announcement of his retirement today. I thank him for his service in this place in Parliament, and also in Government, and wish him well for the future.

explanation: Asked a narrow factual question — is the $669.5m savings figure correct? He says it depends on forecasts and pivots to the previous Government's inflation record and why indexation was changed. The yes/no is never given; a specific question, squarely avoided.
question: Is Louise Upston correct that changes to benefit indexation will save the Government $669.5 million through to 2027-28?
statement: Well, it depends very strongly on what the forecast projections are going forward. As you know, in your previous Government, there was a period where, actually, inflation was running well ahead of wage increases. As a result, that’s why we’ve moved it back to make sure we index benefits to inflation so that people are protected from their purchasing power being eroded by inflation.

explanation: The same $669.5m figure put to him again. Again "it all depends on the forecast" and then a pivot to why indexing to inflation is the right policy. The figure is never confirmed or denied on a second, pointed asking.
question: Thank you. Is Louise Upston correct that changes to benefit indexation will save the Government $669.5 million through to 2027-28?
statement: It all depends on the forecast going forward. But what I’d say to you is indexing benefits going forward, indexing benefits to inflation—that’s the right way to go.

explanation: Asked whether Cabinet was made aware of a $2,300 annual loss for supported living payment recipients, and if not why not. The answer talks only about inflation indexation being the right approach; neither the "was Cabinet aware" nor the "why not" limb is touched.
question: Was Cabinet made aware of the fact that a disabled Kiwi on the supported living payment would lose $2,300 a year by 2028 thanks to changes to benefit indexations; if not, why not?
statement: We’re making sure that benefits are adjusted by the amount of inflation so that the purchasing power of those beneficiaries is not eroded. That is the way we’re managing it going forward, and we think that’s the right approach.

explanation: Same question repeated. He disputes the premise ("they're not losing anything"), which is a small step towards engagement, but still never says whether Cabinet was informed — the actual question asked.
question: Was Cabinet made aware of the fact that a disabled Kiwi on the supported living payment would lose $2,300 a year by 2028 thanks to changes to benefit indexations; if not, why not?
statement: They’re not losing anything. We’re adjusting benefits and indexing benefits to inflation so that the purchasing power of a beneficiary maintains, irrespective of what happens with inflation.

explanation: Asked how the Government books a $669.5m saving if no one loses anything. The reply only re-asserts the first half ("they're not losing anything, we're adjusting by inflation") and never touches where the saving comes from — the core of a narrow arithmetic question is left untouched.
question: If people aren’t going to lose anything because of their changes to benefit indexations, how is the Government saving $669.5 million?
statement: They’re not losing anything, because we’re adjusting benefits by the amount of inflation.

explanation: Asked why he said at his press conference that a cancer patient could be forced to work 10 hours a week. The reply talks about jobseeker obligations, case-by-case assessment and supporting people into work, but never addresses why he made that statement. It stays in the topic without reaching the question.
question: Why did he state at his press conference yesterday that someone undergoing cancer treatment could be forced to work 10 hours a week?
statement: What I’d say to you is we are determined to make sure that people who are on a jobseeker benefit are upholding their obligations. There is a case by case basis. There will be valid reasons why people may or may not meet their obligations. But people who are on a health ticket under the jobseeker benefit actually also want to work, in many cases. We are supporting people into work.

explanation: Asked for the total estimated cost of restoring mortgage interest deductibility including backdating. "That information will be available in the Budget in May" is a plain refusal-to-supply-now rather than a pivot: it engages the question squarely and says what will happen. Unhelpful but not a dodge; short of 1.0 because it neither gives the figure nor says whether an estimate exists.
question: What’s the total estimated cost of the coalition agreement to restore mortgage interest deductibility for rental properties, including the backdating that they have agreed to?
statement: That information will be available in the Budget in May.

explanation: Asked what the Government's first financial decisions say about its priorities. The reply immediately switches to what the previous Government did, recites benefit-numbers statistics, and closes with a personal jab at the deputy leader of the Labour Party. The question is never engaged.
question: What does it say about his Government’s priorities that their first major financial decisions involve backdating tax breaks for landlords, increasing Government revenue from people smoking, and cutting benefits for the lowest-income New Zealanders?
statement: Well, I’ll tell you what we’re not going to do: we’re not going to do what that Government did, which was to increase the number of people on the jobseeker benefit by 70,000 people—increased it by 58 percent, took the number of sanctions and obligations down by 57 percent. We care about young people on a benefit. We want to get people from welfare into work. On that basis, that would exclude the deputy leader of the Labour Party from running for the leader of the Labour Party one day down the road.

explanation: Asked what benefits New Zealanders can expect from the pseudoephedrine bill. The reply names the benefit directly — access to cold and flu treatment that works rather than a placebo — before adding general Government framing. Question engaged and answered.
question: What benefits, if any, can New Zealanders expect to see from the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill?
statement: New Zealanders can indeed expect great benefits from the legalisation of pseudoephedrine cough and cold treatments. The most obvious is that, when people get sick, they will be able to get stuff that works, not what is currently available, which many people regard as being little better than a placebo. In addition to that, it shows we have a Government that, when a law doesn’t work, actually gets rid of it. It shows we have a Government that is prepared to try and make life better and easier for New Zealanders rather than constantly coming up with obstructions and objections.

explanation: Asked why the Government thinks the law needs changing. The reply states the reason directly: the law aimed to stop gang meth supply and failed, with P price down and volume up. A complete answer to the question asked.
question: Why does the Government think this law needs to be changed?
statement: The law was put in place with the intention of stopping gangs supplying methamphetamine; unfortunately, the law did not succeed. The evidence for that is that, since pseudoephedrine cough and cold medicine has been denied from New Zealanders through an effective ban, the price of P has actually gone down, the availability has gone up, and the volume consumed has gone up. The law simply has not worked, and, therefore, we’re getting rid of a law that doesn’t work, so that life can be better and easier for New Zealanders, including getting better cough and cold medication.

explanation: Asked whether safeguards on sale and supply will be kept. "Yes, indeed" followed by exactly which restrictions remain (class C reclassification, import/storage/possession limits, pharmacist-only sale). Direct and complete.
question: Will the Government be keeping in place safeguards for the sale and supply of pseudoephedrine?
statement: Yes, indeed. The law change is a very simple one. It is changing pseudoephedrine from being a class B drug to a class C drug. There will still be significant restrictions around the importation, storage, and possession of pseudoephedrine within New Zealand. There will also be a change in the medicine’s regulations so that pseudoephedrine goes from being a prescription-only drug to a restricted pharmaceutical. That means that, while you will not need a prescription from a GP, you will have to buy it directly from a pharmacist. These restrictions are designed to make sure that there are not negative spillovers from giving everyday New Zealanders the convenience of getting some decent cough and cold meds.

explanation: Asked when pseudoephedrine will be back on shelves. The reply gives the dependencies, states the official advice that full availability may not come until 2025, and says they are pushing for this winter. It reaches the question and answers it as squarely as a timing question can be answered, without an unconditional date.
question: When will pseudoephedrine be back on the shelves in New Zealand, providing effective treatments for Kiwis?
statement: Well, the exact timing depends on two things: first, the Parliament changing the law, and the Government making sure that the regulations are in place and Medsafe is prepared to give the approvals to the products—their approvals have lapsed since they were, effectively, banned over a decade ago; second, it will depend on pharmaceutical companies making applications to Medsafe and being ready to sell the pharmaceuticals that people need by this winter, when the most demand is in place. We’ve had official advice that that may not take place—the full availability—until 2025, but I can tell you that Medsafe, myself, and everyone on the Government side of this operation are doing everything we can to make sure that good cold and flu meds are on the shelves by this winter, when people need them.

explanation: Asked what reports she has received on child poverty impacts of indexing to inflation. The reply names the publicly available report and its finding — up to 7,000 more children on two measures — before adding the Government's counter-framing. The question is answered before the pivot.
question: What reports has she received, if any, advising her of the possible child poverty impacts of indexing benefits to inflation rather than wages?
statement: The publicly available report states that preliminary modelling shows indexing benefits to inflation in isolation as a policy, in the absence of any other Government policy interventions before 2028, may increase the number of children captured by the before-housing-cost moving line measure and after-housing-cost fixed line measures of child poverty by 7,000. The Government will, however, make other policy interventions before 2028, such as delivering tax relief and stopping petrol tax hikes, that will significantly help families with children in modest to low income households, who we know have been doing it particularly tough during the cost of living crisis.

explanation: Asked whether the reports have updated the forecast child poverty figures. "We haven't received updated child poverty figures" is a direct no to a yes/no question; the following material about a collection of policies is padding after the answer, not instead of it.
question: Given that net average wage growth for the purposes of annual general adjustments is now due to outstrip inflation this year, have the reports she’s received updated the forecast child poverty figures?
statement: We haven’t received updated child poverty figures. Every policy and consideration that we will be making in the months ahead will, but, as I have answered in my primary question, it is not one policy intervention on its own that will support us as a country to lift more children out of poverty; it will be a collection of policies that our Government is committed to taking.

explanation: Asked whether any of her reports highlight the disproportionate impact on disabled children. The reply says it would be no surprise that some groups are at higher risk and that the Government will take this into consideration, but never says whether the reports address it. It circles the subject without answering the question put.
question: Do any of her reports highlight the disproportionate child poverty impact on disabled children, given that disabled children or children living with a disabled adult are more likely to live in households where an adult is on benefit?
statement: I don’t think it would be a surprise to this House that there are certain groups where there is a higher risk of children living in poverty, and our Government is focused on those, whether it is Pasifika, Māori, and disabled, that we will of course take into consideration with any policies that we are putting in place to reduce child poverty.

explanation: Asked whether any reports highlight the disproportionate poverty impact on sole mothers and their children. "Absolutely" answers the yes/no question before the reply turns to attacking the previous Government. Marked down slightly because the affirmative may be agreeing with the premise rather than confirming the reports, leaving the answer thinner than a clean yes.
question: Do any of the reports she has received highlight the disproportionate poverty impact on sole mothers and their children, given that 80 percent of sole parent benefit recipients are women?
statement: Absolutely, and what this Government won’t do is allow the number of children in benefit-dependent homes to grow by 45,000 like that Government did.

explanation: Asked whether the MSD figure (5,000 children out of poverty from wage-indexing) is correct, and why she is pursuing changes that raise child poverty. The answer confirms neither, denies neither, and never engages the causal charge — it pivots straight to commitment language and cost-of-living/tax talking points. A narrow factual yes/no was available and was left untouched.
question: Are Ministry of Social Development figures correct that indexing benefits to wage inflation had moved over 5,000 children out of poverty, and, if yes, why is she hell-bent on making changes that increase rather than decrease the number of New Zealand children living in poverty?
statement: This side of the House is really committed to reducing the number of children living in child poverty. We know there’s not one silver bullet; it’s not one policy on its own that will make a difference. Addressing the cost of living crisis, providing tax relief, and getting on top of ridiculous tax hikes for petrol are very practical things that will help low and middle income families as well as those who are receiving benefits.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on breast screening access. He names the announcement precisely — first steps to extend free screening to women aged 70–74. Squarely answered; the foundation thank-you is a tail, not a dodge.
question: What recent announcements has the Minister made in relation to improving access to breast cancer screening for New Zealand women?
statement: Last week, the Government took its first steps towards delivering on our promise to extend free breast cancer screening to women aged 70 to 74. Breast cancer is the most common cancer amongst New Zealand women, and that’s why the Government prioritised this crucial initiative in our 100-day plan. I’d like to thank the Breast Cancer Foundation for their continued advocacy in this area.

explanation: Asked for the next steps in the extension. He gives next steps: grow the workforce, build supporting infrastructure, Health NZ readying the system for extra screening and treatment demand. The steps are broad rather than sequenced or dated, but breadth is a Specificity matter — the question of 'what comes next' is engaged head-on.
question: What are the next steps for the extension of breast cancer screening services?
statement: There is a lot of work to be done in terms of preparation. We need to grow our workforce and support them with the infrastructure required to expand our screening services. Health New Zealand is also working through a process to ready the whole health system for the additional women that will take up screening each year and for those who will, sadly, require treatment. We’re ambitious to advance this as soon as possible.

explanation: Asked what benefits he anticipates. He answers with anticipated benefits directly: two to three extra mammograms on average, ~120,000 additional eligible women, earlier detection, and a lives-saved estimate. Complete on the terms asked.
question: What benefits does he anticipate from extending the age for breast cancer screening?
statement: I’m advised that, once the programme is fully implemented, the extension will mean that women will become eligible for two to three extra mammograms, on average. This means around 120,000 additional women will be eligible for screening every two years. Catching more cancers early means better treatment outcomes. The extension could potentially save 65 lives per year; however, on our current settings, that relates to 22 lives saved. That’s not just 22 women but also their family, friends, and loved ones who won’t have to endure the emotional impact of cancer.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has received. He reports feedback received, including a named, quoted response from the Breast Cancer Foundation chair plus public and professional support. Direct and responsive.
question: What feedback has the Minister received on this announcement?
statement: I have received lots of feedback regarding this announcement. The chair of the Breast Cancer Foundation, Justine Smyth, has said, “We’ve been asking for the breast cancer screening age to be raised to 74 for the past eight years, so it’s fantastic to see work is finally underway on this.” This support has been echoed by many members of the public and health professionals.

explanation: A two-part question: stand by the 'workforce crisis' statement, and accept Te Whatu Ora's July 2023 shortage estimates as accurate. Part one gets an unambiguous yes. Part two gets a yes, but attached to a passage about workforce pressure rather than to the accuracy of the shortage estimates themselves — an affirmative that slides slightly off the core it was asked about. Answered, with a hedge on the second half.
question: Does he stand by his statement that there is a health “workforce crisis” and does he accept the estimates of health workforce shortages Te Whatu Ora published in July 2023 as an accurate reflection of the shortages at the time they were published?
statement: Yes, I stand by my statement that there is a workforce crisis, as I’ve said repeatedly for some time. To the second part of the question, yes, particularly where the document states, “[There] has been pressure on our health workforce which needs to lift; we have heard this message clearly from our workforce.” I have heard that message also.

explanation: Asked what urgent actions he will take that will have an impact this year. He offers something with in-year effect — the incoming GP registrar cohort — but it is a pre-existing intake he is pleased about, not an action he will take. The question's core (what will *you* do, urgently) is approached and then left. Partial engagement, not a clean pivot.
question: What urgent actions will he take to address workforce shortages that will have an impact this year?
statement: We’re very encouraged by the increase in general practice registrars who actually start either this week or next week, which, I understand, is the largest cohort of general practice registrars, which will then feed through into the general practice network, so I’m very pleased with that.

explanation: Asked whether he would like to congratulate the Government that implemented that. 'Yes. Thank you.' — one word plus a courtesy, and the question is fully disposed of. A trap question answered squarely is still answered.
question: Would he like to congratulate the Government that implemented that?
statement: Yes. Thank you.

explanation: Asked a narrow factual yes/no: did he go his first two months without a workforce briefing from Te Whatu Ora? He neither confirms nor denies, saying he would need to check dates — which is a partial, legitimate deferral — then immediately moves to priority-setting talking points instead of undertaking to confirm. The core fact stays unaddressed; some credit for not pretending to know.
question: Is it correct that, after gaining office, talking up a crisis, he did not receive a briefing on the health workforce from Te Whatu Ora in his first two months in office?
statement: I would need to see the exact dates that I’ve received briefings, but I’ve made it very clear to Health New Zealand and to the Ministry of Health that the health workforce is our number one priority, and they clearly have that in their headlights.

explanation: Asked how many jobseekers get jobs as a direct result of mandatory seminars. He answers the question that was asked: MSD cannot provide that measure. That is a real, complete answer to a 'how many' question — the figure does not exist — and refusals and nil-returns count as forthright. The subsequent pivot to check-in announcements is padding after the answer, so it costs only a little.
question: How many jobseeker beneficiaries, if any, get jobs as a direct result of attending work seminars they are required to attend to avoid benefit sanctions?
statement: The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) cannot provide this exact measure, as the member was told by the previous Government. This new coalition Government is not content to allow New Zealanders to languish on the jobseeker benefit without proactive support or checking in on their progress to find work. We want them to experience the independence and opportunities that come from work. That’s why yesterday I announced that 2,500 additional people will receive greater face-to-face support through regular check-ins.

explanation: Asked how she can be confident seminars work when outcomes are not measured. She contests the premise directly — outcomes are measured but not accumulated across beneficiaries — and supplies the basis for her confidence with a seminar where 64 of 82 attendees secured interviews. Whether that basis is sound is a Rigor question; as a response, it meets the question.
question: How can she be confident, then, that these work seminars support people into employment when MSD does not measure any outcomes after attending seminars and people risk losing their benefit if they do not engage with them?
statement: It’s not that the outcomes aren’t measured; it’s just that they are not accumulated across every single beneficiary. So if we look at a recent seminar in the top of the South Island, 82 Kiwi job seekers turned up to that seminar; 64 secured interviews. Had they not been there, they would not have taken that very important step of securing an interview that, for some, would have led to employment.

explanation: Asked precisely which outcomes are measured. The reply opens by restating the collation point rather than naming any measure, then supplies anecdotes about Te Pūkenga training links and an employer who hired 220 people. Illustrations of things that happen at seminars are offered where a list of measured outcomes was requested — it circles the question without landing on it.
question: What outcomes, then, are measured as a direct result of people attending those work seminars?
statement: The outcome is just that it’s not collated as an entire figure. What we do know—and a recent one that I attended in Christchurch showed a number of people who are getting additional support, whether it is being connected to training opportunities, in this instance through Te Pūkenga—employers come along to those work seminars to find staff and find employees. In another business that I visited on the same day in Christchurch, they have employed over 220 people off the jobseeker benefit, who they find at these work seminars.

explanation: Asked how she can be confident sanctions lead to sustainable employment given MSD does not track whether seminar attendees get jobs. She describes what the seminars offer (interview technique, CVs, employer contacts, licences) and asserts "we are doing everything we can", but never engages the core of the question — the absence of outcome data. It gestures at a basis for confidence without addressing why confidence is warranted without evidence.
question: How can she be confident, then, that increasing benefit sanctions will support people into secure, sustainable employment when MSD does not know if any of the people attending work seminars to avoid sanctions, actually, as a direct result, get a job, not just an interview?
statement: When job seekers come into the range of seminars that are available—formal and informal—in Work and Income offices up and down this country, they are getting assistance with interview techniques, they are getting connected to employers, they are getting assistance with CVs. For some of them, it’s getting them on the path to getting a driver’s licence. These are practical things that address the barriers that some people face on their path to employment. There is not one thing that will support, unfortunately, the 190,000 that are on the jobseeker benefit currently. We are doing everything we can. Yesterday was a first important step in the reset of the welfare system to support more people off welfare and into work, and obligations and consequences are part of that.

explanation: Two-armed question: committed to positive Māori health outcomes, and if so which outcomes. He answers the first arm with a plain "yes" and engages the second by pointing to the outcomes in Pae 2 of the Whakamaua action plan and naming diabetes. Both arms reached; the second is answered by reference rather than enumeration, which is a gap in coverage rather than a dodge.
question: Is he committed to delivering positive Māori health outcomes; if so, what are those outcomes?
statement: To the first arm of the question, yes, and to the second arm, I am committed to lifting health outcomes for Māori, and this will be informed by those outcomes identified in Pae 2 in the Whakamaua action plan, including outcomes such as diabetes.

explanation: Asked for a specific percentage uplift in Māori immunisation rates since the $50m announcement and what change he expects over the next 12 months. He answers neither: he describes the new immunisation IT system and weekly monitoring, and defers the targets to a future announcement. A narrow factual question and a forward-looking one, both pivoted away from.
question: What percentage of uplifts in Māori immunisation rates has the Minister seen following his $50 million announcement on 21 December last year, and what changes does he expect to see in the 12 months to follow?
statement: The immunisation project that we announced before Christmas was simultaneously with an announcement around the new immunisation information technology programme, which will give us much more granular and real-time levels of immunisation rates. As a consequence of that, I’ve been asked for weekly monitoring of those new rates, and we’ll be setting what those objectives will be when we announce our priorities and Government policy statement.

explanation: Asked whether he will meaningfully consider the Tribunal's recommendations and whether he will meet the claimants. He invokes sub judice — which would be a legitimate direct refusal if left there — but then substitutes a generality about taking on board "all discussions from all parties" that commits to neither arm. The meeting-the-claimants arm is left entirely unaddressed.
question: Will the Minister meaningfully consider the recommendations following the Waitangi Tribunal’s urgent inquiry into the dissolution of Te Aka Whai Ora, and will he commit to meeting with the claimants?
statement: Those discussions with the Waitangi Tribunal are sub judice, but, in a very general sense, I would say that we’ll take on board all discussions and all dialogue from all parties.

explanation: Asked what consultation he had undertaken, listing five categories of group. He answers the question squarely: he says he has had discussions with Māori, iwi leaders and providers, by Zoom and in person, and about what a post-dissolution future looks like. Community and urban Māori organisations go unmentioned, so coverage is incomplete, but the question was engaged rather than dodged (the thinness of detail is Specificity, not this attribute).
question: What consultation, if any, has the Minister undertaken with hauora providers, iwi, hapū, community organisations, and urban Māori organisations regarding the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority?
statement: I have had discussions in a general sense with Māori, with iwi leaders, and with providers, both on Zoom and in person, and we have discussed what a different future might look like with the dissolution of the Māori Health Authority.

explanation: Asked what actions she has taken to reduce welfare dependency. After a framing preamble she names concrete actions: formalising with MSD that existing obligations and sanctions be applied, and work check-ins from June. The question is directly and near-completely answered.
question: What actions, if any, has she taken to date that aim to reduce welfare dependency in New Zealand?
statement: Our coalition Government is not prepared to accept the welfare system we inherited, where work-ready job seekers were forecast to spend, on average, 13 years on a benefit, and teenagers could become trapped on welfare for 24 years of their working lives. We have higher aspirations for the prospects of New Zealanders. So, last Friday, I formalised with the Ministry of Social Development our Government’s view that all existing obligations and sanctions are applied. If job seekers fail to attend job interviews, complete their pre-employment tasks, or don’t take available work, consequences should be applied. Yesterday, I also announced that, from June, new work check-ins will begin for job seekers so that we can better support people to shift into work.

explanation: Asked why the Government has taken these first steps. She gives the reasoning directly — that work improves financial, social and health outcomes, that jobseeker numbers rose while sanctions fell, and that the system should motivate movement into work. Squarely responsive to the "why".
question: Why has the Government taken these first steps to reset the welfare system?
statement: New Zealanders are better off in work, if they can work. Work improves financial independence, as well as their social and health outcomes. Unfortunately, the number of people on the jobseeker benefit has increased by 70,000 during the past six years, while sanctions applied for breaches of work obligations decreased by 35,259. Sanctions are one part of the tool kit in the welfare system. Because people are better off in work, we want to ensure that the welfare system motivates people to move into available jobs.

explanation: Asked what the purpose of the work check-ins is. The response opens with a statistic about long-duration jobseeker numbers and is cut off mid-sentence ("Vicious cycles—") before any statement of purpose. On the record as given, the question is not reached; note the answer is truncated, so this score reflects an incomplete transcript rather than a confirmed dodge.
question: What is the purpose of the work check-ins the Minister has announced as the first steps of the Government’s reset of the welfare system?
statement: The number of people who have spent longer than one year on the jobseeker benefit has increased by 40,000 by September 2017. Vicious cycles—

explanation: Asked who will be required to attend the check-ins. She answers immediately: people who have been on jobseeker for six months. Slight slippage between "required" and "eligible" leaves a small edge of the question untouched, but the core is answered before she moves to rationale.
question: Who will be required to attend the work check-ins?
statement: People who have been on the jobseeker benefit for six months will be eligible for the proactive work check-ins. The longer people spend on benefits the harder it is to re-enter the workforce. We will not stand by and see New Zealanders’ potential go to waste. By intervening earlier, we can reduce the risk of people becoming dependent on welfare long term and help them experience the independence and opportunities that work provides.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his quoted statement. "Yes." One word, direct, complete.
question: Does he stand by his statement in relation to the Government’s proposed approach to fast-track consenting that “This is not new, by the way, because the COVID fast-track legislation also listed projects in the legislation and also set up a process for Ministers to refer projects to an expert consenting panel”?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked to confirm a specific factual difference from the COVID fast-track regime — that ultimate approval power will sit with Ministers rather than an expert panel. He neither confirms nor denies, deflecting to Cabinet not having settled final design parameters and to the bill's eventual release. A narrow, checkable question answered with process.
question: Can he confirm that a fundamental difference to the COVID-19 fast-track legislation is that, under the proposed new legislation, the ultimate power to approve listed projects will lie with Ministers rather than with an expert consenting panel?
statement: Well, final design parameters of the scheme are yet to be confirmed by Cabinet, and when the bill is ready for tabling and release, it will be done.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about Ministers holding fast-track approval power, framed with a critical quote. He says "No" — a direct and complete answer to the yes/no question — before attacking the quoted critic and pivoting to consenting timeframes. The attack does not reduce the score because the question itself was answered first (rudeness is Civility, not this attribute).
question: Is he concerned that granting Ministers the power to fast track consents for projects, including those that have previously been declined under the existing COVID legislation because of environmental risk, is, in the words of the CEO of the Environmental Defence Society, “a return to the use of unbridled executive power [that] we thought we’d left behind.”?
statement: No, and I’m not going to take lectures from Gary Taylor around what we should or shouldn’t do in this country. What I am concerned about in this country is that the time it’s taken to consent major infrastructure has doubled in the last five years, and we now spend, as a country—

explanation: Asked to confirm at least 59 projects are proposed; he directly confirms and goes further ("actually more than 59"). The added caveat that the precise list is for Cabinet does not displace the answer — the core of the question was engaged head-on.
question: Can he confirm that there are no fewer than 59 projects currently proposed for inclusion in the primary legislation?
statement: I think it’s actually more than 59, to be honest, because we are looking at a vast array of projects, and the precise list and exactly how those processes work with the process we’re setting up will be a decision for Cabinet, and it’s not too far away.

explanation: Asked squarely to rule out one named project. He neither rules it in nor out, deferring to "matters for Cabinet" — a process deflection, not a refusal ('I won't rule it out' would have scored high). A narrow yes/no question left untouched.
question: Will he rule out including the Te Kuha coal mine in the list of projects to be approved in the primary legislation?
statement: Well, decisions as to what projects will be included in the legislation are matters for Cabinet.

explanation: Asked what measures address conflicts of interest. He disputes the premise and defers to the unfinished design, but does gesture at a class of answer — Cabinet, parliamentary and electoral-law mechanisms. Categories where measures were asked for: it reaches toward the question without arriving.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Well, can the Minister, given the extraordinary powers that are being granted to Ministers to approve projects in the primary legislation, without the ability of an expert consenting panel to decline those projects—what measures is he taking to ensure that there are no conflicts of interest?
statement: Well, there are a variety of hypotheses in that question, which may or may not turn out to be true. The member will have to wait for the final design of the fast-track procedure, but, as I’ve said twice now in response to previous questions, there are a variety of mechanisms through the Cabinet process and the parliamentary process and electoral law processes designed to make sure that the type of implications that the member is making are handled appropriately.

explanation: "Does he stand by all his statements and actions?" — answered "Yes" outright. The subsequent attack on the previous Government is a Focus/Civility matter and does not reduce forthrightness; the question itself was fully answered.
question: Does he stand by all his statements and actions?
statement: Yes, including my statement that Auckland light rail was an irresponsible project that would have cost taxpayers up to $29.2 billion, and which the last Government failed to deliver a single metre of track on despite spending $228 million on this project. We’ve already scrapped this wasteful project, which is starting to address the last Government’s $200 billion funding gap in the transport budget.

explanation: Asked to reconcile his 11.5c-for-cycle-lanes characterisation with council data showing safety/active transport was only 16 percent of spend. The 16 percent figure and the contradiction are never addressed; he restates which categories are and are not being funded. Pivots to the message rather than the reconciliation asked for.
question: How does he reconcile his statement that he will not tax Aucklanders an additional 11.5c per litre on fuel to fund “more cycle lanes, redlight cameras, speed [bumps,] and lowering speed limits across the city” when Auckland Council information shows that, of the total funding available for regional fuel tax projects, safety and active transport initiatives represented just 16 percent of the regional fuel tax project spending?
statement: Well, it’s great to be talking about the regional fuel tax again in Parliament and how we’re going to lower the cost of living for Aucklanders, and I’d make the point to the member that there is a range of categories which we will not be funding, which includes bus priority improvements, bus infrastructure, the cycling and the speed bump category—which comes under road safety—and active transport, but we will be making sure that the remaining funding goes towards the projects which the mayor and I have discussed, which includes the Eastern Busway, the City Rail Link, and local roading improvements.

explanation: Asked why it is appropriate to rush the repeal under urgency with no replacement funding commitment. He does supply a reason — an election mandate — which engages the 'why' directly, but the funding-commitment half of the question is ignored. Half the question squarely answered.
question: Hmm. Why does the Minister consider it appropriate to rush through a bill under urgency to cancel the very revenue stream for a number of projects that Aucklanders are relying on—projects that Auckland Council have determined will meet the pressing needs that Auckland faces now and into the future—without any commitment to any additional new funding?
statement: Well, this might sound really, really radical, but we went to the election with a campaign promise, Aucklanders overwhelmingly voted for the coalition Government, and we’re delivering it.

explanation: Asked why he won't give certainty about additional funding. He does not explain the refusal, but implicitly answers by saying the other projects are not priorities and naming what the remaining money will fund. Partial engagement — the 'why won't you' is answered only by inference.
question: Why won’t the Minister give any certainty around what additional Government funding he will give to meet the clear shortfall that he has now left to Auckland Council to deliver on the very projects that they need?
statement: Well, we’ve said the other projects are not priorities for this Government, but we will ensure the remaining funding—over two years’ worth of regional fuel tax money taxed from Aucklanders, sitting in a bank account—will go towards delivering and completing the Eastern Busway, the City Rail Link trains and stabling, and local roading upgrades.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee on all stages of two named projects, or an explanation why not. He describes the money being allocated "to make sure they are being delivered" but never gives or withholds the guarantee, and never gives the 'why not'. Adjacent to the question rather than on it.
question: Will he guarantee, right here, right now, that all stages of the Eastern Busway and the Glenvar Road - East Coast Road adjustment projects will be completed, and, if not, why not?
statement: We are allocating the money—the remaining $340 million—plus the money that will be collected between now and 1 July to those projects to make sure they are being delivered.

explanation: Asked for updates on the repeal; gives the update — the hundred-day commitment and a Cabinet paper next week. Direct and complete for what was asked.
question: What updates can she provide, if any, on the repeal of the Therapeutic Products Act 2023?
statement: The Government has committed to begin work to repeal the Therapeutic Products Act 2023 within its first hundred days. I will be taking a paper to Cabinet next week seeking approval to progress this work.

explanation: Asked why she wants to repeal the Act; she states the reason (not fit for purpose) and elaborates on the regulatory failings. Whether those reasons are true or well-argued belongs to Veracity/Rigor, not here — the question was answered.
question: Why does the Minister want to repeal the Therapeutic Products Act?
statement: The Therapeutic Products Act was not fit for purpose. Appropriate regulation of medicines and medical devices is vital to ensure that these products do what they claim, are high quality, and that product approval pathways do not make them inaccessible or unaffordable. We also know that the current fragmented and outdated approach to the regulation of natural health products means that New Zealand is missing out on a significant proportion of opportunity to grow jobs and the economy. We need to develop a fit for purpose regulatory system for both.

explanation: A yes/no on adverse safety/health impact. She never says "no", but her answer is on-point: no changes are required before the 2026 commencement, and the advice was that implementing on time risked poor outcomes. The answer is discernible, just not stated plainly.
question: Will repealing the Therapeutic Products Act adversely impact medical safety or health outcomes of New Zealanders?
statement: The Act has a commencement date of 1 September 2026, so no changes are required from the health sector or industry. I have received advice that implementing the changes required to meet the commencement date would’ve been extremely challenging. This poses the real possibility of poor outcomes for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked how she intends to progress replacement work. The answer gives an aim (protect consumers without red tape) and one process element (listening to concerns while developing proposals), but no account of how the work proceeds. Partially answers the 'how'.
question: How does the Minister intend to progress work on replacing the Therapeutic Products Act?
statement: The Government has an opportunity to replace the Therapeutic Products Act with legislation that protects consumers without creating unnecessary red tape on industry. We know that communities, the health sector, and industry have concerns, and we intend to listen to those concerns as we develop new proposals.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Opens with "Yes, I do" — a direct, complete answer. The following partisan elaboration is off-topic padding but does not undercut the answer; the core was engaged squarely.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, I do. In particular, I stand by the Government’s action to conduct a ministerial inquiry into problems within the school property system—problems driven by a culture of mismanagement under the previous Government’s Ministers of Education, which have resulted in hundreds of projects facing huge escalations in both cost and scope. I also appreciate the member’s most recent supportive remarks correcting earlier comments from Jan Tinetti denying there was even a problem. This Government stands by all of its actions to address the shocking educational outcomes delivered by that member’s Government.

explanation: Asked to confirm a specific capex figure ($3.7m to $11.9m for Botany) and to name which projects were low value. Confirms nothing and names nothing; instead demands a "specific question" (the question was specific) and pivots to talking points about 350 misled schools. A narrow factual question wholly avoided.
question: Is it correct that school property capital expenditure for the Botany electorate increased from $3.7 million in 2017 to $11.9 million in 2022; if so, which of those projects does he believe were of low value?
statement: If the member would like to ask a specific question, I’m sure I can give him a proper answer for that. But what I would say to you is: 350 schools were misled by the previous Government: “We’re going to rescope your school; we’re going to redesign it.” Twenty before Christmas; 250, now 350; billions of dollars, lots of promises, no delivery, underfunded—a pattern of behaviour we’ve seen many, many times.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with a quoted statement. "Absolutely." One word, complete, unambiguous.
question: Does he agree with Christopher Luxon on the smoke-free law changes made by the previous Government: “We’ve been really supportive. Anything to remove, you know, smoking harm I think is a good thing.”?
statement: Absolutely.

explanation: Asked whether he had seen specific Treasury advice about $500m a year in extra revenue. Answers a different question — what he has seen about smoking rates. The yes/no about the advice is never reached.
question: When he stated, “We believe … we can lower smoking rates with the legislation that exists today.”, had he seen the Treasury advice that repealing the smoke-free environments Act changes will net the Government $500 million a year in extra revenue with more people smoking for longer?
statement: What I have seen is the results from the last year, which has seen daily smokers go from 8.6 percent to 6.8 percent just in the last 12 months, with the legislation that we’re going to readopt.

explanation: Asked whether the Associate Minister advised Cabinet of a $5b health cost and 12 deaths a day, and if not why not. Responds with the Minister's commitment and historical smoking trends; neither the yes/no nor the why-not is addressed at all.
question: Did his Associate Minister of Health advise Cabinet that the Ministry of Health estimated rolling back smoke-free law changes would cost the health system an estimated $5 billion and that smoking currently contributes to an average of 12 deaths per day in New Zealand; if not, why not?
statement: Our Associate Health Minister is very committed to lowering smoking rates. The smoking legislation that we’ve seen over the last decade has actually halved daily smoking in this country. We are very confident that this will continue to lower smoking rates across this country.

explanation: The same question about advice to Cabinet, repeated. Pivots entirely to the decision to readopt existing legislation. The question of what Cabinet was told is not engaged.
question: Did his Associate Minister of Health advise Cabinet that the Ministry of Health estimates that rolling back smoke-free law changes will cost the health system an estimated $5 billion and that smoking currently contributes to an average of 12 deaths per day in New Zealand; if not, why not?
statement: Our decision is very clear: we’re going to adopt the existing legislation—that previously existed just a month before the election—that has driven smoking rates down. Smoking rates are going to continue to fall under the existing legislation that we’re going to readopt.

explanation: Asked why the Associate Minister rejected proposals to stop tobacco sales near schools. Gestures at a reason — "Ministers take a range of advice" — which restates that a decision was made rather than giving the reason for it, then moves to programme talking points. Barely brushes the question.
question: Why did his Associate Minister reject proposals to stop tobacco being sold near schools?
statement: Well, because, as I heard Ayesha Verrall—Ministers take a range of advice on a range of topics, and she’s free to do that. We have a clear programme forward: we want to lower smoking rates across this country and we’re going to do it with the existing legislation.

explanation: Asked why the proposal to raise the purchase age to 25 was rejected, given contrary Ministry advice. "Ministers take a range of advice on a range of topics" is brief but supplies no reason and is not a plain refusal to answer either; the why is dodged. Scored slightly below b02-6 because nothing else in the reply touches the question.
question: Why did his Associate Minister of Health reject proposals to raise the purchase age of tobacco to 25, given the advice from the Ministry of Health: “there is strong evidence that starting smoking after 25 is uncommon.”
statement: Ministers take a range of advice on a range of topics.

explanation: Asked what recent cost-of-living reports she has seen. Cites Statistics New Zealand inflation data and characterises it. Genuinely responsive; a little diffuse at the end, which keeps it short of the top.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the cost of living?
statement: Kiwis are continuing to be hit by high inflation and high interest rates. According to Statistics New Zealand, inflation in New Zealand was higher last year than in the US, the UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, and the European Union, which would suggest that claims made by previous Governments that this was all an international problem are not borne out by the data. Inflation is a big challenge. That’s why we are taking urgent steps through our 100-day plan to beat inflation and rebuild New Zealand’s economy.
