explanation: Asked what reports he has seen in support; he supplies two direct supportive quotations and attributes them. Whether the quotes are fairly used is a Veracity question; as a response, it delivers precisely the thing requested.
question: There is. What reports has he seen in support for charter schools?
statement: One commentator said, “When you look at the success this alternative-style educational model has had for Māori, then it gets an A every day.”, and “Our staff tell us they have seen the change in our tamariki, especially those who have been failed by mainstream schooling.” Another commentator has said, “I support that particular charter school, and the reason I do so is that I’ve seen kaupapa grow from the fetal stages all the way that they have today and I’ve seen the outcomes they’ve achieved, and that’s why I support that particular kaupapa.” I would like to thank Willie Jackson and Peeni Henare for those quotes.

explanation: "Yes, in the context they were given." A yes/no question answered yes. The qualifier is a mild hedge rather than an escape hatch, so slightly below a bare "Yes".
question: Does he stand by his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context they were given.

explanation: Asked to explain why a coalition agreement overrides a Tiriti obligation. He rejects the premise and gives the governing rationale — child wellbeing ahead of cultural needs — which is a partial answer to "why". But the specific charge, the Tiriti obligation and the influence of one minor party, is stepped around rather than addressed. Half an answer.
question: Can he explain why he has allowed one coalition agreement with a minor political party to cause his Government to disregard his obligation under the Tiriti in regards to the repeal of section 7AA?
statement: We are united, in the coalition Government, that we are prioritising the wellbeing of a child ahead of their cultural needs.

explanation: "Yes" answers the question completely in the first word. Everything after it is unsolicited promotion of the Gumboot Friday announcement, but padding after a direct answer is not evasion.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially today’s announcement that the Government will fund $24 million to Gumboot Friday, enabling them to deliver counselling sessions to more than 15,000 young people. I do want to thank the Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, for his tireless advocacy for securing this funding—[Interruption] that’s right—ensuring that Kiwis with mental health challenges can access support earlier. We know community organisations, like Gumboot Friday, can do so much more to solve the big societal challenges we have in New Zealand, and we’re going to keep devolving to the grassroots to get better results for every single New Zealander when it comes to mental health. This is a Government that’s walking the walk, not just talking the talk.

explanation: The question is a specific fiscal comparison: why is spending on new social housing less than the savings from scrapping the grants? The answer asserts more social housing and "tough choices" and cites 1,500 places, but never engages the comparison at all. Talking points where a reconciliation was asked for.
question: If the purpose of scrapping First Home Grants, as his Government announced today, is to increase social housing, why is the Government spending less on new social housing places than it’s saving by scrapping the grants?
statement: Well, as I discussed with that member yesterday, we’re going to increase the amount of social housing in New Zealand and we’re not afraid to make tough choices. The choice that we’re making is to invest in 1,500 new social housing places for Kiwi families, and that will mean that some of those families are out of Labour’s motels.

explanation: A sharpened re-ask with a concrete figure ($105 million less). The response contains no reference to the figure, the shortfall, or Bishop's announcement — only generalities about determination to build houses and pride in 1,500 places. A narrow factual question comprehensively avoided.
question: Why did the announcement by Chris Bishop today indicate that the Government will be spending $105 million less on new social housing places than it will be saving by scrapping the First Home Grants?
statement: Look, I’d just say to that member that we are determined to build more houses in this country. We have more supply needed in the social housing piece, we have more supply of rental properties needed, and more houses that need to be built. I’m very proud of this Government actually spending and investing money to make sure we get 1,500 more places in social housing. It’s important.

explanation: A yes/no arithmetic question about whether $2.9b in tax breaks equals up to 580,000 First Home Grants. The answer never confirms, denies or engages the number, pivoting instead to advice on interest deductibility and rental supply — answering a different question than the one asked.
question: Is it correct that the Government’s $2.9 billion tax breaks for landlords would pay for up to 580,000 First Home Grants?
statement: Well, I want to say to that member that we got exactly the same advice that he received when he was Prime Minister and he was in Government, and that was that interest deductibility would put downward pressure on rents. We are serious in this Government that we want to make sure we expand the rental supply of houses, and so we’re restoring interest deductibility, we’re pulling back the brightline test, and we’re balancing up the tenancy laws.

explanation: Asked whether it is correct that no consent was lodged until 2005 (and whether the RMA case is thin). Bishop opens with a complaint about the House litigating consent timelines, but then engages: he says his information is that preparatory work started in 1999 and expressly concedes "It is true that Meridian applied for it in 2005." The factual core is confronted and contested rather than sidestepped; the deflective preamble and the truncated ending keep it short of complete.
question: Is it not correct that although the land was purchased in the 1990s, as the Minister said, no consent was lodged for building a wind farm on that land till it was transferred to Meridian—in fact, it was lodged on 1 July 2005; a final decision was made on 20 July 2007—and, if this is what this party is hanging its Resource Management Act reform on, it’s pretty thin?
statement: We’re nine days out from the Budget and apparently we’re litigating on exactly what time frame an energy company submitted a resource consent application. But, regardless, the information that I have is that preparatory work on the resource consent for West Wind started in 1999. It is true that Meridian applied for it in 2005, but, of course—

explanation: Asked whether he has received advice that the COVID fast-track referred 1,630 MW of renewables, including Te Rere Hau in under 18 months. "Oh yes, yes" reads as an affirmative to the yes/no question, but he immediately turns to praising the fast-track legislation and his own new regime, never confirming the advice or the figures as such. Half-answered: the yes is there, the substance behind it is not.
question: Has the Minister received advice that under the COVID fast-track consenting process, where Ministers referred projects and independent experts made the decisions, the renewable energy projects referred had a combined generating capacity of 1,630 megawatts—that’s the equivalent of nearly four Clyde Dams’ worth of electricity—and that one of those was Te Rere Hau Wind Farm, which obtained approval in way under 18 months?
statement: Oh yes, yes. I’m a big fan of the COVID-19 fast-track legislation, which is why we have lifted and shifted the vast architecture of the legislation into a new fast-track regime designed to make it easier to build things in this country.

explanation: Asked a narrow yes/no: does the Government's bill retain independent experts as decision-makers rather than joint Ministers? He never says. He jokes about the "troika of Ministers" (an oblique concession that Ministers decide), then retreats to "the bill is before select committee," a general commitment to a one-stop shop, and a dig at the Greens. A pointed factual question about the bill's own text answered with talking points.
question: Under his Government’s bill that is before select committee, has he lifted and shifted the fact that it is independent experts who make decisions and not three wise men of Ministers?
statement: Oh, well, the member is surprisingly complimentary about the troika of Ministers alongside Matua Shane and Mr Brown. As the member knows, the bill is before select committee. We are committed to a one-stop-shop, fast-track regime, which, as the record of the previous Government acknowledges—with the exception of the Luddites and the Green Party—every mainstream political party recognises this as a problem holding New Zealand back. We are also open to sensible changes to the bill.

explanation: Asked whether he will commit to changing the bill to give decisions to independent expert panels, as the generators' submission recommends. He gives a reason for not committing — he won't pre-empt the select committee — and says submissions are being read and refinements are likely. That is a recognisable declination to commit, but it is hedged rather than stated: he never says no, and he never engages the specific change the generators proposed.
question: Will the Minister commit to changing the bill, given the majority of the major electricity generators—under the Electricity Sector Environment Group—in their submission to the select committee have recommended that decisions on whether to approve or decline approvals for eligible projects are made by independent expert panels rather than by the joint Ministers as proposed under the bill as is currently drafted—i.e., they are proposing a very similar scheme to the regime that Labour had?
statement: Well, the bill is before the select committee, so I don’t want to get ahead of the deliberations of the select committee. All I can say is that we are carefully reading the submissions to the committee and the officials are analysing that. There are very few bills that go to Parliament that go to a select committee that don’t come back with sensible refinements to improve the legislation. I’m sure that will be true of the fast-track bill.

explanation: Asked what Police recently announced about policing gangs. He states the announcement directly: a national gang unit and district-level gang disruption units from new and reprioritised resources, plus what they will do. Squarely on the question.
question: What recent announcements has Police made about the policing of gangs?
statement: The Police Commissioner has announced the formation of a national gang unit and district level gang disruption units made up of both new and reprioritised resources. These teams will have a laser focus on the disruption and enforcement of gangs. The new gang units will create and enhance new operational capability in combating gangs. They’ll add significant capability to suppress gangs, their networks, supply chains, and violent, intimidating, and antisocial behaviour.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees that gangs will ignore police. "No, I totally reject that" — an unambiguous answer to the yes/no put to him, followed by his reasoning. Complete.
question: Does he agree with commentators that gangs will ignore police?
statement: No, I totally reject that. Our police officers are an extension of our communities, and threats made against them are made against all of us. We have one of the most professional and capable police forces in the world. I have no doubt that they have the ability to be able to enforce the law and keep the public safe.

explanation: Asked what additional powers the Government is giving police. He enumerates them: patch and insignia bans, dispersal notices, consorting prohibition notices, strengthened firearms prohibition orders with warrantless search. Directly responsive.
question: What additional powers is the Government giving police to use?
statement: The Government has announced several new powers for police, including the banning of patches and insignia in public, dispersal notices, consorting prohibition notices, and strengthened firearms prohibition orders with warrantless search powers.

explanation: Asked how the Police announcement supports the Government's priorities. He links the two — it signals gangs no longer operate in a permissive environment, and restoring law and order is a stated coalition priority. The answer is thin and slogan-like, but thinness is Specificity; the question asked for a connection and a connection is given.
question: How does this announcement from Police support the Government’s priorities?
statement: This is a strong step in the right direction and sends a clear message to gangs and organised crime groups that they are no longer operating in a permissive environment or above the law. Restoring law and order is a key priority for this coalition Government.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the decision to repeal section 7AA. "Yes." One word, and it is the whole answer the question called for.
question: Does she stand by the decision to repeal section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked what she says to a named survivor who called the repeal "another stab in the back." She does address him — an apology for what he went through — and gives her reason for proceeding anyway (children's safety first in the Act). She then turns on the Opposition benches, which drops the thread. An open-ended question given a real if partial reply, with a pivot at the end.
question: What does she say to Tupua Urlich, a former ward of the State, who was the first survivor to speak at the Māori public hearing for the abuse in care royal commission of inquiry, who says, about repealing section 7AA, that “It’s going to take generations to undo that harm. So when the Government turns around and fails to acknowledge our rights, it’s just another stab in the back.”?
statement: I’m sorry that Tupua Urlich had to go through what he went through, and I’m sorry that Tupua Urlich had to stand up and tell his story before the royal commission. But, at the end of the day, this is about making sure that our young people are put first, before any other consideration in the Act. And any member on the other side of the House that can argue that putting the safety and the best interests of our kids first—[Interruption] needs to take a good, long, hard look in the mirror.

explanation: Asked whether she remains unapologetic given her own ministry's regulatory impact statement finds no robust evidence of harm and warns repeal may worsen outcomes. She meets the tension head-on: Ministers' job is to consider official advice, not to agree with it — i.e. yes, and here is why the RIS does not move her. She does not repeat the "unapologetic" formulation or engage paragraph 44's specific finding, which is what holds it below the top band.
question: Does she remain “unapologetic for putting the children first” when her ministry’s regulatory impact statement indicates that there is a lack of robust evidence that section 7AA does anything at all to harm children, and that repealing section 7AA may worsen the safety, stability, and wellbeing of our children with the greatest needs, on page 24, at paragraph 44?
statement: Whilst I respect the work the officials do and the information that they provide, it is also important to note that it is the job of Ministers to consider official advice, not to agree with it.

explanation: Asked for a figure — how much the average renter would save. "Well, that will depend" concedes the question exists but supplies nothing, and he immediately turns to 'putting the policy ideas' before being cut off. The core (a number, or even a range) is never reached.
question: How much does he expect the average renter to save as a result of the $2.9 billion in interest deductibility changes that the Government has introduced?
statement: Well, that will depend, but what I would say is that it’s important that we put the policy ideas—

explanation: A binary question — up or down — and he answers it squarely in the first clause: "They'll have gone down." The subsequent pivot to greenfields and fast-track legislation is padding, but the question was engaged and answered before it. Docked slightly because he never engages that the fall is on his watch, only that it happened.
question: Has the number of building consents for new houses issued increased or decreased since he became Prime Minister?
statement: They’ll have gone down because of the economic cycle, because of the market, but I would say to you that this is a Government that is going to open up more greenfields. And I just encourage the member: why doesn’t he support our fast-track legislation? Because we based it on inspired thinking from David Parker, who would make a great leader of the Labour Party one day, but he had inspired thinking and we’ve built on it, and I encourage the Labour Party to support our fast-track regulations legislation.

explanation: The question asks him to justify a prioritisation. "We are not afraid to make tough choices" and the inherited fiscal situation is the beginning of a justification, so this is not a pure dodge, but he then spends the bulk of the answer attacking KiwiBuild rather than explaining the trade-off he was asked about. Gestures at the question, does not reach it.
question: How is it that his Government is prioritising $2.9 billion in tax breaks for landlords whilst cutting a scheme that ensures that a number of New Zealanders can actually buy their first home?
statement: Again, I just say to the member: we are a Government that is not afraid to make tough choices. We have inherited a fiscal situation left behind by the previous Government. What I don’t understand is how the masterminds that brought us KiwiBuild ended up increasing house prices 15 percent, added $180 to average weekly rents, and four times more people on the social house waiting list. I thought the Labour Party cared about low and middle income, working New Zealanders.

explanation: "Yes, I do" — direct and complete on a yes/no question. The social housing material that follows is unsolicited campaigning and the attack on the previous Government is irrelevant, but neither is a dodge: the question was answered in the first three words.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, I do, and especially our announcement today that we will fund 1,500 more social housing places from community housing providers. The track record from the last Labour-Greens Government was abysmal: billions of dollars spent only to peddle misery with more children growing up in motels and sleeping in cars. We have a comprehensive strategy to fix that mess. We’re fixing the rental market, we’re fixing Kāinga Ora, and we’re funding more places for community housing providers so that Kiwi kids can grow up in a house, not a motel.

explanation: A direct agree/disagree question about the Ombudsman's statement on executive power and oversight. He never says whether he agrees, and never touches checks, balances or accountability at all — he pivots to the need for infrastructure and an appeal for Green support. Talking points substituted for the answer.
question: Does the Prime Minister agree with the Ombudsman on the Fast-track Approvals Bill that “When you get a bill like this that creates enormous executive power, there is ever more need to have a check and a balance unless it’s matched by oversight and accountability. I think democracy itself is the loser.”?
statement: Well, what I’d say to that member, and we’ve had this conversation many times before, is that we need modern, reliable infrastructure in New Zealand. That is how we will make this country more prosperous. We need to get things done, and that means cutting through the red and green tape that’s getting in the way, it means making sure that we take David Parker’s inspired thinking around a fast-track law and we build it out so that we can get things done. And so I just say to the member we welcome the Greens’ support so that we can get renewable energy projects built quicker.

explanation: Two things were asked: does he stand by the statement, and what are the protections for taiao. He answers neither — the select committee process is offered as a reason not to engage. The 'what are these protections' half is a narrow factual request that goes wholly unaddressed, which makes this a worse failure than a vague question half-covered.
question: Does he stand by the statement made on behalf of the Minister responsible for RMA Reform on 9 May that “within the Fast-track Approvals Bill you see various protections for taiao”; if so, what are these protections?
statement: What I’d say to the member is the bill is before a select committee. You’ve heard the infrastructure Minister say himself that he is open to sensible suggestions to improve it. We are going through that process, we will digest that feedback, and we’ll take that on board.

explanation: He never says whether he agrees with the Taxpayers' Union, but the independent expert panel he describes does bear directly on the second half — who decides — and functions as an implicit refusal to commit to removing Ministers. Partial: the substance of the decision-maker question is touched, the agree/disagree and the commitment sought are not.
question: Does he agree with the Taxpayers’ Union, who said that “The Bill places the decision-making authority with the joint Ministers. This places them at the centre of major investment decisions. Effectively, the Bill asks politicians to pick winners. This is never a good arrangement.”; if so, will he commit to removing Ministers as the decision makers?
statement: I don’t know how to be any clearer: the bill is before a select committee; the infrastructure Minister has said himself that he’s open to sensible suggestions. What I would say is we have proposed an independent expert panel that will judge conditions including the environment, including social benefits and economic benefits, the whole lot, and we’ve actually proposed that in the select committee. If you’ve got thoughts about it, make those points now. But the big point is this: we are going to stop the talking and we are going to get things done in this country. I make no apologies for that; it’s what the people of New Zealand expect us to do. It’s what we’re expected to do if we’re going to deliver on our climate change goals—we need to get things done and built. And I’d just say to the member, again, please support the bill. If you care about the environment, if you care about climate change, you’d back our fast-track legislation.

explanation: Four specific commitments were sought. He gives none, and the gas answer supplies an implicit 'no' on the oil and gas item, which is some engagement. Coal, the conservation estate and species extinction are not mentioned at all, and most of the response is a retrospective attack on the previous ban.
question: Will he, in light of his request for the Green Party’s support, commit to no new coal mines, not reopening oil and gas drilling, protecting the conservation estate from mining, and no extinction of native species through his Fast-track Approvals Bill?
statement: Well, I just say to the member: on this side, in this Government, we are deeply committed to delivering on our climate change goals and commitments. But, again, what we saw and what you—in the discussion that we had last week—[Interruption] Would you like me to complete? What we saw was that we actually have some energy security risk in this country. Why? Because there was a banning of an oil and gas ban from the Labour-Greens. There was no follow-up plan to it. It was a bunch of bumper stickers, headlines, and Post-it notes, and, actually, what was needed is we need gas as a transitory energy source so we can keep our energy security in place.

explanation: "I absolutely stand by that statement" answers the operative question directly. The trailing 'is he confused' clause is a rhetorical jab rather than a genuine question, so leaving it unanswered is not a dodge. Terse and unhelpful, but responsive.
question: Does he stand by his statement on 8 May, “support our reversal of the oil and gas ban, support our fast-track legislation, and let’s go get renewable energy built in this country.”, and, if so, is he confused about the difference between oil and gas and renewable energy?
statement: I absolutely stand by that statement and just continue to encourage the Greens to support us.

explanation: A definitional question answered exactly: revenue minus expenses before gains and losses, what gains and losses are, and the total-Crown scope. Nothing asked is left out and nothing extraneous is substituted.
question: What does the operating balance excluding gains and losses (OBEGAL) measure?
statement: The operating balance excluding gains and losses—commonly known as the OBEGAL—is the difference between total Crown revenue and total Crown expenses, before gains and losses. Gains and losses arise from changes in the value of the Government’s assets and liabilities—for example, changes in market prices of equity investments. OBEGAL is a total Crown measure, so it includes the financial results of Crown entities and State-owned enterprises.

explanation: "The OBEGAL is in deficit" — the surplus-or-deficit question is settled in the opening clause. The causal narrative and the 'mess our Government is cleaning up' framing that follow are partisan colour, which does not bear on whether the question was engaged; it plainly was.
question: Is the OBEGAL in surplus or deficit?
statement: The OBEGAL is in deficit and has been since 2019. It is in deficit because Government spending has increased markedly. Now, while some spending increases over recent years were temporary—for example, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and the North Island weather events—there was a permanent increase in other areas. So, after stripping out large, one-off expenses, and adjusting for the economic cycle, the Treasury estimates a structural operating deficit of around 1.5 percent of GDP in the current financial year. A structural deficit, members, is not sustainable in the long term, as it requires continual borrowing to cover expenses, leading to a never-ending accumulation of public debt—a debt spiral. That is the mess our Government is cleaning up.

explanation: Asked for the Government's response and gives one: fiscal consolidation, reducing core Crown expenses as a share of GDP, returning OBEGAL to surplus, with a forthcoming plan. He also volunteers that forecasts have deteriorated further, which cuts against him. Short of 1.0 only because the promised plan is deferred rather than described.
question: What is the Government’s response to this situation?
statement: Fiscal consolidation is required over time to bring revenue and expenses back into balance. As set out in the Budget Policy Statement, the Government is committed to reducing core Crown expenses as a proportion of GDP, and returning the OBEGAL to surplus. These fiscal goals have become harder to achieve as economic forecasts have deteriorated. I can tell the House that the forecasts have continued to deteriorate even since the Budget Policy Statement. None the less, the Government remains committed to its fiscal strategy and will set out a plan to return to surplus.

explanation: Asked WHEN OBEGAL returns to surplus. She engages the question rather than ignoring it — she says the date will be in the Budget forecasts, and offers a related figure (2030-31 under the previous allowances) — but she never gives the date asked for, and part of the answer redirects to the previous Government's settings. A deferral plus a counterfactual: the core 'when' is touched but not reached. Detail and blame-shifting were not counted against her; only the fact that the specific date was withheld.
question: When will the OBEGAL return to surplus?
statement: That will be set out in the fiscal projections and forecasts released as part of the Budget. But what I can tell the House is that in the current economic circumstances, if we continued with the future Budget operating allowances in the half-year update, which was set by the previous Government, there might not be a surplus posted in New Zealand until 2030-31. As a responsible Government, we will not be doing that.

explanation: A simple 'does she stand by her answers' question, answered 'yes' immediately and then reinforced with the statement she most stands by. Direct and complete; the added quote is elaboration, not evasion.
question: Does she stand by her answers to oral questions on Tuesday, 21 May?
statement: Well, yes, and I particularly stand by my statement that “I happen to believe that one of the greatest things we can do for productivity is send New Zealanders the message that there will be reward for their hard work.”

explanation: Two-part question. Part one ('do you stand by it?') is answered squarely: yes. Part two asked WHERE in the coalition agreement the scrapping of first-home grants appears — she never identifies a location, instead rebuking the questioner for not listening and re-reading her earlier answer about 'other savings'. That re-quote gestures at an answer (implying it sits outside the coalition agreement) without ever saying so. Half the question answered, the specific half dodged.
question: Does she stand by her statement “These savings and revenue initiatives are the same as those in the National Party’s tax plan, with some adjustment to reflect coalition agreements.”; if so, where in the coalition agreement does it say that first-home grants will be scrapped?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes. In answer to the second part of the question, the member should’ve listened to the rest of the answers, in which I said, “Tax relief in the Budget will be fully funded through savings and revenue initiatives. These savings and revenue initiatives are the same as those in the National Party’s tax plan, with some adjustments to reflect coalition agreements. There will also”—[Interruption] and the members should listen, because, clearly, members didn’t listen yesterday—“be other savings in the Budget. These savings will be directed towards Government priorities, including front-line public services.”, including social housing for our most vulnerable New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked WHY landlords get a $2.9b tax break while first-home buyer funding is cut. The reply talks about supporting renters and rent pressure — neither the tax break nor the cut is addressed. This answers a different question than the one asked. Note the answer may well be true and on-policy; that is irrelevant here.
question: Why has she chosen to support landlords with a $2.9 billion tax break but cut the funding to help first-home buyers?
statement: We have chosen to support renters because we don’t want to see the acceleration in rents they faced under that Government, and we are taking policy actions to put downward pressure on rents.

explanation: Two-part question answered with 'Yes, and yes' — she stands by the statement and rules out a foreign buyers tax. Terse to the point of curtness, and the trailing tease adds nothing, but both parts are squarely answered. Bluntness is not a dodge.
question: Does she stand by her statement “These savings and revenue initiatives are the same as those in the National Party’s tax plan.”; if so, can she rule out a foreign buyers tax?
statement: Yes, and yes—and I can’t wait to show you what this Government has done next week.

explanation: A narrow yes/no question about new revenue initiatives in the Budget, met with 'Eight more sleeps.' The question is not engaged at all — it is deflected with a quip. A tightly specified question wholly avoided is the worst case for this attribute.
question: Are there any new revenue initiatives not contained in the coalition agreements or the National Party tax plan that Kiwis can expect in the Budget?
statement: Eight more sleeps.

explanation: Asked what he has announced on social housing; he states the announcement — $140m, 1,500 places, delivered by community housing providers from July 2025. The question is answered head-on. (A patsy question from a government member, but that affects Focus/eligibility judgements elsewhere, not whether the question was engaged.)
question: What announcements has he made regarding social housing?
statement: Today, I was proud to announce that the Government is investing in social housing for New Zealanders who are most in need of a warm, dry home. Budget 2024 will allocate $140 million in new funding for 1,500 new social housing places to be provided by community housing providers, not Kāinga Ora, thanks to savings found by ending the First Home Grant. As the House has discussed previously, funding for new social housing places under the previous Government ends in June 2025—another fiscal cliff we’ve had to confront. These places will start to become available from July 2025, giving the sector much-needed certainty about the pipeline, allowing them to plan for the future.

explanation: Asked why CHPs rather than Kāinga Ora; he gives the reason directly — the review found KO not financially sustainable, so no new places until a turnaround plan is approved — plus why CHPs can take it on. The 'why' is squarely met.
question: Why are these places going to community housing providers and not Kāinga Ora?
statement: Well, as the House discussed yesterday and as I announced on Monday, the independent review into Kāinga Ora reveals that it’s not financially sustainable in its current form. And until we have received, as the Government, and approved a turnaround plan from the refreshed board, we will not be giving any new social housing places to them. The community housing sector does an outstanding job of housing people in need—currently over 13,000 social houses around New Zealand. They’ve got the capability, expertise, and desire to grow further, and this Government’s going to back them to succeed.

explanation: Asked how the 1,500 places will be paid for; he names the funding source — ending the First Home Grant — in the first sentence. The rest is justification padding, which neither adds to nor detracts from whether the question was engaged. Answered.
question: How will you pay for these 1,500 places?
statement: As I said before, funding for the new social housing places ends in June 2025, and we are filling in this fiscal cliff by ending the First Home Grant. Budget 2024 is about tough decisions, and we have made a deliberate choice to reprioritise low-value expenditure to more important policy priorities. At a time when the wait-list for social housing is over 25,000 applicants, we have made the tough call to prioritise support for them. The First Home Grant provides a median of $5,000 towards a house deposit, but it is an expensive and inefficient way to support first-home buyers. We are doing the right thing and focusing on supply side solutions to our housing crisis.

explanation: Asked which first-home buyer supports are retained; he lists them — the First Home Loan and KiwiSaver first-home withdrawals. Exactly the question asked, exactly answered.
question: What support for first-home buyers will the Government be retaining?
statement: We’re retaining the First Home Loan scheme, which is effective at supporting buyers over the deposit barrier. This allows first-home buyers to purchase a home with a deposit as low as 5 percent. We’re also retaining the ability for KiwiSaver members to withdraw funds for a first-home deposit. The First Home Loan helps thousands of Kiwis into their first homes every year. It’s more effective at supporting New Zealanders over the deposit barrier, and this is the right thing to do to support New Zealanders in need.

explanation: A closed question — is the report correct? — answered 'Yes.' One word, complete, nothing withheld. Maximum forthrightness.
question: Is it correct, as reported yesterday on Newshub, that the Government intends to scrap grants to first-home buyers?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees many first-home buyers relied on the grant, including 10,000 last year. He answers 'No', disputes the figure with his own (7,800), and addresses the 'relied on' premise by arguing the grant brings purchases forward rather than enabling them. Contradicting the questioner is not evasion; the question is met directly. Whether 7,800 is the true figure is a Veracity matter, not scored here.
question: Does the Minister agree that many first-home buyers have relied on the First Home Grant to purchase their first home, including 10,000 last year?
statement: No, actually, last year—the member’s wrong—7,800 people received the First Home Grant, so the member’s wrong on that. The second point is that the evidence suggests that it brings forward the purchase of a home because it provides money towards the deposit, but it doesn’t actually make the difference for most people between buying a house or not buying a house and that is one of the reasons why we have reprioritised it to higher-value expenditure.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his 28 March statement. Answered "Absolutely" at the top — a direct yes — before elaborating on the five-point plan. The elaboration is padding, but the question itself was squarely answered.
question: Does he stand by his statement on 28 March this year that “The Government is determined to see more New Zealanders in homeownership.”?
statement: Absolutely, which is why we have a comprehensive five-point plan to fix our housing crisis. I’m happy to detail it for the member in response to that patsy, but the member’s heard it before, which is about opening up land supply at the edge of our cities and going up inside our cities; fixing our infrastructure funding and financing system; actually doing what Phil Twyford promised to do five years ago, which is smash the metropolitan urban limit in Auckland; focusing on building and construction changes being led by Chris Penk; fixing the Resource Management Act; delivering better social housing; and fixing the private rental market.

explanation: Asked whether fewer first-home buyers means more renters. Explicitly conceded the point: "Yes, it is true, obviously". The subsequent drift into supply-side talking points doesn't undo the direct answer already given.
question: Does the Minister agree that if there are fewer first-home buyers purchasing a home, then there will be more people renting?
statement: Well, I mean, look, I can’t believe the member is now literally—literally—stating truisms in the House. Yes, it is true, obviously, that if the number of first-home buyers goes down, most of those people will be renting. Homeownership in New Zealand is at record lows. It is down to 63 percent. That is part of the crisis we’ve inherited from the last Government. But, actually, that goes back 20 or 30 years, which is why we have, as I just said, a comprehensive plan around land supply, infrastructure, incentives for councils, lowering the cost of building consents, fixing our planning system, fixing our private rental market. We are determined to focus on the underlying problems afflicting our housing market, which is not demand side measures, like first-home grants, but supply side measures. Because as the member, I think, is learning, unless and until you fix the supply side of the market, everything else is tinkering. We are fixing the underlying fundamentals.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statements and actions on the 7AA repeal bill. Answered "Yes" and quoted which statements. Complete.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions in relation to the Oranga Tamariki (Repeal of Section 7AA) Amendment Bill?
statement: Yes—especially my statement that “Every child deserves the same level of care and support based on their needs, and their safety and wellbeing should always come first.”, and also my statement that “I want our system to ensure that every child in this country is raised in a loving and stable home that sets them up to succeed for life, regardless of race or culture.”

explanation: Two-part: does she accept the repeal ends iwi relationships, and if not, what is her approach to future partnership agreements. She answered both parts explicitly — "no" to the first, and for the second, that strategic partnerships will not change and more will be created where they serve children well.
question: Does she accept that the repeal of section 7AA is a repeal of the relationships Oranga Tamariki have made with iwi, hapū, and kaupapa Māori organisations, and, if not, what will her approach be when “entering into further strategic partnership agreements with iwi or Māori organisations”?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, no. In answer to the second part of the question, I don’t know how much clearer I can make it: I have said over and over again in this House that strategic partnerships will not change and that I will continue to make sure that if these programmes are working well and in the best interest of our young people, they will continue and more will be created if that is what’s best for our children.

explanation: Two-part: does she agree with her statement, and if so, can she give examples of cultural-wellbeing consideration without 7AA. She answered only the first part ("yes") and gave no examples at all. The examples were the substantive half of a narrow request, and they were simply not supplied.
question: Does she agree with her statement that “This Bill does not stop the consideration of cultural wellbeing of children and young people in the care of Oranga Tamariki.”, and, if so, can she provide examples of what consideration of cultural wellbeing will look like without section 7AA?
statement: In relation to the first part of the question, yes.

explanation: Asked what reassurance she can provide to tamariki Māori about severed whakapapa connection. She redirected to who owns the decision (all-of-Government, not ACT) and offered a generic commitment to "the best start in life". The reassurance asked for is gestured at but never reached; most of the reply answers a different question.
question: If the ACT Party “wants to make sure the wellbeing of the child is the paramount consideration of Oranga Tamariki”, what reassurance can she provide to tamariki Māori now that she has committed the further severing of their connection to whakapapa and sense of belonging?
statement: This is not an ACT Party decision; this is an all-of-Government decision, because, as a Government, we are committed to making sure that our young people have every opportunity to the best start in life.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on section 7AA. She named the category of reports and gave a specific case. Directly responsive to what was asked.
question: What reports, if any, has she seen on section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989?
statement: I have seen reports of cases where social workers may have used section 7AA to justify decisions on care arrangements for Māori children which may not have been safe or in their best interests. For example, the members of this House will know about the case of a young girl referred to as “Moana”. After suffering trauma and neglect, Moana was placed with a safe and loving foster family. After a number of years with her foster family and being in a safe environment for the first time, Oranga Tamariki suddenly decided to uplift Moana, because her foster parents were Pākehā and Oranga Tamariki didn’t think they could provide for her cultural needs. Cultural needs can never be at the expense of the safety and wellbeing and best interests of our children.

explanation: Asked what other reports or statements she has seen. She described a specific statement she had seen and began responding to it. Answered, though the reply is cut off mid-sentence.
question: What other reports or statements has the Minister seen on section 7AA?
statement: I have seen a statement claiming that if section 7AA was around when I was a child, I would have been “raised Māori” and would have been connected with my whakapapa and would have known my Māoritanga. The statement goes on to say that I was raised Pākehā with a “disconnection and disdain” for my own people and that my experience is exactly why we need section 7AA. I’m not going to stand here and justify how I was raised—

explanation: Asked whether the repeal will end strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations. Answered unambiguously in the negative — partnerships continue, officials directed to enter new ones, advice cited to that effect. The word "no" is absent but the answer is not in doubt.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Will the repeal of section 7AA mean the end of strategic partnerships that Oranga Tamariki has with iwi and Māori organisations?
statement: I have been very clear, throughout this process, that Oranga Tamariki should continue with strategic partnerships, and I will continue saying that over and over again until people listen. Where these are delivering positive results and better outcomes for our young people, they will continue. Oranga Tamariki currently have 10 strategic partnerships, and I have directed officials to continue with these and enter into new partnerships when and where there are good reasons to do so. I have also received advice from officials that makes it very certain that repealing section 7AA will not prevent Oranga Tamariki from continuing to work with existing strategic partners or entering into new strategic partnerships.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with a quoted statement. "No, I don't." Direct and complete; the rest is explanation.
question: Does the Minister agree with the statement that “The repeal of Section 7AA is a targeted extermination of our babies … exterminating any ounce of culture, identity and any sense of Māori selves.”?
statement: No, I don’t. As I’ve said consistently, this is about ensuring Oranga Tamariki puts the safety, wellbeing, and the best interests of children, not race, at the forefront of social-work practice and decision making. I can’t understand how anyone can think there is anything more important than the safety and wellbeing of our children. Repealing section 7AA is not about disregarding the whakapapa of Māori children; section 7AA places duties on the chief executive that are at odds with the agency’s primary purpose, which is to support the wellbeing of our most vulnerable and at-risk children.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the omission of family violence from the Public Service targets. She said "No" and disputed the premise with a reason — it sits inside the violent-crime target. Directly engaged, then drifted into unrelated law-and-order material.
question: Does she agree with the omission of a reduction in family violence from the Prime Minister’s Public Service targets?
statement: No, because family violence is not omitted from the Government’s nine targets—it is part of the “Reducing violent crime” target. I am proud to be part of a coalition Government which is committed to restoring law and order and putting victims first. This is why we have a series of targets that will focus the public sector on achieving improved results in this area, including reducing crime, with a target of 20,000 fewer people as victims of assaults, robberies, and sexual assaults by 2029. This Government is committed to, and has already announced, a range of measures that help the victims of family violence, including bringing back three-strikes legislation with the addition of the new strangulation and suffocation offence, and backing police to crack down on gangs.

explanation: Asked how she thinks victims of family and sexual violence will respond to targets being limited to what is "responsive" to intervention. She never addressed victims' likely response at all, restating instead that family violence remains a priority and that nine measures were settled on. The core of the question is untouched.
question: How does she think victims of family and sexual violence will respond to the knowledge that this Government will only develop targets that are “responsive” to Government intervention?
statement: Just because family violence is not a stand-alone target among the nine Government targets does not mean it is not a priority. This Government considered a range of targets and measures and settled on nine measures that it believes will best focus the public sector on achieving better results.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the specific DPMC advice that a family violence target was unsuitable, and why not if she disagrees. She answers adjacent to it: she confirms she received official advice that a stand-alone target was not suitable and gives reasons, one of which (measures not suited to quarterly reporting) echoes the DPMC rationale. But she never states her own agreement or disagreement with the cited advice, sheltering behind 'I received a range of advice'. The core is approached, not squarely met.
question: Does she agree with the advice of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet that developing a specific target for family violence was not suitable as “family violence victimisations are unlikely to change over a three- to six-month period and therefore it is not specific enough to drive delivery.”; if not, why not?
statement: I received a range of advice on this topic and I also received advice from officials that a stand-alone family violence target was not suitable for a number of reasons, including that an increase in reporting can be seen as an improvement as more people seek help, and currently, under successive Governments, the key measures regarding family violence are not well suited to the setting of or reporting against quarterly targets.

explanation: Asked whether it was her view that no target was needed because it would show increased reporting. She answers with a flat 'No, that's not what I said' and then states what her position actually is. Direct denial plus correction of the premise — the question is engaged head-on. Slightly short of 1.0 only because the restatement leaves the underlying 'was it necessary' question implicit.
question: Is it the Minister’s view that it was not necessary to develop a specific target for family and sexual violence because it would show an increase in reporting of instances of family and sexual violence?
statement: No, that’s not what I said. What I said was the advice was we could seem like we have achieved something when we actually haven’t. The advice may see that an increase in reporting could be seen as an improvement, when, actually, it just means more people are reporting—doesn’t mean that we’ve made successes in that space.

explanation: Asked whether it is acceptable to develop only targets that are easy to measure and achieve, and where that leaves victims. She answers neither part: she describes travelling the country and listening to NGOs, and ends on a general jab at 'reactionary legislation and targets'. That closing clause brushes against the value of targets, but the acceptability question and the consequences-for-victims question are both left untouched. A pivot to talking points.
question: Does she think it’s acceptable to only develop targets that are easy to measure and easy to achieve, and, if so, where does this leave victims of family and sexual violence?
statement: As I’ve travelled around the country the last couple of months, talking to NGOs and community organisations on where they see the gaps and where they see the Government can help them in this space, I realise there is a lot of work to do and we have to make sure that we’re actually listening to the people on the ground and making a real positive difference in this space rather than reactionary legislation and targets that don’t make a damn bit of difference.

explanation: A two-part question: does he believe everyone should have a secure home, and how does he reconcile that with easier evictions. He answers the first explicitly ('Yes') and offers a reconciliation for the second — the policy is meant to bring more landlords into the market so homes are available. The reconciliation shifts the ground from security of tenure to access, so the second half is answered but only glancingly; both parts are nonetheless engaged.
question: Does he believe everyone in New Zealand should have a secure home; if so, how does he reconcile this with his Government’s intention to make it easier to evict people from their homes?
statement: Yes, I believe everyone should be able to access a warm and dry home to live in. The intent of our tenancy policy changes is to encourage more landlords into the market so that people can access those homes.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts HUD's advice on the two specific evidential findings. He acknowledges it is HUD's official advice but never says whether he accepts it, moving instead to what he personally believes about landlords taking a chance on tenants. A listener can infer non-acceptance, but the yes/no on the ministry's evidence is stepped around rather than given. Note the answer's detail and plausibility are irrelevant here — it is the accept/not-accept core that is avoided.
question: Does he accept the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) advice that evidence is uncertain that no-cause evictions will put downward pressures on rents but that the evidence is clear that security of tenancy for renters will be negatively impacted?
statement: Well, that’s the official advice from HUD. What I do believe, as I’ve heard from many landlords and many people out there who work with vulnerable tenants, is that bringing back no-cause evictions will enable landlords to take a chance on often quite vulnerable tenants who are trying to access rental properties. That is a good thing for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with a named person's quoted claim, and why not if he disagrees. He gives the yes/no plainly — 'generally, I disagree with that' — with a caveat that he hasn't seen the full context. The 'why not' half is simply not supplied. Direct on the main question, incomplete on the follow-up; the caveat is a genuine qualification, not a dodge.
question: Does he agree with the president of the Canterbury Property Investors’ Association, who said about no-cause evictions, “Instead of getting maintenance, they get a 90-day notice to end their tenancy.”, and, if not, why not?
statement: I haven’t seen the quote from that particular individual in its full context, but, generally, I disagree with that.

explanation: Asked what he says to a specific renter's account of a 90-day notice after a healthy homes report. He does answer it — he says he supports the healthy homes standards and would say exactly that to the renter, and adds that retaliating on those grounds is illegal. He then expands into a general housing-policy statement, which pads the answer, but the question posed was addressed before the broadening rather than instead of it.
question: What does he say to one renter who told us that they remember their “mum crying because we received a 90-day notice just days after we filed a healthy homes report because my room was completely covered in mould, there were slugs entering under doors every night, and none of the walls were insulated”?
statement: The Government supports the healthy homes standards, and I would say to that renter exactly that. It is also illegal to do that on the grounds of what the member is talking about. I would say more generally the whole thrust of our housing policies, as I discussed with Manawatu Tenants’ Union and a whole range of people working in this advocacy space this morning, is to improve homeownership for New Zealanders and improve the lives of renters by putting downward pressure on rents. It is too expensive to own houses in New Zealand. It is too expensive to rent in New Zealand. We are fixing the underlying issues in our housing market that have caused that to be the case.

explanation: Asked what he says to a person whose elderly grandfather was repeatedly evicted. He offers sympathy — a partial answer to a 'what do you say' question — then explicitly declines to comment on individual circumstances, which is itself a forthright refusal, before pivoting to the policy balance and the questioner's misreading of intent. Half of the response engages, half redirects; the person's situation is acknowledged but not really responded to.
question: What does he say to one person who told us that “My elderly grandfather was kicked out each year for three years in a row, from three places, and it was so sad seeing him shuffled along every year. It was such an ordeal moving him. He wasn’t eligible for funding for a place in a rest home and didn’t have enough money to pay for one.”?
statement: I have every sympathy with people in those situations, but I can’t comment on those individual circumstances. What we are trying to do is get the balance right between tenants and landlords, and also make it clear that landlords that wish to provide properties to people who they might otherwise have turned down are willing to take a chance on people. The member needs to appreciate that the policy intent is positive not negative.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made about coastguards and lifeguards. He names the announcement, the date, who he made it with, the vehicle (Budget 2024), the amount and the recipients. Squarely and completely answered; the closing colour about the Kiwi way of life does not displace the answer.
question: What recent announcements has he made regarding coastguards and lifeguards?
statement: Last Friday, I announced with the Prime Minister and Minister of Transport, the Hon Simeon Brown, that through Budget 2024 the Government would be providing an additional $63.6 million over four years to fund Coastguard New Zealand and Surf Lifesaving New Zealand so that these NGOs can continue to deliver their essential front-line water safety and rescue and prevention services across New Zealand. Heading to the beach, lake, or a river for a fun day of activity in the water is part of the Kiwi way of life, particularly in the summer. With that comes inherent risk, and these front-line organisations do critical work to help ensure people can head home safe.

explanation: Asked how much funding each organisation will receive. Both figures are given, each attributed to the right organisation and the right period. Nothing about the question is left unaddressed.
question: How much funding will each organisation receive?
statement: Coastguard New Zealand will receive $19.5 million over four years, while Surf Lifesaving New Zealand will receive $44 million over the same period. This is operational funding to help address cost pressures faced by these organisations. This will ensure they’re able to continue to deliver their essential front-line water safety, rescue, and prevention services across New Zealand. Coastguard New Zealand and Surf Lifesaving provide an essential public service that benefits the health, safety, and wellbeing of New Zealanders. The Government is committed to ensuring that these services continue to prevent harm and save lives on our beaches and in the water.

explanation: Asked what other announcements he has made regarding lifeguards. He describes presenting the Search and Rescue Awards and gives the particulars. An awards presentation is a slightly loose fit for 'announcement', but he supplies the other lifeguard-related thing he did rather than evading, so the question is engaged.
question: What other announcements has he made regarding lifeguards?
statement: Last night, I was pleased to present the 2023 New Zealand Search and Rescue Awards at Parliament. These awards are presented annually in recognition of outstanding achievements. Forty nominations were received in 2023, with two gold awards and 10 certificates of achievement being awarded at this year’s ceremony. A quick count of the support category recipients last night revealed they have over 170 years of search and rescue experience between them. I’d like to take a moment to acknowledge the people at Coastguard, Surf Lifesaving, and other organisations working in search and rescue for their dedication and commitment to ensuring New Zealanders’ safety.

explanation: Asked whether the Minister stands by a stated expectation of Oranga Tamariki. Answer: "Yes." One word, but it is the complete and direct answer to a yes/no question.
question: Does she stand by her expectation of Oranga Tamariki “that the best interests of our young people are at the forefront of all their decision making”?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked how it serves children's best interests to shift specialist legal work onto untrained, short-staffed social workers. The reply explains the rationale for the restructure (functional leads, accountability, legal services focused on court roles) and closes on "still a proposal", but never engages the training gap or the 160-social-worker shortfall that were the core of the question. It gestures at the subject without reaching the question.
question: How is it in the best interests of children and young people to add specialist legal work to Oranga Tamariki social workers, work that they are not trained for, and in an organisation where they are already 160 social workers short?
statement: One of the premises of the consultation document is lifting performance and accountability across the organisation, whereby functional leads would have sole responsibility for delivery in areas that they own. As a result, Oranga Tamariki proposed that legal services should focus on their core court-related roles and for some other functions that they are doing to be led and delivered by those who are responsible and accountable for them. Every part of this is still a proposal and no final decisions have been made.

explanation: Asked whether the Minister agrees with the Law Society that lawyers' and social workers' roles are distinct and non-substitutable, and if not, why not. The reply says "No, I don't agree, because..." and supplies the definitional reasoning. Both halves of the question — the position and the reason — are answered squarely.
question: Does she agree with the Law Society that Oranga Tamariki lawyers and social workers have distinct specialist front-line roles, and that the services these lawyers provide cannot simply be carried out by others in the organisation—for example, social workers who already face complex and heavy workloads—and, if not, why not?
statement: No, I don’t agree, because “front line” has been defined—the advice is that front-line staff roles are considered to be children’s workers, as defined in section 23 of the Children’s Act, and the definition of “front-line service” is an operational matter for Oranga Tamariki. I’m advised that Oranga Tamariki considers front-line services to be those provided by staff directly to children and families. While Oranga Tamariki solicitors provide valuable support to social workers in carrying out their statutory functions, they do not provide direct services to children or their families.

explanation: Asked whether the Minister agrees with the family law section's stated safety concerns. The reply — that this is still a proposal and no decisions are final — is responsive to a different question (what stage is this at). Agreement or disagreement is never expressed.
question: Does she agree with the family law section of the Law Society, who say that they hold significant concerns about the potential consequences for the safety and wellbeing of whānau and vulnerable tamariki, should there be a reduction in either of those roles, as well as the proper functioning of the Family Court?
statement: Can I just make this very clear: this is still a proposal and no final decisions have been made.

explanation: Asked how cutting the Safety of Children in Care team serves children's best interests. The reply does engage: it contests the premise (the work continues, this is consolidation under fewer managers) and offers better decision-making as the justification. The answer is garbled and thin, but garbled reasoning is Rigor — the question itself was addressed rather than sidestepped.
question: How is it in the best interests of children to slash the Safety of Children in Care team, which reports on children abused while they are in care?
statement: There are many departments that the work will still continue, they’re just being consolidated under less managers so that the managers can get out of the way so they can make better decision-making.

explanation: Asked for an update on the Gumboot Friday commitment. The reply gives exactly that: $24 million over four years, the contracted provider, and the coalition-agreement origin. Directly on the question asked.
question: What update can he provide on the coalition Government’s commitment to Gumboot Friday?
statement: The coalition Government announced yesterday that Budget 2024 will provide $24 million over four years, contracting the I Am Hope Foundation to provide under-25-year-olds with free counselling services through the Gumboot Friday initiative. This funding was a commitment made under the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement. Gumboot Friday helps youth with mental health needs—

explanation: Asked why investing in this organisation matters for young New Zealanders. The reply answers the "why" head-on — return on investment, counsellor numbers, faster intervention. A friendly patsy question, but it is answered.
question: Why is investing in this grassroots organisation so important for young New Zealanders?
statement: This Government is focused on investing in our front-line services that will deliver real results. For every $1 invested in I Am Hope, it results in a social return to New Zealand of $5.70. This is a grassroots organisation that works and delivers results. I Am Hope has over 500 accredited counsellors and, with this funding, 300 more are on the way. This is a common-sense investment, and by providing better access to targeted, faster intervention now, youth will get the help they need sooner.

explanation: Asked whether the Minister stands by all the Government's statements and actions. Answer: "Yes." Complete.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether the Minister stands by the decision to appoint a particular MP as Parliamentary Private Secretary. Answer: "Yes." Direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by his decision to appoint Todd Stephenson MP as Parliamentary Private Secretary to the Associate Minister of Health (Pharmac)?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked HOW specific conflicts of interest in named pharmaceutical shareholdings were managed. "Appropriately and properly" asserts a verdict on the management without describing any of it — the mechanism asked for is never touched. It stays on-topic and is not an attack or a pivot, so it is not a total dodge, but the core of a "how" question is left unanswered.
question: How were Todd Stephenson’s conflicts of interest managed in respect to his shares in Johnson and Johnson, Chimeric Therapeutics, and Commonwealth Serum Laboratories—all being pharmaceutical companies that stand to benefit from Pharmac’s decision-making powers?
statement: Appropriately and properly.

explanation: Asked whether the MP was involved in drafting the letter of expectations to Pharmac's board chair. The reply declines on portfolio grounds and offers to transfer the question. That is a plain, non-evasive refusal — no filibuster, no counter-attack — and a refusal can be forthright; but unlike "No, I won't", it leaves the factual question open by handing it elsewhere. Partial credit.
question: Was Todd Stephenson involved in writing the letter of expectations to the board chair of Pharmac?
statement: With respect to that questioner, that answer does not belong with me; it belongs with the Minister in charge, and I’m happy to redirect it, because at a certain level of—

explanation: Asked whether it is acceptable that the Minister's letter to Pharmac was drafted in part by a shareholder in pharmaceutical companies. The reply back-references an earlier content-free assurance that the issues were handled properly. Acceptability is at most implied, never stated, and the specific concern raised is not engaged.
question: Is it acceptable that the Minister’s main way of expressing his views to Pharmac were drafted in part by a person who holds shares in pharmaceutical companies?
statement: The third answer given to that questioner covers the issue. I said that those issues were handled properly and appropriately.

explanation: Asked whether Stephenson's shareholding is a conflict of interest while he attends Pharmac meetings. Peters never says yes or no — he tells the questioner she doesn't understand Pharmac's construction and independence. That is at best an oblique implication that independence makes it moot; the actual question is left unanswered, and the answer partly targets the questioner. (Response is truncated, but nothing in what exists reaches the question.)
question: Is it a conflict of interest for Todd Stephenson to be at meetings with Pharmac where details of drug funding will have been discussed while Mr Stephenson holds shares in pharmaceutical companies?
statement: With respect, I don’t think the questioner understands the actual construction of Pharmac and the independence of that organisation. We’ve all made—

explanation: Asked whether he will stand Stephenson down. "No" is a direct, complete answer to that — a refusal that answers is forthright, and the follow-on clause is cut off. Marked below the blunt-refusal ceiling only because the question was a two-part alternative and the second limb (unwillingness to challenge Seymour) goes untouched, not because the reply is unhelpful or terse.
question: Will he maintain the standards that New Zealanders expect of their Government and stand down Mr Stephenson from his role, or is he unwilling to challenge David Seymour’s exploitation of a loophole which allows a pharmaceutical industry plant to assist the Minister responsible for Pharmac?
statement: No, I think there is a—

explanation: Two-part question: is she committed to no disability-based barriers, and if so why the health-standards test. The second limb is answered squarely — the certificate is limited, health requirements exist to identify needs and weigh public health costs — and she supplies the decline figures. The commitment limb is never stated as a yes or no, so it engages most, not all, of what was asked.
question: Is she committed to ensuring that disabled asylum seekers and refugees face no barriers to obtaining residency on the basis of their disability; if so, why are their residency applications tested against the “acceptable standards of health” requirements?
statement: New Zealand has made international commitments to refugees and protected persons that we are meeting. Those services are provided by a team of dedicated, amazing hard workers who support the refugee programme. Those who have successfully claimed asylum in New Zealand only need to provide a limited medical certificate in their residence applications. This certificate only assesses a small number of the most serious health conditions. Health requirements help us identify and manage the health needs of those refugees and their protection status and understands the support they need when settling in New Zealand as well as considering costs to the public health system. I am advised that between 16 April 2014 and 16 April 2024 only two residence applications for recognised refugee or protected persons were declined based on determinations that an applicant did not meet the acceptable health standards requirements. These applications in both cases were subsequently granted their residence by ministerial intervention.

explanation: Asked why have a policy that creates barriers. She contests the premise head-on ("I refute the claim that this creates barriers"), then says what the policy is for and points to the 75-place medical quota. Denying the premise and explaining the alternative is engagement with the question, not a dodge; the truth of the denial is a Veracity matter and does not move this score.
question: Why, then, have a policy that creates barriers and hurdles for the proper resettling of asylum seekers and refugees when some of the events that they’re escaping create those serious health conditions that she just spoke about?
statement: I refute the claim that this creates barriers. What it is actually doing is ensuring that those medical needs can be fully assessed and services provided to meet those needs. As I’ve said, there have been none in the last two years that have resulted in a barrier, and, in addition, there is a separate medical refugee quota category of 75 places per annum, which will accommodate those high needs that would not meet the criteria.

explanation: A narrow factual ask — does she accept at least 46 declines across the quota and family reunification categories — plus a fairness follow-on. The 46 figure is neither confirmed nor denied nor addressed at all. The fairness limb gets an implicit defence ("that is a barrier for health considerations"), which is the only reason this is not near zero. Dodging a specific number counts heavily against.
question: Does she accept that at least 46 people have also been declined on medical grounds across the refugee quota programme and the refugee quota family reunification category, and, if so, does she think that is fair or justified?
statement: As has been stated on numerous occasions, in this category we have to balance the needs of New Zealand’s health system and ensure that we are able to meet the needs of those people, and in some circumstances there will be considerations that will mean they don’t meet the criteria. That is not a barrier for disabled people; that is a barrier for health considerations.

explanation: Asked whether she thinks a refugee with renal issues should face resettlement delays, and if not why the policy applies. She gives neither: "All I can say, again, is that there is a limited health assessment" restates the process already described and asserts it will stand. The opinion asked for is never offered and the why is not re-engaged.
question: Does she think a refugee with renal issues should face delays to be able to properly resettle in Aotearoa after escaping genocide, and, if not, why is the acceptable standard-of-health policy applied to refugees seeking residency visas?
statement: All I can say, again, is that there is a limited health assessment applied to assess the needs of those who are entering the refugee programme. That assessment will stand and is an important part of the process.

explanation: A confirm-or-deny question about whether kidney failure or cancer could delay residency. She queries which programme is meant and then falls back to "there is a process that needs to be followed" — no confirmation, no denial. The clarification request is a sliver of engagement, but the yes/no core is avoided and the answer is explicitly a repetition ("yet again").
question: Can she confirm, then, that people facing issues such as kidney failure could face delays for residency applications that could delay their proper resettlement in Aotearoa, or for conditions such as cancer?
statement: Mr Speaker, it’s unclear whether he’s asking about the refugee programme or a migration programme, but, as I’ve stated—yet again—there is a process that needs to be followed to ensure that the medical needs of those who are in the programme are assessed.

explanation: Asked what he recently announced on roadside drug testing; he states the Monday announcement — legislation this year enabling roadside oral fluid testing. Directly and completely responsive to what was asked.
question: What recent announcements has he made on roadside drug testing?
statement: On Monday, I announced that our Government will introduce legislation this year to enable roadside drug testing as part of our commitment to improve road safety and restore law and order. Oral fluid testing is common overseas and it’s an easy way to screen for drugs at the roadside. Our approach will bring New Zealand in line with Australian legislation and will remove unnecessary barriers that have delayed the fight against drug-driving.

explanation: Asked what advice he has seen on the impacts of drug-driving. He supplies the substance of that advice — alcohol and drugs as the top contributing factor, 200 fatal crashes in 2022 — and so engages the question, though he never separates the drug component from alcohol and drifts into the policy response. The drift, not any judgment about detail or accuracy, is what keeps this off the top.
question: What advice has he seen on the impacts of drug-driving?
statement: Alcohol and drugs are the number one contributing factor in fatal road crashes in New Zealand. In 2022 alone, alcohol and drugs were contributors to 200 fatal crashes on our roads. That is why our Government is introducing legislation to enable roadside drug testing, will set targets for police to undertake 50,000 oral fluid tests each year.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen; he opens "I have seen reports that" and names them — the 2022 legislation's evidentiary-standard problem, the Police Association and AA responses. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What reports has he seen on roadside drug testing in New Zealand?
statement: I have seen reports that despite legislation being passed in 2022 to enable roadside drug testing, roadside testing has not been rolled out as the legislation required the test to be suitable for evidentiary purposes and not just for a screening intent. The Police Association said this was “really disappointing” and the Automobile Association said that the failed roll-out was “another blow to road safety”. Our Government will pass workable legislation to target the highest contributing factors to fatal road crashes.

explanation: Asked how the new legislation will differ from the 2022 regime. He states the difference directly: screening-purpose oral fluid tests at the roadside with laboratory testing for evidentiary purposes, versus the old requirement that roadside tests themselves be evidentiary.
question: How will the Government’s legislation differ to roadside drug-testing legislation passed in 2022?
statement: Our roadside drug-testing regime will use oral fluid testing devices at the roadside, for screening purposes. If two oral fluid tests are positive, then an oral fluid sample will be tested in a laboratory for evidentiary purposes. This differs to the previous roadside drug-testing regime, which required tests at the roadside to be used for evidentiary purposes and resulted in police being unable to roll out roadside drug testing.
