question: What actions is the Government taking to reduce harm caused by gangs and make communities safer?
statement: The Government is taking action to reduce harm caused by gangs by progressing legislation that will reduce the ability of gangs to operate and cause fear, intimidation, and disruption to the public. The Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill, which inched closer to its third reading last night, is a significant step in making our communities safer. Gangs peddle misery and cause fear and intimidation, and this Government is taking the safety of the public seriously.

explanation: Asked for examples of gang-caused fear and intimidation; he supplies a concrete one (the Tokoroa "we don't really wear red" remark) and explains why he reads it as fear. The question asked for an example and an example was given.
question: What examples, if any, has he heard of the fear, intimidation, and disruption that gangs cause in our communities?
statement: Well, I heard an example from a member of Parliament from the Greens last night saying, “we don’t really wear red in Tokoroa, and that’s just the way things are.”, and the only reason why people wouldn’t wear a particular colour in a particular place is because of fear of the consequences—ultimately, fear of violence. No New Zealanders should live in fear, and that’s why this Government is intending to ban the display of gang insignia and is passing this piece of legislation.

explanation: Asked for a further example; he gives a second, distinct one (the Whangārei "don't wear red" remark). Squarely answers the follow-up as put.
question: What other examples has the Minister heard of the fear, the intimidation, and disruption that gangs cause in our communities?
statement: Well, I heard another example from another member of Parliament, also from the Greens, last night. It said, “I know, just like in Tokoroa, don’t wear red. Don’t wear red in Whangārei”, and, like I said before, no New Zealanders should be living in fear. The Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill will provide extra tools for the police to deal effectively with gangs.

explanation: A "why" question answered with reasons: 51 percent growth in gang membership and 33 percent growth in violent crime over six years. Whether those figures are accurate is Veracity's business; as a response, it lands directly on what was asked.
question: Why is the Government taking action against the fear, intimidation, and disruption that gangs cause in our communities?
statement: Well, because gang membership increased by 51 percent in the previous six years and, at the same time, violent crime in our communities had gone up by 33 percent. New Zealanders should be able to go about their normal lives without fear of being intimidated or preyed upon by organised crime. If that means banning the presence of gangs and gang patches in public, this Government is quite happy to justify that so people can expect to go about their lives in safety.

explanation: A two-part factual question answered part by part — "To the first part, yes" concedes the 2 August advice outright, and the second part is met with a counter-account (the Minister spoke to officials first thing Monday). It engages the delay allegation head-on, though it never quite settles whether Monday morning preceded the matter becoming public, leaving a sliver of the question unresolved.
question: Is it correct that he was advised of Health New Zealand’s plan to block early access to the cancer drug Keytruda on Friday, 2 August, and that he did not take action to address this issue until after it was made public?
statement: To the first part, yes. To the second part, first thing on Monday morning, the Minister spoke with health officials regarding this issue. I’m pleased to see that Health New Zealand has taken a pragmatic approach informed by clinical advice to deliver these treatments, thanks to the Government’s transformative investment to deliver up to 26 cancer treatments.

explanation: Asked how much advice he needs to see that blocking access to the drug is a bad idea. The reply relocates the decision to Health New Zealand's clinicians and expresses confidence in them, which rejects the question's premise without ever engaging the question itself. It contests the framing rather than pivoting to unrelated talking points, so it sits above a pure dodge, but no answer is given.
question: Well, how much advice does he need in order to recognise that blocking early access to a life-saving cancer drug is a bad idea?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, these decisions are clinical decisions made by Health New Zealand, and he has faith in Health New Zealand to come up with pragmatic solutions based upon clear clinical advice.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: is it correct that officials thought the delay was acceptable because expectations were not set? Answered "no" — a flat denial with no elaboration, but it engages the question squarely and completely. Brevity and unhelpfulness are not evasion.
question: Is it correct that Health New Zealand officials had the impression that the delay in implementation of the Government’s flagship health policy was acceptable because he failed to set clear expectations on delivery?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, no.

explanation: Two parts: (a) do the OIA documents show work was not progressed to a Cabinet paper until public backlash, and (b) don't New Zealanders deserve a Minister who will fight for them. The response explicitly answers only the second, rhetorical part, and does so with talking points about "transformative investment". The factual core — the timing shown in the documents — is never touched.
question: Is it correct that documents released under the Official Information Act show he did not progress work on his original promise to fund cancer medicines to a Cabinet paper until public backlash against the Budget, and don’t New Zealanders deserve a Minister that will fight for better healthcare for them?
statement: In answer to the second part of the question, they deserve a Minister that will fight for better health outcomes, and this Minister is fighting for better health outcomes by delivering a transformative investment in cancer treatments for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what recent passport announcements had been made. The answer states the announcement directly: wait times halved, five weeks down from a peak of ten. Directly and completely on the question asked.
question: What recent announcements has she made about passports?
statement: I was pleased to announce yesterday that wait times for New Zealand passports have halved, and New Zealanders should now allow up to five weeks for a standard New Zealand passport, down from a peak of 10 weeks. I’ve been advised that many passports are being issued faster than this time frame as well. The recent delay in passport wait times was caused by a software upgrade in March. Since then, the department and I have been focused on reducing passport processing times as a top priority. Getting passport wait times down to the standard two weeks continues to be a priority for me. I want to provide Kiwi families and businesses with certainty on how long it will take to receive their passport.

explanation: Asked what benefits New Zealanders have received from the passport system upgrade. The answer enumerates benefits — single online group form, online lost/stolen reporting, online referee verification. Squarely responsive.
question: What benefits have New Zealanders received from the upgrade to the passport system?
statement: The new system allows families applying as a group to use one online form, rather than multiple paper ones. Kiwi families are making good use of this feature, as 91 percent of passports last month were applied for online and 32 percent of these were group applications. The upgrade also makes it easier to report a lost or stolen passport, and allows referees to verify an applicant’s identity online, rather than through a phone call. This is the largest upgrade to the passport system in over a decade.

explanation: Asked how New Zealanders can ensure passports arrive in time. The answer gives the two actions asked for: apply early, and submit a compliant photo. Direct and complete.
question: How can New Zealanders ensure they get their passports in time for their overseas trips?
statement: The top action New Zealanders can take to ensure they get their passport on time is to apply as soon as they start planning an overseas trip and, secondly, it’s to make sure that the photo they send through is of a good quality and meets the requirements. For context, 11,598 photos were rejected by the Passport Office in February alone this year, which delays the application process. There is an online photo checker available to use on the passport website, and, remember, selfies are not accepted.

explanation: Two parts: does she stand by the Budget description, and how is Oranga Tamariki ensuring no reduction in front-line provision. The first is answered "yes" outright; the second is engaged — the mechanism given is clawback of unspent contract money and re-funding based on prior delivery. It reaches the question, though the assurance about front-line provision is asserted more than explained.
question: Does she stand by the Government’s Budget description of the Oranga Tamariki Contracting Service Costs savings initiative that “This initiative improves the efficiency of service delivery, with no reduction in frontline services”; if so, how is Oranga Tamariki ensuring no reduction in frontline service provision?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes, and in answer to the second part of the question, that savings initiative is money Oranga Tamariki expects will be returned where a provider has been funded and services have not been delivered. Previously, organisations were allowed to sit on funding, even if they weren’t using it. Now, where services and outcomes are not delivered, Oranga Tamariki will be asking for the money back. I think taxpayers would be alarmed to learn that this was not happening in the past. In terms of front-line service provision, what is happening is where contracts are being changed, it is because this Government is making sure that funding is delivering outcomes for children and young people and that taxpayers are getting value for money. Where organisations have not delivered on the full value of their contracts last year, Oranga Tamariki will be funding them this year based on that prior delivery. Going forward, we will be funding these organisations that are delivering outcomes for children, and not funding those who don’t.

explanation: Asked to reconcile the no-reduction commitment with Family Start Nelson losing staff after a funding cut. The answer takes on that specific provider and gives the reconciliation: the FTE reduction (12.75 to 10) follows measured underdelivery against contract. It does not address the 40 percent / $14 million figures in the question, so it engages the case without fully meeting the numbers put to it.
question: How does she reconcile this commitment to no reduction in front-line services with Family Start losing 40 percent of their front-line staff due to their funding being cut by $14 million per year, compromising their ability to support at-risk infants in Nelson?
statement: I would like to refer to a media release released this morning by Oranga Tamariki, speaking to specifically this provider. For example, He Matapuna Ora, the Family Start provider in Nelson, stated they are in the top four performing Family Start providers in the country. Based on their own quarterly reports and our internal review of all Family Start contracts between 2022 and January 2024, they achieved, on average, 80 percent of the whānau volumes, lower numbers of home visits than were expected, and based on this information, we have reduced their fulltime-equivalents (FTEs) from 12.75 to 10. At one point, He Matapuna Ora reported in previous financial years that they had had 17 FTEs, despite being contracted for 12.75.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees that whānau workers are front-line workers and, if not, for her definition of front-line services. Neither is answered — the response redirects to the previous answer about delivery volumes. Both branches of a narrow question left untouched, which is a clear dodge.
question: Does she agree with Family Start Nelson manager Rebecca Ravenscroft, who said, “our whānau workers are frontline workers, they are in the homes of these whānau and whenever they visit they have to sight the baby so they are definitely frontline workers”, and, if not, what is the Minister’s definition of front-line services?
statement: I’ll refer to the previous answer where I stated that this organisation, in particular, only met 80 percent of the whānau volumes and lower numbers of visits than were expected. So that money that was not delivered on will be redirected to a front-line service that can deliver that.

explanation: Asked whether the Family Start Nelson cut meets her expectations for the savings initiative, and if not why. Answered directly: "it does meet my expectation", with the reason (unspent money redirected). The "if not, why" branch is moot given the yes. Ignoring the 42 percent mortality evaluation cited in the question weakens the reasoning but not the engagement — that is Rigor, not Forthrightness.
question: Does cutting funding for Family Start Nelson meet her expectations for Oranga Tamariki’s savings initiative, when evaluation found that their programme reduced overall post-neonatal mortality in the first year of life by 42 percent, and, if not, why is Family Start facing these cuts?
statement: I think I’ve actually answered part of that in my previous answers, but what I would say is it does meet my expectation if money cannot sit in these organisations’ bank accounts that’s not being spent when it could be redirected to organisations that could be delivering a service for our young people.

explanation: Asked to recommit to no reduction in front-line services and, if so, how the gaps already created will be filled. The response asserts the substance of the recommitment ("not reducing front-line services") and addresses the gap question by disputing the premise — savings are redirected, some providers up, some down. Engaged, but it never quite delivers the recommitment as asked and answers the gap question by denying gaps exist.
question: Will she recommit, as the Government did in the Budget, to there being no reduction in front-line services because of the $120 million of cuts to Oranga Tamariki - contracted services, and, if so, how will Oranga Tamariki fill the gaps already created by these cuts?
statement: Overall, the Government and Oranga Tamariki are not reducing front-line services. Savings coming from getting money back where it hasn’t been used are redirected to other front-line services. Separate to this, what we are doing, unlike previously, is reviewing contracts and making sure we are getting what we pay for. Changes have been made based on previous utilisation and delivery, and where demands and needs have changed in particular regions, Oranga Tamariki has also looked at where there is duplication of services in the same areas. This means some providers will see a decrease in funding and others will see an increase. Funding does not equal delivery. As we saw under previous years, you can throw more and more money at a problem, but unless you demand results, things can get worse.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the "abject disaster" statement and, if so, why. Answered "yes" and then supplied reasons — deficits across ITP business units, international and domestic enrolment decline, loss of regional decision rights. Both parts met head-on.
question: Meitaki, Mr Speaker. Kia orana koutou katoatoa. Does she stand by her statement that “the previous government’s Te Pūkenga mega-merger has been nothing but an abject disaster”; if so, why?
statement: Yes, and to name a few reasons why, in 2023 all previous Institutes of Technology and Polytechnics of New Zealand (ITPs) individual business units recorded deficits, with at least three recording deficits in excess of $20 million and all but two previous ITP individual business units forecasting deficits in 2025. Further, international student numbers recovery for Te Pūkenga is behind universities, is behind schools, and is behind language schools. Overseas, no one knows what Te Pūkenga is. Further, Te Pūkenga has overseen a 9 percent decline in domestic enrolments. Polytechnics are unable to make decisions about their domestic and international fees. ITPs have been unable to make decisions that meet regional needs of their communities.

explanation: Asked how stopping construction of schools/hospitals/houses helps the economy. The response contests the premise directly ("we're not stopping the construction"), which is a legitimate engagement, but then leaves the actual question — the economic case — untouched and pivots to inherited-recession talking points. Partial engagement via premise denial only.
question: How does stopping the construction of schools, hospitals, and houses, when 6,000 people in the construction industry have lost their jobs, help the economy?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, we’re not stopping the construction; we are actually getting on and fixing the fundamentals in this economy. We inherited an economy that was in recession, interest rates that were at record highs, and inflation was well outside the bounds. The previous Government was addicted to spending. We are turning this country around, unlike the mess we got left behind.

explanation: A narrow factual question: what estimates of the cost of lost rail freight capability has the Minister received? The response never says whether any estimate was received, redirecting to the ferries still operating and being certified to 2029. It disputes the framing rather than answering; a specific factual ask squarely avoided.
question: What estimates has she received of the cost to New Zealand businesses and the economy of the loss of rail capability on the Interislander ferries, given those ferries currently carry over half a million metres of train freight per year?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, I’m not sure if she has realised, but the ferries are still operating, providing freight services between the North and South Islands. What we are doing is going through a process to secure their resilience into the future, but, as KiwiRail has made very clear, those ferries are safe to operate until at least 2029.

explanation: Asked whether health delivery is failing because named clinics are unstaffed overnight. The response mentions none of the clinics, gives no yes or no, and consists entirely of blame for the previous Government's restructure. Complete pivot to talking points.
question: Are they not delivering in health because her Government is leaving clinics like those in Dargaville, Wellsford, Kenepuru, Napier, and Rotorua unstaffed overnight?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, we have inherited a mess when it comes to our health system, and this Government has a plan to turn it around; unlike the previous Government, who decided the best time to reorganise the health system was during the middle of a pandemic. It’s unbelievable the mess that was left behind and the challenges that this Government is having to clean up, but, unlike them, we’ve got a plan.

explanation: Two-part question: is Tākai a "cash cow", and what would the Minister say to the parents who used it? The response never mentions Tākai or the parents at all, offering only generic inherited-mess rhetoric. Nothing of the question is engaged.
question: Does she believe that Tākai, which has shut down because of her cuts after 20 years of social service, is a cash cow, and what does she say to the tens of thousands of parents who have benefited from their support?
statement: Again, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, we have inherited a number of challenges as a Government, which we are having to clean up with the mess left behind by the previous Government. They were spending like drunken sailors, they were borrowing, they had interest rates and inflation through the roof, and this Government has been elected to fix this economy, to ensure our public services are delivering on the front line for New Zealanders, but we have a huge mess to clean up.

explanation: Asked how a $216 million tobacco tax break helps the economy. The response flags "a range of assumptions in that particular question" — a gesture at contesting the premise, but it is never spelled out — then moves to smoking rates and an attack on the previous Government. The tax break's economic justification is never addressed.
question: How does giving the tobacco industry a $216 million tax break, leaving less money for health, help the economy?
statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, there was a range of assumptions in that particular question, but what we are very focused on is reducing smoking rates. We’ve got a plan to address that on this side of the House, but we’ve also got a range of challenges that we need to sort out, and we’ve been elected to fix it. If that last Government were still in charge, they’d be spending more, they’d be taxing more, and delivering less.

explanation: Asked what steps the Government is taking to support jobseekers into work. The response enumerates steps: phone case management for 4,000 young jobseekers, 2,100 extra community-led places, mandatory work check-in seminars at two weeks and six months. Directly and completely on the question.
question: What steps is the Government taking to support people on the jobseeker benefit into work?
statement: The coalition Government has delivered a series of initiatives to support job seekers into work. Recently, we established a new over-the-phone case management service for 4,000 young job seekers and expanded the number of places for young job seekers in community-led employment programmes with coaching, by 2,100. We have also introduced work check-in seminars that job seekers must attend within two weeks of coming on to benefit and again after six months. Our Government is working hard to make changes to the welfare system to ensure New Zealanders are able to reap the rewards and opportunities of work.

explanation: Asked for the key features of the announced community coaching. The response names them — funding to proven community organisations, needs assessment, job plan, tailored support including job coaching. Answers what was asked.
question: What are the key features of the community coaching the Minister has announced as part of the Government’s Welfare that Works?
statement: This is our Government’s new approach that will see more funding for community organisations with a proven track record of supporting young people off welfare. This will see more young people getting a needs assessment, a job plan, and tailored support, including job coaching, to help them access employment opportunities. This programme highlights our Government’s commitment to putting young people on a pathway to a better future through work.

explanation: Asked why He Poutama Rangatahi providers were chosen for the programme. The response gives an actual reason: 77 percent of participants are Māori and Māori jobseeker numbers are rising, so the provider targets the group of concern. The "why" is engaged, with a preamble of background before reaching it.
question: Why has the Minister chosen He Poutama Rangatahi providers for this programme?
statement: Five hundred places for the community-led programmes will be with a selection of He Poutama Rangatahi which was launched by the previous National Government in 2017 for people aged 18 to 24 who have been on jobseeker support longer than a year. We know that 77 percent of participants in this programme are Māori. I am concerned about the increasing number of Māori job seekers. Community coaching delivered through He Poutama Rangatahi will help young Māori improve their employment opportunities and reach their potential.

explanation: Asked why additional jobseeker support is needed now. The response answers with the reason — jobseeker numbers forecast to rise until January 2025 and vulnerability to tougher labour market conditions, hence acting now. Squarely responsive.
question: Why is additional support for job seekers needed now?
statement: The challenging economic situation we have inherited inevitably means that job seeker numbers were expected to increase until January 2025, before decreasing. We know job seekers are vulnerable to tougher labour market conditions, which is why our Government is working hard to make our welfare system proactive in helping as many job seekers as possible in the current economic climate. Even though we have a challenging economic environment, our Government will not stand by and allow New Zealanders to languish on welfare and waste their potential. We are acting now to support job seekers into work so they can experience the independence and opportunities that work provides.

explanation: Asked whether unemployment figures show New Zealand is back on track, and if not why not. The response asserts the country is getting back on track and supplies a causal explanation for rising unemployment (inherited low-growth economy), so the "why not" limb is engaged, but it never confronts what the figures themselves show. Partial: answers around the core rather than at it.
question: Do recent unemployment figures show New Zealand is back on track; if not, why not?
statement: Our coalition Government is getting New Zealand back on track, and, as I’ve acknowledged before, too many New Zealanders have been denied the independence and opportunities that work provides. We’ve inherited a low-growth economy from the previous Government, which, unfortunately, means rising unemployment. That’s why we’re implementing a more proactive welfare system to support people off benefit and into work. In the six years before we took over, the number of people receiving the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent.

explanation: Asked how the country can be "back on track" when 1,000 more people are out of work each month. The response offers a reason for the job losses — the inherited economy — which engages the tension, but never reconciles it with the "back on track" claim the question targets. Answers half of what was put.
question: How can New Zealand be back on track when, on average, every month since she’s been in office there’s been an additional 1,000 people out of work?
statement: As I explained, unfortunately we inherited an economy that saw the previous Government absolutely mismanage the economy, and, unfortunately, New Zealanders are paying the price. For every New Zealander that loses a job right now, it comes back to the broken economy that we inherited and the damage that that side did.

explanation: Asked whether Māori employment rates are back on track given the rise from 8.2 to 9.1 percent. No yes or no is given, but the response engages the substance — conceding unemployment is rising and jobseeker numbers are getting worse, while attributing it to inherited conditions. An implicit concession rather than a clean answer or a clean dodge.
question: Does the Minister consider Māori employment rates to be back on track when, under her watch, in just nine months, Māori unemployment has increased from 8.2 percent to 9.1 percent?
statement: Unfortunately, the economic conditions that we have inherited mean rising unemployment. We have seen the unemployment rate rise—fortunately not as far as those forecast—and the job seeker numbers are, of course, getting worse. That is the reality of the economy we have inherited. Our job is to fix it. That’s exactly what we are doing, because we want to see more New Zealanders and more Māori in work.

explanation: Asked why her own officials' regulatory impact statement ranks her preferred option as 'worse' than the status quo on system sustainability and learner/employer needs. The answer never touches the RIS ranking at all — it points to a consultation document, cites 'a range of advice' and 30 years in the sector, and invites submissions. The core of the question (the officials' adverse assessment) is untouched. Process talking points in place of an answer.
question: Why, then, in the regulatory impact statement prepared by her own officials, does the Minister’s preferred option rank as “worse” than the status quo when it comes to system sustainability and to learner and employer needs?
statement: There is a consultation document out at the moment for the sector to give their thoughts on. I have taken a range of advice and, as well, I have relied on the over 30 years that I’ve spent in the sector, and so options are there for the sector to submit on.

explanation: Asked why the RIS ranks her preferred option 'much worse' on implementation cost and complexity and worse overall. The response is a set-piece on regional access to vocational education and the Open Polytechnic supporting smaller regional polytechnics. It never mentions cost, complexity, or the RIS ranking. A narrow, document-anchored question answered with unrelated advocacy.
question: Why, in the regulatory impact statement prepared by her own officials, does the Minister’s preferred option rank as “much worse” than the status quo when it comes to implementation cost and complexity, and ranks her preferred option overall as “worse” than the status quo?
statement: This Government is very focused on ensuring that all regions have access to vocational education and training. We understand that it is a pathway to employment for individuals such as school leavers and those returning to the workforce. It is absolutely critical that options that we look at ensure that regional delivery can occur. The proposal that is out for consultation enables the Open Polytechnic to support those smaller regional polytechnics to be able to maintain that level of provision.

explanation: Asked why she is ignoring the advice of her seven specialist advisers who told her to keep the Te Pūkenga model. She engages squarely: she contests the premise (they were Te Pūkenga's advisers, not hers) and then answers the substance — they gave a range of options and the one being consulted on was among them, i.e. she is not ignoring them. Whether that is true is Veracity's problem; the question was met head-on rather than dodged. Marked below full because the 'why' behind choosing that option over their recommendation is left implicit.
question: Why is she ignoring the advice of her seven specialist advisers, who—at a cost of $2,000 a day each—told her to keep the Te Pūkenga model with some regional groupings?
statement: Well, I would note that they were not my specialist advisers. They were Te Pūkenga’s specialist advisers, and they gave a range of options, of which the option that we are consulting on was one. [Interruption]

explanation: A two-part question: why she told RNZ the advice had been proactively released when it had not, and when it will be released. Both parts are actually answered — she says she noted it 'would be' released and was unsure whether it had been (an explanation of the discrepancy), and gives a timeframe of 'the next week'. The tail then drifts into an unrelated Te Pūkenga surplus recitation, but the padding comes after the answer rather than instead of it, so it does not convert this into a dodge.
question: Why did she tell Radio New Zealand—RNZ—that she had proactively released the advice she received from her seven specialist advisers when she has done no such thing, and when will she release the advice?
statement: I noted that it would be proactively released. I wasn’t sure if it had been or not, and I understand that it’s due to be proactively released in the next week. I would note, again, that they were not my specialist advisers, but I would also note that under a new chief executive at Te Pūkenga, who has experience in and understanding of the sector; a new chair; and a clear set of expectations from this Minister, Te Pūkenga is at last undertaking the cost-out work and is forecasting a year-to-date surplus for the six months to 30 June 2024 of $28.5 million.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on Local Water Done Well. He names the announcement made that morning with his colleague on the enduring components of water service delivery. That is the thing asked for. The self-congratulation and jab at the Opposition are Focus/Civility issues, not evasion — the question was answered before them.
question: What recent announcements has he made on Local Water Done Well?
statement: This morning, my colleague the Hon Andrew Bayly and I shared great news for ratepayers and local government, announcing the enduring components of water service delivery under our Government’s fantastic Local Water Done Well plan. This is about providing local government with the certainty it needs to deliver the water services that Kiwis rely on, while minimising costs for ratepayers. Members on the other side said that Local Water Done Well could not be done, but after just nine months we’ve delivered for communities across our country.

explanation: Asked what the enduring components are. He enumerates them: new models for financially sustainable water organisations, and Local Government Funding Agency financing for water organisations. Directly responsive to the exact thing asked.
question: What are these enduring components of Local Water Done Well?
statement: The enduring components of Local Water Done Well announced today will enable new models for financially sustainable water organisations across the country and financing from the New Zealand Local Government Funding Agency for water organisations, which will reduce the financial burden on ratepayers who were faced with higher rates under three waters.

explanation: Asked what the announcement means for councils. He answers in council terms: access to the lowest-cost financing available to local government, and leverage support up to 500 percent of revenue, roughly twice existing levels. The closing contrast with three waters is Focus, not evasion; the question itself was squarely engaged.
question: What does this mean for councils across the country?
statement: Councils will be pleased with today’s announcement. The New Zealand Local Government Funding Agency provides the lowest cost financing that is available to local government. From today, it will be able to support leverage for water council-controlled organisations (CCOs) up to a level equivalent of 500 percent of revenue—around twice that of existing financing levels for councils, subject to water organisations meeting prudent credit criteria. This would not have happened under the co-governed, mega-entity, three waters model. Our plan restores local ownership, it restores local control of water assets, and it recognises the importance of local decision-making.

explanation: Asked about the financial implications. He addresses them: lower financing costs for councils than under the previous reform, with LGFA lending available immediately. No dollar figures are given, but thinness of detail is Specificity — on the forthrightness axis the question was taken and answered on its own terms.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. What will be the financial implications of this announcement?
statement: Today’s announcement is great news for ratepayers. Local Water Done Well will provide lower costs to New Zealand councils for financing than could have been achieved under the previous Government’s three waters reform, which we swiftly repealed to restore local control of water assets to communities. It will do this with the New Zealand Local Government Funding Agency being able to immediately lend to water CCOs. This financing is available as of today and means that communities will have the flexibility and the tools they need to meet their unique needs.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that the review will not lead to the scheme's disestablishment. He never gives or withholds a guarantee in terms — a plain 'no, I can't guarantee that' would have scored high. What he offers is adjacent: the review is yet to begin and no terms of reference have been decided, which implies the guarantee cannot be given without saying so. Partial credit for that implication, then a pivot to the Health New Zealand merger that leaves the core untouched.
question: Can he guarantee that the proposed review of the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme, which has admitted more than 700 Māori and Pasifika students to medical school in the last 10 years, will not lead to its disestablishment?
statement: As part of our coalition agreement with ACT, we have agreed to review the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme (MAPAS). This review is yet to begin, and no decisions about terms of reference have been made. That’s because we have been laser-focused on addressing the financial challenges left to us by the botched merger of Health New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the associate minister's 'lazily looking at everyone through the lens of race' characterisation. He explicitly substitutes a different question — 'what I do agree with is the review of MAPAS' — and closes with a rhetorical question of his own. The specific proposition he was asked to endorse or disown is stepped around by construction. A textbook answer to a question that was not asked.
question: Does he agree with the associate health Minister that the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme is an example of “lazily looking at everyone through the lens of race”?
statement: Well, on behalf of the health Minister, what I do agree with is the review of MAPAS in line with the coalition agreement. When you think about it, what is wrong with reviewing a programme to ensure it’s meeting its objectives?

explanation: Two things asked: does he still hold his stated belief about culturally competent care, and what is the plan to get more Māori doctors into the workforce. Neither is reached. The reply asserts the Government does not accept poor Māori health outcomes and is focused on lifting outcomes for all New Zealanders — a generality that never revisits the quoted belief and never describes a workforce plan.
question: Does he still believe that “if you’re treated in a culturally competent context, you get a better outcome.”, and, if so, what is his plan to get more Māori doctors into the workforce, following the review?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, we don’t accept the poor outcomes for Māori in health, unlike the last Government. That’s why we’re focused on ensuring we lift health outcomes for all New Zealanders, including Māori and Pasifika and our communities in need.

explanation: A yes/no question on whether she agrees with the Prime Minister's statement, with 'if not, why not'. The answer opens with an unambiguous 'Yes' and then confirms the specific elements — recession, health system, education. The subsequent list of Government fixes and the swipe at the Opposition are Focus and Civility matters; the question itself was answered completely in the first word.
question: Meitaki maata, Mr Speaker. Does she agree with the Prime Minister’s statement, “This is a country where our economy is in real trouble. This is a country where we cannot deliver health and education services as well as we need to”; if not, why not?
statement: Yes. We inherited an economy in recession, a broken health system following a botched merger, and an education system that has been failing too many children for too long. But good news: we have got a plan to turn things around. We’re fixing education, we’re fixing health, we’re growing the economy, we’re reining in wasteful spending, and we’re reducing the amount spent on external consultants, unlike members opposite, who seemed to outsource—

explanation: Asked whether Pacific employment is on track given unemployment rose 6%→8.3% under her watch. The Minister never addresses the figure or the 'on track' claim; she pivots to what the Government 'won't do' and attacks the questioner's own record. Pure dodge.
question: Does the Minister consider Pacific employment rates to be back on track when, under her watch, in just nine months, Pacific unemployment has increased from 6 percent to 8.3 percent?
statement: I can tell that member what this Government won’t do with Pacific unemployment: we will not oversee an increase in six years of 93 percent in Pacific unemployment—that’s outrageous, and that’s your record.

explanation: Asked how she can say youth employment is on track when youth unemployment rose 15.1%→20.7%. She opens by needling the questioner, then talks about long-term welfare dependency and 'taking action' — the specific figure and the 'on track' assertion are never engaged. A faint gesture at the topic keeps it above zero.
question: Can the Minister tell us how she can say youth employment is on track when recent figures show that youth unemployment has increased from 15.1 percent to 20.7 percent just in the last June quarter of 2024?
statement: I’m pleased that that member is finally interested in youth unemployment, because what we saw, unfortunately, was a welfare system stagnating so much that a young person who goes on to benefit under the age of 25 now is forecast to spend two decades on welfare. That’s the record of that member. We’re not standing by to watch it, which is why we are taking action.

explanation: Asked whether she has any plan to get people into work. She answers squarely with the plan: the 50,000-by-2030 target, sanctions regime, two-week and six-month work check-ins, expanded case management, He Poutama Rangatahi. The Australia jibe is rhetorical and needs no reply. Not fully 1.0 only because the answer is asserted rather than tied back to the trajectory implied by the question.
question: Does the Minister have any plan to get people into work, or is she just planning for the figures to get better once a whole lot of Kiwis move to simple, old Australia?
statement: I’m very proud to again put on record the changes this Government has made to reduce the number of job seekers by 50,000 by 2030. We have made sure that the sanctions regime is utilised and people are clear about their obligations to look for work. We have introduced a work check-in within two weeks of someone going on to the jobseeker benefit, and again after six months. We have increased case management, and, for young people, 4,000 young people will now get case management over the phone. We have also, last week, increased the number of young people that will get access to the very successful He Poutama Rangatahi programme launched by National in 2017, including community coaching.

explanation: Asked why the Government is reviewing earthquake-prone building legislation. After a 'back on track' preamble, the reason is actually given: owners cannot meet deadlines because of remediation costs and layered regulation, so the review was brought forward to balance safety against real-world cost. Answered, with some padding.
question: Why is the Government reviewing the earthquake-prone building legislation?
statement: Our Government is focused on rebuilding the economy as part of our broader aim of getting New Zealand back on track. The earthquake-prone building system attempts to manage risk by requiring earthquake-prone buildings to be remediated by set time frames. However, many building owners are currently unable to meet deadlines due to high remediation costs and excessive layering of regulations. This is why we have acted with urgency to bring forward the review to provide certainty and ensure we have a good balance between protecting lives and real-world costs.

explanation: Asked when the review will begin. Answered directly — it is already under way, with the Amendment Bill having its first reading that afternoon. Direct and complete.
question: When will the review into earthquake-prone building legislation begin?
statement: We are moving at pace and the review is under way as we speak. This very afternoon, in fact, the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill will have its first reading in this very House. The bill extends the remediation deadlines for earthquake-prone buildings by four years to give temporary relief to Kiwis while the review is under way.

explanation: Asked what the review will focus on. Four foci are enumerated plus the report-back timing. A complete, on-point answer.
question: What will the review focus on?
statement: The review will be extensive and report back in the first half of 2025, with four key foci. The first is the costs of mitigating earthquake risk and improving buildings resilience; the second, proposals for managing earthquake risk, including the effect on private property owners; the third, barriers and the types of incentives that would help building owners better manage seismic risk; and, fourth, changes that align with broader Government objectives, such as going for housing growth and rebuilding the economy.

explanation: Asked how the public can have their say. Answered with the specific channels: the building.govt.nz website, the MBIE email address, and the select committee process.
question: How can the public have their say?
statement: The public can provide feedback and share their views on the earthquake-prone building system via the building.govt.nz website or by emailing building@mbie.govt.nz or, of course, via the select committee process. This is all about listening to Kiwis to ensure that we have rules that work for them.

explanation: Asked what evidence substantiates her 'cash cow' statement. She supplies evidence directly: $22 million recovered for undelivered services, accumulated provider surpluses, and a lawyer's email. Whether that evidence is adequate or true is Veracity/Rigor, not Forthrightness — the question was engaged head-on.
question: What evidence does she have to substantiate her statement, “For too many years, Oranga Tamariki has been the cash cow for community service providers who say they will provide services, and then don’t”?
statement: I refer the member to the $22 million Oranga Tamariki has already recovered from the last financial year where services weren’t delivered, with more expected to come. In previous years, some providers have accumulated significant surpluses and this is unacceptable. Every cent of taxpayer funding that providers receive needs to reach the children and young people for its intended purpose, not sit idle in their bank accounts. I also refer the member to an email I received this morning from a lawyer who works in this space, who said, “I have been appalled over the past few years at how much taxpayer money has been wasted on agencies that make big claims yet deliver nothing but a glorified babysitting service.” This is a Government that is making sure that that money will be used where it is needed, with organisations that are struggling for funding when it’s sitting in bank accounts unused.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: does 'nothing more, nothing less' mean preventative family services will no longer be funded? She replies only that she instructed Oranga Tamariki to return to its core purpose, leaving the funding question to be inferred. The core of the question is skirted, though the reply stays on the topic rather than pivoting away.
question: When she stated in her press release, “The funding they provide is for the care and protection of children in state care. Nothing more, nothing less.” when referring to Oranga Tamariki, does this mean that family services that prevent children going into State care will no longer be funded?
statement: I instructed Oranga Tamariki to get back to their core purpose and do their core purpose well, which is in the best interests of children in care and that come to the attention of Oranga Tamariki.

explanation: Asked whether Oranga Tamariki has a role in assisting families at the earliest opportunity. Answered with 'Absolutely' — a complete answer to a yes/no — before broadening to shared responsibility across agencies and society. The expansion neither adds to nor detracts from the direct answer given.
question: Does she consider that Oranga Tamariki has a role in assisting families, whānau, hapū, iwi, and family groups at the earliest opportunity to meet the needs of their children and young persons; if not, who holds this responsibility?
statement: Absolutely, but it’s not just up to Oranga Tamariki to fix this problem; it’s up to all of Government agencies and also society itself. Step up when you see something is wrong with our young people. Speak up when you see something is happening with our young people. Don’t just rely on Government to fix it.

explanation: Asked two things: is she aware the purpose is statutory, and does she intend to repeal it along with section 7AA. Neither is answered; she restates Oranga Tamariki's job in general terms. The repeal question in particular is left entirely untouched.
question: Is she aware that the previous statement is one of the statutory purposes of Oranga Tamariki in the Act, and, if so, does she intend to repeal the purpose of the Oranga Tamariki Act along with section 7AA?
statement: Oranga Tamariki’s job is to protect the children in their care and to make sure they’re protecting any children that come to their attention with reports of concern.

explanation: Asked HOW Oranga Tamariki can meet its early-intervention duty without prevention funding. The answer never touches funding at all — it restates that OT has a responsibility to intervene early, which is the premise of the question, not a response to it. It stays on topic but never reaches the point being pressed.
question: How can Oranga Tamariki fulfil their statutory requirements to act at the earliest opportunity to meet the needs of children and young people if they are not funded to undertake preventative services that would occur before a child or young person enters into State care?
statement: There are many ways a child can come to the attention of Oranga Tamariki, not just being placed into State care. And when a child is brought to the attention of Oranga Tamariki, it is their responsibility to intervene as early as possible.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with a named provider's claim that cuts will end prevention work. She declines plainly rather than filibustering, which is creditable — but she declines by recasting a question about the effect of cuts on prevention into a question about an individual contract, which is not what was asked. A plain refusal to a narrower question than the one put: partial.
question: Does she agree with Zoe Hawke, the chief executive of E Tipu E Rea Whānau who says of the cuts to their services, “The core of our mahi, the core of our work is prevention, preventing uplift … We have prevented so many uplifts, unfortunately we may not be able to do that any longer.”; if not, why not?
statement: I can’t comment on individual contracts without that information in front of me—but if you’d like more information, please put that in writing.

explanation: Asked for a reassurance that uplifts will not rise. "I cannot make guarantees about anything" is a direct no to the thing asked — a refusal that answers. The subsequent pivot to what she can guarantee is talking-point material, but the core was reached first and unambiguously.
question: Can she reassure New Zealanders that there will not be an increase in Oranga Tamariki uplifts as a result of her cuts?
statement: I cannot make guarantees about anything. What I can guarantee is that Oranga Tamariki will get back to their core purpose, which is the care and protection of young people in their care and children that come to their attention. If a child is unsafe and needs care and protection, that’s what will happen.

explanation: Asked what announcement she made about KPIs. She names the letter, the recipient, the reporting cadence and the specific indicators. Complete and direct; the closing rhetoric doesn't displace the answer.
question: What recent announcement has she made regarding key performance indicators for Oranga Tamariki?
statement: This morning, I wrote to the chief executive of Oranga Tamariki, instructing him to report to me every three months on key performance indicators. These include the frequency of social worker visits to children in care, the timeliness of responses to reports of concern, and whether or not caregivers feel supported by Oranga Tamariki. These areas are going to make the biggest difference to the safety and wellbeing of children and young people in care. Too many children in the care of their family or their caregivers die or are abused and neglected every year in this country. It is a national disgrace and I’m not willing to accept it. As Minister for Children, it’s my expectation that Oranga Tamariki is relentlessly focused on its core purpose of ensuring the safety and wellbeing of children in their care.

explanation: Asked why quarterly public reporting is necessary. She gives the reason squarely: existing compliance reports come annually, and quarterly ones surface problems earlier. Directly responsive.
question: Why does the Minister think it’s necessary to have quarterly public reporting on these performance measures?
statement: Oranga Tamariki has oversight from the likes of the Independent Children’s Monitor. However, these compliance reports are only provided to me once a year. Quarterly updates in areas that are most vital to ensuring the safety of children will allow me and the public to identify earlier any areas where Oranga Tamariki is not meeting expectations. This will mean that we can address any issues as they arise, rather than waiting for a yearly report to find out what is going on and needs to be fixed. Providing greater transparency and accountability will give Oranga Tamariki the focus it needs to ensure it’s delivering on its core purpose, which is keeping children and young people safe in their care.

explanation: Asked why accountability and transparency matter. She answers the why directly — the scale of harm means a new approach is needed and public reporting creates focus. A soft patsy question, but it was engaged, not dodged.
question: Why is this accountability and transparency so important?
statement: Clearly, things need to change. When a child is killed every five weeks in this country and so many more are abused and neglected by those who are meant to care for them, then a new approach is desperately needed. By making Oranga Tamariki report every three months and making these reports public, it will give Oranga Tamariki the focus it needs to ensure that it is delivering on its core purpose: keeping children and young people safe.

explanation: Asked why supporting caregivers is a priority. She answers the why directly: many children cannot live at home, caregivers fill that role, and too many report feeling unsupported. On point throughout.
question: Why is supporting caregivers one of the Minister’s priorities?
statement: The reality is that many children and young people are not able to live with their immediate family. For whatever reason, their home is not a safe, loving environment for them. In these circumstances, caregivers, including wider family or whānau, play an essential role. They open up their hearts and their homes to look after our most vulnerable. However, I have heard too many accounts of caregivers who say they do not feel supported by Oranga Tamariki. It is so important that we have skilled and experienced caregivers available for situations where a child is not able to stay in their family home.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by a statement and why. "Yes" plus the itemised debt components. Both halves of the question answered completely.
question: Does she stand by her statement that Te Pūkenga is a “financial mess, drowning in debt of over $250 million”; if so, why?
statement: Yes. Te Pūkenga has $8.426 million of commercial debt, $35.391 million of Crown debt, and $207.311 million of intercompany debt, amounting to a total debt of $251.128 million.

explanation: Asked why she includes intercompany debt in the total. She corrects the figure and then explains the reasoning — reserves from some institutions offsetting others' debt — and asserts it is real debt. That is the question answered on its own terms, whether or not one accepts the accounting.
question: Why is the Minister including the $150.6 million of internal debt, of intercompany borrowings, in that total debt figure?
statement: If I can just help the member on that, it’s $207.311 million of intercompany debt. When Te Pūkenga was set up, different industry training organisations (ITOs) and polytechnics came in with different financial positions. Some came in with reserves; some came in with debt. Those with reserves have had to allow their reserves to go to offset commercial debt that was being held by the other institutions. That is real debt.

explanation: Asked to reconcile the $250m claim with $45.3m of external borrowings. She addresses the gap by pointing again to intercompany debt and adding that it must be dealt with at disestablishment. Largely a repeat of the prior answer, but it does engage the discrepancy rather than sidestep it.
question: Why does she claim that Te Pūkenga is awash with and drowning in debt of over $250 million when, at 30 June 2024, total external borrowings were only $45.3 million?
statement: As I’ve outlined, there is $207.311 million of intercompany debt, which has been taken from reserves of some institutions and applied against the debt that other institutions have. As Te Pūkenga is disestablished, that debt will have to be dealt with. It is real.

explanation: Asked why Crown, non-interest-bearing borrowings count toward the claim. "Debt to the Crown is debt" meets the premise head-on — blunt and thin, but it is a direct answer to the point raised, and the response is cut off by interruption rather than trailing away from the question.
question: Why does she claim that Te Pūkenga is $250 million in debt when, of those total external borrowings, at 30 June 2024, of $45.3 million, $44.6 million is with the Crown and is non-interest bearing and only a tiny portion is external to the Crown?
statement: Debt to the Crown is debt, and so we have significant debt being held—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked to reconcile a $77m deficit told to RNZ with a $28.5m forecast surplus told to the House. She explains that the $28m is a half-year figure and that polytechnic income arrives early in the year — which does account for the two figures coexisting. She never revisits the $77m number itself, so the reconciliation is implied rather than completed.
question: Why did she tell Radio New Zealand this week that Te Pūkenga was running a $77 million deficit when she told the House just yesterday that it is now forecasting a surplus of $28.5 million?
statement: That’s the half-year surplus. So when you run a polytechnic or an ITO your income comes early, your income comes in the first half of the year, your expenditure goes throughout the year. It will bounce around a little bit, but that $28 million was their half-year to date surplus.

explanation: Asked why she is breaking up Te Pūkenga against official advice when it is posting a surplus. She disputes the surplus premise and then gives her actual reason — the business cases required $400-900m to make it operational and she will not spend that on structure rather than tertiary education. That squarely answers the 'why'. She never engages the 'against the advice of officials and her own special advisers' clause, so it is not complete, but the core of the question is reached rather than dodged.
question: Meitaki, Mr Speaker. Why, given that she was advised that the benefits of the Te Pūkenga merger would take at least five years to materialise, is she spending millions and millions, against the advice of Government officials and her own special advisers, breaking up an organisation that is finally posting a surplus?
statement: Te Pūkenga hasn’t posted a surplus yet. However, I can advise the member that in October 2022 a business case was done that was going to require Te Pūkenga to have over $900 million spent on it to make it fully operational. The Minister at the time understandably rejected that. They came back and said, “Oh, well, over five years, it will need over $400 million to be operational.” Again, the Minister understandably rejected that. This is an organisation that would need to have hundreds of millions of dollars spent on it to make it operational, to have its systems interoperable, and I am not prepared to see that sort of money be used on setting up a structure when it should be used on tertiary education.

explanation: Asked what announcements the Government has made on economic regulation of water services. The answer states the announcement directly: a new economic regulation regime for water providers overseen by the Commerce Commission. Direct and complete.
question: What announcements has the Government made regarding the economic regulation of water services?
statement: This morning, the Government announced that it is establishing a new economic regulation regime for water providers, overseen by the Commerce Commission. The new regulatory regime will ensure that water providers invest in the right infrastructure at the right time so that Kiwis can rely on having fresh, clean water at an affordable price.

explanation: Asked what regulatory tools will be available. The answer names them — information disclosure first, then minimum/maximum revenue thresholds, quality standards, performance targets, and price-quality regulation. Exactly the question that was asked.
question: What regulatory tools will be available?
statement: We’ve designed the economic regime to provide the Commerce Commission with a flexible range of regulatory powers. The initial regulatory tool will be the use of what we call information disclosure, which will require water providers to disclose important information such as the nature or state of their infrastructure and their financial situation. The Commerce Commission will also have the ability, if necessary, to set minimum or maximum revenue thresholds, impose quality standards or performance targets, and, ultimately, it could implement price-quality regulation.

explanation: Asked what consumer protections will be put in place. The answer identifies information disclosure covering complaint procedures and customer engagement, and the commission's power to require further protections such as external dispute resolution. Engages the question directly.
question: What consumer protections will be put in place?
statement: The new information disclosure will allow the commission to collect and analyse information relating to consumer protections, such as complaint procedures and customer engagement. If deficiencies are identified, the commission will have the power to require further protections. These could include strengthening complaints procedures or adoption of an external dispute resolution arrangement.

explanation: Asked how the regime will ensure appropriate investment. The answer opens with a jab across the House at Twyford, but that is a Civility/Focus matter and does not count here; the substance then answers the mechanism asked about — revenue is ring-fenced and can only be spent on water infrastructure, not diverted to unrelated activities. The core is reached.
question: How will the economic regulation regime ensure appropriate investment?
statement: But you should have listened, Mr Twyford; that’s the difference. The difference is we’re putting it in place; you talked about it. So an important ingredient is that the economic regime requires that the revenue collected by the water providers will be ring-fenced and only spent on investing in their water infrastructure. In essence, we’re not going to allow spending to be directed into unrelated activities. Local Water Done Well not only keeps water in local ownership and control but also ensures that we get the right level of investment at the right time into our water assets so that Kiwis have access to high-quality, affordable water.

explanation: A two-part question. She answers the first part with an explicit 'yes', and takes on the second directly by rejecting the premise and giving her own account of the figure ($30m a year in recoveries, not a cut). Both halves are engaged head-on; whether her account is correct is Veracity, not this attribute.
question: Does she stand by her statement that “Savings coming from getting money back where it hasn’t been used are redirected to other front-line services”; if so, how is the budget for contracted services being cut by $120 million?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes. In answer to the second part of the question, the member is incorrect. The figure the member is referring to is $30 million a year over four years, which is not a cut. This is the amount Oranga Tamariki has forecast it will be able to recover from providers at the end of a contract period where they have not delivered everything we have paid for. If taxpayers pay for a service and they don’t get it in full, I expect that money to be repaid. If this had been happening over the last six years, there would have been at least $132 million that could have gone to children, rather than letting some providers build up significant surpluses.

explanation: Two parts: what evidence for the 'cash cow' claim, and is it fair to accuse providers. She supplies evidence for the first ($22m already recovered, accumulated surpluses in previous years). The 'do you think it's fair to accuse' half is never answered — she restates the accusation instead of addressing its fairness. Half the question squarely met, half sidestepped.
question: What evidence, if any, does she have to support the claim that “Oranga Tamariki has been the cash cow for community service providers”, and does she think that it’s fair to accuse valued, not-for-profit community providers at the front line of banking funding, instead of caring for at-risk tamariki?
statement: I refer the member to an answer from a previous question today. The member would have heard about the $22 million that Oranga Tamariki has already recovered from the last financial year where services weren’t delivered, with more expected to come. In previous years, providers have accumulated significant surpluses, and this is unacceptable. Every cent of taxpayer funding that providers receive needs to reach the children and young people it is intended for, not sit idle in bank accounts.

explanation: Asked (a) does she accept the Independent Children's Monitor finding, and (b) how can she be confident the 332 providers were fairly evaluated. She never says whether she accepts the finding — the monitor is not mentioned at all — and answers the confidence half only by asserting she instructed a thorough process and believes it was done. Partial engagement: the second half is touched, the first is stepped around entirely.
question: Does she accept the recent finding by the Independent Children’s Monitor that Oranga Tamariki does not have the systems in place to properly monitor their own practices, and, if so, how can she be confident that each of the 332 front-line service providers who have had all or part of their funding cut have been evaluated fairly and accurately?
statement: All decisions are at Oranga Tamariki level, but I instructed Oranga Tamariki to do a thorough process of checking through contracts to make sure we were getting the services that we were paying for and make sure that we were actually targeting the right areas for the care and protection of our young people, and I believe they’ve done so.

explanation: A narrow two-part factual question: will the $14m be redirected, and which comparable Nelson service is being funded. Neither is answered — no yes/no on redirection, and no service named. She pivots to why the provider's funding was adjusted and a general assurance that money will go to a provider that can deliver. The specific core of a narrow question is avoided, which is the worse kind of failure.
question: Will the $14 million cut from Family Start Nelson be redirected to other front-line services, and, if so, which comparable service in Nelson is being funded to fill this gap?
statement: I believe we’ve already spoken about that provider previously, where they did not deliver the full services that they were paid for. Their funding has been adjusted based on the information they provided to Oranga Tamariki, and Oranga Tamariki will make sure that that money is not sitting in a bank account and that it is going to a provider that can actually provide a service.

explanation: She declines plainly — she does not have the information in front of her and asks for the question in writing. A stated refusal or inability to answer, given openly, is forthright rather than a dodge, so this is not scored low for being unhelpful. It falls short of a clean 0.9 refusal because she then appends unrelated boilerplate about taxpayer money instead of leaving the decline to stand, and she gives no answer to the 'if not, why are you comfortable' half.
question: Is she concerned that the cuts to Presbyterian Support South Canterbury’s funding mean that “There will no longer be any free counselling services available within South Canterbury”, and, if not, why is she comfortable with creating these gaps in front-line service provision?
statement: I cannot make an answer on information I don’t currently have in front of me. If that member would like information on that specific question, please put it in writing. But what I would say is we are making sure that every dollar of taxpayer money that is being spent is actually going towards a service that is being provided to our young people who are in the care and protection of, or the attention of, Oranga Tamariki.

explanation: Asked how she can claim savings are redirected when the money goes back into the overall bucket. She answers the premise head-on: that is not what is happening, the money is not going back into the main Budget, it is being redistributed to front-line services. Thin on supporting detail, but detail is Specificity — the question itself is answered without evasion.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. How can she continue to claim that the savings are being redirected to other front-line services when the Government is simply cutting the budget for contracted services by $120 million and putting it back into the overall bucket?
statement: I can stand here and say that because that is not what is happening. That money is not going back into the main Budget; that money is being redistributed back to front-line services.

explanation: A standard 'does he stand by' question, answered with an unambiguous 'Yes'. The trailing partisan gloss about AUKUS and Andrew Little does not detract — the question asked for a position and got one, completely.
question: Mālō e lelei, Mr Speaker. Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, particularly continuing Labour’s work which began in September 2021 on AUKUS Pillar Two, with the help of the honest Hon Andrew Little’s endorsement.

explanation: Asked which of two ministers was correct about keeping the firearms registry. Peters names neither and says the final product is not yet produced. That is a partial engagement — it implies no position is settled — but the binary 'who is correct' put to him is never answered, and it defers to a future occasion.
question: Who is correct: Mark Mitchell, who said on Newstalk ZB this morning that the Government would keep the firearms registry as it is, or Nicole McKee, who said, “The full category A licensing regime is not going to be effective, it’s going to be too costly, and it’s going to make people fearful of their safety.”?
statement: The reality is that the final product has yet to be produced, and Ministers and the Cabinet are working on those. When that’s complete, we’ll be delighted to answer you in full.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: was Mitchell incorrect? The response restates that Cabinet is working on it and is hearing submissions, then adds a jab about cheap political points. The yes/no is squarely avoided; a tight factual question met with process language.
question: So was Mark Mitchell incorrect when he said that the Government would be keeping the firearms registry as it is?
statement: One more time: the Cabinet, alongside the Ministers in charge of this legislation, is working on it at this point in time. We’re hearing submissions. We’re taking as wide as possible a look at this in the interests of New Zealand’s long-term safety, and not trying to make cheap political points out of it on the way through.

explanation: Asked WHY he won't say the register is safe. He gives an actual reason — the Government is still hearing both sides before deciding, and won't pre-empt it. It ignores the premise about the earlier vote and National's pre-election position, and is padded with rhetoric, but the 'why' asked for is engaged.
question: OK. Why won’t he say that the Government won’t be changing the firearms register, given every party in Parliament except the ACT Party voted in favour of it, and his party, the National Party—to the Prime Minister—indicated before the election it would keep the firearms register?
statement: One more time: it’s been a longstanding habit of members of this side of the House to, as Phil Collins said, hear both sides of the story. We are finding out what that is, and when we know what both sides of the story are, in the interests of New Zealand’s long-term safety, we seek to make the right decision and not to cheaply politicise what was a disastrous event.

explanation: Asked whether HE agrees with Seymour's refusal to rule out leaving the coalition, and what he would do to prevent a collapse. He declines on the ground that it would be wrong to answer for another leader — but he was asked for his own view, so the refusal is aimed at a question that wasn't put. Neither limb is answered.
question: Does he agree with his soon to be Deputy Prime Minister’s refusal to rule out leaving the coalition over the so-called Treaty principles bill, and, if so, what measures will he take to avoid the coalition collapsing?
statement: It would be not respectful or democratic of me to seek to answer on behalf of the person—the Minister—he’s talking about.

explanation: Same two-part question repeated. The same misdirected refusal, but he adds that the coalition is 'the epitome of harmony', which glances at the second limb (what will he do about a collapse — implying there is no risk). Still no answer on whether he agrees.
question: Oh, in that case, excellent. Does he agree with the soon to be Deputy Prime Minister’s refusal to rule out leaving the coalition over the so-called Treaty principles bill; if so, what will he, as Prime Minister, do to avoid that?
statement: As I said before, it would not be respectful or democratic for me to seek to answer on behalf of another party’s leader. But I can say, in comparison with a previous coalition I was in in 2017 to 2020, at this present time, what you see over this side of the House is the epitome of harmony.

explanation: Asked whether he will support a second reading immediately after the first. He points to the coalition agreement and tells the questioner to go read it, then attacks him for wasting Parliament's time. Directing to a document that contains the answer is minimal engagement; he never states the position himself.
question: Will he support a second reading of the Treaty principles bill immediately following the first, given he has already said that he won’t support the second reading—meaning the select committee hearing would be a waste of time and money and, in his own words, be divisive?
statement: Can I just say, on behalf of the Prime Minister, this is in a document called the coalition document of the last election’s decision, which has been out now for over seven months. I’d invite him and his ministerial colleagues babbling away now, because they know he’s in difficulty—he can’t even ask questions properly—and I’d invite the people in the gallery up there to go and read the coalition agreement and stop wasting Parliament’s time. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked to choose between three conflicting statements from Jones, Luxon and Seymour. He opens with 'it's clearly in the coalition agreement', then departs into Ngata, Pōmare and the existence of Treaty principles. The disagreement he was asked to adjudicate is never resolved; the bulk of the answer is a different subject.
question: Does he agree with Shane Jones, who said, “the Treaty of Waitangi Principles Bill will not be voted for by New Zealand First [after its] introduction [to] Parliament”; Christopher Luxon, who said National will pursue a Treaty principles bill to select committee and “that’s as far as it will go”; or David Seymour, who said he won’t believe the Prime Minister won’t “change his mind if the public really wants it”?
statement: It’s clearly in the coalition agreement, but I think one is entitled to believe that despite all of the previous statements, if there was prevailing compelling evidence to change one’s mind, as a famous economist once said, “When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do?” However, in this case, we take the view of the most learned Māori or, dare I say it, lawyer to come to this Parliament, who got a degree in two years flat, and in 1922, 102 years ago, he set out what Māori then believed and which we believe today, unlike these new people who decide in their woke manner, like Willie Jackson—all over the place. He doesn’t even stand up for the greatest leader Ngati Porou ever had, and decides he knows better. No, sir. We’re going to stick with a man called Ngata, Pōmare, Buck, and a famous guy who was Deputy Prime Minister in my position all those years ago—there’s only two of us, mind you—and he said the same. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether the PM is open to changing his mind on the second reading. He does answer it — one can change one's mind when facts change, but 'I don't think it will happen in this case' and 'that will not happen at this point in time'. The answer is buried in a long digression about the Treaty, but the core is reached.
question: So is the Prime Minister indicating—as he seems to have in his last answer—that he’s open to changing his mind on the second reading of the Treaty principles bill?
statement: What I was enunciating was what the Prime Minister said in the coalition agreement, as did we. But I did offer the opinion that sometimes—and I don’t think it will happen in this case, of course, obviously—you do have a faint hope that others might have it right. But in the examples that I’ve given, that will not happen at this point in time. Do you know why?
