question: Has he seen any announcements that will support cancer patients?
statement: Yes, I most certainly have, and I referred to them earlier. What I would say is that, right across the world, the rate of progress in creating new treatments for cancer is truly astonishing. As someone who believes soundly in science, I am hesitant to describe it as a miracle, but what is presently happening and the number of cancer treatments coming online could be described as that, if anything was to be. This Government’s commitment is to keep finding ways to fund more and more of them to increase New Zealanders’ survivability.

explanation: Two parts: is he concerned, and what steps is he taking to reduce cost. The first is answered flatly ('Yes'). The second is not — he recites existing settings (free care under 18, low-income funding) and calls it 'a longstanding issue that needs very careful consideration', which is a hedge rather than a step he is taking. Half the question engaged.
question: Is he concerned about the impacts of poor access to dental care, as outlined in this week’s report from Dental for All; if so, what steps, if any, is he taking to reduce the cost of dental care?
statement: Yes. We know that good oral health is important for the wider health of New Zealanders. Currently, free dental care is provided to children and adolescents until the age of 18. There is also funding in place to support adults on low incomes. It’s a longstanding issue that needs very careful consideration. However, as outlined in the Government policy statement, the importance of ensuring primary and community healthcare services, including oral health services, are responsive to need remains a priority.

explanation: Asked what he says to those deferring dental care, framed around his failure to name an initiative. He does not address the people in the premise, but he directly rebuts the embedded charge by naming initiatives — $250m of Vote Health, fluoridation, the toothbrush programme. Engages the operative core (name one) while ignoring the rhetorical framing.
question: What does he say to almost half of New Zealanders who put off going to the dentist because of cost when he was unable to name a single initiative he has taken to reduce the cost of dental treatment?
statement: This Government has spent $250 million approximately on oral health as a proportion of Vote Health. We’re also committed to increasing community fluoridation, which will provide community benefits. We also provide support for the toothpaste to toothbrush programme which provides care to vulnerable populations, and also to whānau of those vulnerable populations.

explanation: Asked whether he will take any action to lower dental costs. He answers about what already exists — low-cost access, a 2022 increase to the emergency dental grant — and never says whether any further action will be taken. Backward-looking answer to a forward-looking question; barely grazes it.
question: Will he take any actions to lower the cost of dental care, or will he allow families to go without being able to afford getting basic health care as a result of cost?
statement: Vulnerable families have access to low-cost access dental care, including recent increases—2022, as I recall—to the emergency dental grant, which, I believe, is now called the special needs dental grant for immediate and essential treatment.

explanation: Asked to choose between two positions: should low-income people go into debt, or should dental care be free and public. He restates his earlier point about access and adds 'of course we'd like to do more'. Neither horn is taken; the closing clause is the only faint contact with the question.
question: Does he think low-income communities should go into debt to access dental care, or should dental care actually be part of the public healthcare system and be made free?
statement: I’ve already expressed that low-income and vulnerable families have access to dental care, but of course we’d like to do more.

explanation: A narrow yes/no of opinion: is the for-profit private model fit for purpose. The reply — improve the economy and we can fund a wider range of services — is about something else entirely and never states a view on the model. A specific question fully pivoted away from.
question: Does he think the current for-profit private model that prevents people from accessing dental care when they need it is fit for purpose in Aotearoa?
statement: What I think is that if we improve the economy, we’ll then have the ability to provide a wider range of health services.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements had been made on building and construction. He names the self-certification regime immediately and adds the accompanying crackdown on poor builders. Directly on the question.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made about building and construction?
statement: Among other things, we’ve recently announced the basis of a self-certification regime. The context is that we’re also looking to crack down on incompetent, careless, and unethical builders. But we know that in order to reform the building and construction sector to support more affordable homes and a stronger economy, we know that at the same time we need to provide more streamlined processes for those who are worthy of that trust.

explanation: Asked why the system needs reform. He gives reasons: 569 days average to build and consent, 10-15 inspections on a standard single-storey home, control resources better spent on higher risk. The question is answered on its own terms.
question: Why does the current system need reform?
statement: It currently takes on average 569 days for a home to be built and consented. Amid a housing shortage that has persisted for some time, that is simply too long to wait. Currently, a single-storey home of standard dimensions might feature some 10 to 15 separate inspections. The resources of the building control system would be better spent mitigating more significant risk elsewhere.

explanation: Asked who will be eligible to self-certify. He identifies both categories — individual tradespeople such as plumbers and drainlayers, and businesses with a proven track record. Directly and completely responsive; the caveat about consultation does not dodge the 'who'.
question: Who will be eligible to self-certify their own building work?
statement: The scheme will undergo a robust consultation process, but there are two key pillars that will feature. The first is at the individual tradesperson level, such that plumbers and drainlayers will be able to self-certify their own work in the same way that electricians and gasfitters already currently can. The industry’s been calling for this for years. The second pillar is that businesses with a proven track record—which, I admit, we do need to define carefully—for example, homebuilders who build hundreds of similar homes every year, will be able to enjoy a more streamlined consent process.

explanation: Asked what feedback he had received. He reports it: largely positive from the sector, cautious cross-party support in principle, and three named industry figures. Squarely answers what was asked.
question: What feedback has he received on these proposals?
statement: The feedback from the sector has largely been very positive. I do actually also want to acknowledge the constructive approach across the political aisle. We’ve enjoyed cautious support in principle, and I do want to acknowledge that, and also willingness to engage on the details, so we will be doing that. Within the sector, Greg Wallace of master plumbers has been advocating for self-certification for his members for four years. Ankit Sharma of master builders, the CEO, points out that this will enable his organisation’s members to build more affordably and efficiently. And Aidan Jury from Jennian Homes highlights the time factor as being critical to builds, including as to costs. So we’re determined to make these changes for the betterment of all Kiwi consumers.

explanation: Asked how the US election result affects New Zealand. He asserts that it will have a significant impact and moves to congratulations and an intention to work with the incoming administration, without saying what the effects are. The question was broad, so the generality is a partial rather than a flat dodge — he engages the subject without reaching the 'how'.
question: How does the result of the recent US election affect New Zealand?
statement: The result of every US presidential election, as in the last 100 years, has had and will have a significant impact on New Zealand, our region, and indeed, the world. Donald Trump’s election as the United States’ 47th President will be no exception. We congratulate President Trump and J D Vance on their election victory, and we look forward to working with them and their incoming administration. But also, we acknowledge the contribution of outgoing President Joe Biden and his administration towards relations between New Zealand and the United States. The United States is one of New Zealand’s closest and most important partners, and we plan to further enhance our relationship with the US and the American people over the next four years.

explanation: Asked whether the Picton Wharf and terminal will need rebuilding regardless of the option chosen. Answer: "Yes." One word, but it is the complete answer to the question asked.
question: Isn’t it the case that regardless of what option is progressed, the Picton Wharf and terminal will be required to be rebuilt?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked why she cancelled the Hyundai ferry contract prematurely rather than first seeking port-side infrastructure options. The answer concedes only that port-side infrastructure would be required, then relabels the question as hypothetical and declines. The declination is not a forthright refusal of the question asked — the question was about a decision already made, not a hypothetical — so the core (why cancel first) is never engaged.
question: Why did she prematurely decide to cancel the Hyundai ferry contract when what she should have done is sought options for the port-side infrastructure instead?
statement: There are a couple of things going on here. The first thing is the member is making some presumptions around the Cook Strait solution that the Government will come to. What she is right to assume is that that would require some port-side infrastructure. There are a couple of relevant facts. One is that the infrastructure at CentrePort and the infrastructure in Picton may require upgrades in the future. There are of course a number of options available to the Government. There are a number of people who use port infrastructure. There are a number of ways in which Cook Strait ferries can be arranged. It is not helpful for me to address hypotheticals such as those that the member is presenting.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on the fiscal position. She names the report — the Treasury-released Crown financial statements for the September quarter — and what it covers. Directly responsive.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the Government’s fiscal position?
statement: Well, I have released today the financial statements of the Government for the first quarter of the financial year. In fact, they were released by Treasury. The statements detail Crown revenue and expenditure for the three months to 30 September and update the operating balance before gains and losses (OBEGAL) and the Crown’s debt position.

explanation: Asked what the financial statements showed. The answer states the revenue, expenses, OBEGAL deficit and net debt figures. Squarely the thing asked for.
question: What did the financial statements show?
statement: The statements show core Crown revenue in the first three months of the year totalled $32.3 billion and core Crown expenses totalled $34.9 billion. Those numbers are broadly in line with Treasury’s last set of forecasts made for the Budget in May. However, the OBEGAL deficit was $700 million larger than forecast, at $4.2 billion for the quarter, and net core Crown debt was also $700 million larger than forecast, at $177.6 billion.

explanation: Asked why the OBEGAL deficit was larger than forecast. The first sentence answers it — mostly the performance of Crown entities — before drifting into blame for the previous Government. The causal question was reached and answered; the later pivot is Focus, not evasion.
question: Why was the OBEGAL deficit larger than forecast?
statement: The increase is mostly attributable to the performance of Crown entities. The results do show that the Government has slowed the growth of Government expenditure; however, they also show that it is going to take time to deal with the additional costs that have been baked into the system by the previous Government. These include the cost of servicing the additional debt incurred between 2017 and 2023. That extra debt amounts to $118 billion, which for the members’ knowledge is the equivalent of $22,000 for every person in New Zealand. In light of this, I note a statement made on Radio New Zealand today from a member who said, “That’s why we’re calling on the Government strongly to get”—

explanation: Asked how the Government will get the books back in balance. Three levers are named — careful spending, better value for money, economic growth — which engages a broadly framed "how" at the level it was asked, though it stops at the level of levers and trails off into contrast with predecessors. Partially answers.
question: How is the Government going to get the books back in balance?
statement: Today’s result does reinforce the need to maintain careful spending, get better value for money, and drive economic growth. Driving growth is a really important part of the equation. If we not only want to get the books back in order but lift living standards, we need to grow the economy faster. Unlike our predecessors, the Government understands that it is business—

explanation: Asked which of the Government's policies, if any, risk increasing material hardship and child poverty. The answer lists policies intended to reduce poverty and historical figures under a previous Government; no policy is identified and no explicit "none" is given. It answers the opposite question.
question: What policies of this Government, if any, risk increasing material hardship and child poverty?
statement: Our Government is focused on reducing material hardship and lifting children out of poverty. That’s why we made significant investments in Budget ’24, with policies that support families experiencing hardship, including tax relief, FamilyBoost, and increasing the in-work tax credit. Treasury modelling shows the investments in Budget 2024 are estimated to lift around 17,000 children out of poverty, on the after-housing-cost measure, by 2026-27. Our Government is focused on practical solutions, including breaking the cycles of welfare dependency; improving educational outcomes to help keep children out of poverty in the long term. We know this approach works because during the last full four years of the previous National-led Government, from the year 2013 to 2017, the number of children in material hardship fell by 56,200.

explanation: A narrow yes/no factual question — was she advised that the school lunch and public transport discount changes would harm progress on her child poverty targets. The answer speaks only of pride in the school lunch programme and never touches whether such advice was received. A specific question squarely avoided.
question: Is it true she was advised that changes to school lunches and public transport discounts would have a negative progress towards meeting her child poverty targets?
statement: I’m really proud of the Government school lunch programme because, in effect, what we are doing is actually providing school lunch to an additional 10,000 children that we know are struggling—their families are struggling with food. So I’m really proud of the changes that our Government has made possible to alleviate the burden for families.

explanation: Asked to confirm she received no such advice. "Ministers receive advice and then further advice" hedges around the core — it neither confirms nor denies receiving the advice described — but it does gesture at the advice question rather than ignoring it, and then reverts to the school lunch defence.
question: Is she saying that she has received no advice indicating that several of her Government’s policies would lead to negative progress towards meeting her child poverty targets?
statement: What I would say is, as I said in answer previously to that member, Ministers receive advice and then further advice, and the further advice and what the Government actually announced around Ka Ora, Ka Ako will absolutely buffer families who are currently experiencing challenges putting food on the table. In fact, our Government has found a way to make it possible to ensure that 10,000 additional children receive the school lunch programme.

explanation: Asked whether she accepts the Government's actions are making the 2028 targets unachievable. "I absolutely disagree with that" is a direct, complete no. The talking points that follow do not undo the answer, and the rest of the response is unresponsive only in the sense of being extra.
question: Does she accept that this Government’s actions are contributing to the 2028 child poverty reduction targets becoming increasingly unachievable because of their multiple policies locking more children into poverty?
statement: I absolutely disagree with that. Our Government has been clearly focused on dealing with the cost of living crisis, growing the economy, and improving things like school attendance and school achievement, which we know contribute to the long-term impacts and effects on children, which is why we’ve got targets in these areas.

explanation: Asked how she can disagree given she was advised her policies would set back the targets. She does supply grounds for the disagreement — Budget 2024's projected 17,000 children — which engages the "how can you" framing, but sidesteps the advice premise the question was built on. Partial.
question: How can she disagree with the previous question when she has been advised that several of her Government’s policies would negatively contribute to meeting her child poverty reduction targets?
statement: Because, as I said in my primary answer, I’m proud of Budget 2024, which will lift 17,000 children out of poverty. We saw six years of the previous Government; material hardship went up by 4,100 when it was supposedly the priority.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements had been made on breast cancer screening access. The answer states the announcement — free screening extended to 70- to 74-year-olds, starting in Nelson-Marlborough ahead of a national roll-out. Directly responsive; the surrounding justification does not displace the answer.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made about improving access to breast cancer screening for New Zealand women?
statement: Last week, the Government announced that free breast-screening is being extended for 70- to 74-year-old women, starting in the Nelson-Marlborough district, ahead of a national roll-out late next year. This is something that has been called for over many years. The aim of breast screening is to find breast cancers early before there are any noticeable signs and symptoms, with early detection improving management options and outcomes. We know that breast cancer is one of the most common cancers in New Zealand with about 3,400 women diagnosed with the disease each year. So, extending screening can save lives. That is why this initiative is a priority for our Government.

explanation: Asked how NZ intends to engage with the incoming administration. The answer does describe the engagement approach — preparation, and the right people posted in Washington, across the US and at home. It opens with a brief detour ("a decision for the American people") and stays at the level of posture rather than substance, but the question's core is reached. Thinness here is a Specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: How does New Zealand intend to engage with the second Trump administration?
statement: We are ready and have hit the ground running with the incoming Trump administration. This was a decision for the American people, not for us. But we have prepared for President Trump’s re-election. That preparation has included ensuring we have the right people working on the New Zealand - US relationship in Washington, DC; around the United States; and back here in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked how the world will change in policy terms. The answer declines to characterise any change, noting only that Trump will pursue his own agenda and that the Government will spend the 2.5 months to inauguration trying to understand it. Giving a reason for having no view yet is partial engagement, but the question as asked is never answered.
question: How does New Zealand think the world will change in policy terms under a new administration?
statement: As happens after any change of leadership, President Trump will no doubt pursue his own policy agenda. But it’s important to note that President Trump will not take effect—in terms of the office, being sworn in—until 20 January 2025. Over the next 2½ months until President Trump’s inauguration, the New Zealand Government will be working hard to better understand the incoming administration’s policy agenda. We’ll also be working on how we can best engage with the new administration on policy cooperation for the mutual benefit of both of our countries and our peoples.

explanation: Asked what advice was received on rail freight cost impacts before the cancellation. The answer engages squarely: advice was received on aspects of iReX, it has been proactively released on the Treasury website, and it focused on transport system efficiency rather than the specific cost of freight. That last clause is a direct response to the actual question — it says what the advice did and did not cover.
question: What advice, if any, did she receive on the potential impacts on the cost of moving freight by rail between the North Island and South Island before announcing the cancellation of the order for rail-enabled ferries?
statement: The question reflects some misunderstanding on the part of the member. Ministers received several pieces of advice about various aspects of Project iReX before Cabinet decided in December last year to not meet KiwiRail’s request for further funding for the project. The advice we received has been proactively released and is on the Treasury website. The advice focuses on the efficiency of the transport system as opposed to the specific cost of freight. Ministers’ assessments was that Project iReX was inherently flawed, with large cost blowouts for landside infrastructure, and the project needed to be reset.

explanation: A narrow yes/no question — was advice received on the fiscal impacts of extra truck movements. The entire answer attacks the premise ("littered with assumptions") without ever saying whether such advice was received. A tight factual question left wholly unengaged.
question: Did she receive any advice on the fiscal impacts of adding thousands of trucks to the road as a result of not having rail-enabled ferries, as has been indicated by the managing director of Mainfreight—will be the result of not having rail-enabled ferries—before announcing the cancellation of the order?
statement: Well, that question is littered with assumptions, many of which are completely wrong.

explanation: Asked which assumptions were erroneous. The answer names one directly — that more freight would go on trucks. "I'll start with" signals only one of several, so it is incomplete, but it does exactly what was asked rather than pivoting.
question: Could the Minister please tell me which of the statements that were made in the previous question are erroneous assumptions, as she claims?
statement: Well, I’ll start with the assumption that there would be more freight going on trucks—that’s a big assumption.

explanation: Asked a binary about the Mainfreight managing director: wrong or lying. The answer neither affirms nor rejects either option, instead reporting that conversations have occurred and that assessments are premature because Cabinet has not decided. "Premature" gestures at rejecting the claim without ever engaging the question put.
question: Does the Minister, therefore, think that the managing director of Mainfreight, our largest freight operator in the country, is wrong or is lying when he says that his company will put at least 5,000 additional truck and trailer movements on the roads as a result of the loss of rail-enabled ferries?
statement: Well, I’ve had many conversations with a range of people involved in getting freight across the country, including Don Braid from Mainfreight. What he would reflect to the member is that decisions have not been made by Cabinet on what kind of ferries there will be or what the arrangements for freight would be, so it’s very premature to be making those sorts of assessments.

explanation: Asked a general principle question — should all evidence be reviewed before cancelling projects. The answer is a long recitation of the iReX cost blowout ending in "then, yes ... it needs to take action," where the "yes" attaches to the case for acting rather than clearly to the review principle. It hedges around the core of the question instead of stating a position on it.
question: Does she think Government should review all the evidence about the costs, benefits, and impacts of infrastructure decisions before cancelling or announcing projects?
statement: When an infrastructure project changes from being an investment in ships that is expected to cost less than a billion dollars into an investment that is expected to cost at least $3 billion dollars—80 percent of which are costs for port-side infrastructure and not ships—when a project has consistent blowouts, and when a previous Government chooses to ignore those, then, yes. When a new Government is elected, it needs to take action.

explanation: Asked why $3bn was unaffordable for iReX but committed for the Mount Victoria tunnel. The response is entirely directed at the questioner — an invitation to campaign against the tunnel in Miramar, closing with "Good luck." The reason asked for is never given at any point.
question: Why has she considered that $3 billion for this iReX project, which had a business case and clear strategic value of retaining a rail connection between the North and South Islands, was unaffordable but, yesterday, has committed to at least $3 billion to add less than 2 kilometres of one-car lane in each direction in central Wellington before an investment case has even begun?
statement: Well, if the member for Rongotai wishes to tell the people of Miramar that they don’t deserve a duplicate Mount Victoria tunnel, that they should sit in traffic, that their buses should go slowly, and that they should have inadequate ability to cycle through the tunnel to get to work, then she is welcome to go and campaign on her commitment to get rid of the second tunnel. Good luck.

explanation: "Does she stand by all her statements and actions?" answered "Yes" in the first word, with a specific statement volunteered as illustration. Complete and direct. The counter-question tacked on at the end does not subtract from an answer already given.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes. In particular, I stand by the statement I made yesterday, which was that “today’s unemployment statistic is yet another reminder of how letting inflation get a grip on the economy was so damaging.” I wonder if the member agrees with that statement.

explanation: Asked whether this is a good use of taxpayer funds. The answer never addresses the value-for-money question, pivoting to a general observation about how legislation reaches the House and why that matters for democracy. It touches the surrounding subject without reaching the question asked.
question: Is it a good use of taxpayer funds to support a piece of proposed legislation that will not proceed past the select committee stage but will cost the country more in racial disharmony?
statement: Legislation progresses to the House in a number of ways. There are, for example, a number of members’ bills that I would not wish to progress, but it is important for democracy that legislation can come to the House.

explanation: "I am struggling to see what responsibility I have for that question as the Minister of Finance" is a plain declination on portfolio grounds — the same shape as the worked "No, I won't release that advice" example, and delivered without filler. It is scored below a blunt "no" because the stock "struggling to see" phrasing leaves the refusal implied rather than stated outright.
question: Is it important to democracy to support a piece of proposed legislation that will have a cost to racial disharmony and will not proceed anywhere past the second reading?
statement: I am struggling to see what responsibility I have for that question as the Minister of Finance.

explanation: A two-part question — does she stand by the statement, and when is "shortly". Both parts answered in five words: "Yes; it'll be this year." That "this year" is a loose commitment goes to Specificity; as an answer to what was asked, it is complete.
question: Does she stand by her statement regarding the Interislander ferries from six weeks ago that “We will ensure that we will make an announcement shortly.”; if so, when is shortly?
statement: Yes; it’ll be this year.

explanation: Asked what the age extension means for NZ women. Reti answers squarely: 22 lives potentially saved per year, a 34 percent lower breast-cancer death rate for participants, earlier detection and better treatment outcomes. The core of the question is met head-on.
question: What does this age extension mean for New Zealand women?
statement: This age extension could potentially save 22 lives per year. That’s not just 22 women but also their families, friends, and loved ones who won’t have to endure the attendant impact of cancer. Data shows that women who participate in the BreastScreen Aotearoa programme are 34 percent less likely to die from breast cancer. Increasing access through this age extension allows us to catch more cancers early, which means better treatment outcomes. We’ll also be looking to improve the outcomes for women such as the more than 60 women who succumbed in this age group in the latest data of 2019.

explanation: Asked HOW the scheme will be deployed across the country. The answer says deployment takes planning, workforce and physical infrastructure, and that it will roll out nationwide next year — that is scope and timing, not mechanism. It reaches the edge of the question (nationwide, next year) without ever describing the deployment itself, so it partially answers.
question: How will this scheme be deployed across the country?
statement: Extending breast screening to an approximately 60,000 additional eligible women per year takes an immense amount of planning, including investment in workforce and the physical infrastructure. I want to thank everyone involved for their efforts to date, and I look forward to seeing this programme rolled out nationwide next year. Early detection will save lives.

explanation: Asked what other actions the Government has taken on cancer. The answer enumerates them directly: a faster-cancer-treatment target, more CT access, the $604m Pharmac expansion, a radiotherapy machine at Whangārei. Exactly the question that was asked.
question: What other actions has the Government taken to improve outcomes for New Zealanders with cancer?
statement: This extension of breast screening is just one action we’ve taken for better cancer care. We’ve also introduced a target for faster cancer treatment, increased access to CT scanning, expanded access to life-extending cancer medicines through our transformative $604 million investment in Pharmac, and started building a new cancer radiotherapy machine at Whangārei Hospital. We remain committed to improving outcomes for the thousands of Kiwis and their families affected by cancer each year.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by 'I'm not worried that some are now homeless', and why. Potaka contests the framing but then restates the question in his own words and answers it: none of the 726 households and 1,452 tamariki moved through priority one were homeless when placed. He never utters a plain 'yes I stand by it', which costs him, but he engages the substance and supplies his reason rather than dodging.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “I’m not worried that some are now homeless” regarding people who have left emergency housing; if so, why?
statement: This was a similar question asked by the Hon Willie Jackson in August. As I said then and as I will now, the member mischaracterised the context in which the comments were made around the Government’s priority one fast track to get whānau with tamariki who had been staying longer than 12 weeks in emergency housing out of that moral, financial, cultural, and social catastrophe. The question asked: am I not worried that some are now homeless? My answer is that none of the 726 households and 1,452 tamariki living in emergency housing and transitioned through priority one by 30 September 2024 into social housing were homeless when placed. Every single one of those 1,452 children were placed into warm, dry homes.

explanation: Asked whether what he is really worried about is reducing costs. The answer recites target No. 8, the 62 percent progress figure, accuses the questioner of chicanery, and restates a commitment to moving children into warm dry homes. The proposition put to him — that cost is the real motive — is never accepted, denied or addressed. Talking points in place of an answer.
question: When he says he is worried about emergency housing numbers but isn’t worried that “some are now homeless”, isn’t he just saying that all he’s really worried about is reducing costs?
statement: This Government has a target—target No. 8—to reduce the number of households living in emergency housing by 75 percent by 2030. We are up to 62 percent in nine months. The member may use chicanery and innuendo to try and trap me into an answer, but I’ll repeat that, in this House, we are absolutely dedicated to ensuring that those with genuine need for short-term stays in temporary accommodation in most urban and city centres in New Zealand can access that, but we have been absolutely committed to ensuring that many thousands of tamariki living in that catastrophe move into warm, dry homes.

explanation: A two-part question: how can the claim of success be credible given (a) official advice predicting more homelessness and (b) the 20 percent figure. He engages (b) directly and on its merits — they now track 80 percent of exits versus 50 percent before, and the remaining 20 percent are simply unknown rather than known-homeless. The official advice and the credibility claim itself go untouched. Half the question squarely met.
question: How can he credibly claim this policy is a success when his official advice was that these changes to entry criteria for emergency housing would increase homelessness, and when asked why 20 percent of people that have left emergency housing are now homeless, his response was “I’m not worried.”?
statement: Again, the member uses fuzzy maths to describe the actual situation. The actual situation is when we arrived, we knew where around 50 percent of those leaving and exiting emergency housing were going to. Now, through the dedicated diligence and professionalism of our officials and, of course, the Ministers who are involved with housing, we know where nearly 80 percent of people are going to when they exit. The other 20 percent we may not know, because it’s not required of people leaving emergency housing to actually tell officials where they’re going to.

explanation: A narrow factual question — how many declined since the criteria changed. He declines to supply it in the House and redirects to the written-question process, which is a real response rather than silence, and a refusal can be forthright. But he then pads with an unrelated statistic (2,000 tamariki having left), which is answering a different question. A deferral plus a pivot, on a question narrow enough that the dodge is conspicuous.
question: How many people have been declined emergency housing since he changed the entry criteria?
statement: That is a written question that the member can send to my office, but what I can say is that by September, over 2,000 tamariki had left emergency housing in the nine months to date.

explanation: Asked for a number: how many moved into housing built by this Government. He disputes the premise that the builder matters, notes housing has been built by many Governments, says occupants are comfortable, then pivots to emergency-housing availability. No figure, and no engagement with the attribution the question turned on.
question: How many people have been moved into social or community housing, paid for and built by this Government?
statement: Again, I can reiterate and respond to the member, who asked a very similar question last week, that social housing has been built by a number of Governments over the years, and those people that have moved into those social houses built by a number of Governments over many years are very, very comfortable. What I can also say is this: there continues to be availability for emergency housing for those with genuine need for a short-term stay in temporary accommodation in most urban centres in this country.

explanation: Two propositions put to him: that the homes are Labour-built, and that the emergency-housing decrease comes from criteria changes blocking entry. He effectively concedes the first — taxpayer-funded housing built by successive Governments, and the jibe about regulatory molasses implicitly grants that his Government could not have built them in nine months. The second proposition, which is the sharper accusation, is never touched.
question: No, I’m not. Is it not the case that any people that are now homed from emergency housing are in homes funded and built by the previous Labour Government, and the decrease in emergency housing numbers is because he in his changing criteria is stopping people getting into emergency housing in the first place?
statement: It is the case that the taxpayers of Aotearoa New Zealand have paid for social housing that has been built by a number of Governments over time. And, just to add this, in the event that the member has ever been involved in building houses before, I think it would be pretty incredible for you to buy the land, plan the house, get the funding support, and go through all the regulatory molasses to build a house within nine months.

explanation: Asked what recent reports he has seen on gang policing. He reports a specific one: yesterday's Christchurch arrests of three Mongols associates and recovery of stolen property. Directly responsive.
question: What recent reports has he seen on the policing of gangs?
statement: Yesterday, police arrested three associates of the Mongols gang in Christchurch, recovering stolen property from the gang’s headquarters. This comes in advance of an event they were organising in Canterbury this week. Police have prepared for this event and have been working to prevent it disrupting members of the public going about their lawful business.

explanation: Asked what steps Police are taking to disrupt gang events. He names two — maintaining law during the Mongols event, and working with Immigration NZ to block international members entering. Thin, but thinness is a Specificity matter; the question itself is answered.
question: What steps is Police taking to disrupt gang events?
statement: Police will be working to ensure the maintenance of law during the Mongols’ event this week. They are also working closely with Immigration New Zealand to prevent international members of the gang entering New Zealand to celebrate and glorify their criminal activity.

explanation: Asked WHY the Government is blocking Mongols members from entering. He gives the reason: border alerts and suspended visa-waiver status send the message that they are not welcome to celebrate criminal behaviour here. The 'why' is answered as a 'why'.
question: Why is the Government working to prevent Mongols gang members entering New Zealand?
statement: By placing border alerts and suspending visa-waiver status on known Mongols members, the Government is sending a clear message that they’re not welcome in New Zealand for a celebration of their criminal behaviour. This Government does not tolerate gangs and the misery that they peddle, and refuses to allow others to come into our country and glorify that misery.

explanation: Asked what he says to recent rhetoric around police anti-gang operations. He responds about the operations themselves — praising the 10-month North Island operation and the police service — which engages the subject matter, but never addresses the 'rhetoric' the question pointed at. The question was sprawling and soft, so partial coverage is a mild rather than severe miss.
question: What does he say to recent rhetoric around police operations cracking down on gangs?
statement: Police have done an outstanding job on a 10-month operation across the North Island, and in particular targeting the Mongrel Mob Barbarians for drug dealing, possession of illegal weapons, and planning hit jobs. We are lucky in this country to have a world-class police service deeply connected to the communities that they serve and who take their responsibility of keeping Kiwis safe seriously.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on AML/CFT regulation. She names a specific report (Business New Zealand's 'Reducing compliance burden on New Zealand small businesses') and summarises its findings. Squarely the thing asked for.
question: What recent reports, if any, has she seen in relation to anti-money laundering and countering terrorism financing regulations?
statement: Business New Zealand recently released a report: Reducing compliance burden on New Zealand small businesses. The report highlights that the current anti - money-laundering law places an unnecessary burden on small businesses. It points to repetitive information requests, too many procedural steps, inconsistent requirements, excessive costs, and a lack of coordination in the system as serious issues weighing heavily on small business productivity.

explanation: Asked what work is under way to address the report's issues. She answers with the first phase of her AML reforms and the consolidation of three regulators into DIA. Directly responsive to 'what work'.
question: What work is currently under way to address the issues raised in that report?
statement: The first phase of my anti - money-laundering reforms has taken initial steps to address some of the concerns Business New Zealand has raised. This work will consolidate the three current regulators: the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, the Financial Markets Authority, and the Department of Internal Affairs into a single regulatory body under the Department of Internal Affairs. This consolidation will cut red tape, streamline processes, and reduce the high compliance costs that the report identifies as obstacles for small businesses.

explanation: Asked how the three-phase programme addresses the report's specific recommendations. She maps the Statutes Amendment Bill and the single-supervisor move onto the report's calls for simpler compliance. It reaches the question, though 'specific recommendations' is answered at a somewhat general level.
question: How does the Minister’s three-phase work programme address specific recommendations from the Business New Zealand report on anti - money-laundering?
statement: My three-phase work programme directly addresses the recommendations to simplify and streamline anti - money-laundering (AML) processes. Through the Statutes Amendment Bill, which is currently before the House, I’m introducing immediate relief that targets the report’s call for straightforward compliance. Moving to a single AML supervisor will also ensure that clear, consistent guidelines are available for small businesses, allowing them to meet compliance standards more efficiently without having to jump through the unnecessary regulatory hoops.

explanation: Asked whether she will focus on simplifying customer due diligence. Answer opens with 'Yes' and states where in the programme it happens. A clean yes/no to a yes/no question.
question: Will the Minister focus on simplifying customer due diligence to address the report’s specific recommendations?
statement: Yes. Businesses have highlighted excessive customer due diligence as a primary challenge for small business. I’m addressing this directly through the adoption of a risk-based approach in the first and third phases of my reform programme. By streamlining these due diligence requirements, I am to reduce compliance costs and improve productivity for small businesses, allowing them to operate more freely and contribute to New Zealand’s economic growth.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all the Government's statements and actions. Answer is 'Yes' plus an example. Complete.
question: Te Arawhiti: Does he stand by all the Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, anā, particularly the resolution between three Kurahaupō iwi in the top of the South Island, Te Tau Ihu o Te Waka-a-Māui, who have received $25 million in alternative redress after the Woodbourne airport could not be transferred to them because of PFAs, or chemical poisoning, under the land.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by introducing the Treaty principles bill early, and what does he say to iwi leaders calling it dishonourable and reckless. He answers the first part squarely ('I stand by the decision') and gives only a thin gesture at the second ('I recognise and acknowledge the genuine concerns'), with the 'earlier than expected' element untouched. Half the question engaged.
question: Does he stand by the Government’s action to introduce the Treaty principles bill earlier than expected, and if so, what does he say to iwi leaders who have described this as “dishonourable and reckless”, and if not, why not?
statement: I stand by the Government’s and Cabinet’s decision to introduce the Treaty principles bill, and I recognise and acknowledge the genuine concerns expressed by iwi leaders.

explanation: Asked whether Rahui Papa was correct in a specific quoted statement, and if not why not. The reply — 'Rahui Papa has his own principles' — declines to say correct or not and gives no reason, sidestepping a narrow yes/no. Not a refusal either; it answers a different question about whose view it is.
question: Is Rahui Papa correct when he said, “Get rid of the Māori-bashing, racist bills, policies, and procedures of this Government”; if not, why not?
statement: Kei a Rahui Papa tōna ake piki amokura. [Rahui Papa has his own principles.]

explanation: Asked a binary: is the Māori-Crown relationship better or worse under his leadership. He pivots to Māori tamariki leaving emergency housing and never says better or worse. A specific question replaced with an unrelated favourable data point.
question: Is the Māori-Crown relationship better or worse under his leadership?
statement: I believe that many, many Māori communities are very enthusiastic about the number of Māori tamariki who have left emergency housing. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked why he prioritised cutting jobs at Te Arawhiti. He offers a talking point about better public services, then declines the substance by classing jobs as operational matters. The deflection-to-operational is at least a stated position on why he won't engage, so it is not a pure dodge, but the 'why' asked about is never given.
question: Why has he prioritised cutting jobs at Te Arawhiti, whose primary role is to help make the Crown a better Treaty partner, when iwi leaders are speaking out against his Government’s anti-Māori agenda?
statement: As we are all aware, this Government is very focused on delivering better public services. Any matters in relation to jobs and employment are operational matters and will be left at the appropriate operational levels.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to front up on the forecourt for the hīkoi. He calls the hīkoi important, lists competing responsibilities, and ends with 'the first step is to get to the weekend' — no commitment either way. A plain 'no, I won't' would have scored high; talking around it without reaching yes or no does not.
question: Will he commit to fronting up on the forecourt of Parliament to listen to the tens of thousands of New Zealanders who will march against his Government’s anti-Māori agenda?
statement: The hīkoi in question is very important for many, many people. As the Minister for Māori Crown Relations, I have a number of responsibilities that I have to attend to here and in many other places throughout the country, including, for example, resolving some of the issues that were left extant by the previous Government. However, the first step is to get to the weekend.

explanation: Asked what recent conservation announcements he has made. He names one: the opening of the Tuatapere Hump Ridge Track as the 11th Great Walk. Directly what was asked for.
question: What recent announcements has he made about conservation matters?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I recently had the pleasure of celebrating the opening of New Zealand’s 11th Great Walk, the Tuatapere Hump Ridge Track and revealing the exemplary waharoa carved by Steve Solomon. The Hump Ridge Track is steeped in cultural and historical significance, and its Great Walk status will make it more of a draw card for both Aotearoa New Zealanders and international manuhiri. This is a great example of Te Papa Atawhai collaborating with iwi, the local Hump Ridge trust, and local government to bring a conservation project to life and bring benefits to local businesses and the economy.

explanation: Asked what his conservation priorities are. He names four priorities explicitly. Direct and complete; the closing slogan doesn't detract.
question: What priorities does the Minister have for conservation?
statement: I’ve established four clear priorities for conservation: targeting investment into high-value conservation domains; generating revenue and recalibrating costs so we can ensure to focus on delivering better public services with conservation; strengthening relationship with iwi, hapū, and other communities to shared goals; and reducing red and green tape to make it easier for businesses and others to undertake mahi on public conservation lands. We’re getting things done for conservation.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. Answers "Yes, I do" and then elaborates. The elaboration is padding, but the question was squarely answered.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, I do, especially our efforts to restore law and order, ensuring that Kiwis feel safe in their homes, their businesses, and in their community. As part of that objective, on Sunday the Government announced that legislation will be introduced this year, making stalking illegal, with a maximum penalty of up to five years in prison. The new offence comes as a part of a wider package of changes to actually keep Kiwis safe, including a change to prevent those convicted of a stalking offence from holding a firearms licence, and a recognition of the Family Violence Act that stalking is a form of psychological violence. Our message is very simple: if you are perpetrating a culture of fear in your community—whether that’s breaking into a shop or stalking and intimidating someone—we are coming after you. This is a Government focused on restoring law and order.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Tribunal's characterisation of the bill, and if not, why not. He answers neither — he pivots to the procedural point that the bill won't be enacted, which is a different question.
question: Does he agree with the Waitangi Tribunal that, if enacted, the Treaty principles bill would “be the worst, most comprehensive breach of the Treaty in modern times.”, and that if it isn’t repealed it would constitute the “end of the Treaty”; if not, why not?
statement: Unless Opposition parties support the bill, it won’t be enacted.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware of two specific Tribunal findings and how he can support the bill in good conscience. He ignores the awareness question and the conscience question, but does partially engage by narrowing what "support" means (first reading only) — a hedge around the core rather than a full dodge.
question: Is he aware that the Waitangi Tribunal has determined that principle 2, as contained in the bill, would “abrogate rights of Māori that article 2 guaranteed and protected, and revoke the promises and guarantees the Queen made to Māori in 1840.”, and that principle 3, as contained in the bill, “bears no resemblance to the texts and meaning of article 3.”; if so, how can he support the bill in good conscience?
statement: Well, as I explained to the member last week, we are supporting the bill through first reading. But the Government parties in the coalition are free not to support it after that point in time.

explanation: Asked whether the reason his Ministers attack the Tribunal unchecked is that the Tribunal has highlighted the bill's damage. He never addresses the alleged reason or his own inaction; he offers a general defence of questioning the Tribunal's role. Effectively a different answer to a different question.
question: Is the reason why his Ministers have consistently sought to undermine the Waitangi Tribunal without any censure from him, even calling for its disestablishment, because the tribunal has brought attention to the profoundly negative impacts the Treaty principles bill is having on the Crown’s relationship with Māori?
statement: What I’d say to that member is that many commentators have said in a post-Treaty settlement world it’s quite a legitimate question to ask what the role of the Waitangi Tribunal is going forward. That is something that we as a coalition Government will explore in due course.

explanation: Asked how National's support ending before second reading addresses concerns, given the claimed prejudice and select-committee risk. He rejects the premise and gives an actual reason for the position (MMP compromise), which engages the "how can he claim" core, but leaves the prejudice and select-committee elements untouched.
question: How can he claim that the National Party’s support of the bill ending before the second reading will address the widespread concerns, when the mere introduction of the bill will, according to the Waitangi Tribunal, “prejudice Māori” and there is a risk that the select committee process will be hijacked by racists and purveyors of misinformation for six months?
statement: I disagree with the characterisation of that question. As I explained to the member last week, we live in an MMP world. Parties in this Parliament have different views and different constituents they represent here in Parliament. We didn’t get what we wanted; the ACT Party didn’t get what they wanted. We came to a sensible compromise. We’re supporting it at first reading, not beyond that. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what responsibility he takes for division and hurt caused by the bill. He answers about not being responsible for Finlayson — a reframe onto the quoted person rather than the division he was asked about. It reads as "none", but only by answering a substituted question.
question: What responsibility does he take as Prime Minister for the fact that, as former National Minister Christopher Finlayson has said, “there is too much division and hurt in New Zealand caused by, among other things, pernicious nonsense like the Treaty Principles Bill.”?
statement: Well, I don’t take responsibility for Chris Finlayson.

explanation: Asked why he didn't tell voters his pre-election commitment was tradeable. He never addresses the disclosure question at all, restating his current position instead.
question: When he told New Zealanders before the election that he thought the Treaty principles bill was divisive and that National would not support it, why didn’t he tell them that commitment was something he was willing to trade away in coalition negotiations?
statement: Well, we’re not supporting the bill into law; we’re not supporting the bill out to a national referendum. We’ve been very clear about that from the get-go.

explanation: Asked what recent economic reports she has seen. She names the Treasury fortnightly summary and what it contains. Direct and complete.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: Every fortnight, on its website, Treasury publishes a summary of economic data and events. The most recent of these contains a number of data points that suggest the New Zealand economy is recovering after a long recession. The number of building consents is beginning to rise. New Zealand’s goods export prices, particularly dairy, are continuing to climb. On Monday—and Grant McCallum was pleased to tell me all about it—Fonterra lifted its forecast milk price from a mid-point of $9 a kilogram to $9.50, and business confidence, firms’ expected activity, and employment intentions have all risen.

explanation: Asked when the next Treasury forecasts will be released. Gives the date — 17 December. Complete; the added commentary is extra, not evasion.
question: When will the next Treasury forecasts be released?
statement: Treasury will release a full set of economic and fiscal forecasts in the half-year update on 17 December. I expect those forecasts will show a strengthening economy, lower interest rates, and reducing unemployment over the next few years. That’s not just me; that’s what almost all economic commentators anticipate. What will also be of interest, though, is how the economic and fiscal forecasts compare to previous expectations.

explanation: Asked how forecasts have changed in recent years. States they changed for the worse and explains the direction and cause. Squarely answered.
question: How have the economic forecasts changed in recent years?
statement: Economic forecasts have generally changed for the worse over successive updates, as it became clear that the current recession started earlier, was deeper, and persisted for longer than was earlier understood. With the benefit of hindsight, earlier forecasts attributed too much weight to an apparent pick-up in productivity over the COVID period. This pick-up proved to be illusory. Earlier forecasts were therefore too optimistic. So, incrementally, Treasury has been lowering its assumptions around labour productivity.

explanation: Asked how economic forecasts flowed through to fiscal forecasts. Describes the transmission channel and the resulting downgrades. Direct answer to the mechanism asked about.
question: How have these economic forecasts flowed through to the fiscal forecasts?
statement: Economic forecasts flow through to the fiscal forecasts in several ways, especially through the impact of nominal GDP on tax revenue, which subsequently impacts on debt and the operating balance. Steadily deteriorating economic forecasts, plus some big spending increases in Budgets 2022 and 2023 have led to a series of downgrades in the fiscal forecasts. For example, since the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update 2021, every forecast for the return to operating balance before gains and losses surplus has been revised downwards.

explanation: Asked what statements he had seen about the bill; he characterises them ("many and varied but overwhelmingly positive") and begins quoting them directly. Squarely on the question. The answer is cut off mid-quote, but what is there engages.
question: What recent statements has he seen about the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill?
statement: Many and varied but overwhelmingly positive. To take just three that I received in the hour leading up to question time: “I never thought I’d see a politician take on the Treaty grift in my lifetime, especially not a Māori politician. I support redress in the tribunal but I know you’re right to wonder if the expansion of the organs of State for us becomes more a crutch than a helping hand. It’s patronising to hear TPM argue we need special treatment to compete. I worry the next generation might hear that and start believing it. Kia kaha, bro.” Another—

explanation: Asked what statements he had seen from principals opposing the bill; he describes exactly those statements (urging opposition, urging absence from school) before adding commentary. The editorialising afterwards is not a dodge — the question was reached first.
question: What statements has he seen from school principals opposing the Treaty principles bill?
statement: I’ve seen statements from school principals to their community, urging people to oppose the Treaty principles bill and to even be absent from school to participate in hīkoi activations. I can’t miss the opportunity to say to those principals that they have a duty to adhere to political neutrality, and there is nothing in the Treaty principles bill that will disadvantage any student even one iota. However, students are disadvantaged by missing school. [Interruption]

explanation: A yes/no question answered with an explicit "Kāhore—or no" followed by elaboration. Direct and complete.
question: Will the Treaty principles bill affect Māori language and culture?
statement: Kāhore—or no. As I said at Waitangi last year, one of my goals is ki a maimoatia te reo me te ahurea Māori—that is, to cherish the Māori language and culture. The Treaty principles bill protects the rights of hapū and iwi Māori as they stood in 1840. It also ensures that those basic rights of tino rangatiratanga and self-determination extend to all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether the bill affects Treaty settlements; he points to clause 8 stating it must not be used in interpreting settlement-related statute, which is a clear negative answer with its basis. The "read the bill" aside is extra, not evasion.
question: Will the Treaty principles bill affect Treaty settlements?
statement: The Treaty principles bill is very clear that in clause 8 it says it should not be used in interpreting any statute in relation to a Treaty settlement. What I say to people who have these fears or anxieties about the bill—and I know that there are some—or anyone saying “Kill the bill”, my advice is to read the bill because you will find such details as that that often show you there’s nothing to worry about.

explanation: A sprawling question about what the bill means for rights and the country's future, answered on its own terms — defining the undefined 1975 principles, equal rights, shared citizenship. Vague, but vagueness here is the question's shape, not a dodge.
question: What will the Treaty principles bill mean for the rights of New Zealanders and our future as a country?
statement: Most importantly, it will fill in the blanks that this House left in 1975 when it said that there were Treaty principles but failed to define what they were. It will give us a conception of our founding document that is based upon equal rights for all and that, in turn, enables us to solve together the many challenges we face with health and housing and jobs, education and the economy, and that, in short, will allow New Zealanders to overcome our real and tangible challenges with a shared and equal understanding of our citizenship and our rights in this country.

explanation: Two parts: agreement with the Luxon quote, and why weekly reporting stopped. She says "Of course" to the first and gives a reason for the second (COVID-era demand has passed, reverting to pre-COVID reporting). Both halves are engaged.
question: Does she agree with Opposition leader Christopher Luxon, who said, “I can tell you we’re going to be straight with the New Zealand people, tell it as it is—the good, the bad and the ugly”; if so, why has the weekly reporting of income support and hardship figures stopped?
statement: Of course. Our Government is committed to having 50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker benefit by 2030. Monthly and quarterly data is a better decision-making tool to achieve this and it’s my intention to continue this reporting. I was advised that weekly reporting was originally produced in response to demand for more timely information as required during COVID. That period, of course, has now passed. Like many things, we are simply returning to the pre-COVID reporting. We want our department’s resources to be focused on the analysis that we need to get more people into work, not on unnecessary reporting.

explanation: A narrow either/or — was it MSD's request or the Minister's? She says she "had looked at the different reporting mechanisms", which hints at her own decision but never names who requested it. The core of a tightly specified question is left unanswered.
question: Was the weekly reporting cancelled at the request of the Ministry for Social Development and Employment, or at the Minister’s request?
statement: I had looked at the different reporting mechanisms. The weekly reporting is very volatile and the more detailed analysis that’s provided in the monthly and quarterly report provides us the ability to do what we want to do, which is to support more people into work.

explanation: A counterfactual — would she have cancelled reporting if the numbers were falling? The response restates the COVID/volatility rationale already given and never touches the hypothetical. The question's core is entirely bypassed.
question: Would the Minister have cancelled weekly reporting had jobseeker numbers been going down?
statement: As I said, weekly reporting was introduced during COVID. We’re not during those times. The weekly reporting wasn’t as accurate—very volatile. We want to make sure we’re using data that is more meaningful in terms of making decisions to actually achieve our Government’s target to reduce the number of people on jobseeker benefit by 50,000.

explanation: "Has reporting been stopped because it shows numbers rising?" is answered with a flat "No." That is a direct, complete response to what was asked; the subsequent attribution of unemployment to the previous government is surplus, not a substitute for the answer.
question: Has the weekly reporting been stopped because it shows that jobseeker numbers have risen by over 22,000 since she took office, as unemployment continues to climb to record heights?
statement: No. Unfortunately, as the Minister of Finance said, the economic climate that we took over, with a recession that was deeper and longer, has meant that unemployment has continued to rise. Treasury has forecast that, including a year ago, where the numbers have not yet peaked. For every single person that loses their job, I feel for them. Unfortunately, we are dealing with the circumstances we got from the last Government.

explanation: Two parts. The second (why stop weekly reporting now) is answered — monthly/quarterly give the needed analysis. The first (does she acknowledge benefit numbers match or exceed pandemic peaks) is never acknowledged or denied, and she moves to a favourable exit statistic instead. Half the question is reached.
question: Does the Minister acknowledge that unemployment figures, or the numbers of people on benefit, are now as high or higher than what they were during the height of the pandemic, and, if so, why does she think that now is the time to stop regular weekly reporting?
statement: As I said, monthly reporting and quarterly reporting provides us the level of analysis that we need to make decisions that actually support us to ensure that we are able to do more to support job seekers into work. What I’m really proud to say is the last quarterly report showed us that despite this very challenging economic time, we had 16,100 people in this quarter exit jobseeker benefit into work—2,400 more than the same quarter a year ago. What we’re doing is working.

explanation: A two-part question answered part by part — "yes" to the first, "yes, absolutely" to the second. Terse and unelaborated, but nothing is dodged; brevity is not evasion.
question: Does she accept that the State’s failures “to consider or recognise an ao Māori … view, tikanga, te reo and mātauranga Māori” were circumstances that led to abuse; if so, is she confident that the proposal to repeal section 7AA is not a continuation of this?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, in the context of the findings of the royal commission of inquiry, yes. In answer to the second part of the question, yes, absolutely.

explanation: Asked to name empirical evidence justifying the repeal of section 7AA. She gives a motivation (clarity, safety and wellbeing first) and repeats it, but names no evidence of any kind. The specific thing requested is never supplied.
question: What empirical evidence can she name to justify the repeal of section 7AA when advice states that keeping it will help strengthen safety policy and guidelines, and Whanaketia found cultural safety to be a requirement of care safety?
statement: I have repeated this over many occasions that the core reason for looking at section 7AA was to bring clarity to the fact that we need to put the safety and the wellbeing of our young people at the forefront of every decision we’re making when it comes to placements and when it comes to removal of young people in care. So I have thought about the safety and wellbeing of children, and I repeat it over and over again that that should be the first thing we’re thinking about in every decision we make about our young people.

explanation: Asked whether she believes repealing s7AA hinders implementing Whanaketia recommendations, and if not, why not. She says "No" outright and gives the reason (partnership arrangements with hapū and iwi will not change), then adds she will await the select committee. The core yes/no was answered and a why-not supplied; the select-committee line is an addition, not a substitute.
question: Does she believe that repealing section 7AA hinders the Government’s ability to implement Whanaketia recommendations and achieve its vision of holistic redress, which require the Government to partner with Māori and give effect to Te Tiriti, and, if not, why not?
statement: No. I’ve repeated over and over again that nothing will change when it comes to partnership agreements with hapū and iwi around the country, but I will wait for the select committee to finish their deliberation of this bill and will commit to carefully considering their report once it’s tabled in the House.

explanation: Asked why she is removing the requirement to report on Māori outcomes and disparities. She does supply a reason — she considers repeated reporting a resource drain that restates a known problem — so the "why" is engaged. It is a reason rather than a rebuttal of the ethnicity-data point the question rested on, so it reaches the question but not squarely all of it.
question: Thank you. Why is the Minister removing its requirement for reporting on outcomes and disparities for Māori when Whanaketia recommends strengthening ethnicity-specific data collection to ensure better-informed decision-making?
statement: Whilst I appreciate that question, we have spent years and years going back to when I was dealing with Child, Youth and Family Services over 20 years ago doing reports. I’m sick of reports that say the same thing over and over again from multiple spaces that take resources away from our young people, when we know what the problem is and we just need to get on with it and deliver for our children.

explanation: Asked why she is removing s7AA given Whanaketia's minimum safeguard of connection to whānau, hapū, iwi and whakapapa. She never states a reason for the removal; she asserts nothing will change and reframes to safety and wellbeing taking priority. That reframing brushes the tension in the question but the "why remove it" core is left unanswered.
question: Why is she removing section 7AA when Whanaketia states that a minimum safeguard for protecting tamariki in care is ensuring Māori “are connected to their whānau, hapū, iwi, whakapapa, whenua, reo, and tikanga”?
statement: I’ve repeated this over and over again. Nothing will change when it comes to working with whānau, hapū, and iwi to make sure that they have a voice at the table. But we must make sure that safety and wellbeing are the forefront of all our decision making. If whānau is the right place for a young person to be placed, that’s what should happen. But, unfortunately, that’s not always appropriate and we need to make sure that the safety and wellbeing come first.

explanation: "Does he stand by his reported statement?" — "Yes." One word, direct, complete. Nothing was avoided.
question: Does he stand by his reported statement that previous National Governments had made good progress on Treaty settlements, and they hoped to restore some of that momentum; if not, why not?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked how the Treaty Principles Bill restores momentum given iwi leaders calling it reckless. He disputes the premise by noting views vary and that some leaders still want progress, but never addresses the mechanism the question asked for. Contesting the premise is engagement of a sort, so not a total dodge, but the "how" is never reached.
question: How does introducing the Treaty Principles Bill “restore some of that momentum.” when the bill has been described by iwi leaders as “reckless”, “dishonourable”, and “callous”?
statement: Well, I’m sure there’s a wide variety of views amongst iwi leaders, but there are still plenty who are very keen to make progress on Treaty negotiations.

explanation: A two-part question: does he agree Don Brash is a "true New Zealand patriot", and would that help or hinder settlement momentum. He answers the second part squarely ("I'm not sure it will make any difference whatsoever") but sidesteps the first with a reference to having written a book about Brash. Half the question is answered directly, half is deflected.
question: Does he agree with Paul Goldsmith that former ACT Party leader and current leader of Hobson’s Pledge, Don Brash, is a “true New Zealand patriot”, and, if so, will this help or hinder the momentum of Treaty settlements?
statement: I’m not sure it will make any difference whatsoever, but I did write a book about that particular fellow 20-odd years ago, and that’s on the record.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Nicola Willis's quoted remark and whether the debate would restore settlement momentum. He declines the framing ("drawing a long bow") and moves to the state of Ngāpuhi negotiations. Neither the agree/disagree nor the momentum question is answered; the rejection of relevance is the only engagement with what was asked.
question: Does he agree with Nicola Willis with regard to the Treaty Principles Bill, who said on Radio New Zealand: “The debate, I think, can be healthy, but if one party seeks to impose their view on the other without consent, I think that’s dangerous.”, and, if so, will this debate restore some of the momentum of the Treaty settlement process?
statement: Well, I think, again, that question is drawing a long bow from Treaty negotiations, which is work which is steadily working its way through the system. Now, it’s true that one year in, I have not yet concluded a settlement with Ngāpuhi, and that is challenging work and many Ministers in the past have worked in that way. Ultimately, it requires engagement on both sides, and that’s what we’re doing.

explanation: Asked why the Government is proceeding despite advice and warnings. He opens by attacking the Opposition's choice of questions, then restates a general commitment to Treaty settlements. No reason for proceeding is offered; the question is answered with tactics commentary and talking points.
question: If the debate on the Treaty Principles Bill is considered dangerous, why are he and his Government choosing to ignore all the advice and warnings, and proceeding with a select committee process that is going to be one of the most divisive in Aotearoa’s history?
statement: Well, clearly, the other side have woken up this morning and decided to have every question on this particular area today in the House, and so they’re straining to draw different bills into different ministerial responsibilities. In terms of making progress on Treaty settlements, we are very committed to continuing to make progress on those Treaty settlements. It’s been something that, across the House, Governments of all persuasions have worked together towards. We’ve got some progress, and we’ve got more progress yet to make.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government is taking to reduce victims of crime. He names a specific action — legislation this year making stalking a jailable offence of up to five years — and ties it to the aim. Directly on the question asked.
question: What actions is the Government taking to reduce the number of victims of crime?
statement: The Government has agreed to introduce legislation this year which will make stalking an illegal and jailable offence for up to five years. It is often a precursor to more serious and violent crime—there are established links between stalking and intimate partner violence—which is increasing in prevalence. Every New Zealander deserves to feel safe, and this is another part of the Government’s plan to reduce the number of victims of crime.

explanation: Asked how the new offence will protect stalking victims. He answers in terms of recognition, more effective prosecution and prevention, and why existing law falls short. The mechanism is stated at a general level but it is the mechanism the question asked about; vagueness is a Specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: How will the new offence protect victims of stalking?
statement: A stalking offence will provide better recognition, more effective prosecution, and support greater prevention of stalking offences. The current legislation’s not adequately responding to the challenge. While some stalking behaviours can be prosecuted through existing laws, they do not cover modern stalking methods. Victim advocates have long called for the Government to create a bespoke offence and we have listened to them.

explanation: Asked what the new offence covers. He gives the threshold (three specified acts in 12 months) and enumerates covered behaviours. Complete and squarely on the question.
question: What will be covered by the new offence?
statement: Well, the new offence will capture patterns of behaviour, being three specified acts occurring within a 12-month period that amount to stalking and harassment. It includes damaging reputation, recording, tracking, loitering, as well as the use of technology and modern stalking methods.
