She contests the premise directly — there has been no cut to the overall contracted spend — explains what is actually happening to contracts (expiring, reduced, increased) and gives the reason (no longer tolerating underutilisation). Denying the premise on the record is engagement, not evasion; slightly short of full because the 'if so, why' limb is answered only through the reframing.
question: Does she stand by cuts to community provider contracts; if so, why?
statement: For one last time this year: there has not been a cut to the overall amount Oranga Tamariki is spending on contracted providers. There are contracts that will expire and not be renewed, some that Oranga Tamariki has decided to reduce, and others that will be increased. Oranga Tamariki spent more than $500 million with providers last year, and I’m advised we’re on track to do so again this year. However, unlike in the past, Oranga Tamariki is no longer accepting underutilisation and under-delivery, and it’s making sure it’s actually getting what it is paying for. This is what taxpayers expect and deserve when the Government is spending their hard-earned money and, actually, it’s what most vulnerable children and young people deserve too.

explanation: Asked a pointed yes/no: is she seriously saying cutting Stand Tū Māia's contract is the right thing to do? She recites contract values, states that a resolution was reached, that its terms are confidential, and that procurement talks continue. She stays on the subject matter but never touches the question of whether the decision was right, and does not even say plainly that she won't answer — a blunt refusal would have scored far higher than this.
question: Is she seriously saying that cutting Stand Tū Māia’s contract in April next year—an organisation that provides specialised trauma treatment and intensive wraparound family support for thousands of highly vulnerable children and their families, with a waiting list of over 450 children—is the right thing to do?
statement: Oranga Tamariki have two contracts with Stand Tū Māia, plus pay equity: integrated outcome agreement, originally $18.77 million per year; services in schools, $1.34 million per year; pay equity uplift, which was $5.18 million for the year. And Oranga Tamariki has reached a resolution with Stand Tū Māia and legal proceedings were withdrawn. The terms of this resolution are confidential to all parties involved and Oranga Tamariki is still having discussions with Stand Tū Māia about future procurement.

explanation: Asked why she didn't go back to the Minister of Finance for extra money. The answer supplies exactly that reason — she rejects more spending as the solution, because outcomes worsened under an output-based approach. The reason is implicit rather than framed as 'I didn't ask because…', so it is a shade short of complete, but the core of the question is reached.
question: Why didn’t she go back to the Minister of Finance to ask for extra money when Stand Tū Māia has been told the reason their contract for last resort services to thousands of children has been cut is that there is no more funding left this year?
statement: To be perfectly frank: that is the reason why we’re in this problem in the first place, because spending more money seems to have been the solution to all the problems. But we’ve seen it actually isn’t. Outcomes got worse; children were suffering because nothing was based on outcomes. It was based on output, and we’re not going to do that any more.

explanation: Asked whether there will be more cuts to front-line community providers next financial year. She gives a conditional rather than a yes or no: contracts are reviewed as normal, performers continue, underperformers 'won't continue'. That conveys real information bearing on the question — some contracts will end — but stops short of answering whether more cuts are coming. A partial answer that hedges around the core.
question: Will there be more cuts to community providers delivering front-line services in the next financial year?
statement: It’s normal process to go over contracts when they’re being renewed. If they are providing the service that is required of them and that is required of the priority spaces which this Government is doing, then they will continue. If they are not providing the service that they’re supposed to, if they are underutilising and if they’re not providing the service they should, then they won’t continue.

explanation: Asked whether she has broken a promise that front-line services would not be impacted. She pivots to restating what she campaigned on — that more money doesn't fix problems — and to outcomes over the last six years. The broken-promise allegation and the front-line impacts are never addressed; the answer relocates to ground of her own choosing. Not quite the floor, since the reframing gestures at what she says her promise actually was.
question: Is it true that despite all the word games, in fact, she has broken a promise to the people of New Zealand that front-line services would not be impacted, when across the country we have seen cuts to vital services for our most vulnerable children and whānau?
statement: I campaigned saying that more money does not fix a problem. What fixes a problem is actually making sure that we’re delivering the outcomes that are needed for our most vulnerable children. The outcomes have not got better over the last six years. They will get better when the focus is clear and precise that we need to concentrate on children and young people in care and children that come to the attention of Oranga Tamariki.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he had made regarding regulatory sector reviews. He identifies the ECE regulatory review report, its 15 recommendations, his acceptance of all of them, and the intended Cabinet paper. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent announcements has he made regarding regulatory sector reviews?
statement: Today, I released the early childhood education, or ECE, regulatory review report, the first major report from the Ministry for Regulation. The report makes 15 recommendations to modernise and simplify regulations across ECE so that service providers can get on with what they do best: providing safe, high-quality spaces for children to reach their potential. The ministry has recommended removing, changing, or merging approximately three-quarters of the 98 licensing criteria for centre-based services, simplifying the system so it focuses on children’s welfare and education instead of paperwork. I’ve accepted all 15 of the review’s recommendations for regulatory changes, ranging across licensing workforce compliance and regulation. In order to promote innovation, quality, and growth, I’ll be taking a paper to Cabinet in the new year with the intention of implementing these recommendations.

explanation: Asked two narrow factual questions: when Willis made the request, and whether Cabinet agreed. The answer gives neither a date nor a Cabinet decision, pivoting to 'asset sales are off the table', economic growth and SOE performance. A specific factual question squarely avoided.
question: When did Nicola Willis ask the Treasury to produce a list of public assets that could be privatised, and did the Cabinet agree to that course of action?
statement: Well, again, as I’ve said very clearly, asset sales are off the table for this term. What we’re focused on is economic growth. Of course, we will look at the performance of our State-owned enterprises because many of them are underperforming and they need a good curry up and they need to deliver.

explanation: The same two-part factual question, re-put. The response stays entirely on SOE performance and concedes only 'there'll be a range of asks' — no date, no answer on Cabinet. The closing 'that's all that's happened here' brushes at the topic without reaching either part of the question.
question: When did Nicola Willis ask for the list that she just referred to, and did the Cabinet agree to that course of action?
statement: What we’re focused on is making sure we get better performance out of those State-owned enterprises. It’s quite normal as we want to make sure we’ve got excellence, that that capital’s being well deployed, and that the performance of those organisations is improving. There’ll be a range of asks about their performance. That’s all that’s happened here.

explanation: Asked why the public should have confidence in his knowledge of his own Government. He does not address the confidence/knowledge point, but he does engage the question's premise head-on with an unambiguous denial ('no asset sales this term—period'). Partial: the core charge is met by flat contradiction rather than answered.
question: Why should the public have confidence that he knows what’s going on in his Government, that when he tells them that asset sales aren’t something that are being actively considered—if they believe him—when he doesn’t actually know?
statement: Asset sales are not being discussed, debated, or delivered in this parliamentary term. I don’t know how to be any clearer with the member of the Opposition. I’ve said very, very clearly, there will be no asset sales this term—period.

explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should believe him given Willis's alleged catalogue. He rejects the characterisation, restates the commitment, and offers a competing account of what the Ministers are actually doing (SOE performance). That is a real engagement with the 'why believe you' core, though he never addresses the catalogue claim directly.
question: Why should New Zealanders believe him when he says that asset sales aren’t something the Government is considering, when Nicola Willis is currently preparing the catalogue for the fire sale?
statement: I reject the characterisation of that question. As I have said consistently before the election, asset sales are off the table over this Government. But it is quite appropriate and entirely appropriate that we have State-owned enterprise Ministers and a Minister of Finance that want to make sure that we have high-performing State-owned enterprises. When they haven’t been delivering properly, we want to make sure there’s excellence and we want to make sure that the New Zealand taxpayer, who has capital tied up in those assets—that they are delivering well for those taxpayers.

explanation: Asked why privatisation would leave Kiwis better off given the energy-company precedent. The reply dismisses the questioner ('gone down the rabbit hole') and repeats that asset sales are off the table. The denial has some bearing on relevance, but the question about privatisation's effects is never engaged.
question: Oh, well, if you’re going to set that as the standard, Mr Speaker, I’m sure it will be evenly applied across the House! Why should Kiwis believe privatisation and asset sales will leave them better off, given that the last National Government’s privatisation of energy companies led to higher power prices, bigger profits, and less investment in electricity generation?
statement: Look, I think the Leader of the Opposition has gone down the rabbit hole, and, actually, I don’t know how to be any clearer: asset sales are off the table for this Government.

explanation: Asked why he should be believed given he had called an earlier questioner a conspiracy theorist and then conceded consideration. He directly addresses the specific charge, explaining what the 'conspiracy theorist' comment referred to, alongside the SOE framing. Engages the core, without conceding or resolving the inconsistency alleged.
question: Why should New Zealanders believe the answer he’s just given, when having been asked the question on asset sales in the House last year, he accused the person asking it of being a conspiracy theorist, only to admit that the Government has actually been considering it?
statement: The Government has been looking at the performance and the excellence and the management of our State-owned enterprises to make sure that the public is getting a good return on the capital being employed. The comment I made to the Green member was the idea that you would actually run an organisation down before you sell it—that makes no sense.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made on speed limits; he names the announcement made that morning — reversal of blanket speed limit reductions, starting tonight, complete by mid-year. Direct and complete. The swipe at the last Government is surplus but does not displace the answer.
question: What announcements has he made regarding speed limits?
statement: I’m pleased to say that this morning, the Prime Minister and I announced another commitment of this Government has been met, with reversals to the last Government’s blanket speed limit reductions beginning tonight. They will be in place by the middle of this year. We’re focused on speeding up New Zealand’s economic growth, and in this case, we mean it literally. The last Government was obsessed with imposing illogical and untargeted speed limit reductions on State highways and local roads. We are reversing that.

explanation: Asked how this benefits Wairarapa; he names the specific change — SH2 Featherston to Masterton back to 100 km/h overnight. The benefit itself is left implicit in the change rather than stated, and the opening interjection is off-topic, but the question is squarely engaged.
question: How will this benefit the people of Wairarapa?
statement: Oh, no, no—not after this morning’s announcement, he isn’t. We have announced this morning that the speed limit on State Highway 2 between Featherston and Masterton will return to 100 kilometres per hour overnight. Previous members of this House, including Associate Ministers of Transport, have claimed that this is not able to be done. We changed the rule in relation to the setting of speeds, and it will now happen.

explanation: Asked what other areas benefit; he enumerates 38 roads reverting, 49 further State highway sections going to consultation, and the council process for local roads. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What other areas will benefit from quicker and more efficient travel?
statement: We’ve announced 38 roads for which the speed limits will revert back to what they were pre-2020. That will take effect, in relation to Wairarapa, from tonight, and in relation to the other 37, between now and 1 July. There are also 49 further sections of State highways that will go out for public consultation. These will run for six weeks. In relation to local roads, councils have until 1 May 2025 to advise the New Zealand Transport Authority (NZTA) of the roads subject to reversal under the new rules. And I should note, in passing, that I want to thank the Hon Simeon Brown, the former Minister, for his hard work in this area.

explanation: Asked how safety was taken into account; he answers with the variable school-zone speed limits, then moves onto drug-driving testing and breath tests. The core is reached, but a large share of the answer drifts to a different safety policy than the speed-limit decision asked about.
question: How has the Minister taken safety into account?
statement: Safety is important, and the new rule requires variable speed limits outside schools during pick-up and drop-off times. That is important. But we’re also focused on the leading factors in road deaths, which is drugs and alcohol. So the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Bill passed its second reading last night, which brings New Zealand into line with other jurisdictions, in which we will be able to test people by the roadside for whether or not they have recently used drugs. I believe we will look back in a few years’ time and regard this move in a similar way to the way in which we regard blood-alcohol testing, which is a perfectly normal part of life: controversial when first introduced, amongst some, but actually par for the course. And the idea that you can drive on our roads and not be tested regularly, or at least have the chance of being tested regularly, whilst being high is nuts and we are changing that. At the same time, we are increasing the amount of breath tests done by the police, and that is an extremely important move.

explanation: A 'does he stand by' question answered with 'Yes' before elaborating. Complete and unambiguous; the campaigning that follows does not detract from the answer having been given.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to increase speed limits so that Kiwis can get to where they need to go to faster. If we want to go for growth, we need to get serious about powering up our regions. That’s why we’re so pleased with the changes that the Minister has just outlined in the Wairarapa this morning. That’s all part of our plan to end a culture of no, a culture of slow, and my message to the other side is: if you’re serious about growth and getting Kiwis moving faster, back our changes and back the communities who are sick of being slowed down.

explanation: Asked whether phasing out fossil fuels and their subsidies is still NZ's negotiating position. He answers only that Cabinet has held no discussion on subsidies — which is about internal process, not the standing position, and ignores the phase-out half entirely. Touches the topic without reaching the question.
question: Is it still our country’s negotiating position on the international stage to phase out fossil fuels and to phase out subsidies for fossil fuels?
statement: We have not had a discussion about subsidies for fossil fuels—no debate, discussion, or decision made in Cabinet at all.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware ACCTS bars subsidy or backstop support for fossil fuels. 'We honour our trade obligations' glances at the substance, but he never confirms or denies awareness of the requirement and falls back on the same no-Cabinet-discussion line. Partial engagement.
question: Is the Prime Minister aware that the Agreement on Climate Change, Trade and Sustainability, which his trade Minister announced we’d signed last year, requires that we do not subsidise, de-risk, or provide any backstop support whatsoever for fossil fuel exploration or import?
statement: Well, we honour our trade obligations, and, as I said, there haven’t been any decisions, discussion, or debate happening in Cabinet on that topic.

explanation: Asked to rule out underwriting or subsidising fossil fuel exploration or import. He explicitly swaps the question ('what I can rule in is...') and delivers renewables and energy-security talking points; the ruling-out is never addressed. The closing 'we are going to use gas' is about supply, not subsidy.
question: So, then, can the Prime Minister rule out that his Government will be underwriting or providing any form of subsidy for fossil fuel exploration or import?
statement: What I can rule in is that we’re going to be Government that actually doubles the amount of renewable energy in this country and we’ll make sure that we can also keep the lights on and keep electricity abundant and affordable for New Zealanders. And we are going to use gas, whether it’s domestic or imported.

explanation: Asked directly whether he will rule out subsidising fossil fuels. He restates that Cabinet has not debated or decided, which answers a different question (what has happened) than the one asked (what he will commit to). A narrow yes/no left unanswered.
question: Can the Prime Minister be straight up with the country and tell us whether he will rule out subsidising fossil fuels?
statement: As I’ve said, we haven’t had any debate, discussion, or decisions made in Cabinet on that subject.

explanation: Asked whether he is open to subsidising fossil fuel exploration or import. The reply is process description of how Cabinet works plus a repeat of 'no conversation on that subject'; his own openness is never addressed.
question: Can the Prime Minister be straight up with the country and tell us whether he is open to subsidising fossil fuel exploration or import in this country?
statement: We work as a Government. We have Cabinet conversations and decisions, and we take them as a Cabinet. As a result, what I’d say to you is we haven’t had any conversation on that subject.

explanation: Two-part question — what responsibility she has for growth, and whether the recession reflects on her execution. She states the responsibility concretely (macroeconomic and fiscal settings) and gives an explicit 'no' to the second part. The blame directed at the previous Government is a Focus/Civility matter and does not lower this; both parts were squarely engaged.
question: What responsibility, if any, does she have for economic growth, and does the current recession reflect on her execution of that responsibility?
statement: Like all Ministers in this pro-growth Government, I have a responsibility to look across my portfolio for opportunities to support and promote economic growth. In the case of finance, that means, in particular—among other things—ensuring macroeconomic and fiscal settings are supportive of growth. For example, having low and stable inflation, which in recent years has definitely not been the case, but which has now been brought back in target, and working to bring discipline in our fiscal policies to support interest rate reductions, which have come down 125 basis points since this Government was elected. To the second part of the question, no, but it perhaps reflects on some people’s execution of their responsibilities—people whose big spending pushed inflation to 7.3 percent and required 525 basis points of interest rate hikes to bring it down. Those would be Ministers in the previous Government. I don’t take responsibility for the damage they did to the New Zealand economy; I do take responsibility for fixing it.

explanation: Asked why it took a recession and other indicators for her to realise she needed a growth plan. 'It didn't' rejects the premise head-on — a complete, if terse, response to a loaded question. The absence of elaboration is a Specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: Why did it take a recession, record net migration levels, higher unemployment for her to realise that she needed a plan for economic growth?
statement: It didn’t.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. 'Yes' — one word, direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that Invest New Zealand will not lead to foreign ownership of public assets. He substitutes his own guarantee about faster infrastructure and better outcomes; foreign ownership of public assets is never mentioned, let alone ruled in or out.
question: Will he guarantee that his Invest New Zealand initiative will not lead to the foreign ownership of public assets if he is re-elected next term?
statement: What I can guarantee is it’s going to get infrastructure built quicker, it’s going to get renewable energy projects built faster, and anything else that means that we can actually deliver for New Zealanders—Māori or non-Māori—who actually want higher incomes. They want better housing, they want better health outcomes, better education outcomes, so we’re going to do whatever it takes to power up growth in New Zealand, period.

explanation: Asked what role Te Tiriti o Waitangi will play in the Invest New Zealand plan. 'This Government will honour the Treaty' is a general assurance rather than a role, and the pivot to iwi appetite for foreign capital answers a related but different question. Gestures at the question without reaching it.
question: Ka pai. What role will Te Tiriti o Waitangi play in his plan to open up Aotearoa through Invest New Zealand?
statement: Well, this is a Government that will honour the Treaty. But what I’d say is that the iwi partners that we have talked to are very open to partnering and working with pools of international capital and domestic capital to build infrastructure and to do things that advance the wellbeing of their hapū and whānau.

explanation: Asked whether opposing the Treaty principles bill matters given his support for the Regulatory Standards Bill, which the questioner says will limit Treaty clauses. He refutes that premise directly, which engages the core of the alleged inconsistency, but 'our position is very well understood' sidesteps rather than states it. Half engaged, half deflected.
question: Does it make a difference that he is voting against the Treaty principles bill when he has already guaranteed his support for the Regulatory Standards Bill, which will limit Treaty clauses in future legislation?
statement: Well, our position is very well understood on the Treaty principles bill, and I refute the assertion that that’s what the Regulatory Standards Bill’s doing.

explanation: Asked whether he is committed to equitable healthcare for all New Zealanders. He commits to timely, quality access 'based on need' for all New Zealanders, which brushes the question, but never affirms or denies the commitment to equity that was actually asked about, and spends much of the answer on funding figures. Partial.
question: Is he committed to equitable healthcare for all New Zealanders; if not, why not?
statement: My priority as the Minister of Health is ensuring that all New Zealanders have access to timely, quality healthcare. This Government has invested more in health services than ever before, an additional $16.88 billion, and my expectation is that those services are delivered based on need. Kiwis rightfully expect to see their doctor or attend emergency departments without long waits and get the surgeries they need as quickly as possible. My focus, and the focus of this Government, is on ensuring that those expectations are met and delivered upon for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether he is merely blocking entry to emergency housing to cut costs rather than reducing the underlying need. He answers with exit/outcome numbers (2,500 fewer tamariki in emergency housing, 2,000 into homes), which rebuts the implication obliquely but never engages the actual mechanism put to him — whether the fall comes from restricted entry. Partial engagement; the core of the question is stepped around, not reached.
question: Is it not actually the case that he is simply stopping people from entering emergency housing to reduce costs instead of actually reducing the need for emergency housing in the first place?
statement: It is actually the case that we have seen a reduction of nearly 2,500 tamariki living in emergency housing and we’ve also seen nearly 2,000 tamariki under Priority One go to dry, warm homes. That is actually the case.

explanation: Asked what recent growth announcements the Government has made. He names one directly — the Prime Minister's establishment of Invest New Zealand — and says what it is for. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made about boosting economic growth?
statement: Last week, the Prime Minister announced the establishment of Invest New Zealand as the country’s one-stop shop for attracting highly productive capital. By increasing foreign direct investment, we’ll accelerate the growth of New Zealand businesses, create better and higher-paying jobs, and provide the infrastructure that New Zealanders need.

explanation: Asked why Invest New Zealand was set up. He gives the reason squarely: New Zealand's FDI stock is below the OECD average and growing slowly, so the Government wants to lift it. Directly responsive.
question: Why has the Government decided to set up Invest New Zealand?
statement: We’re not getting our fair share of international investment. Currently, the New Zealand stock of foreign direct investment sits at 38 percent of GDP, compared to an OECD average of 50 percent of GDP. Last year, by comparison, New Zealand’s foreign direct investment grew by 5 percent, compared to Singapore at 31 percent. The Government’s committed to increasing direct investment and growing the New Zealand economy so that Kiwis get their fair share and the services that come with that.

explanation: Asked what Invest New Zealand will do. He lists its intended functions (drive investment into high-potential sectors, lift R&D, streamline funding processes). The question is answered on its own terms.
question: What will Invest New Zealand do?
statement: Invest New Zealand will be a new agency modelled on the Irish and Singaporean best practice. It’ll drive direct investment into high-potential sectors to boost New Zealand’s innovation in productivity, increase R & D investment in New Zealand by overseas companies, making us attractive and increasing the value of our exports, and streamline processes to significantly increase funding for new and existing businesses and public and private sector projects.

explanation: Asked why attracting foreign investment matters to the economy. He answers with the claimed benefits — unlocking global investment for road and energy projects, jobs, businesses, infrastructure. Engages the question directly; only the closing plan-of-government line drifts.
question: Why is attracting foreign investment important for the economy?
statement: Because the initiative will unlock tens of billions of dollars in global investment opportunities that support the delivery of key road and energy projects, creating better-paying jobs, support and create new businesses, and help the Government deliver core infrastructure the country needs. As the Prime Minister said, this year is about growing the economy, and Invest New Zealand is part of the Government’s plan to make all New Zealanders better off.

explanation: Asked two narrow quantitative things: projected additional tourists and estimated economic benefit. She states plainly that specific numbers are hard to predict — which does answer the first part as 'no projection exists' — but offers no estimate of economic benefit at all, and pads with tourism totals and website-hit counts. Half the question is met with a stated non-answer, half is left untouched.
question: How many additional tourists are projected to visit New Zealand as a result of the digital nomads policy, and what, if any, is the estimated amount of economic benefit from this policy?
statement: Encouraging digital nomads to stay for up to nine months is part of this Government’s plan to unlock economic growth by making New Zealand a more attractive place for people to work remotely while travelling. Tourism is New Zealand’s second-largest export earner, generating almost $11 billion and creating nearly 200,000 jobs. Unfortunately, we are only at 86 percent of pre-COVID, 2019, numbers and this policy will help get New Zealand back on track. While it’s hard to predict specific numbers, we do know from overseas examples that staycations are extraordinarily popular. Immigration New Zealand has already seen an incredible amount of interest—just since Monday—when there were over 4,000 hits on the first day we announced this policy. This has more than doubled, so over 8,000 yesterday. New Zealand is open for business. On this side of the House, we are pulling every lever to encourage more people to visit.

explanation: Asked whether she plans to address regional infrastructure gaps to cope with any influx. She responds by commenting on how the member ought to feel about more visitors and notes digital nomads travel around and pay GST. Infrastructure is never addressed; the reply pivots to the questioner's attitude.
question: Given we’re open for business, does she plan to address current infrastructure gaps in regions, like Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, which are already under strain, to ensure that the tourism sector in our regions can thrive while supporting any potential influx?
statement: I would have thought that that member would be really excited about the possibility of more visitors coming into Hawke’s Bay, into Wairarapa, into Gisborne, to see the very beautiful environment that we have. We’re talking about digital nomads—they’ll be travelling around the country. Every dollar they spend is a dollar in GST and good for New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether the Government raised the international visitor levy by 185 percent to prop up the books. She confirms the levy was increased — engaging the factual half — but neither confirms the figure nor addresses the stated purpose, and closes on electorate talking points. Partial.
question: Did that Government increase the international visitor levy by 185 percent to prop up Government books?
statement: We have increased the international visitor’s levy. We are open for business. We are very keen to see more visitors come to New Zealand, including digital nomads. I, for one, hope they come to my electorate, and I would have thought that member hoped they come to hers as well.

explanation: Two parts: does she accept hardship harms schooling through lack of food, and why was food insecurity removed from the Child Poverty Related Indicators. The first is answered squarely ('yes'). The second is deflected — she asserts food insecurity is still measured elsewhere rather than saying why it was removed from that indicator set — then moves to lunches and work programmes. One part answered, one dodged.
question: Does she accept that children living in material hardship are more likely to do poorer in school due to a lack of food; if so, why did the Government remove food insecurity from the Child Poverty Related Indicators?
statement: To the first part of the question, yes, and that’s why our Government has continued to invest in the things that reduce material hardship, lift educational achievement, and help families get ahead. Food insecurity continues to be measured and remains an indicator under our children’s Child and Youth Strategy. I’m also proud that we have extended the Healthy School Lunches Programme to 10,000 children so more students will have access to food. Our efforts to help more parents into work will also lift household incomes and improve their ability to put food on the table. Reducing material hardship is a key priority in our child and youth strategy, which is why we have a target to lift 17,000 more children out of material hardship by 2027.

explanation: Asked whether hardship will fall at a rate matching or exceeding promised economic growth, and if not, why children in poverty won't benefit proportionally. She replies only that growth creates jobs and therefore fewer children in hardship. The comparative-rate question is never taken up in either branch; this is a pivot to the general growth argument.
question: Will the number of children living in material hardship decrease at the same or higher rate than the Prime Minister’s promised economic growth; if not, are children living in poverty not going to benefit from economic growth at the same rate as the rest of the population?
statement: Economic growth is a fantastic opportunity because, of course, if we see jobs being created, then we will see more parents in work, which means fewer children in hardship.

explanation: Pressed for a yes or no on whether hardship will decline at a rate equal to or greater than economic growth. 'Well, they go together' gestures at the link but restates the same jobs-to-incomes chain rather than accepting or rejecting the proposition put to her. The narrow question asked twice is still avoided.
question: Is she saying, then, that we’re expected to see a decline in the number of children living in material hardship equal or greater to the amount the economy grows?
statement: Well, they go together, because the more the economy grows, the more jobs there are, the more opportunities there are for parents, the fewer parents that we will have on benefit. They’ll have greater incomes and have better ability to provide for their children, which will mean fewer children in material hardship.

explanation: Asked whether it is true that child material hardship will keep rising for the rest of the term. She points to a target to reduce the number, which amounts to an implicit 'no' and does engage the question, but she never addresses the trajectory over the term itself and finishes on recessionary conditions and growth talking points. Answers around the edge of the question rather than at its centre.
question: Is it true that material hardship for children will continue to increase under her watch until the rest of this Parliament’s term?
statement: I just said in my answer to the primary question that we have a target to reduce the number of children living in material hardship. I hope the member has noticed that we have had very challenging economic times, including recessionary conditions, and families have been doing it incredibly tough. And I do want to acknowledge that the start of the school year is incredibly tough for parents. That’s why we are focused on economic growth, that’s why we are focused on creating more jobs and enabling more families to look after their children so that there will be fewer children in material hardship.

explanation: Asked whether the researchers' claim about private-insurance-based systems is correct, and if not why not. The answer never says correct or incorrect: it offers a balanced compliment to both the public system and private insurers and closes on "that's my focus as Minister of Health." The core proposition is left entirely untouched — a pivot to talking points on a narrow yes/no-plus-reason question.
question: Are top health researchers correct in saying, “Health systems that rely on funding via private insurance are … less accessible, less efficient, less equitable, and [generally] have worse health outcomes.”, and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, many, many New Zealanders rely on our public health system, and many, many New Zealanders have private health insurance. The private health companies do an amazing job, as does our public health system, to ensure that New Zealanders can access the timely, quality care that they need so they can live healthy lives. That’s my focus as Minister of Health.

explanation: Asked whether Mulholland is correct that more private involvement would only benefit the well-off. Opens by attacking the questioner's party, then pivots to funding figures. The tail does glance at the core — noting GPs and clinics are already private, an implicit counter to "only the well-off" — but he never states whether the claim is correct or gives the "if not, why not". Partial engagement at best.
question: Is health advocate Malcolm Mulholland correct that “opening the health system up to more private sector involvement would only benefit the well-off”, and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, I think the Labour Party is in a very dark and conspiratorial place. I mean, we are focused on delivering the quality and timely healthcare that New Zealanders need and focusing the system on results. This Government has invested a record $16.88 billion into our public health system. But I also say there are many, many parts of our healthcare system in New Zealand which are operated by the private sector—our entire GP system, our doctors, our doctor clinics—and I thank them for the work that they do delivering healthcare for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked to explain why people wait longer and pay more. He gives an explanation — the previous Government's pandemic-era restructure. Blaming the questioner's party is the substance of the causal claim here, not a dodge, and whether that explanation is true or well-reasoned is Veracity/Rigor, not this attribute. Marked down because only the waiting-times half is addressed; the "paying more for doctors appointments" limb is never touched, and the answer trails into a focus-on-outcomes line.
question: Then, can he explain to New Zealanders why they are waiting longer for health appointments and paying more for doctors appointments?
statement: Well, because we’ve inherited a system which the last Government decided to restructure during a pandemic. Instead of focusing on outcomes, they were focused on bureaucracy, and my focus is on getting the outcomes that New Zealanders need.

explanation: Two limbs. The first is answered squarely and briefly: "that is not the Government's position" — a clear no on the opt-out proposal. The second limb, what he will do to prevent defunding and privatisation, gets only faster appointments, more elective surgeries and record funding, which never reaches the question. Half the question answered directly, half replaced with talking points.
question: Does he agree with David Seymour’s state of the nation speech, which asked if we should, “allow people to opt out of the public healthcare system, and take their portion of funding with them so they can go private?”, and, if not, what’s the Minister going to do to prevent the health system from being defunded and privatised?
statement: Well, that is not the Government’s position, but what we are focused on doing is about focusing on delivering the outcomes that New Zealanders need: faster specialist appointments, doctor visits quicker, making sure there are more elective surgeries being completed. We have invested a record amount of funding in our public health system, and now we need to focus on making sure it is delivering the results that Kiwis deserve and expect.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken on literacy and numeracy achievement. The reply lists actions: the new curriculum, structured literacy, classroom resources, targeted interventions, teacher PLD and the phonics check. A friendly question, but it is answered on its own terms and completely; the promotional framing does not make it a dodge.
question: What actions has the Government taken to lift achievement in literacy and numeracy as part of its plan to teach the basics brilliantly?
statement: With the 2025 school year kicking off, this Government is relentlessly focused on lifting student achievement and closing the equity gap in classrooms by teaching the basics brilliantly. From this term, parents can expect their children to benefit from a new year-by-year knowledge-rich curriculum grounded in the science of learning, structured approach to literacy and numeracy, new classroom resources, targeted interventions for kids who need extra help, teachers’ professional learning and development, and the roll-out of a phonics check.

explanation: Asked what changes have been made to the curriculum, and the answer describes the changes — a knowledge-rich, structured, internationally comparable English and maths curriculum, consistent across schools. Directly responsive; no pivot.
question: What changes have been made to the curriculum?
statement: This year, 65,000 young New Zealanders starting school will benefit from an internationally comparable, knowledge-rich, and structured curriculum in English and maths, that has been very well received by the sector. Parents will know exactly what their children are learning each year in school in English and maths. And no matter which school or classroom in the country they are a part of, they will receive exactly the same teaching and learning from the same high-quality curriculum.

explanation: Asked what changes parents can expect in how children learn to read and write. The answer stays on that exact point throughout: structured literacy for years 0–3, 18,000 teachers trained, phonics checks at 20 and 40 weeks, resourcing, reading intervention teachers. Direct and complete.
question: What changes can parents expect for how their kids are learning to read and write?
statement: Every single child in years zero to 3 learning to read will start school this year being taught to read using structured literacy, including the young six-year-old Angus Bates, who’s in the gallery today. Eighteen thousand teachers have already been trained or are in training. Phonics checks are available after 20 and 40 weeks at school to catch our young learners who are falling behind. Schools across the country are getting up to $5,000 for additional structured literacy resources each year for four years. And, finally, 970 schools applied for and received staffing allocations for reading intervention teachers for young learners who are falling behind in their reading.

explanation: Asked what changes parents can expect in maths this year; the answer names them — workbooks and teacher guides shipped, curriculum-aligned resources, maths PLD, the years 7–8 acceleration trial. It closes on a slogan, but the question itself was squarely engaged before that.
question: What changes can parents expect for how their kids are learning mathematics this year?
statement: Nearly half a million maths workbooks, textbooks, and teacher guides are being shipped to primary and intermediate schools around New Zealand where they will benefit over 430,000 students as they engage with their new maths curriculum this year. High-quality curriculum-aligned resources will not only support teachers to implement the new curriculum but increase the consistency of teaching and learning. They are supplemented by teacher professional learning and development in maths and our maths acceleration trial for years 7 and 8 students, set to benefit 3,000 of them. A world-leading education system is a key driver for our economic growth, and we need all children to be proficient in reading, writing, and maths, which is why we are so unashamedly focused on teaching the basics brilliantly.

explanation: Two limbs. Limb one is not answered with agree/disagree, but he says explicitly why he won't — the question conflates the wait-list, emergency housing and severe housing deprivation. Contesting a premise openly is engagement, not evasion, though it stops short of an answer. Limb two is answered directly: he remains confident, with the 81 percent reduction cited. More engaged than dodged, but not complete.
question: Does he agree with Andrew Crisp, Chief Executive of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, who said that “both the register and people that apply does not represent effectively … severe housing deprivation”; if so, is he confident that the need for emergency housing has reduced?
statement: I acknowledge that tens of thousands of New Zealanders, disproportionately Māori, are doing it tough with the cost of living crisis and severe housing challenges. Limb one of the question is unnecessarily ambiguous because it conflates the social housing wait-list with emergency housing and severe housing deprivation, all of which have different characteristics. In relation to limb two, blue shoots—the country has reached the Government target, reducing by 81 percent the number of households living in emergency housing. Emergency housing, I remain confident, remains an option for New Zealanders with genuine need for short-term stay, temporary accommodation in most towns and cities.

explanation: Asked whether he seriously believes the need for emergency housing is down to only 591 households. He restates the 80 percent reduction and the 2,500 children, and adds "I'm very serious about that" — which hedges toward yes without ever addressing whether the household count reflects need. The core distinction the question turns on is talked around rather than met.
question: Does he seriously think that the need for emergency housing in this country has been reduced to only 591 households?
statement: I’m very proud that this Government has taken serious action to ensure that the number of households in emergency housing has reduced by over 80 percent, and I’m particularly comfortable and enthusiastic that over 2,500 children have left emergency housing since we became the administration. And I’m very serious about that. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked to admit he is masking true need by stopping people entering emergency housing. He effectively answers no by denying the premise: in most towns and cities those with genuine need have a pathway in, alongside other placements. That is a direct response to the central allegation. The "growing homelessness crisis" limb is left unaddressed, which caps the score.
question: Will he admit that by stopping people from entering emergency housing, as front-line agencies have told him is happening, he is masking the true need for housing and overseeing a growing homelessness crisis in this country?
statement: In most towns and cities in this country, those people who have a genuine need for a short-term stay in temporary accommodation, known as emergency housing, have a pathway to do that. Yes, there is a responsibility framework that goes with that, but there are also a number of other support products and brokering services that enable people stay out of emergency housing and be placed in social service transitional housing and social housing and other options.

explanation: A pointed either/or — believe the front-line agencies or the Minister. He acknowledges the providers' concerns, which is a small step toward the question, but never resolves the choice put to him and moves quickly to build programmes and housing numbers. The core of the question is avoided.
question: Who should New Zealanders believe: agencies working on the front line that told the Minister to his face that his policy changes are stopping people getting the emergency housing they need and are leaving them on the street, or the Minister, who focuses on the savings of a million dollars a week?
statement: I acknowledge there is genuine concern that is being expressed to me by a number of social service providers and others around the health and housing crisis that continues to confront many New Zealanders, disproportionately Māori. We have also committed to continuing a build programme with Kāinga Ora, with over 1,500 net homes to be built; support for community housing providers, with 1,500 additional funded places over the next couple of years; and others, like Tainui and many Māori housing providers, with another 300 affordable rentals to be built in the next couple of years. We acknowledge that there are genuine concerns and are also taking steps in order to ensure that going for housing growth, the housing renaissance led by the Manu Pūtea Nicola Willis and the Manu Pīhopa Chris Bishop is carried through.

explanation: Asked whether the Government will keep referring people to food banks while denying ongoing funding to bodies like the Auckland City Mission. Upston's first sentence engages the core factual limb head-on — the Government is continuing to fund the Auckland City Mission — which rebuts the question's premise directly. The rest pivots to inherited spending and 'our focus is on fixing it', leaving the 'continue referring people to food banks' limb untouched. Partial engagement: the answerable half was answered, the other half absorbed into talking points.
question: Will the Government continue referring people to food banks while denying ongoing funding to food banks like the Auckland City Mission, or is kids going hungry just the necessary casualty of the Government outsourcing basic social services to underfunded charities in the private sector?
statement: The Government is continuing to fund organisations like the Auckland City Mission. As I said, I accept that it is incredibly challenging right now. I would like to stand here and say that we didn’t inherit a period of prolific Government spending that has led to incredibly challenging economic times that mean more families are doing it tough, but our focus on this side of the House is on fixing it.

explanation: Two limbs: does she stand by 'nicotine is incredibly addictive', and what evidence-based actions has she taken to help people quit nicotine. The first is answered flatly and immediately ('Nicotine is incredibly addictive; there's not a single person in this House who would dispute that'). The second is answered on a reframed basis — action taken is supplying lower-harm nicotine products and, post-quit, stop-smoking services for vaping — which is helping smokers manage nicotine addiction rather than quit nicotine, so it reaches the question at an angle. The swipe at 'members opposite' and the length of the smoking-harms detour are Civility/Specificity matters and did not move this score.
question: Does she stand by her statement that “Nicotine is incredibly addictive”; if so, what evidence-based actions, if any, has she taken to support people to quit nicotine?
statement: Nicotine is incredibly addictive; there’s not a single person in this House who would dispute that. Unfortunately, yet again, the members opposite continue to conflate two different issues, so I will try again to clarify. Smoking kills. It harms nearly every organ of the body, causing cancer, heart disease, stroke, lung disease—the list goes on. But let’s be clear. Nicotine is what keeps people smoking; it is not what makes it deadly. That’s why this Government is focused on supporting smokers to manage their addiction to nicotine by accessing lower-harm nicotine products as alternatives to cigarettes. This has been standard practice for a considerable period of time. Once smokers have successfully quit, stop smoking services are able to support individuals to shift their focus to quitting vaping.

explanation: Asked why RELX vapes are funded as cessation devices given (a) no Medsafe approval and (b) no robust procurement. Costello answers (b) squarely and immediately — 'The procurement process has been complied with' — and gives a genuine 'why': the innovation fund is trialling alternative products, restricted to adult smokers in quit programmes. The Medsafe-approval limb is never mentioned, which is the part of the question left unengaged. Whether her procurement claim is true is Veracity, not this.
question: Why is her Government funding RELX vapes as smoking cessation devices when unlike all other smoking cessation tools, they have not been approved by Medsafe and have not been through a robust procurement process?
statement: The procurement process has been complied with. The product is completely compliant and safe. It is supplied by a company with no affiliations to the tobacco industry and it is a completely compliant product and is New Zealand - owned. The issue that we are talking about is that this product is being funded by the innovation fund as a tool to apply to alternative products that will help smokers quit smoking. It is only provided through quit smoking services and only to adult smokers and only to those who have committed to a programme of quitting smoking.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: does she acknowledge RELX set an unusually high nicotine content relative to approved cessation tools. The response never touches nicotine content, comparison, or acknowledgment — it declares the questioner is 'conflating the issues' and restates that the product is less harmful than smoking. That is an answer to a different question (is it safer?) than the one asked (is it more addictive, and was that for RELX's gain?). A sharply specific question wholly avoided, so it sits near the floor.
question: Does she acknowledge that RELX determined an unusually high nicotine content for these vapes compared to approved smoking cessation tools, making them more addictive, and therefore maximising RELX’s financial gain?
statement: Yet again we are conflating the issues. We are talking about a product that is less harmful than smoking and therefore will allow long-term addicted smokers to quit smoking.

explanation: Asked for her response to leaked recordings quoting RELX employees on bribes. She asked for the question to be repeated rather than responding. No part of the question is engaged, so it cannot score as answered; it is graded above a pivot because it is not a substitute answer or an attack on the questioner, and the following pair shows she did then respond. A genuine mishearing and a stalling tactic are indistinguishable from the text, and the rubric here scores what the response did, not the intent behind it.
question: What is her response to leaked recordings of RELX employees stating, “We’ve made effing bribes in New Zealand and Australia.” and “That’s the thing, right? Especially in difficult markets or markets with heavy strict regulations, all you have to do to circumnavigate them is to go into the grey channels.”?
statement: Mr Speaker, could she repeat the question? I’m not sure what the question was.

explanation: Asked what her response is to the leaked RELX recordings. She gives one directly: the quotes are selectively excerpted and omit the speakers saying 'No, no, no. That's not what we do', and the recording is from Singapore in 2023 with no bearing on New Zealand. That squarely engages the thing asked about. Whether her characterisation of the recording is accurate is a Veracity question and was held out of this score.
question: What is her response to the leaked recordings of RELX employees stating, “We’ve made effing bribes in New Zealand and Australia.” and “That’s the thing, right? Especially in difficult markets or markets with heavy strict regulations, all you have to do to circumnavigate them is to go into the grey channels.”?
statement: My response to that summation of quotes is the fact that she’s missed out the section where the people in the recording are saying “No, no, no. That’s not what we do.” and also that this is a 2023 recording in Singapore, which has no connection to New Zealand markets or New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked for her response to further leaked quotes about 'Government payments' being subtle. She responds by rejecting the premise outright — the inference that this Government received bribes is abhorrent. Rejecting the premise is a real response to 'what is your response', and a blunt refusal to accept the framing is not a dodge. Marked below the previous pair because she engages only with the implication drawn, not with the quoted material itself, which the question put directly in front of her.
question: What is her response to leaked recordings of RELX employees stating, “I’m talking about making, like, Government payments.” and in response, “We don’t do that visibly in Australia and New Zealand, but Government payments are not a problem for us because these are extremely—how do I put it—subtle.”?
statement: The inference that this New Zealand Government has received bribes is abhorrent and I reject the premise of that question.

explanation: Asked (a) will she ensure an independent investigation, and (b) if not, how will she address public concern. She never says yes or no, but 'I have met with officials today. I'm confident in the procurement processes' reads as a clear implicit no, and the meeting with officials is offered as the response to concerns. The core is reachable but she does not state it, so this is answering while hedging around the point rather than a refusal — which, said plainly, would have scored high.
question: Will she ensure the procurement process for RELX vapes undergoes independent investigation in light of these comments from RELX employees, and if not, how will she address the concerns from New Zealanders about the procurement of these devices?
statement: I have met with officials today. I’m confident in the procurement processes. We have produced a product that will allow smokers to quit smoking, and we stand by that programme of work.

explanation: Asked for updates on Customs improving services using technology. The answer is entirely on that subject: digital traveller declarations now outnumber paper ones, the app can be completed 24 hours ahead and covers multiple declarations, and the benefits for border processing. A friendly question, but the test is only whether it was engaged, and it was, directly and completely.
question: What updates can she provide about the New Zealand Customs Service’s efforts to improve services using technology?
statement: I am pleased to announce that the New Zealand Customs Service, who are an exemplary Government department, recently announced that more travellers are now using the digital traveller declaration than the paper version. Everyone entering New Zealand must complete a declaration, and Customs and its border partners have worked tirelessly to encourage Kiwis and overseas visitors to use the declaration, which can be done 24 hours in advance of travel, rather than on board a flight, and makes it easy to fill out multiple declarations before getting off a plane. Downloading the New Zealand Traveller Declaration app has additional benefits for families and frequent travellers. The digital declaration delivers better public services by supporting efficient processing by border agencies, and streamlining passengers’ experience entering New Zealand. I would encourage everyone to give the digital declaration a go the next time they return to New Zealand.

explanation: Asked what other technology improvements are helping arriving and departing passengers. Answered directly and on point: e-gate access extended to all 27 EU member states from September, now 37 countries and over 85 percent of travellers, with further visa-waiver countries being planned. Nothing asked was left unaddressed.
question: What other technology improvements are delivering better services for passengers arriving to or departing New Zealand?
statement: From September last year, e-passport holders from all 27 EU member States became able to use e-gates on arrival to and departure from New Zealand. This expansion means that travellers from 37 countries have access to automatic border processing in New Zealand. This represents over 85 percent of all arriving and departing travellers. I’m also advised that Customs is finalising plans to progressively open e-gates’ access to remaining visa-waiver countries. Seamless and efficient border processing not only improves traveller experiences, it also frees up front-line customer staff to increase their focus on critical tasks, like assessing high-risk travellers.

explanation: Asked whether technology improvements are also supporting businesses. Effectively 'yes', with the supporting instances named — the alcohol Excise Duty Estimator, updated duty forms, and the MyCustoms account platform with deferred payment balances and statements. Direct and complete engagement with the question put.
question: Are technology improvements also supporting New Zealand businesses?
statement: In the environment of saying “yes” and committing to economic growth, Customs has made significant progress in making it easier for businesses to spend less time on paperwork, and more time focused on their business. Last year, Customs launched the alcohol Excise Duty Estimator on its website, and updated duty alcohol application forms and permits. Both of these updates aim to support businesses to make excise-related information easier to understand and more readily available. In addition, the launch of the MyCustoms account platform in June last year delivered improved accessibility, with deferred payment account holders given the ability to view their balance and transactions, download statements, and immediately access the information that they need online. Customs’ deferred payments scheme allows importers to defer payments on their Customs’ charges, consolidating them into a monthly invoice. This frees up cash flow, and means low-risk imports can move across the border faster. I’m advised that further options for online services are being developed, with the aim of being rolled out for clients later this year.

explanation: Asked what feedback on the technology improvements Customs has received. She answers the question asked: the feedback is positive, from both Customs' operational side and the public, and stakeholders such as airlines, freight and Customs brokers are enthusiastic. The answer is thin on specifics — no volumes, no survey — but thinness is Specificity; on the only question here, the feedback question was met rather than sidestepped.
question: What feedback related to technology improvements has been received by Customs that she’s aware of?
statement: I’ve been advised that the digital advances made by Customs are being positively received and providing improved efficiencies for both Customs’ operational needs, as well as the public using their services. Further stakeholders that Customs work with, such as airlines and fast freight and Custom brokers, are all enthusiastic about the agency’s development of digital services.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered "Yes." One word, complete, no hedge — the canonical forthright answer.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked WHY the Government approved a $575,000 purchase from RELX. Never addresses the approval decision: redirects the bribery implication back at the questioner's own former government, then argues vaping products work. The fragment "the product works and all evidence says so" glances at a rationale, which is why this is not at the floor, but the specific procurement decision asked about is never engaged.
question: Why did the Government approve the purchase of $575,000 worth of vaping products from RELX, a company accused of bribing the New Zealand Government?
statement: As that member was just told, the date of that so-called phone call was to a Government that she was a member of with the help of the Greens in 2023. So any implication of a bribery comes straight back to her own back door. Now, having dismissed that because I don’t believe it did happen in that way—I think it’s a typical Green fiction—the reality is that the product works and all evidence says so. It says so in other countries, and we’re in the first three in the world in reducing cigarette smoking and we should salute that because we’re ahead of our target now.

explanation: Asked whether he can confirm any Minister or official knew of the bribery allegations before procurement. He says plainly that he cannot confirm it, and gives a reason. That is a direct and complete response to a can-you-confirm question. The reason is a jab at the questioner and its accuracy is contestable, but neither is Forthrightness — the question was answered, not dodged.
question: Can he confirm whether any Minister or official was aware of the bribery allegations against RELX before the procurement of these vaping products?
statement: We most definitely cannot confirm that because we weren’t in Government at the time; she was.

explanation: Asked whether a formal tender process was followed. Does not say yes or no; points at a review and an answer given to a prior question. Referring the questioner elsewhere is a thin form of engagement — it acknowledges the question and asserts an answer exists — but it does not deliver the yes/no that a narrow factual question demanded.
question: Was a formal tender process followed for selecting a vaping supplier at Health New Zealand?
statement: The Minister in charge has had a review today and she’s given that answer to a prior question in this House already.

explanation: Asked directly for his own view on whether the spending was appropriate. Offers no view at all; converts the question into a demand that the questioner's side explain how the process started. A narrow question about his own belief, squarely avoided.
question: Does he believe it is appropriate for Health New Zealand to use taxpayer money to purchase products from a company with a documented history of regulatory breaches?
statement: Well, again, if that is the case, then that Minister and her colleagues owe us an explanation as to how they began the process in the first place.

explanation: Asked whether he can confirm any undisclosed meetings, correspondence or lobbying with RELX. He engages the core: says his side had not heard of the company, and that the inquiry would need to be on notice to be answered properly. That is a real response to a can-you-confirm question. Marked down from there because he then pivots into a counter-attack about 2021 policy rather than closing on the question asked.
question: Can he confirm whether any Minister, official, or Government agency has had undisclosed meetings, correspondence, or lobbying interactions with RELX or it’s representatives?
statement: I have to tell that member that many of us on this side have never heard of that company before today, and for such an inquiry to be answered we would need to have it on notice so we can go and find out and give you an honest answer in this House. Bear this in mind, though: the survey that began this process was done when she was in Government in 2021, and it said that the evidence says that smoking goes down as the less harmful vaping goes up. She got that information and she was acting on it then. Why the change in policy from the Opposition now?

explanation: Asked to rule out that anyone in Government received direct or indirect benefits, and if not, why not. He does not rule it out, but he does engage the second limb — the stated reason is that full inquiries are needed — and undertakes to come back with an answer. Half credit: the "why not" limb is answered, the central ruling-out is deferred and entangled with redirection at the other parties.
question: Can the Prime Minister rule out that any Government officials, Ministers, or parties in this Government received direct or indirect benefits from RELX or its affiliates in relation to that purchase; if not, why not?
statement: I am very grateful, as it turns out, for the Greens’ disclosure today, because the year 2023 says that everything about this question relates to their time in office. So we can’t account just for our side without finding out about her side. So perhaps we can come back next week and answer the question, having made full inquiries of the Labour Party and the Green Party.

explanation: Asked whether he has confidence in the Associate Minister's handling of the procurement. He answers explicitly: "Yes, I do have confidence in the Minister, total confidence in the Minister." The long preamble attacking the questioner and the media is a Civility and Focus problem, and deliberately does not count here. Slightly below the top only because the confidence stated is in the Minister generally rather than in her handling of this process specifically.
question: Does he have confidence in Associate Minister of Health Casey Costello’s handling of this procurement process, given the lack of transparency and due diligence?
statement: Sometimes, you know, you can give an answer; you take a horse to water, but you can’t make it drink. The answer is profoundly in her own court. This began in 2023 when they were responsible. They started the process and all of a sudden, now, all sorts of allegations are falsely made and probably taken up by a very compliant media as part and parcel of the future history of this matter, but none of it will be true. Yes, I do have confidence in the Minister, total confidence in the Minister, because she’s got an impeccable record on matters like that, as a former policewoman.

explanation: Asked to commit to an independent public inquiry, and if not, why not. Never says yes or no. The remark that he could barely explain why an inquiry is needed reads as an implicit refusal with a gesture at a reason, which keeps it off the floor, but it dissolves into rebuking the questioner rather than plainly declining. A blunt "No, and here's why" would have scored high; this does not reach that.
question: Will he commit to an independent public inquiry into the influence of the tobacco and vaping industry on its smoke-free policies; if not, why not?
statement: I’d barely be able to explain why they’re going to have an inquiry when the tobacco companies are screaming blue murder that they’re being treated unfairly. Can’t that member get through her head what’s actually happened here? You’ve got the insinuation, and the facts are a thousand miles away from them.

explanation: Asked what reaction he has seen to the speed limit announcement. Delivers exactly that — named reactions from Transporting New Zealand and the Masterton Mayor, quoted. Directly and completely responsive. That this is a friendly question from a government member makes it uninformative, but it does not make the answer evasive.
question: What reaction has he seen to the announcement yesterday that the previous Government’s speed limit reductions are being reversed by 1 July 2025?
statement: There’s been a fantastic response due to yesterday’s announcement around the reversal of the untargeted blanket speed limit reductions. For example, Transporting New Zealand saying they are “pleased to see the programme of speed limit reversals getting underway” and “changes will reduce journey times and help avoid dangerous behaviour by frustrated drivers.” It was good to see that Masterton Mayor Gary Caffell, His Worship, told Morning Report “the three-minute saving journey [time] meant a lot for transport firms, ambulances and emergency services like the fire brigade.”

explanation: Asked what feedback he has seen on the economic growth potential of the announcement. Supplies feedback from Transporting New Zealand and New Zealand Couriers on journey times and freight costs. Answers the question asked; a little of the response is general growth framing rather than feedback seen, which is the only reason it sits below the previous pair.
question: What feedback has he seen regarding the economic growth potential of this announcement?
statement: Well, we are very focused in this Government on speeding up economic growth and these measures will make a difference. Time savings make a difference across the country when it comes to making it easier to get from A to B. Transporting New Zealand said their members have been frustrated by blanket speed restrictions; the impact of increased journey times and increased freight costs were not adequately considered. New Zealand Couriers said that speed limits are an issue for couriers. The answer to unlocking growth in this economy is not one silver bullet policy; it’s hundreds of different actions like this one taken across Government to speed New Zealand’s economy up.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the PM that Crown-Māori relations are 'probably worse'. He opens with 'e tika ana te kōrero a te Pirīmia' — the Prime Minister's statement is correct — which is an unambiguous yes, followed by a reflection that governments come and go but the Treaty endures. The follow-on is padding, not evasion; the core yes/no was given.
question: Te Arawhiti: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that Crown-Māori relations are “probably worse” under the coalition Government?
statement: I te ao, i te pō, e tika ana te kōrero a te Pirīmia. Tēnei āhuatanga, te Kāwanatanga, pērā i ngā pāti o tēnei Whare me ngā mema Pāremata: he wā ka tae mai, he wā ka hoki ki te kāinga. Engari me toitū te Tiriti ki te āke āke.

explanation: A two-part question: does he stand by his statement, and if so why support the Regulatory Standards Bill. The first half is answered flatly ('Ae, e tino tautoko ana au i tāku kōrero'). The second half — the substantive part — is deferred with 'tāria te wā', wait and see how the bill is implemented. Half the question squarely engaged, the harder half postponed rather than answered.
question: Does he agree with his statement that “te iwi Māori and Te Tiriti are fundamental to the country’s past, present, and future”; if so, why is he supporting the Regulatory Standards Bill, which would limit the role of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in future legislation?
statement: Ae, e tino tautoko ana au i tāku kōrero ai, me te mea nei, tāria te wā ka rongo hoki ki ngā kōrero a te Pirīmia; tāria te wā, mō tērā pire, ka kitea hoki tōna whakatinanatanga.

explanation: Asked whether he advocated for Māori issues to be included in the PM's statement. The reply — the content of the PM's speeches is for the PM, not for Tama Potaka — is crisp and on-topic but answers a different question: who owns the speech, not whether he advocated. It implies a no without ever stating one. Closer to a deflection than a refusal, since a refusal would at least concede the question was put to him.
question: Did he advocate for the inclusion of Māori issues in the Prime Minister’s statement, considering that the Prime Minister has admitted what the Māori-Crown relationship is worth under his Government?
statement: The content of the Prime Minister’s speeches is for the Prime Minister, not for Tama Potaka.

explanation: A does-he-stand-by-it question, answered 'āna' — yes — with the qualifier 'i te nuinga o ngā tāone o Aotearoa' (in most of New Zealand's towns). The qualifier slightly narrows the original claim rather than dodging it; the yes is delivered directly and the question is engaged.
question: Does he stand by his answer to oral question No. 9 yesterday that “those people who have a genuine need for a short-term stay in temporary accommodation known as emergency housing have a pathway to do that”; if not, why not?
statement: Ki te arero o ōku tūpuna, āna, i te nuinga o ngā tāone o Aotearoa.

explanation: Asked how he reconciles his position with front-line providers telling him directly that his policy changes are blocking people with genuine need. The answer restates that the process is clear and that officials apply it properly — an assertion about the process, not a reconciliation. The providers' contradiction is never touched. The narrowness of the 'how do you reconcile' framing makes the miss a squarer one.
question: How does he reconcile that with numerous front-line providers telling him at the Community Housing Aotearoa Conference 2024 that the policy changes he brought in are stopping those with genuine need getting into emergency housing?
statement: We have been very clear about the process through which the assessment of genuine need is undertaken, and we’re very confident that the officials are undertaking that process in a pono and tika manner.

explanation: Asked how a specific young mother in a tent does not have genuine need. He says he cannot respond fully without further information, calls it an operational matter, and encourages follow-up. That is a hedged non-answer, but it is a response to the question actually asked rather than a pivot or an attack — he engages with the case and states why he will not address it. Partial engagement, not a dodge.
question: How does the young mother and her four-month-old in Tauranga, who was told she can’t apply for emergency housing and is now living in a tent, not have genuine need?
statement: In relation to that particular example, without further information, it’s very hard to respond fully, and I’m sure that is a matter that should be dealt with at an operational end, and I encourage that to be followed up.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on employment. She names the Stats NZ monthly employment indicator and MSD quarterly benefit statistics, with the figures each carries. Direct and complete — the question asked for reports and reports were given.
question: What reports has she seen on employment in New Zealand?
statement: Stats NZ’s monthly employment indicator released this week showed the number of filled jobs increased on a seasonally adjusted basis in December.
