explanation: Asked what else the Government is doing. Three further items are named — paid parental leave increase, FamilyBoost, extended breast screening. The closing jab at opponents is a Focus/Civility matter and doesn't reduce the fact that the question was answered.
question: What else is the Government doing?
statement: The Government is committed to supporting women. That is why we have increased paid parental leave by 6 percent, we have introduced the FamilyBoost payment to help meet the cost of early childhood education, and we have rolled out an extension to breast screening services to include 70- to 74-year-olds. We are all about action, not press releases and empty, hollow promises.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. The answer opens with an unqualified 'Yes' — complete on its own terms. The infrastructure material that follows is padding, not evasion.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Yes, especially our action to unlock infrastructure investment. The Waikato Expressway is a great example of the impact that modern, reliable infrastructure can make for families and for businesses, and now we’re bringing the same experience to Northland—more jobs, more growth, more connectivity, and more opportunity for every New Zealander living north of Auckland. It’s no surprise that I saw today the Northland Corporate Group said the expressway is “exactly what our economy needs to drive growth, create jobs, reduce costs, and enable export expansion.” We’re serious about economic growth and ensuring that Kiwis can get ahead, and delivering infrastructure like the Northland Expressway is just one part of that vision.

explanation: Asked why he is willing to wait until term 2 to fix the school lunch programme. He concedes the incident was unacceptable and describes the Minister working through the issues, but never addresses the timing — why term 2 rather than now — which is the specific thing asked. It gestures at the subject without reaching the question.
question: Why is he willing to wait until term 2 for the chaos David Seymour’s caused to the school lunch programme to be fixed, given kids are going hungry; lunches are still arriving late or not at all; some of the food is inedible; and, in the worst cases, kids are being physically injured by exploding lunches?
statement: Well, the incident we saw last week was unacceptable and not something we want to see at all. I think the Minister has fronted really clearly on that, actually suspending those type of lunches. Importantly, he is working his way through the issues to make sure that we get better-quality food and better on-time performance.

explanation: Asked what it would take for him personally to step in, and about Seymour ignoring Stanford. He restates that the Minister is working hard and improvements are coming by term 2 — a repeat of the previous non-answer. Neither the threshold for his own intervention nor the Stanford point is touched.
question: What will it take for him to finally step in and fix the mess his Government has made of the school lunches programme, particularly given the one Minister who actually seems to want to get it sorted out, Erica Stanford, is being ignored by David Seymour?
statement: Again, this is a Minister that’s working incredibly hard through some very challenging issues to make sure that we get our food back to scratch and to make sure that we deliver on time, in full. There’s some improvement happening; there’s a lot more that needs to happen; and, as I said, the Minister is wanting to make sure there are improvements in place for term 2.

explanation: Asked to guarantee that the collective partner's insolvency won't leave kids hungry. He addresses it squarely: he has been assured the programme is not at risk despite the liquidation. Short of the personal guarantee sought — he reports an assurance rather than giving one — but the question was engaged, not dodged.
question: Will he guarantee that one of the three partners in the school lunch collective going insolvent won’t lead to any kids going hungry; if not, why not?
statement: That is what we have been assured: that, despite the liquidation, the school lunches programme is not at risk. Obviously, that’s a commercial matter, but our key thing is to make sure that we are getting what we have contracted for and that that is delivered.

explanation: Asked why rough sleeping rose 53% and whether that coincided with 690 households leaving emergency housing. The answer never touches the 53% figure, the 690 households, or the causal link — it pivots entirely to a record-comparison talking point ('I put our record up on housing against yours any day'). Neither limb of the question is engaged.
question: Why has the number of rough sleepers in Auckland increased by 53 percent over the last four months, and is it a coincidence that that occurred at the same time his Government kicked 690 Auckland households out of emergency housing?
statement: Well, I am incredibly proud of our record on housing, unlike that last Government. We have stable rents; we have 4,000 to 5,000 people off the social housing wait-list, which went up four times under Minister Megan Woods; and, importantly, we’ve taken 2,000 kids out of motel accommodation and got them into proper homes and houses through community housing providers in Kāinga Ora (KO). I put our record up on housing against yours any day of the week. [Interruption]

explanation: Two limbs: does he agree with Potaka that the link is real, and if not will he provide evidence of where the kids went. He never says whether he agrees, and never commits to providing evidence. Repeating the 2,000-kids line brushes the 'where did they go' limb for the cohort that was moved, which is why this is above zero, but the core — agree or not, evidence or not — is untouched.
question: Well, does he agree with Tama Potaka that the link between people getting kicked out of emergency housing and a rise in homelessness is “not anecdotal, it’s real”, and, if not, will he provide evidence of where the kids in emergency housing actually went?
statement: As we have said before, we have taken 2,000 kids that were being raised in motels under the last Government, and we now have them in proper homes and proper houses through community housing providers in KO. I thought that member would actually want to celebrate that and actually think that was a good thing.

explanation: Asked what happened to the 20% not moved into sustainable housing. The reply asserts they haven't needed assistance, which is a substantive claim about that group rather than a pure pivot, but it answers 'are you helping them?' instead of 'what happened to them?'. Partial engagement; the asked-for account of where they went is never given. (Its vagueness is not what lowers the score — the substitution of a different question is.)
question: What happened to the 20 percent who haven’t been moved into sustainable housing?
statement: The message, very clearly, is that if they need our assistance and help, we are there to help and assist them. They haven’t needed it.

explanation: Asked when the next Treasury forecasts will be released. Answer names the occasion and the date — 22 May, with the Budget. Direct and complete.
question: When will the Treasury’s next set of economic and fiscal forecasts be released?
statement: Each year, Treasury does two sets of forecasts: one to accompany the Budget, and another at the half-year update. In an election year, as a bonus, there’s also a pre-election update. Looking ahead, the next Treasury forecasts will be those that accompany the Budget, on 22 May.

explanation: Asked what the new economic forecasts will show. Answer states expectations squarely: return to growth in the December quarter, picking up through the year, unemployment peaking in H1 2025 then declining. Caveats about forecaster uncertainty are appended after the question is answered, not used to avoid it.
question: What will the new economic forecasts show?
statement: Broadly in keeping with other published economic forecasts, I expect the Treasury’s forecast to show a return to growth in the December quarter of last year, then picking up over this calendar year. Consistent with other forecasts, they are also likely to show unemployment peaking in the first half of 2025 and then declining. Treasury is currently working through its detailed forecasting process. What I would say is it’s a hard time to be a forecaster, with a lot of uncertainty around the impact of other countries’ economic policies and responses.

explanation: Asked what the fiscal forecasts will show. Answer engages directly given the forecasts are unfinished: some elements up, some down, higher finance costs from global bond yields, and an explicit expectation of no positive fiscal surprise. It reaches the point rather than circling it.
question: What will the new fiscal forecasts show?
statement: Well, again, the Treasury is still working through their process, and the Government is still working through our Budget decisions. What I do know from previous updates is that within the overall fiscal picture, some elements will show an improvement over the previous forecasts, and some will show a decline. For example, the outlook for global bond yields means that finance costs are likely to be greater than they were at the half-year update. That is to say, the costs of servicing New Zealand’s debt will be higher. And, given my experience of forecast revisions last year, I am not holding out hope for an overall positive fiscal surprise. That seems unlikely, but it is still early days. As with the economic forecasts, there are many risks that could affect the fiscal forecasts.

explanation: Asked what her approach to the new forecasts will be. Answer states the approach plainly: medium-term consolidation, no overreaction to movements either way, Budget allowances driving restraint, with options considered before Budget 2025. Squarely responsive.
question: What will her approach be to the new forecasts?
statement: The Government has a deliberate medium-term approach to fiscal consolidation, and we’ve always said that we will not overreact to movements up or down in the forecasts. We have set Budget allowances that drive spending restraint and require savings to fund Government priorities. None the less, the Government will look at options during the lead-up to Budget 2025 and consider whether the new Treasury forecasts warrant any further action.

explanation: Two limbs. On 'does she stand by the statement' she hedges — 'I may well have said that' plus an unverified-quote caveat — without confirming or denying. On the growth target she answers directly and completely: no explicit target for variables other than inflation. One limb dodged, one answered cleanly.
question: Does she stand by her statement that “We are taking steps to ensure that we will grow faster than we otherwise would”; if so, what is her growth target for jobs and incomes?
statement: I may well have said that—it sounds like something I would say—but my office has not been able to access the verification, so I don’t know the context and am mindful that that member has quoted me out of context and incorrectly in the past. To the second part, the Government has a target for inflation but no explicit target for other economic variables. Needless to say, my ambition is to deliver policies that support more job creation and higher incomes.

explanation: Asked why there are 6,248 fewer filled jobs. The answer gives an actual causal account — inflation left unchecked, interest rates hiked, hitting growth and job creation — and then argues the unemployment level matches pre-election forecasts. Whether that explanation is correct is Veracity, and its partisan framing is Focus; as a response to 'why', the question is engaged.
question: Why, then, are there 6,248 fewer filled jobs than this time last year, according to Statistics New Zealand?
statement: As we have gone through in this House again and again, unfortunately, when inflation is left to go out of control and interest rates are hiked very far, that has a negative impact for both economic growth and for job creation. What I would highlight for the member is that the number of people unemployed today is markedly similar to that which was predicted in the pre-election fiscal update. Members, for your reference, if we go to Q1 for 2025, the number of people unemployed predicted at the pre-election update was 165,000. The half-year update confirmed exactly the same number. If the member wishes to say that this is a result of Government policies, I would commend to her that she then explain why the previous Labour Government were predicting exactly the same levels of unemployment.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to beat the forecast 3.4% growth for 2026. The answer restates an 'ambition' and pleads factors outside its control, never saying yes or no to the commitment, then redirects to the questioner's colleague. It hovers around the core without landing on it — a plain 'no, I won't commit to a number' would have scored high.
question: Is she therefore committing to “grow the economy faster than [it] otherwise would”, as stated in a Radio New Zealand interview, than the annual growth figures of 3.4 percent for 2026, as forecast by Treasury in the half-yearly fiscal update?
statement: Well, my ambition in all of the policies that we deliver is to drive our growth rate, and therefore job creation and income growth, higher. I have, however, within my arsenal, a small piece of humility, which is to say that, while our Government should be driving policies on a daily basis that will help the growth outlook, we should always be mindful that there are factors that remain outside of our control, not least of which are global economic conditions and the decisions made by other Governments. While that member is welcome to say that those factors somehow wouldn’t affect her, I’d suggest she consult with the new spokesperson for jobs and incomes as to what her view is.

explanation: Asked why Treasury and the Reserve Bank have not upgraded their forecasts. The answer supplies the reason directly: Treasury forecasts twice a year, so no update was due, and the next comes at the Budget. Short and dismissive in tone, but it answers.
question: Why then have the Treasury or the Reserve Bank not upgraded their forecast, given her claims that the Government will grow the economy faster?
statement: As I outlined in my patsy question, the Treasury actually update their forecasts twice a year: at the half-year update and at the Budget update. The member can look forward to updated forecasts at the Budget.

explanation: Asked how she can claim faster growth when jobs data and forecasts don't reflect it. She offers a first reason that genuinely engages — unemployment tracking the pre-election forecast — then abandons the question for an attack on what Labour would have done. Half the answer addresses the challenge, half substitutes a comparison that was not asked for.
question: How can she claim that she will grow the economy “faster than we otherwise would” when current job statistics, Treasury, and Reserve Bank forecasts do not reflect any of her claims?
statement: Because of two things. The first is, as I have outlined to that member laboriously, the forecast rate of unemployment is markedly similar to that which was forecast prior to the election. Second, I can stand here with great confidence and say that a Labour-led Government, at this juncture in history, would have done more economic vandalism—

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made on the Northland Expressway. He states directly what was announced yesterday (opening registrations of interest for stage one, at the infrastructure summit). The question is answered squarely; the self-aware 'patsy' remark and the promotional framing do not affect whether the question was engaged.
question: What announcements has he made on the Northland Expressway?
statement: I thank the member for that excellent patsy. Yesterday, I was thrilled to announce, alongside the Prime Minister, the Government would formally open the registrations of interest for the first stage of the Northland Expressway at the infrastructure summit later in the week. This marks a significant milestone in this Government’s commitment to build roads of national significance around the country. Connecting Northland to Auckland in a new, resilient, safe, and efficient new expressway will unlock growth, boost productivity, and drive higher living standards.

explanation: Asked what benefits Northlanders can expect. He answers with benefits — unlocking economic potential, the Waikato Expressway precedent, growth and productivity. The benefits named are broad rather than concrete, but thinness of detail is Specificity, not Forthrightness; the question asked was engaged and answered on its own terms.
question: What benefits can Northlanders expect from this Northland Expressway project?
statement: The Northland Expressway will unlock the true economic potential of the North. The right analogy is the Waikato Expressway, delivered by the last National Government, which was a game-changer for Waikato and Hamilton, and the Northland Expressway will do for the North what the Waikato Expressway has done for Waikato. This is an investment in the upper North Island area—the economic powerhouse of the country, with 53.7 percent of our population and 55 percent of GDP. This is an investment in growth and productivity.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has received. He supplies the feedback directly: named quotes from the Northland Regional Transport Committee chair and the Northland Corporate Group co-chair, plus an NZIER report. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What feedback has the Minister received on this announcement?
statement: It is great news, and that’s been reflected in the feedback. The chair of the Northland Regional Transport Committee says it will be “a real game-changer”. Northland Corporate Group co-chair Andrew McLeod says it will be “transformative for the upper North Island. Without it, the ability for Northland to support Auckland from the North, via logistics, energy, food … forestry, and construction … will remain underutilised and [barricaded].” And, of course, there is an New Zealand Institute of Economic Research report into the Northland Expressway, which shows significant economic interest.

explanation: Asked when construction will begin — a narrow factual question, and he reaches the point: procurement this week, RFP mid-2025, preferred bidder early next year, contract by mid-year, construction on the Warkworth to Te Hana section starting late 2026. The date asked for is actually given.
question: When does the Government plan to begin construction on the Northland Expressway?
statement: Formal procurement will begin this week on the first section. Registered parties will be invited to submit a formal expression of interest, with a request for proposal in mid-2025 for up to three short-listed bidders. The preferred bidder is expected to be announced early next year, and a public-private partnership contract finalised by the middle of the year, with construction expected to begin soon afterwards on the first section from Warkworth to Te Hana, which is expected to start in late 2026. We will be getting on with the other sections of the expressway, particularly around the Brynderwyns, which is a very important corridor to look at as well.

explanation: The standard 'does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions' question. He opens with 'Yes' — a complete answer to what was asked — and the added healthcare material is elaboration, not evasion.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes, and especially our actions to get our healthcare system focused on patients, not the back-office bureaucracy. We are already spending a record amount in health, but last week the Minister of Health, Simeon Brown, announced a range of new actions we’re taking to make it easier for Kiwis to see a doctor. We’re training more doctors and nurses, we’re paying them more, and we’re creating more opportunities for them to work in primary care, serving the community. We’re putting more funding into GP clinics so that they can enrol more patients, and we’re introducing a 24/7 digital platform so that Kiwis can see a doctor when they need it. Kiwis deserve timely, quality care and access to healthcare, and we won’t stop until we deliver exactly that.

explanation: A narrow binary question: is Auckland homelessness increasing or decreasing? He never says either. He substitutes adjacent metrics he prefers (emergency housing exits, social housing wait-list, stable rents) without touching the direction of homelessness. Answering a different question than the one asked, and the question was specific enough that the avoidance is squarely on its core.
question: Is homelessness in Auckland increasing or decreasing as a result of his Government’s decisions?
statement: Well, what I can say is that we’re getting more people out of emergency housing, we’re taking more people off the social housing wait-list, and rents are stable.

explanation: Asked whether answers of that kind explain his earlier refusal to guarantee nobody would be made homeless. He does not engage the refusal at all, pivoting immediately to the previous Government's housing record. The question is argumentative but it is a real supplementary with an attributable answer; it was dodged.
question: Are answers like that why, when I asked the Prime Minister a year ago in this House, he refused to guarantee that nobody would be made homeless by his Government’s policies?
statement: What I can tell you is that our Government is doing everything that it can after the legacy that was left by a Greens-Labour Government that did an appalling job on housing. We are working on making sure we get more houses available for sale. We’re making sure that we get rents stable, we’re making sure we take people off the social housing wait-list that went up four times, and we’re making sure we get kids out of motels. That’s a good thing, and I think that that member would be wanting to celebrate that.

explanation: Asked to confirm that every person sleeping rough in Auckland can access housing under current settings. He does engage rather than pivot, asserting that people can come to the Government and get assistance — but he substitutes 'the assistance they need' for housing and never confirms or denies the 'every person' claim put to him. Partial: it reaches toward the question without closing on it.
question: Can the Prime Minister confirm if every person currently sleeping homeless on the streets of Auckland City is able to get access to housing under his Government’s policy settings?
statement: They are able to come to the Government and actually ask for and get the assistance that they need, and we will take anyone’s efforts to come and actually get the support that they need.

explanation: Asked whether more people sleeping rough after tightened emergency housing access is what he means by a growth strategy. He offers only the motel and emergency housing count before being cut off — again the preferred adjacent metric, with no engagement with the premise or the 'growth strategy' framing he was asked about.
question: Is more people sleeping on the street, following his Government’s decisions to tighten access to emergency housing, what he means by his “growth strategy”?
statement: What I can tell the member is there are less people in motels and emergency housing, and more—

explanation: A simple yes/no invitation: will he spend a few hours in Auckland Central meeting people made homeless? He rejects the characterisation of the question and moves to the previous Government's record and the 2,000 kids out of motels, never saying whether he will go. A plain 'no, I won't' would have scored high; talking past the request without reaching it does not.
question: Will the Prime Minister spend just a few hours in Auckland Central to come and meet the people who his Government’s decisions have made homeless?
statement: I reject the characterisation of the question. The last Greens-Labour Government made housing worse for all New Zealanders, whether they own a house, whether they rent a house, whether they need a community housing provider or a social house, or whether they’re in emergency housing. We are proud that through focused and good management, we have taken 2,000 kids out of motels and put them into proper houses. That’s a great thing.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made about increasing visitor numbers. She names the announcement ($3m for international business events), what it funds (bids from 90 to 110, incentive programmes), and situates it among prior announcements. Squarely the question asked.
question: What recent announcements has she made about increasing visitor numbers to New Zealand?
statement: I have recently announced a range of investments and initiatives to boost tourism in New Zealand. This includes yesterday’s announcement of a $3 million boost to secure more international business events in New Zealand. This investment will allow Tourism New Zealand to increase their annual conference bid development from 90 to 110 bids, attract high-value incentive programmes, and sell New Zealand as a world-class location for business events. This is the next step in our tourism boost package, following previous announcements, including the Australia campaign and a regional fund to attract more international visitors to our fantastic regions.

explanation: Asked how the announcements will improve visitor numbers. She gives the causal mechanism: conferences bring large groups who would not come as holidaymakers, and business visitors return later and refer others. It engages the 'how' directly; the opening line about 85 percent of pre-COVID levels is context rather than dodge.
question: How will these announcements improve overall visitor numbers?
statement: Our visitor numbers remain at 85 percent of pre-COVID numbers, so we need to keep pushing to get back to those levels. Large-scale conferences result in large numbers of extra visitors, who may not have made the trip for a holiday alone. When people come to New Zealand for business, we want them to go home and to consider returning for a holiday, as well as telling their friends and families about our wonderful country and our warm hospitality.

explanation: Asked what economic benefits she expects. She gives them: $30m incremental spend, $175 more per day per business visitor, off-peak travel, downstream spending. Directly and completely on the question.
question: What economic benefits does she expect to see as a result of these announcements?
statement: Every visitor who comes to New Zealand puts more money in the back pockets of Kiwis. The additional investment in securing business events will deliver more than $30 million in incremental spend to the economy. Business event participants spend, on average, $175 more a day than other visitors and often travel during the off-peak season, boosting tourism and economic activity year-round. More tourists mean more people in cafes, more people spending in our shops, more bookings for local accommodation, and more job opportunities for Kiwis.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has seen. She reports feedback: a named industry chief executive's assessment, industry support for the Australia campaign, 900 deals on offer. The cartwheel joke is padding but the question is answered.
question: What feedback has she seen on these announcements?
statement: I’ve recently announced a range of investments, and the feedback has been incredibly positive. Business Events Industry Aotearoa chief executive, Lisa Hopkins, said the business events announcement was one of the best investments in the sector she has seen in her career. And she only managed to get 19 cartwheels in, hearing the news! The “Everyone must go” campaign has exceeded our expectations in terms of its reach into Australia. It has had unprecedented support from the industry and has created a sense of urgency, with over 900 deals now on offer for Australians. It is clear that New Zealand is open for business, and we are looking forward to welcoming more visitors to our shores.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions. 'Yes.' One word, complete, no hedge.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked specifically for a growth strategy using the LOCAL wealth base so as not to rely on offshore capital. He does state a strategy — partnering with private capital to build infrastructure — but explicitly collapses the distinction the question turned on ('whether it's international pools of capital or whether it's domestic'), so the core of what was asked is engaged only partly.
question: What exactly is his growth strategy to utilise and develop our local wealth base here in Aotearoa so we aren’t reliant on risky offshore capital?
statement: Well, I reject outright the characterisation of that question. New Zealand has done a very, very poor job, over a number of decades, of attracting capital to New Zealand. Frankly, whether it’s international pools of capital or whether it’s domestic pools of capital, we want to be able to partner with that private capital so that we can actually get infrastructure built—more roads, more hospitals, more schools. That’s what New Zealanders want, and that’s how we deliver better public services for them.

explanation: A yes/no fairness question about bank and supermarket profits. He never says whether it is fair; he pivots to what the Government is doing about competition and then to the last Government. Adjacent to the topic, but the question's core — is this fair — is left untouched.
question: Is it fair that the overseas banks New Zealanders bank with bring in $3.5 billion of excess profits a year and the half-overseas-owned supermarkets New Zealanders have no other choice but to shop at squeeze them out of $1 million in excess profits daily when most people are struggling to get by?
statement: Well, I’ll just say to the member, that’s why this Government wants to make sure that there is real competition in banking and in energy and across all of our sectors in this economy. That’s what we’re doing. Sadly, it didn’t happen under the last Government.

explanation: Asked whether it is fair that the largest ECE provider made $32m tax-free. After an opening attack on the Greens, he answers: it is OK for commercial enterprises to make a fair return, 'that's quite OK.' That is a yes. The attack and the unaddressed tax-free element cost some marks, but he reaches the question — the rudeness is Civility's concern, not this one's.
question: Is it fair that the biggest early childhood education provider, which New Zealanders have to send their tamariki to so they can go to mahi, pulled in $32 million of tax-free profits last year while most people are struggling to get by?
statement: I mean, this just characterises the Greens’ position, doesn’t it? It’s a de-growth agenda of living in a hermit kingdom. Actually, it’s OK that commercial enterprises that provide products and/or services to consumers or customers or to the New Zealand public actually make a fair return for their efforts. That’s quite OK.

explanation: Asked whether he will acknowledge that borrowing costs plus shareholder dividends make privatisation more expensive overall. He declares the question disjointed, says he will answer 'the first part', and talks about private hospital capacity shortening waits. He neither acknowledges nor denies the cost-of-capital claim; rejecting the public-versus-private frame is engagement of a sort, but the specific proposition put to him is never met.
question: Will the PM acknowledge that the higher costs of borrowing and the need to pay dividends to shareholders mean that privatisation ultimately ends up costing New Zealanders more than if public services stayed in public ownership?
statement: Well, I mean, there’s quite a lot to that question that is, I think, rather disjointed and doesn’t hang together, but I’ll answer the first part. I can give you very good examples where, actually, New Zealanders can get operations that they need in the healthcare system, and, frankly, whether it’s delivered through the public system or the private system, we want them to get the procedures and the help that they need. Private hospitals in many cases are geared up at scale to deal with a number of procedures and operations that New Zealanders can get quicker if we use that capacity, so it’s not a private versus public argument.

explanation: A two-branch question — will he increase public ownership, or sell off assets? He answers neither branch, calls the Greens deluded, and says the question makes no sense. 'I reject it' rejects the question rather than answering it, which is the opposite of the blunt refusal that would score high ('no, I won't').
question: Will the Prime Minister increase public ownership of the basic things we all need just to live—like school lunches, healthcare, and childcare—or will he choose to sell off Aotearoa and funnel even more profits to offshore corporates instead?
statement: I have to say the Greens are totally deluded on economics. I mean, I don’t know how to say it any other way, but, honestly, that is a question that just makes no sense, and I reject it.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement. He says "yes" — qualified by "in the context in which that statement was made" and "in most towns and cities", which hedges the edges but does not avoid the core. A yes/no question got a yes.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “Emergency housing will always be available as a last resort for those who need it”?
statement: In the context in which that statement was made, yes. Emergency housing was intended to be a last resort—not the first resort—and it remains a last resort in most towns and cities in Aotearoa New Zealand for those with a general need for a short-term stay in temporary accommodation.

explanation: Asked whether he is saying Auckland's homeless aren't in genuine need. He affirms that many people in NZ have genuine need, which implicitly rejects the premise, but never engages the Auckland-specific claim (53 percent in four months) and redirects to transitional housing supply. Partially answers while hedging around the core.
question: Is the Minister saying that those who are homeless in Auckland, which has risen 53 percent in only four months, aren’t in genuine need of emergency housing?
statement: There are many people with a genuine need for emergency housing in New Zealand, and there continues to be transitional housing places in Auckland.

explanation: Same narrow question, this time for Wellington. The answer never addresses whether those people are in genuine need — it pivots to a list of programmes and pathways (Housing First, rapid rehousing, etc.). Answering a different question than the one asked. A narrow question dodged squarely.
question: Is he saying that those who are homeless in Wellington, which has risen over 40 percent, aren’t in genuine need of emergency housing?
statement: I’m also saying that there are a number of programmes and pathways for those who are either homeless or with severe housing deprivation to actually reset their situation. For example, there is Housing First, rapid rehousing, transitional housing, single site supported housing, and even private housing that people can access by way of housing support products, which continue to be supported by this Government.

explanation: Asked whether front-line providers are wrong. He offers census deprivation data and notes those providers can engage with other programmes — never says whether they are wrong. The reply is on-topic but sidesteps the yes/no put to him.
question: Is he saying that front-line providers, the very people who administer those programmes and pathways he just outlined, are wrong when they provide him with examples of people unable to access emergency housing because of the policy changes that he brought in?
statement: I can observe, as does the census data from 2018 to 2023, that severe housing deprivation actually increased over 10 percent during those five years. I can also observe that those providers which the member refers to also have the opportunity to engage on these other programmes which I’ve enunciated in my previous answer.

explanation: Asked whether he will meet providers with cameras present. The answer speaks only about the Opposition's "frustration" and government delivery figures; no yes, no no, no engagement with the request at all. A plain refusal here would have scored high — this is a pivot to talking points instead.
question: Thank you. Will he meet with front-line providers, with cameras present so everyone can see, and tell those very people who are dealing with increased homelessness every day, looking them in the eye and saying that he is right and they are wrong?
statement: I sense and completely understand the member’s and the Opposition’s frustration at our successful delivery and commitment around over 3,000 children leaving emergency housing in the last 15 months and 2,000 by way of the Priority One decision making. And I sense the member’s frustration that—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked what recent red-tape announcements he has made. He names the 27 February Invercargill release, the review, the 16 recommendations and the accepting agencies. The question is soft, but it is answered directly and completely — detail and self-promotion are not this attribute's business.
question: What recent announcements has he made about cutting red tape?
statement: On 27 February in the mighty Invercargill, Ministers Penny Simmonds, Andrew Hoggard, and I released the findings from the Ministry for Regulation’s review into agricultural and horticultural products. Rapid access to veterinary medicines and agricultural chemicals is essential for lifting agriculture productivity and growth in the agricultural and horticultural sectors. Yet some firms have waited over five years for Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) and Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) approval, costing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost productivity. The review has made 16 recommendations to approve the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act 1996 (HSNO) and agricultural compounds and veterinary medicines (ACVM) processes, which Cabinet has accepted. EPA and MPI have begun implementation, and the two Ministers responsible expect to get it done very quickly.

explanation: Asked for the potential economic benefits. He gives them: a $272 million productivity lift from halving approval times, and a quarter-billion-dollar downside risk from lost EU market access. Squarely responsive; whether the figures are true is Veracity, not this.
question: What are the potential economic benefits of improving access to regulated agricultural and horticultural products in New Zealand for these products?
statement: The costs of getting this wrong, as we have been, are substantial. Sense Partners, an economic consultancy, estimate that halving approval times for agricultural products could lift productivity in the sector by $272 million. Conversely, losing EU market access for fruit and vegetables due to delayed product approvals as the EU moves on with its standards and our farmers and horticulturalists can’t get the right products, that is estimated to risk a quarter-of-a-billion-dollar loss. Being able to get these products through a sound regulatory system is vital to our productivity. By bringing together two disparate ministries that have been dis-coordinated, the Ministry for Regulation is making that happen.

explanation: Asked what announcements have been made about delivering critical infrastructure. He states them: the 15 percent early-agreement incentive, the 5 percent recognition payment, and the streamlined objection process. Directly on the question.
question: What announcements has the Government made about making it easier to deliver critical infrastructure projects?
statement: A wide Public Works Act reform is under way, but we’ve announced recently critical infrastructure streamlined proposals, whereby incentive payments of an additional 15 percent of the value of the land will be made available to landowners for early agreement; an additional 5 percent of the value of the land in addition, as a recognition payment, acknowledging the special significance of the land in question for these critical infrastructure projects; and a streamlined objection process, whereby the landowner, himself or herself, can object directly to the decision maker, saving time and money, while preserving Land Valuation Tribunal and recourse to judicial review if necessary.

explanation: Asked which projects benefit from the streamlined pathway. He names the category (Schedule 2 fast-track consents, roads of national significance) and then names actual projects — Mill Road, Woodend Bypass, Cambridge to Piarere, the Northland Corridor, a second Ashburton bridge. Complete answer to what was asked.
question: What projects will benefit from this streamlined land acquisition pathway?
statement: Thank you very much for the question and the opportunity to answer it. This faster and fairer process will apply to projects consented in Schedule 2 of the Fast-Track Approvals Act, along with, and including, roads of national significance, as identified by this Government in its ambitious work programme. These might include, for example, Mill Road, Woodend Bypass, Cambridge to Piarere, the Northland Corridor—aka expressway—and a second Ashburton bridge.

explanation: Asked how Kiwis will benefit. He answers with benefits: faster emergency-services response, shorter commutes, quicker freight to ports. It is rhetorical and boosterish, but the question was a soft "how will people benefit" and he addresses it head-on rather than pivoting elsewhere.
question: How will Kiwis benefit from these changes?
statement: New Zealanders will benefit enormously from these changes. As I say, these will be faster and fairer for all involved, including the payments and processes that will benefit the landowners themselves. But, of course, the transport infrastructure, for example, will enable emergency services to get much more quickly to the scenes of accidents when they occur, as opposed to being stuck in traffic or having to take the long way round. Parents will get home much more quickly on the way home from school, or out to their workplace for that matter, and our farmers will get their food and fibre to tables around the country and to our ports that much more quickly. This is a real gain for New Zealand families.

explanation: Asked whether the Government will honour the promise of an India FTA within its first term. After a long preamble about Labour, he reaches the question: "yes, we remain committed to delivering... a trade agreement with India this term." The core is engaged and answered affirmatively; slight softening from "free-trade agreement" to "improved access through a trade agreement" keeps it just short of complete. The attacks on the previous government are a Focus/Civility matter, not a dodge.
question: Will the Government honour Christopher Luxon’s pre-election promise for a free-trade agreement with India within its first term?
statement: Well, New Zealand’s relationship with India had been run down over the past six years, much more than we realised. There had hardly been any ministerial visits, no Prime Minister visited in the six years of the Labour Government, and the then Labour foreign Minister, Nanaia Mahuta, during a press conference with the Indian foreign Minister in New Zealand, said that a trade deal with India was not a priority for New Zealand. Well, I can confirm that Prime Minister Luxon is much more ambitious for New Zealand, and we have increased engagement, at official and ministerial levels significantly, including a meeting between Prime Minister Luxon and Prime Minister Modi. Of course, the Prime Minister will lead one of New Zealand’s largest business delegation visits to India next year. And for the member, yes, we remain committed to delivering improved access for Kiwi exporters through a trade agreement with India this term.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the PM that dairy is a "difficult conversation" with India. Opens "Well, yes, I do." Direct and complete; the following remarks about not negotiating via the Chamber and the Ardern jab are additions after the question has already been answered.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister on Radio New Zealand this morning, who said that dairy is a “difficult conversation” with India?
statement: Well, yes, I do. It’s clear that dairy is important for both our countries and both Governments, but the one thing that we won’t be doing is litigating or negotiating trade deals with any country of the world via this Chamber or via the media. I know that member was opposed to that when the Labour Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern, in that very chair, said she was off to Europe to do a deal and didn’t allow that Minister to bring back the meat and dairy access he would have got without that Prime Minister selling him out.

explanation: Asked a narrow yes/no with a follow-up: will he set a minimum dairy market-access threshold, and if not, why not. Neither limb is answered — no position on a threshold, no reason for declining one. Pivots to Labour-era export decline and a generic "we work hard to get the very best deal". A specific question squarely avoided.
question: Will he set a minimum threshold for agricultural market access for dairy in any free-trade agreement with India, given that it is our single largest export industry; if not, why not?
statement: Well, I think it’s clear that successive Governments have always argued for a better deal for New Zealand exporters, particularly the high-quality food producers from New Zealand. Most concerningly, what we do need to address before we even have a chance to negotiate with a country like India is the decline in trade we saw over the six years of the Labour Government, where our exports to India fell by $550 million. In the very same period of time, Australia increased their exports by $7 billion into that market. That member, like every New Zealander, can rest assured that we work hard to get the very best deal that we can with India for New Zealanders, because our relationship with India is a priority for this Government.

explanation: Asked whether he will rule out signing an agreement that excludes dairy. He states plainly that he won't negotiate via the Chamber or the media — an explicit, unambiguous refusal to state a position rather than a filibuster, which counts for something. But unlike "No, I won't release that advice", it never resolves the question put; the ruling-out is neither given nor refused on its merits. Middle score: openly declines, does not reach the substance.
question: Will he rule out signing the promised comprehensive free-trade agreement with India if it excludes dairy?
statement: Well, it will be called a comprehensive economic partnership agreement, like the one with the UAE in six months and the NZ-Gulf Corporation Council that the previous Government said wasn’t possible—all done within a year. But I won’t be negotiating via this Chamber or the media with any Government around the world.

explanation: Asked whether the PM was correct to say "We didn't even have a relationship with India". Answers "Well, yes, it was correct" and gives his reason. Direct and complete. Whether the claim is true is Veracity, and the swipe at Labour is Civility/Focus — neither lowers this.
question: Was it correct for the Prime Minister to say on Radio New Zealand this morning, “We didn’t even have a relationship with India”, given the commitment and efforts of Indian and New Zealand business people and politicians over many years to build that relationship?
statement: Well, yes, it was correct. The reason for that is that member’s foreign Minister stood in public in Auckland, beside the Indian foreign Minister, and said a trade agreement with India is not a priority for New Zealand. How unambitious can you be? Businesses around New Zealand, New Zealanders, Indian - New Zealanders have worked hard on that relationship. They always did. They were let down by a Labour Government over six years.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statements and actions on the Cook Strait ferries. "Yes", followed by elaboration on which statement in particular. Direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by his statements and actions regarding the Cook Strait ferries?
statement: Yes, and by my statement that a project in 2020 with $400.1 million in Government funding and the balance coming from KiwiRail and the ports somehow blew out by billions by 2023 and the Treasury warning the last Government it was on track to go above $4 billion. We are hard at work on a cost-effective solution. It’s possible to bring new ships to New Zealand and take a pragmatic approach to infrastructure, so watch this space.

explanation: Asked what feedback the Government has had from commercial shipyards. He describes the process instead — a worldwide search, meeting Hyundai, approaching many yards, narrowing the list shortly — without ever reporting what the shipyards said. The imminent shortlist implies a positive response, so it gestures at the question without reaching it.
question: What feedback has the Government had in its engagement with commercial shipyards?
statement: We are in a worldwide search for a good commercial deal. Good business people seek multiple quotes towards a competitive price, and also treat prospective partners with the utmost respect. That’s why we met with Hyundai and it’s why we directly approached many shipyards around the world. We intend to narrow our list very shortly to a selection of capable shipbuilders, and the final cost will be a massive saving to the New Zealand people.

explanation: Asked how the infrastructure work is tracking. Answers "Extremely well" and substantiates with the specific engagements (CentrePort, Port Marlborough, KiwiRail, Ferry Holdings). Squarely responsive; the media aside is on-topic.
question: How is the work on the infrastructure element of this programme tracking?
statement: As former Labour Minister Maharey would say, more good news. Extremely well; we have been to see CentrePort, we’re in contact with Port Marlborough and we’ll visit them directly soon, and are regularly working with KiwiRail and our new company Ferry Holdings Ltd. It was curious to see reports in the media yesterday suggesting that ports were reluctant to work with KiwiRail. In our experience, both ports and KiwiRail have worked constructively, collaboratively, and collegially to focus on cost-effective infrastructure. In a few weeks’ time, this House will see just how productive work can be when the Government is disciplined in its objectives.

explanation: Asked who has been appointed to the Ferry Holdings Ltd board. Begins naming them immediately — Chris Mackenzie, Heather Simpson — before the transcript cuts off. Engagement with the question is direct; the truncation is a transcript artefact, not a dodge.
question: Who has the Government appointed to the Ferry Holdings Ltd board?
statement: Again, more good news. Chris Mackenzie, with a deep operational knowledge of rail and ferries; Heather Simpson—

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. "Yes." One word, complete.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Two-limb question: does he agree with the Peters quote about a globalised sell-out, or is disagreement why the Foreign Minister was barred from the investor summit. The "No" plus the account of the Minister's schedule addresses the second limb (rejecting the barring premise); the first limb — whether he agrees with the quoted view — is never touched. Half the question engaged.
question: Does he agree with the Rt Hon Winston Peters, “We don’t want a globalised sell-out of New Zealand, which is what many of the neo-liberals have recommended”, or is his disagreement with Winston Peters the reason the Minister of Foreign Affairs has been barred from speaking at his international investor summit?
statement: No—the Minister of Foreign Affairs is going to be here tomorrow, ensuring that the Government maintains control of this House. Then, in the evening, he will be on a plane to the United States to ensure that the best representation possible in our country’s interests—hopefully in a bipartisan way—is put to the American people.

explanation: Asked whether the PM will signal openness to privatising school and hospital buildings. Redirects it to the Prime Minister and his forthcoming speech without giving a yes or no. He does state a reason for not answering rather than reciting talking points, which lifts it slightly above a pure pivot, but the substance of a narrow question is left unaddressed.
question: Will the Prime Minister be indicating to international investors tomorrow that his Government is open to the privatisation of school and hospital buildings?
statement: The reality is that the Prime Minister is giving a speech today setting out what the coverage and span of the two days—the 13th and 14th—will be. That should be asked of the Prime Minister because that’s covered in his speech—

explanation: Asked whether the PM's $6b hospital pipeline remark meant the Government is open to private investors OWNING those hospital buildings. The answer never touches ownership: it pivots to the inherited economy, the general need for international investment, and a call for cross-party agreement. A narrow yes/no about ownership was put and entirely sidestepped.
question: When the Prime Minister said on Monday that there’s $6 billion of hospital building work in the pipeline he’d be presenting to international investors tomorrow, was he indicating that the Government is open to private investors owning those hospital buildings?
statement: The Prime Minister was indicating that he inherited a wrecked economy where the main mantra was borrow and hope, and that if we’re to turn this around, we need international investment and we need it now. Our job is to provide the international investors with the answers as to why New Zealand is the right place to invest. That’s why we hope to have agreement across political parties on the essentialities now brought upon us by an infrugal, wasteful, spendthrift Government.

explanation: Asked whether Simeon Brown's statement about maximising elective surgery in private hospitals reflects Government policy. The answer engages the underlying public-vs-private issue ('how they get the operation is not helped by blind, stupid ideology'), which implies endorsement, but never states whether it is Government policy. Gestures at the question without reaching it.
question: Does health Minister Simeon Brown’s statement that he wants as much elective surgery as possible to be done in private hospitals reflect Government policy?
statement: The wisdom of Simeon Brown is that he understands one thing: the patient’s everything—the patient’s everything. How they get the operation is not helped by blind, stupid ideology.

explanation: Two limbs: does he agree with Seymour's claim about partial privatisation improving accountability, and if so how does he explain the mixed-ownership power companies' behaviour. The Dick Seddon reply obliquely affirms the first limb ('that was always understood to be the case') but the explanatory limb — the specific one — is not addressed at all.
question: Does he agree with David Seymour, “If you partially privatise corporations and allow private shareholders to own part of them, the company is much more accountable”; if so, how does he explain the mixed-ownership - model power companies decreasing their investment in new generation, increasing power prices, and withdrawing record profits following that partial privatisation?
statement: If one has a grasp on this country’s political history, going all the way back to Dick Seddon, that was always understood to be the case.

explanation: Asked whether the Government is considering relaxing the foreign home-buyer ban. 'But that's not what the Government's doing' is a direct denial, which answers the operative limb and moots the conditional 'if so'. The rest is an attack on the questioner's party, but the core question was engaged before the pivot. Marked below the top band because the denial is brief and the bulk of the reply leaves the topic.
question: Is the Government considering relaxing the foreign home-buyer ban as part of its bid to attract more wealthy foreign investors; if so, what happened to putting New Zealanders first?
statement: But that’s not what the Government’s doing. So why is he speculating on something that his party was prepared to do? His party, for example, is the only one that in 2002 signed a deal with Singapore and sold that right down the drain. And I had to go across there and try and change it.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements have been made about positive health outcomes for pets. The answer names the announcement (regulatory change letting authorised non-veterinarians do certain dental procedures) and links it to pet health outcomes. Direct and complete; the closing partisan jab does not bear on whether the question was engaged.
question: What recent announcements has he made about positive health outcomes for pets?
statement: Yesterday, I announced a regulatory change to allow non-veterinarians to carry out certain dental procedures on cats and dogs when authorised by a vet. As a farmer, I know how busy vets are around the country and that we have talented vet nurses who are capable of doing subgingival procedures like teeth scaling. This change will give them the legal protection to do that. Animals’ dental health is a really good marker for overall health and so expanding the number of people that can provide this service will lead to really positive outcomes for pets. And we actually give a toss about pets over here.

explanation: Asked why the change was necessary. The answer gives the cause directly — a previous amendment to the Animal Welfare Act restricted the procedures to vets, and these regulations restore prior practice. The blame framing and the pun are irrelevant to Forthrightness; the 'why' was answered.
question: Why was this change necessary?
statement: Well, these changes were necessary because of an amendment to the Animal Welfare Act made by the previous Government that was nothing short of a “cat-tastrophe”. It meant that surgical procedures can only be provided by a vet. Vet nurses were routinely conducting subgingival dental procedures prior to the law change. These regulations will restore that right and mean that pets who have potentially serious health concerns don’t have to wait for a vet and can be seen more quickly.

explanation: Asked how the change will be positive for pet owners. The answer addresses exactly that: expected cost reduction over time, work still done by trained clinical staff, and freed-up vet time improving availability. Squarely on the question asked.
question: How will this be “paws-itive” for pet owners? [Interruption]
statement: Sorry, end of the puns, I promise. The hope is that over time we will see a reduction in cost for this sort of procedure. It will still be done by trained, capable, professional, clinical staff, but not necessarily by a registered vet. But most of all, it’ll go some way to freeing up vets’ time so that they can be more available to pet owners who need them for more complex procedures. The overall ability of vets to provide services to their clients will therefore improve.

explanation: Asked how the change will support vets and vet nurses. The answer covers both groups — freeing vets' time, and vet nurses being able to use their skills once the regulation takes effect. Some of the reply is acknowledgment of sector bodies, but the question is reached and answered.
question: How will this change support vets and vet nurses?
statement: This will be welcome news to vets and vet nurses. I would like to acknowledge the work of the New Zealand Veterinary Association and the New Zealand Veterinary Nurses Association who have been advocating for their sector in this area since 2021. In addition to freeing up vets’ time, I’m sure that vet nurses will be relishing the opportunity to use their skills to care for even more animals when this regulation comes into force on 10 April this year.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned that two offshore wind investors have withdrawn or paused, and if not, why not. Answered 'No' outright and then gave the reason (no enabling regime existed before; legislation is coming). Both limbs engaged. Slightly short of the top because the two specific investors are never acknowledged, but the question put was about concern, and it was answered.
question: Is he concerned that two international offshore wind investors have now withdrawn or paused their New Zealand projects, citing current Government policy as their reason; if not, why not?
statement: No, I am confident in the work this Government is doing to enable offshore wind. When we came into office, there was no regime or legislation to enable offshore wind, but thanks to this Government, we will soon have both.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned that investors say their investment is at risk, with a PwC jobs estimate attached. Answered 'No, I'm not' and gave his grounds (100+ investors in the country signalling intent to invest; removing regulatory obstacles). A flat denial with reasons is a direct answer, whatever its accuracy.
question: Is he concerned that international investors are telling his Government that their investment is at risk because of his Government’s policies that could cost New Zealand, by PricewaterhouseCoopers’ estimations, between 5,000 and 30,000 highly skilled, well-paid jobs?
statement: No, I’m not. We’ve actually got over 100 of those investors currently in the country telling us and telling this Government that they want to invest in this country, and we are a Government that’s going to ensure that the red and green tape that is currently in place is out of the way so that they can invest in our country and make Kiwis’ lives better.

explanation: Asked whether he, the Prime Minister, or ANY other Minister met with Sumitomo after their 11 October letter, and if not, why the Government had not acted. He answers only for himself (four weeks in post, no meeting request received) and says nothing about the PM or other Ministers, which he would be expected to address. The 'why not' limb gets an implicit partial answer before the reply moves to generic remarks about meeting investors and renewable generation.
question: Has he, the Prime Minister, or any other Minister met with Sumitomo Corporation following their letter on 11 October to the Prime Minister and other Ministers seeking reconsideration of Government policies, and, if not, why has the Government not worked to ensure international investment in New Zealand has not been paused because of their policies?
statement: I’ve been the Minister for Energy for just under four weeks, and I haven’t had a request from that organisation to meet. But I do meet regularly with a large number of investors who are looking at opportunities to build renewable generation in this country. That is one of the single-biggest things that this country can do in order to improve livelihoods and our economy. More renewable generation will aid energy security and affordability, and grow our economy.

explanation: Two-part question: (a) does Watts agree with the PM's quote, and (b) has Watts told the PM that Government policy settings are driving offshore-wind investment away. Part (a) is answered squarely in the first clause ("I obviously always agree with our Prime Minister"). Part (b) — the actual point of the question — is never touched; there is no statement about whether any such conversation happened, and the reply moves to abundant-energy and legislative-framework talking points. Half of a two-part question answered, with the sharper half dodged.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister, who, in question time yesterday, said, “We know we need the investment, because it’s actually capital to grow our businesses, which actually creates higher-income jobs and more jobs for people.”, and has he had a conversation with the Prime Minister to say, actually, in the case of offshore wind, it’s his Government’s policy settings that are driving away international investment that would lead to well-paid jobs in New Zealand?
statement: Well, I obviously always agree with our Prime Minister, but what I also agree with is the fact that this country needs more abundant and affordable energy, and this is a Government who is taking the steps to put in place the legislative regime to make that a reality. I will reinforce: we had no legislative framework in place when we came into Government, but we will do by the end of this year, and that is good for New Zealand and it’s good for the New Zealand economy.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Infrastructure New Zealand's point about delays under this Government and work under way under the previous one. Watts never says agree or disagree, but he does engage the substance by contesting the premise — the regulatory regime was not in place on taking office, so offshore wind cannot be built today. That directly rebuts the 'previous Government had work under way' half. The 'delays from this Government' half is left alone and replaced with a delivery promise. Partial engagement rather than a pivot to unrelated talking points.
question: Does he agree with Infrastructure New Zealand, who has pointed out the delays from this Government and the work that the previous Government had under way to establish a regulatory regime for offshore wind?
statement: I only go back to what I noted in my primary response, which is: when we came in, that regulatory regime was not in place. You cannot build offshore wind in this country today, because the regulations are not in place. This Government is taking the action to make sure it is in place, and this Government will deliver upon that promise.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements have been made on increasing penalties for illicit drug use. Brown names the announcement made yesterday, the Cabinet decision, the fentanyl-analogue class A reclassification and the 23 substances, and ties it to tougher penalties. The question is engaged head-on; the closing rhetorical flourish about peddlers is additional, not a substitute for the answer.
question: What recent announcements has he made on increasing penalties for illicit drug use?
statement: Yesterday, I announced that Cabinet has agreed to progress with stronger drug classifications to crack down on harmful substances and protect New Zealanders from the devastating impact of illicit drugs. Proposed changes include classifying three fentanyl analogues as class A drugs as part of stronger controls on 23 harmful substances, which will lead to tougher penalties for offenders. Peddlers of illicit drugs cause significant harm in our communities and inflict misery on our streets. Our Government is committed to keeping Kiwis safe from dangerous substances.

explanation: Asked why the Government is proposing increased controls on 23 illicit drugs. The reply gives an actual causal answer — it is responding to the Expert Advisory Committee on Drugs' recommendation — and states what the change enables (police and Customs preventative action, harsher penalties). That is a direct response to a 'why' question.
question: Why is the Government proposing to increase controls on 23 illicit drugs?
statement: Well, the Government is responding to the Expert Advisory Committee on Drugs, which recommended to limit the risk of harmful and potential misuse of drugs to include these classifications. This will enable police and Customs to take preventative action and allow harsher penalties for those caught making or possessing these drugs.

explanation: Asked which substances besides fentanyl analogues are being more tightly controlled. Brown lists them: synthetic cathinones, synthetic cannabinoids, and amphetamine precursors. The question asked for a set of items and the set was supplied; the trailing drug-harm framing does not displace the answer.
question: What substances besides fentanyl analogues are being more tightly controlled?
statement: Our Government is proposing to impose stricter controls on a number of illicit substances. This includes synthetic cathinones, often marketed as bath salts; synthetic cannabinoids; and amphetamine precursors, used in the manufacture of meth. We know how important it is to reduce the impact of drug harm. Ensuring there are stronger controls in place for these harmful substances is a step towards our goal.

explanation: Asked when the new drug laws come into effect. The reply names a date — in force by mid-year — along with the intervening process steps, and flags it as conditional on agreement. A timing question asked, a timing answer given; the conditionality reflects genuine process, not hedging around the core.
question: When will these new drug laws come into effect?
statement: Well, good news. The process to strengthen drug controls is already under way. The planned changes have been approved by Cabinet and will now be drafted as an Order in Council, tabled in Parliament, and considered by the Health Committee before again being referred back to Cabinet. If agreed, these changes will come into force by mid-year, ensuring stronger protections against harmful substances as soon as possible.

explanation: The standard omnibus 'does she stand by all her statements and actions'. Stanford opens with 'I absolutely stand by actions to...', which affirms rather than dodges, but she narrows the scope from 'all her statements and actions' to a chosen subset and spends the remainder on phonics checks and a supportive teacher quote. Because the question itself is sprawling, the partial coverage is a lesser failure than dodging a narrow one; the affirmation is present but curated.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: I absolutely stand by actions to build a world-leading education system that delivers equitable and excellent outcomes for every child—in particular, this Government’s introduction of phonics checks in English and te reo Māori. So far this year, more than 800 teachers have already completed their training module, and feedback I’ve received from teachers has been extraordinarily positive. One wrote that “The phonics check is an easy-to-administer assessment that provides teachers with valuable information about a child’s phonics knowledge and their ability to blend sounds and read words. It enables teachers to target their instructions to meet their children’s needs.”

explanation: A narrow factual question — did the Government receive official advice that the school lunch changes would not work, and if so why did she agree to them. Neither part is answered. The reply is a clean portfolio deferral to Minister Seymour rather than a pivot to talking points or an attack, which keeps it above the floor, but 'ask someone else' leaves the question asked entirely unresolved. It is not the same as a refusal that settles the matter.
question: Did the Government receive official advice that its changes to the school lunch programme weren’t going to work, and, if so, why did she agree to them?
statement: While I am kept up to date on the broad direction of this area, this area of school lunches, as you know, is delegated to Minister Seymour, and detailed questions should be directed to Mr Seymour.

explanation: Asked whether she personally put a contingency plan in place for a provider going into liquidation, and if not, why not. The answer explicitly reiterates the previous deferral to Minister Seymour and supplies nothing on either limb. A directly personal question about her own actions met with a redirect leaves the core untouched; the deferral is plainly stated, which is why it is not scored at zero, but a narrow question was squarely avoided.
question: Did she put in place a contingency plan in case something went wrong, such as a provider going into liquidation, and, if not, why not?
statement: I will respond to that question by reiterating the previous answer: while I’m kept up to date on the broad direction of this area, those questions need to be directed to Minister Seymour.

explanation: Asked when she first learned of the Libelle issues and when she told Minister Seymour. She gives a precise date for the first limb — Seymour informed her of high-level supply challenges on 11 February — which also resolves the second limb by inversion, since the information ran the other way. Direct and near-complete; the 'if at all' limb is answered implicitly rather than explicitly.
question: When did she first find out about issues with Libelle, and when did she tell Minister Seymour, if at all?
statement: In answer to that question, Minister Seymour informed me of some high-level supply challenges relating to Libelle on 11 February.

explanation: Asked why she did not act once she learned lunches were at risk. She supplies an actual reason: she found out only recently and the area is Seymour's delegation, with support offered. That engages the 'why not' rather than sidestepping it, so it lands well above the deferrals on the earlier supplementaries. It sits short of the top because the reply does not reconcile 'only found out recently' with the 11 February date she had just given — an engagement with the question that leaves its edge blunted.
question: Why didn’t she, as Minister of Education, act when she found out that hundreds of thousands of school lunches were at risk due to Libelle’s issues?
statement: I only found out about these issues recently. This is a delegation for Minister Seymour, and I know that these are very challenging and complex issues that he is working through, and I’ve offered him my full support in anything that he might need.

explanation: Asked what recent changes have been made to the Accredited Employer Work Visa. Stanford enumerates three concrete changes — removing the median wage threshold, reducing minimum experience for level 4 and 5 roles to two years, and extending visa duration from two to three years. The question is answered squarely; the closing economic framing is appended to a complete answer, not standing in for one.
question: What recent changes have been made to the Accredited Employer Work Visa to support businesses to access the skills and experience they need?
statement: This week, we’ve implemented a number of changes to the Accredited Employer Work Visa to help support businesses access the skills and experience they need to help us grow the economy. These changes include removing the median wage threshold, reducing the minimum experience required for level 4 and 5 roles to two years, and increasing the visa duration for new applicants in level 4 to 5 roles from two to three years. This Government has listened to businesses and stakeholders from around the country, and these changes will support businesses to grow the economy so that all New Zealanders can thrive.

explanation: Asked why the changes were made; gives the reasons directly — coalition agreement on the median wage, labour-market distortion, work-experience and visa-length settings. Some campaign framing at the end, but the question is reached and answered.
question: Why were these changes made?
statement: These changes were made because the success of New Zealand’s businesses is critical to growing our economy. Removing the median wage was a Government coalition agreement as it has distorted the labour market and meant that in some instances New Zealanders were being paid less than their migrant colleagues doing the same job. As Minister, it was also clear to me that some of the settings around relevant work experience and visa lengths could be improved. Our focus remains on attracting higher-skilled workers while managing migration responsibly to help Kiwi businesses expand and help grow the economy.

explanation: Asked what the impact was; states an impact (prioritising Kiwis, more fit-for-purpose visa) and cites a farming-sector quote naming concrete effects — cost savings, less uncertainty. It leans on a third party's testimonial rather than her own account, and the impact is prospective, so it engages the question without fully owning the answer.
question: What was the impact of these changes?
statement: These changes will support the right balance of ensuring Kiwis are prioritised for job opportunities while providing a more fit for purpose visa so New Zealanders can have access to the skills they need to grow the economy. Richard McIntyre from Federated Farmers said, “These changes are a significant step forward and will be welcome news for many farming families across New Zealand”. And it, “… will cut thousands of dollars in costs for farmers, but will also mean a lot less stress and uncertainty for both the farmer and the employee who just want to get on with … farming.”

explanation: Asked what feedback she had seen; answers 'lots of positive feedback' and quotes two named sources. Exactly the thing asked for.
question: What feedback has the Minister seen?
statement: I have seen lots of positive feedback. BusinessNZ chief executive Katherine Rich said, “The changes are a positive start to what will need to be a continuing programme of refinement to immigration settings to ensure that businesses can get the skills they need to support economic recovery and growth.” And, “It is positive to see [this] Government signalling greater responsiveness to business needs…”.

explanation: Asked whether he supports his Government's statements and actions; answers 'Āe' — yes. One word, complete, no dodge.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Āe.

explanation: The question had an 'or' (productivity or just growth) and a 'how' (how does offshore investment address the productivity crisis). Answering 'āe and āe' fits neither: yes is not a choice between two options, and it supplies no mechanism. The core of the question is never touched.
question: Does the Prime Minister care about productivity or just growth, and, if so, how exactly does relying on offshore money from big corporates attending his privatisation festival address New Zealand’s productivity crisis, which is created by entrenched social inequality?
statement: To the manifestation of a number of questions, first two questions, both the answers—tahi, rua—are āe and āe.

explanation: Two-part question. Part one is answered flatly — the PM agrees with the statement.
