explanation: A two-part question: does he stand by the 'glass half empty' statement, and does he think the jobless should cheer up. He answers both explicitly — 'Yes, I do stand by that statement' and 'no', with a statement of who he was actually referring to. Direct on both limbs.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “Some New Zealanders have got themselves into the habit of what I call glass half empty economics”, and, if so, does he think that those people who lost their jobs should just cheer up?
statement: Yes, I do stand by that statement, and, no, I was referring to most members of the Opposition, including the shadow Minister of Finance, who said in a podcast a couple of days ago, “We don’t have to provide the solutions to issues,” and “It’s not my job to find the solutions.” I do stand by those statements as well.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on the building and construction sector. He names a specific report (Kennards Hire 2025 Construction Confidence Check) and its findings. Squarely on point.
question: What reports has he seen on the building and construction sector?
statement: This week, Kennards Hire released its 2025 Construction Confidence Check survey and found that an overwhelming 93 percent of construction business leaders are confident in the industry’s growth and performance over the next five years. Better still, more than half—52 percent, in fact—are “very confident” that we will see strong growth in New Zealand’s building industry. This Government is backing the building industry, and it’s great to see that—after reports that the industry activity had levelled out—the vast majority of business leaders believe that we are now moving forward.

explanation: Asked what other findings the survey made. He gives further survey findings (drivers of optimism, infrastructure investment, foreign investment) before adding government-policy commentary. The question is directly answered; the trailing policy material doesn't displace it.
question: What other findings did the survey make?
statement: The survey also highlights factors driving such surge in optimism among our building industry leaders. Around half—47 percent—point to increased Government investment in infrastructure as a reason to feel that the future is brighter. They are also celebrating increased foreign investment and growth in regional infrastructure projects. These are all priorities for the Government, so it is that, for example, we are reforming the Overseas Investment Act to bring wealth into New Zealand, we are investing into our regions, and we’ve committed to $6 billion worth of infrastructure projects before Christmas.

explanation: Asked what common challenges the survey identified. He names them — materials quality/availability and outdated equipment — then moves to the government's response. The asked-for content is delivered.
question: What common challenges face the industry, according to the survey?
statement: The survey highlights a couple of major challenges. One is a lack of quality and availability of building materials, and outdated equipment. This is exactly why the Government has introduced Investment Boost—this helps tradies and other businesses to invest in the technology and tools that they need to grow by immediately allowing them to deduct 20 percent of the cost from the income tax due that year. We’ve also changed the law to remove unjustifiable barriers, making it easier for Kiwis to access high-quality building products, increasing availability and innovation, boosting competition, and driving down prices.

explanation: Asked what other recent construction data he has seen. He cites Stats NZ consent figures for the year to June 2025 and their trend. Directly responsive, notwithstanding the partisan aside.
question: What other recent data on the construction sector has the Minister seen?
statement: Stats NZ data shows that for the year ending June 2025, nearly 34,000 new dwellings were consented. While the rise of 1 percent may seem small to some, it does mark the end of a downturn period that started several years ago. It represents hope, despite the hope on the benches opposite that the reverse were true. It’s hope for the sector, hope for our housing supply, and commentators say that this data signals activity is stabilising and recovery is on the way.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Reti's quote and, if so, what that looks like. He states agreement and then sets out what it looks like in practice — IMPBs advising, not commissioning, feeding the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee. Both limbs engaged.
question: Does he agree with Hon Dr Shane Reti when he said, “I want to see IMPBs (iwi-Māori partnership boards) powered up to support the health outcomes for your whānau and your communities”; if so, what does that look like?
statement: I agree with the Hon Dr Shane Reti, who was very clear that iwi-Māori partnership boards, IMPBs, should be providing advice on the health needs of Māori across the country and that they should not be commissioning agencies. That’s why we’re strengthening the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee and clarifying the role of iwi-Māori partnership boards. Local IMPBs will continue to engage with local Māori communities about their health needs, aspirations, and health outcomes and will provide that advice directly to the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee. That advice will then support decisions made by the Minister and the Health New Zealand Board. This is about putting patients back at the centre and ensuring the voices of Māori communities are clearly heard where they can make the most difference.

explanation: Asked to explain why he minimised the boards' role given their expressed concerns. He describes what the change does (streamline advice, clarify roles, strengthen the advisory committee), which gestures at rationale, but never engages the 'why' in the face of the boards' opposition. Partial.
question: Can the Minister explain to the iwi-Māori partnership boards why he has made such a decision regarding the minimisation of their role after they have expressed extreme concern with the proposals led by this Minister?
statement: The Government has been very clear that, as part of the legislative changes that are being made, we want to streamline the advice that the IMPBs are providing, we want to clarify their roles—that they are not to be commissioning services; that is the role of Health New Zealand—and we want to strengthen the role that the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee does play to provide advice both to the Minister and to the Health New Zealand Board.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Thompson's statement about needing a plan and whether his plan will include meaningful engagement with Māori. He neither agrees nor disagrees and says nothing about engagement, pivoting to immunisation statistics under the previous government. Both limbs dodged.
question: Does he agree with Hingatu Thompson from Te Taura Ora o Waiariki iwi-Māori partnership board, who said, “There’s no way New Zealand is going to achieve improvement to Māori health without having a plan”, and, if so, will his plan include meaningful engagement with Māori on the matter?
statement: Our plan is to make sure that we are actually delivering better outcomes for all New Zealanders, including Māori, and I would just point out one of the facts that the Opposition doesn’t like to talk about, and that is the immunisation rate for two-year-olds, which fell from 89 percent of Māori in 2017 when they came to office to 64.8 percent when they left. That is, ultimately, what drives better outcomes for Māori: actually getting better outcomes.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Ministry's Te Tiriti obligation statement and how minimising IMPBs delivers on it. He answers the first limb affirmatively ('Of course the Government... does have a role'), but the 'how' is met only with a restatement that Health NZ must focus on delivery for all New Zealanders. Half answered.
question: Does he agree with the Ministry of Health website, which states, “As a department of the public service, the Ministry of Health - Manatū Hauora has a responsibility to contribute to the Crown meeting its obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi.”, and, if so, how does minimising iwi-Māori partnership boards deliver on this commitment?
statement: Of course the Government, through its agencies, does have a role to ensure that it is delivering on Treaty settlements and making sure that it is doing that through relationships. However, we have been very clear that Health New Zealand, as a delivery agency, must be focused on delivering better services for all New Zealanders, including Māori.

explanation: Asked whether Reti and Durie are both wrong, and what makes him surer than Māori health experts. He doesn't say yes or no, but does engage the premise by disputing it — the bill retains a role for IMPBs — so the question is contested rather than ignored. The second limb about his own authority is left alone.
question: Are the Hon Dr Shane Reti and Sir Mason Durie ONZ both wrong in their support for iwi-Māori partnership boards, and, if so, what makes the Minister so sure that he knows more about Māori health than the Māori health experts themselves?
statement: If the member was to read the bill before Parliament, the bill continues to have a role for iwi-Māori partnership boards. However, we want to make sure we are streamlining that function and focusing it on delivery for services—something the previous Government forgot about, as evidenced by the appalling immunisation rate for two-year-old Māoris. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked how he justifies the targeted killing of named journalists in Gaza. The recorded answer is a single broken-off fragment ("Well, there is—") containing no engagement with the question at all — nothing of the asked-for justification, or a refusal to give one, ever reaches the point. Scored as effectively unanswered.
question: How does the Prime Minister justify the targeted killings of journalists in Gaza, including Anas Jamal al-Sharif and the entire Al Jazeera journalist team based there?
statement: Well, there is—

explanation: A yes/no question: does he believe the killing of the Al Jazeera journalists is justifiable? He neither says yes nor no; instead he relocates the question to a jurisdictional point about not being responsible for Israel's actions. That is at least an explanation for why he is not going to opine (unlike pure talking points), but the core belief question is squarely stepped around rather than refused outright.
question: Does the Prime Minister believe the killing of journalists in Gaza, including Anas Jamal al-Sharif and the entire Al Jazeera journalist team based there, is justifiable?
statement: I have no responsibility for the actions of Israel or any other country; I am responsible, as Prime Minister of New Zealand, for New Zealand.

explanation: Asked what will be left to protect if he waits until September to act. He never addresses the September timing, the escalation, or what would remain; he restates the Government's consistent positions (hostage release, humanitarian access, ceasefire, two-State solution). Classic pivot to standing lines — the specific temporal challenge in the question is untouched.
question: What will be left to protect in a month’s time if the Prime Minister waits until September to act, with the Israel Government approving further escalation in Gaza, including measures that will deepen the starvation and killing of Palestinians?
statement: I would just say to the member that there are strongly held views on all sides of this debate across the whole of New Zealand, and, in fact, all around the world. What this Government has been consistent in doing since this conflict started is actually calling for the immediate release of hostages from Hamas. I’m sure that member would agree with that—that that is the appropriate action. What this Government has been calling for is for Israel to give unfettered humanitarian access to protect civilians and to honour its obligations under international law, and what this Government has consistently called for is a ceasefire. That is the way in which we get ourselves to a pathway on the two-State solution.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions. Answer: "Yes." One word, complete, unambiguous.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked why he thinks worker-led collectives call his Government the most anti-worker in decades. "You'd have to ask them" is a genuine, direct (if minimal) response to the why — he declines to speculate about their reasoning — but he then fills the rest with unrelated economic talking points rather than engaging the characterisation. Partial engagement.
question: Why does he think worker-led collectives are describing his Government as the most anti-worker Government in decades?
statement: You’d have to ask them, but what I can tell you is we’re on the side of low and middle income working New Zealanders because we believe they deserve tax relief—first time in 14 years. We’re backing fast track to create more jobs and opportunity to get things built in this country. We’re the ones that have lowered inflation. We’re the ones that are lowering our interest rates. We’re the one that’s getting the economy growing again. We are doing everything we can to get this country put on a pathway to economic growth, and I think it’s got a very exciting future.

explanation: Asked why the legislation was designed with Uber in mind rather than vulnerable migrant workers. He rejects the assertion and characterisation outright. That denies the premise squarely rather than wandering off, which is a real (if bare) response to a loaded 'why' — but he offers no account of the design rationale, so the question is only half-met.
question: Why was his employment relations legislation designed with big businesses like Uber in mind, instead of their workers, who are predominantly vulnerable, low-paid migrant workers?
statement: I reject the assertions and characterisation in that question.

explanation: Asked to reconcile wage-growth rhetoric with three specific decisions (real-term minimum wage cuts, scrapping fair pay agreements, cancelling pay equity claims). He engages the wage-growth half by pointing to wages outpacing inflation, but none of the three named decisions is addressed, so the reconciliation actually asked for is never attempted.
question: How does he reconcile his focus on growing wages with his Government’s decisions to offer real-term cuts for minimum-wage workers and cancel fair pay agreements and pay equity claims for low-paid wāhine workers?
statement: I’d just say to the member that I would encourage her to look at the records. Since this Government has been formed, we have had wages growing faster than inflation. Compare that to the previous Labour-Greens Government, where we had 13 quarters where inflation was well ahead of wage growth. Wages being higher than inflation is how Kiwis get ahead, and that’s what we’re supporting.

explanation: Two-part question: does he accept collective bargaining is the main driver of wage increases, and if so why undermine it? He gives no yes/no — he implicitly demurs by listing bargaining as one option among several — and the 'why the bill' half is not touched. Gestures at the subject without reaching either part.
question: Does he accept that collective bargaining is the main way workers’ wages increase, and, if so, why is he pushing through a bill that will undermine the collective bargaining power of hundreds of thousands of workers in Aotearoa?
statement: There are ways in which employees reach employment arrangements with their employers, and that can be an independent contracting arrangement or it can be collective bargaining. We support lots of options.

explanation: A narrow factual question: which Māori education providers has she consulted, if any? She spends most of the answer on the content of her reforms, then names only categories — her Māori education advisory group, 'Māori education leaders', ministry experts — without identifying a single provider. The asked-for list is gestured at, not given.
question: What Māori education providers has she consulted with, if any, regarding the impact her proposed education changes will have on all Māori learners across Aotearoa?
statement: My proposed education changes include the introduction of Rangaranga Reo ā-Tā, a new structured programme to teach reading, writing, and speaking, including a suite of decodable books. For the first time ever, we’ve printed and made freely available the introduction of Hihira Weteoro, the first ever phonics check in te reo Māori, new pāngarau maths resources including professional learning and development teacher guides and practical resources, and the refresh of Te Marautanga o Aotearoa to be a knowledge rich year-by-year curriculum in te reo Māori. Across my education reform programme, I regularly engage with my Māori education advisory group and Māori education leaders regarding kaupapa Māori. The Ministry of Education engages with a range of experts in Rangaranga Reo ā-Tā, pāngarau, aromatawai, and curriculum development—all of this because I have high aspirations for the success of Māori learners in all parts of our education system.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with Te Rūnanga Nui's stated criticism. "I don't" — an explicit answer to the yes/no put to her, followed by her reasons. Directly and completely responsive.
question: Does she agree with Te Rūnanga Nui o Ngā Kura Kaupapa Māori o Aotearoa that replacing NCEA level 1 with a Foundational Award in literacy and numeracy “narrows the purpose of learning and risks disengaging students who benefit from a broader kaupapa Māori programme.”?
statement: I don’t, and I think the important thing to note is the Education Review Office report, which said that 60 percent of teachers did not see value in NCEA level 1, that 70 percent of employers did not value it, and that half of parents didn’t understand it. Now, if that’s the award we want to give to Māori learners to set them up for success, then that’s not being aspirational enough. A Foundational Award in literacy and numeracy and a whole year of learning through a deep curriculum to make sure that they go into Year 12 ready for learning for that first important year of national qualifications is going to set them up for success.

explanation: Asked why she prioritised standardisation over cultural relevance despite kura kaupapa warnings. She answers a different question — what consultation is happening and who sat on the advisory group — never engaging the prioritisation choice the question was about, nor denying that she made it.
question: Why has she decided to prioritise standardisation over cultural relevance when kura kaupapa providers have warned that this approach is not fit for purpose for kura kaupapa?
statement: Look, we have already started and are going to continue to work with Te Rūnanga Nui and Ngā Kura ā Iwi and the kura kaupapa leaders to make sure that they have their say in this process. We’ve already set up meetings, we’ve already had initial conversations, and I would also like to point out that there was a principal from Ngā Kura ā Iwi and a principal from Te Rūnanga Nui on the professional advisory group that was helping to set this up.

explanation: Asked how banning nearly all Māori words from junior resources affects the Crown's duty to protect te reo. She meets the premise head-on — Māori words remain, forthcoming books will contain them, 'to say they're being banned is absolutely wrong' — and asserts she takes the duty seriously. The premise-rejection is squarely on point; the impact question itself is only lightly touched because she disputes its basis.
question: How will her decision to ban nearly all Māori words from junior teaching resources impact the Crown’s responsibility to actively protect and promote te reo Māori?
statement: I take that responsibility very seriously, which is why we produced the first ever set of Rangaranga Reo ā-Tā, structured literacy books, in te reo Māori. No Government has ever done that before. Let me be clear: these are the very first books that are tools to teach children to learn English. The Māori words in them will remain. In the new books that will round out the series, a dozen or so that still need to be produced will still contain Māori words, and to say they’re being banned is absolutely wrong.

explanation: Asked whether she supports a rigorous, culturally grounded assessment framework consistent with kura kaupapa Māori strengths. She engages the assessment-framework topic squarely — a new aromatawai has been procured, will be required twice yearly, and will be available in te reo for Māori-medium classrooms — which amounts to an implicit affirmative on assessment. But the specific hook of the question, whether it would be grounded in the proven strengths of kura kaupapa Māori, is never taken up; the answer describes a nationally-imposed tool instead and closes on the previous Government. Substantially engaged, core partly sidestepped.
question: Does the Minister support the establishment of a rigorous, culturally grounded assessment framework consistent with the proven strengths of kura kaupapa Māori?
statement: In answer to that question, we have just recently procured a new aromatawai, or assessment tool. Now, that assessment tool next year will be required twice yearly to measure progress, to measure progress from Year 3 all the way up. It will also be provided in te reo Māori as well, to measure progress of Māori students—not only in the mainstream but also in those Māori-medium classrooms—to make sure their learning is on track, to make sure their parents can see their progress, but, more importantly, for the Government and the Minister of Education to know where to put resource when those young people start to fall behind. We know that they are falling behind and if we do nothing, like the previous Government, then we end up with children who don’t get qualifications.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to extend the consultation timeline. She gives a clear refusal — 'we are not slowing down our reforms' — and explains the alternative engagement path with Ngā Kura Iwi and Te Rūnanga Nui plus an offer of a briefing. A plain no is a forthright answer; only slight deduction because the refusal arrives after preamble rather than being stated as such.
question: Will she commit to extending the consultation time line, in line with calls from kura kaupapa providers, to ensure that ākonga Māori are not left behind by her education reforms?
statement: We have been in the washing machine of change at least for the last five years. We have got to make change. I’ve already committed, as has the ministry, to dealing with Ngā Kura Iwi and Te Rūnanga Nui in a special and different way, where we hold constant meetings and receive their feedback on a different path than the mainstream consultation progress. We will continue to work collaboratively with them, but we are not slowing down our reforms, because our young people deserve a qualification that sets them up for success, and NCEA does not do that. If the member would like a briefing, I’d be happy to offer that to her. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, complete, unambiguous.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Two-part question: why he stands by the 86 percent cut to State house builds, and whether that is why 755 construction firms collapsed. He answers the causal half directly and explicitly — no, it is not Kāinga Ora, it is interest rates — which is a genuine engagement with the second limb. He never addresses why he stands by the build cut itself, pivoting to the previous Government's spending and then to what his Government is building. Half the question met.
question: Why does he stand by his Government’s decision to cut State house builds by 86 percent, given construction leaders have stated that house construction is an anchor for the sector, and is that why 755 construction firms have collapsed in just one year under his leadership?
statement: Well, the reason that the construction industry is doing it incredibly tough isn’t because of Kāinga Ora; it’s because interest rates skyrocketed under the previous administration, as my colleague just alluded to. The previous Government spent $66 billion, created high inflation, and, as a result, created high interest rates. The construction industry is required to go out and actually borrow money at higher interest rates. That makes it difficult to do projects, and that’s the reason the construction industry has been doing it tough. But, of course, we are building things and getting things done in this Government, and that will help construction.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts that a lack of Government work contributed to a 48 percent rise in liquidations and 18,000 fewer construction jobs. He neither accepts nor rejects the proposition; he recites pipeline figures and then lists the previous Government's abandoned projects. A denial can be inferred from the boasting, but the question 'do you accept' is never actually answered, and the jobs and liquidation figures are left untouched.
question: Does he accept that a lack of Government work has contributed to a 48 percent rise in construction firm liquidations and to 18,000 fewer jobs in construction today than when he became Prime Minister?
statement: Well, I’m actually proud that we’ve got an infrastructure pipeline now of $207 billion. I think we have $125 billion of projects under construction. We have announced another $6 billion of infrastructure projects to be built or commenced before Christmas. I’d just say the track record on this side of the House is we don’t have phantom projects like three waters at $1.2 billion, we don’t have $300 million Auckland light rail projects, and we don’t have harbour crossings that never come to fruition. [Interruption]

explanation: A narrow comparative question: will infrastructure spending in 2026 be more or less than in 2023? He explicitly frames a non-answer ('the way I can answer the member is...') and substitutes pipeline totals, which are a different quantity, then diverts to projects cancelled by the previous administration. Neither 'more' nor 'less' is ever said. Dodging a question this precise is a serious failure.
question: Will the $6 billion of projects that he claims are going to be starting before Christmas result in Government spending on infrastructure in 2026 being more or less than it was in 2023?
statement: Well, the way I can answer the member is by saying our pipeline has continued to strengthen through the course of this Government. We now have $207 billion worth of infrastructure. I would highlight to the member that a number of those projects that we are getting going on before Christmas were actually either cancelled by the previous administration—I think about the projects that are happening at Auckland Middlemore Hospital: recladding projects announced in 2018. This is a Government that’s going to get on and do it.

explanation: The same more-or-less question put again after the first evasion, giving him a clean second chance at a binary. He repeats the same pipeline figures, concedes he is repeating himself, then turns to demanding the questioner's support on fast track and closes with a rhetorical appeal. The comparison asked for is again never made; the second attempt makes the avoidance more pointed.
question: So will the Government be spending more on infrastructure in 2026 or less than it did in 2023?
statement: As I said in my earlier answer, I can encourage the member that we have strengthened our infrastructure pipeline to now sit at $207 billion. We have $125 billion under construction, $6 billion before Christmas. I’d just say to that member, I’d really love his support in supporting the construction industry, because I think it would be very important for him to reverse his decision on fast track so that we can actually get more projects up and running and away like the $200 million at the Auckland wharf. That’s going to create more jobs and more opportunities for New Zealanders. So why don’t you come on board and support us?

explanation: Asked whether he will admit that putting transport projects on hold had a chilling effect. He opens with 'No.' — a direct refusal of the proposition — and then explains his position with project examples. The question was engaged head-on at the first word; the subsequent counter-attack does not undo the answer already given.
question: Will he admit that putting existing transport projects on hold straight after the election has had a chilling effect on the sector, increasing uncertainty and stopping work?
statement: No. What I would say is that where the previous Government cancelled Ōtaki to Levin in 2018, reannounced it in 2020, and then did nothing, we’re actually building it. Where you cancelled Melling in 2018 and reannounced it in 2020, we’re now getting it going. When it was announced by the previous Government in 2018 that recladding Middlemore Hospital was very important, they did nothing for six years; we’re doing it. When you spend $1.2 billion looking at three waters and don’t do anything, that’s not good enough. We’re getting things built.

explanation: Asked whether a named industry figure is wrong to say further stimulus is needed. The question invites a yes or no on that person's claim; he never says whether the man is wrong, instead reporting his own conversations with the sector, blaming interest rates on the previous administration, and citing $6 billion of upcoming work. The stimulus proposition is only obliquely resisted, and the specific judgement asked for is never delivered.
question: Is the former chief executive of construction firm Naylor Love wrong when he says that further stimulus is needed from the Government “otherwise, we’re going to see … continuing downturn in [the] construction industry, more people losing jobs, and more misery.”?
statement: Well, I’d just say to the member, again, that in my conversations with people in the construction sector, they’re very conscious that poor economic management from the previous administration created high interest rates, and interest rates are critical for developments to happen. This is a Government that has got $6 billion worth of infrastructure happening and commencing before Christmas. That’s a good thing.

explanation: Asked why he cannot point to a single family receiving the promised $250 a fortnight under FamilyBoost. He does not name a family, does not explain why he cannot, and does not contest the premise; he thanks the questioner for the publicity and turns the answer into a promotional appeal for more families to sign up. The question is used as a platform rather than answered.
question: If he thinks that his FamilyBoost policy is such a “simple process”, as he said yesterday, why can’t he point towards a single family that’s received the $250 a fortnight that he promised them?
statement: Well, I just want to thank the member for his question, because every time he draws attention to FamilyBoost, we appreciate it, because we want 22,000 more families to actually sign up for FamilyBoost. That’s why we’ve expanded the thresholds; that’s why we’ve expanded the contributions that are being made, and I encourage everyone to do it.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made about seasonal worker access. She names both new visa pathways, their durations, entry conditions and example occupations. Directly and completely responsive to what was asked.
question: What recent announcements has she made about supporting businesses to access seasonal workers?
statement: I recently announced that the Government is introducing two new seasonal visa pathways to help businesses access the surge support they need during peak times. The Peak Seasonal Visa is up to a seven-month visa for short-term seasonal roles such as wool handling and meat processing. The Global Workforce Seasonal Visa is a multiple-entry, three-year visa for highly skilled workers in roles such as winemaking, snow instruction, and sheep scanning. The success of our seasonal industries is crucial for growing the economy, which is why we are backing industry.

explanation: Asked how the visas will help grow the economy. She answers on point: they give businesses with seasonal peaks certainty of workers at critical times, get product to export, fill roles hard to staff locally, and let employers retain specialists across seasons. The closing detail on local advertising obligations is adjacent rather than on the growth question, but the core is squarely addressed.
question: How will these visas help to grow the economy?
statement: Well, businesses with seasonal peaks need certainty they’ll be able to access the workers they need during critical times to get products to export and meet the demand for roles such as snow instructors and adventure tourism guides. While employing New Zealanders is always our top priority, these visas will help our industries fill roles that are currently difficult to staff locally, as well as make it easier for employers to retain highly skilled, specialist workers across multiple seasons. For the Peak Seasonal Visa, businesses will still have to advertise their jobs locally and engage with Ministry of Social Development to ensure New Zealand workers have first opportunity.

explanation: Asked what feedback came from the primary industry; the answer names Federated Farmers and the Meat Industry Association and quotes both. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What feedback has she received from the primary industry on this announcement?
statement: Federated Farmers have welcomed the changes, saying that these visas will make a huge difference to the agricultural sector. Immigration spokesperson Karl Dean said, “It’s awesome, because it’s the training and getting people used to your processes, your health and safety, the farms you deal with, is what does cost a business.”, and Meat Industry Association chief executive Sirma Karapeeva said, “Improving the ability to employ migrant workers on a seasonal visa means meat processors can ensure shifts run at maximum capacity on a regular basis. This results in more sustainable employment and income for New Zealanders employed by the sector.”

explanation: Asked for tourism-industry feedback; the answer relays named responses from Lake Wānaka Tourism/Destination Queenstown and Cardrona/Treble Cone. Directly responsive.
question: What feedback has she received from the tourism industry on this announcement?
statement: Lake Wānaka Tourism and Destination Queenstown chief executive Mat Woods said that the new visa is great news for Wānaka and Queenstown tourism operators. It will help create more consistency and less disruption across the tourism sector, ensuring visitors can enjoy world-class experiences across all four seasons. Cardrona and Treble Cone chief mountain officer Laura Hedley said that the visa will provide greater confidence for the Aotearoa ski industry and many of its key staff. This new visa pathway gives both them and us more certainty, and we welcome the change.

explanation: A yes/no agreement question; the Minister opens with 'Yes, I agree' and then supports it. He narrows 'heat pumps' to 'efficient heating' and doesn't tick off every clause (jobs, public health), but the core agree/disagree question is answered.
question: Does he agree with the chief executive officer of Consumer NZ and the managing director of Simplicity, in the Protecting industry, jobs and household budgets as the gas runs out report, that accelerating heat pump adoption will reduce reliance on gas, protect jobs, improve public health, and lower energy costs for New Zealand families and businesses?
statement: Yes, I agree that accelerating the uptake of efficient heating is vital for Kiwi families. That’s why I was pleased to announce the expansion of the Warmer Kiwi Homes programme last week. This will make an additional 300,000 more households eligible for support, including for heat pump installations. That’s an additional 300,000 households who could potentially save up to $340 a year. This expansion, along with the Government’s other work, will help more New Zealanders enjoy warmer, healthier homes and lower energy costs.

explanation: Asked squarely whether he will reinstate the $100m cut. He never says yes or no; he defends the Budget 2025 refocus and the programme's history. An implicit 'no' can be inferred, but the question's core commitment is left unstated.
question: Will he, then, reinstate the over $100 million cut from the Warmer Kiwi Homes programme in Budget 2024 to convert households to heat pumps for room and hot water heating, given the report shows these measures could save households up to $1.5 billion annually in energy bills?
statement: Budget 2025 refocused the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority (EECA) budget to deliver value for money and align this with Government priorities of secure, affordable energy. We’ve brought it back to core priorities like insulation, efficient heating, and technology that reduces bills and strengthens energy security, and we’re getting better results for less money. The reality is that this programme has been in place since 2009, and the Warmer Kiwi Homes programme has already had good progress with over half a million installations and heating retrofits across this country. We are now expanding the reach of this programme to provide more opportunities to more middle-income households so that they can benefit too. The Government is still committed to accessing hard-to-reach households.

explanation: A narrow factual question — has he seen specific Budget 2024 advice? The reply never mentions the advice at all and pivots to cost of living, electricity prices and blaming the previous government. A clean dodge of a yes/no.
question: Has the Minister seen the advice, given with decisions in Budget 2024, that the changes he has made to the Warmer Kiwi Homes programme will result in less homes being retrofitted and/or households needing to contribute more to access support?
statement: This Government is focused on tackling the cost of living and keeping electricity prices under control. The first thing that we did as a Government is undo those reckless policies from the last Government that pushed up prices and scared off investment. This sector is now delivering market-led solutions, including demand response deals and long-term supply agreements. We strongly support this approach because it delivers results and lowers prices for Kiwis.

explanation: Asked for a figure: how much new money since 2023. He asserts he has already answered, then repeats the 'refocused priorities / 300,000 households / half a million installations' lines. No new-money figure and no answer to the alternative posed either.
question: How much new money since 2023 has gone into the Warmer Kiwi Homes programme, or is he just spreading an already reduced amount of money, allocated by Labour in 2023, even thinner?
statement: I have already answered this question. As I have said, we have refocused EECA’s priorities to deliver more value for money. We are ensuring that that programme delivers outcomes, and, as a result of those decisions, we have expanded the reach of that programme to more than 300,000 additional Kiwi households. This programme has been under way since 2009—half a million installations. We have predominantly dealt with the very difficult homes, and we are now expanding that to more middle-income households in this country, and that is a positive step.

explanation: Asked whether he will reinstate the $40m commercial buildings initiative. He labels the question a patsy and pivots to Investment Boost. It is at least in the same policy area (commercial heat pumps), but the will-he-reinstate question is never answered.
question: Will he reinstate the $40 million cut from the commercial buildings initiative in the 2023 mini-Budget to partner with industry to replace fossil fuel boilers used for space and water heating with more energy-efficient technologies such as hot water heat pumps, given that the report shows policies such as this can lead to more security in our energy supply and prevent further job losses?
statement: I thank the member for that patsy, and I will remind the member of the great policy that this Government announced at the Budget: Investment Boost. Investment Boost allows a 20 percent upfront reduction in year one on heat pumps for commercial buildings. This Government is doing everything it can to increase the uptake of efficient options for businesses and households, and that is a great example of a policy that this Government has done. It’s also a recommendation in the report that the member asked in her oral question.

explanation: Asked to accept that his Government's cuts are making things worse and leaving no plan. He engages the substance — concedes prices are high and gas is running short, attributes cause to prior governments, and cites the $200m initiative as the plan — but never directly addresses the cuts or accepts/rejects the charge about them.
question: Isn’t it the case that cuts in the energy portfolio from his Government are making things worse, costing jobs, and leaving New Zealand without a plan as the gas runs out?
statement: I want to be very upfront with New Zealanders in regards to the challenges they face with energy. Energy prices in this country are higher than where they need to be. Gas is running out faster than what we expected. The result of those outcomes is because of decisions made by prior Governments, but this Government is not standing by and doing nothing. We are taking leadership. We have announced initiatives, including the $200 million investment in order to increase oil and gas, which is critical to burn electricity, and we’re delivering a variety of other mechanisms. The member needs to understand that.

explanation: Asked what the report said. He does state a finding ('it signalled real sovereign risk for the first time in decades') before sliding into a defence of reversing the ban and attacking 'virtue-signalling'. Partially answers, then leaves the question for talking points.
question: What did this report say?
statement: It signalled real sovereign risk for the first time in decades. That risk has been priced in by the market and passed on to New Zealand consumers. The reversal of the ban gives industry the certainty to invest in the gas we need for dry years and industrial heat while new generation comes on line. This Government supports the transition to renewables, but we will not risk energy shortages and skyrocketing prices through reckless virtue-signalling policy.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made on caregiver experience; she cites the caregiver work programme and the $16m over four years in Budget 2025. Responsive, though it opens with general sentiment before reaching the announcements.
question: What recent announcements has she made about improving the experiences of Oranga Tamariki caregivers?
statement: I want to ensure all caregivers feel supported and valued so that they can provide the best possible care for the children and young people they’ve opened their homes to. Since becoming Minister, I’ve asked Oranga Tamariki to progress work on a caregiver work programme focused on upholding rights and responsibilities of caregivers. We have listened to the caregivers about what makes the biggest difference for them, through both annual satisfaction surveys and more targeted consultation with caregivers. This has led to a range of caregiver support changes in the way we strengthen and simplify practices and policies—all designed to improve the experience of caregivers. In Budget 2025, we committed $16 million over four years to make care environments safer and to better support and train caregivers in the wider workforce.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions; answer: 'Yes.' One word, complete and direct.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked for a number of jobs lost as a direct result of Government decisions. The answer never gives any figure and never accepts the causal framing, pivoting immediately to blaming the previous Government's spending, debt and inflation. A narrow factual question answered with attribution of blame instead.
question: How many jobs were lost as a direct result of his Government’s decisions?
statement: Well, as the member will be aware, we have seen an increase in people on the jobseeker benefit. That’s a function of a previous Government that increased spending by 84 percent, tripled the debt, drove up inflation and interest rates, and put the economy in recession. Sadly, when you’re in a recession, with less demand for products and higher costs because of inflation and interest rates, people, sadly, lose their jobs. That is a very challenging situation for individuals, and it’s something this Government’s working incredibly hard at.

explanation: Two-part question: is the 46 percent figure correct, and was it his Government's choice. He neither confirms nor denies the figure and never addresses choice; he offers a counter-aggregate (wages growing faster than inflation) which implicitly contests the premise but does not engage either part directly.
question: Is it correct that 46 percent of workers, such as teachers, nurses, and firefighters, received a pay rise lower than inflation, and, if so, was that his Government’s choice?
statement: Well, I’m very, very proud of the fact that under this Government, we have had wages growing faster than inflation, unlike the previous Government, which had 12 or 13 quarters where inflation grew faster than wages. Ultimately, wages need to go ahead of inflation so that people can get ahead.

explanation: Asked whether 'parties of workers' included the women affected by the pay equity changes. He talks about pay equity continuing and money being set aside, but never says whether those women were among the workers he meant. Adjacent to the topic, but the specific question is left unanswered.
question: When he said yesterday, “We are the parties of workers,” did he refer to the women affected by the changes to pay equity claims?
statement: Well, there is continued pay equity, as we’ve talked about many times in this House. This Government continues to support it. We’ve put money aside to support future claims, and any individual or any employee is free to make a claim.

explanation: A yes/no question with a stated fallback ('if not, why not') about supporting 35,000 additional State homes. He never says yes or no and never engages the 35,000 figure; he recites Kainga Ora build numbers and then attacks the questioner's record as former Minister. Opposition is implied but never stated.
question: Does he support building an additional 35,000 State homes to tackle growing homelessness and create thousands of jobs, and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, I’m very proud that Kāinga Ora has actually built 7,000 new homes under this Government. That is more than the 5,700 under the last term of the previous Government. Importantly, there will be about 2,000 extra homes each and every year being built. Most importantly, there’s been probably close to 6,000 people taken off the State house social housing wait-list. There’s been 2,100 kids put into warm, dry homes. You see rents falling, under $5 a week versus $180 a week. As that member knows, as the former Minister of homelessness—where homelessness went up 37 percent under her watch while the Government spent a billion dollars on emergency housing—those are difficult challenges.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made about the Conservation Act. He names the date, the announcement, and its two components (easier business/activity on conservation land; charging foreign visitors). Squarely on the question.
question: What recent announcements has he made about the Conservation Act 1987?
statement: On 2 August 2025, the Prime Minister and I announced changes to unlock growth on conservation lands. We’re going to fix the Conservation Act to make it easier to conduct business and other activities on conservation lands, supporting activities like tourism, agriculture, and—one of my personal favourites—infrastructure, where that makes sense. In addition, we are giving the Department of Conservation more support by introducing the ability for the department to charge foreign visitors a fee to access high-volume sites. By charging foreign visitors to visit popular sites they currently enjoy for free, we can invest more in one of the key reasons they come to this country: our iconic nature, biodiversity, and world-class visitor, or manuhiri, experiences.

explanation: Asked how simplifying the Act leads to regional economic growth. He answers the mechanism directly: jobs, businesses operating on conservation land, faster permit and concession processing, greater investment certainty.
question: How will simplifying the Conservation Act lead to greater economic growth in our regions?
statement: Exactly—jobs. Thousands of businesses operate on conservation land, bringing in millions of dollars a year for local and regional economies, and, indeed, jobs. Changes announced will enable faster processing of permits and other concessions for businesses and community organisations, amongst others. They also simplify the rules for doing business and undertaking other activities on conservation land, giving people greater certainty to invest and recreate. We can balance thriving natural environments with responsible development without unreasonably compromising conservation values.

explanation: Asked how charging tourists leads to greater protection of biodiversity. He gives the causal chain asked for: revenue from access charges ring-fenced and reinvested in bridges, tracks, pest control and habitat restoration.
question: How will charging international tourists lead to greater protection of our biodiversity and natural environment?
statement: International visitors, like many Kiwis, love nature. Sixty-five percent go walking or tramping, and 45 percent visit a national park while they’re here in New Zealand. Access charging will allow us to provide world-class manuhiri experiences while protecting nature through reinvesting this revenue. The access charges will focus on popular tourism experiences, creating a more sustainable way to fund their upkeep and improvement by those who use them. Charging international visitors at four majestic sites is estimated to generate around $60 million a year for conservation, to be ring-fenced for conservation work like upgrading bridges and tracks, pest and predator control, and habitat restoration.

explanation: Asked for the next steps in implementing access charging. He lists them: infrastructure planning, targeted consultation with concessionaires, communities and iwi, and a target date of summer 2027.
question: What are the next steps for implementing access charging?
statement: We are carefully planning the next steps, including suitable physical and digital infrastructure required to support execution. The Department of Conservation want to take targeted consultation with concessionaires, local communities, and iwi for feedback on implementation options. New charges are intended to be in place by summer 2027.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Bishop's quoted characterisation. He opens with 'Yes' and qualifies it by reference to the full quote, then expands on homelessness generally. The yes/no is delivered before the elaboration.
question: Does he agree with Hon Chris Bishop that homelessness has “potentially ticked up a little bit, up a little bit more in the last couple of years”?
statement: Yes, in the context of the full quote, homelessness is a long-running issue for New Zealand. I have said in this House previously that homelessness has, unfortunately, been increasing in New Zealand for many years. No one here wants to see Kiwis living homeless and particularly without shelter, but homelessness is not just a housing issue; it is driven by a range of structural and systemic failures that may reflect—and do reflect—the broader economic environment. This Government takes homelessness seriously, particularly those living without shelter, and that’s why we are fixing the fundamentals of our housing market and making sure we have the right houses in the right places with the right support for people in genuine need.

explanation: Asked whether a 90 percent increase counts as 'a little bit'. He never characterises the figure or the phrase, deflecting to the existence of various data reports and then to actions taken and advice awaited. The core comparison is entirely avoided.
question: Does he consider a 90 percent increase in homelessness in Tāmaki-makaurau to be “a little bit”?
statement: There are a range of data reports and comments that have been made over many years by councils, by community housing providers, and, indeed, by members of the Opposition. We have taken action by directing officials to provide advice on short-term, targeted interventions to provide help and support to those living without shelter. Officials and Ministers have liaised with numerous providers on these matters, and we await final advice.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Auckland City Mission's claim. He engages the question only to the extent of saying it is the first he has heard of that quote, then substitutes a different, favourable quote from another housing figure rather than saying whether he agrees or disputes the claim.
question: Does he agree with Auckland City Mission that his decision to refuse emergency housing to people suffering from pneumonia or undergoing dialysis has forced them to live on the streets and is putting pressure on already overrun hospital emergency departments?
statement: That is the first that I’ve heard of that particular quote, but what I have heard from the CEO of the community housing association of New Zealand, Paul Gilberd, is that the work we undertook with Priority One, in ensuring that over 3,000 children have come out of motels over the last 18 months, is an absolutely fantastic result, delivered in a timely manner, with absolute empathy for those young children, who were living in a social, moral, and financial catastrophe that remained when we came into this administration.

explanation: Asked why he is not acting immediately to remove emergency housing barriers. He rejects the premise as conflated and points to officials being directed to advise on short-term interventions, which partly answers ('we are acting'), but the specific 'why not immediately' is not reached before he moves to a broader list of housing work and an attack on the previous Government.
question: Why, if Chris Bishop has said he is open to making it less difficult for people to access emergency housing, is he not acting immediately to remove the barriers preventing people from getting a roof over their heads?
statement: There are a number of issues that are conflated in the member’s question. We have taken action to direct officials and seek their advice over short-term interventions targeted to help particularly those living without shelter and rough sleeping. We’ve also undertaken a range of activities, both short-term and long-term, to make it easier for New Zealanders to build houses and to access affordable housing, whether or not that’s the mahi of Minister Chris Penk around building and construction laws, the mahi of Minister Bishop around the Resource Management Act and a number of other matters, or, indeed, the mahi that Minister Luxon and others have undertaken for emergency housing. We are absolutely clear: we will not return to the utopic boondoggles of 100,000 KiwiBuild homes or the moral catastrophe that was emergency housing on a large scale that affected places like Ulster Street in Hamilton West.

explanation: Asked why 86 percent fewer State homes are being built while homelessness rises. The answer never engages the figure or the reduction; it pivots to the position that government is not the only builder and to a commitment about 'genuine need'. An implicit rationale (reliance on private/community providers) is gestured at, which is why it is not zero, but the specific 'why the cut' is left unanswered.
question: Why, when reports from his own officials suggest there are more homeless people than ever, is he constructing 86 percent fewer State homes in 2025 than there were being built in 2023?
statement: As the members of this House are very aware, this Government does not believe it is only the Government that can build homes for New Zealanders. There are a range of parties, whether or not that’s community housing providers, Māori housing providers, or, indeed, a range of other potential housing providers—but particularly private developers—that can build supply into the demand that is currently happening here in New Zealand. What we do know, though, and what we are absolutely committing to, is ensuring that those with genuine need get the right places and the right houses with the right support to address their needs.

explanation: Asked why the Government is cutting State home builds and refusing to act on Chris Bishop's admission. The reply talks about Māori-led housing delivery in Utakura and Te Kao, whakapapa connections, and transitional housing costs inherited from the previous administration. Neither the cut nor the Bishop point is addressed.
question: Why, when Māori are disproportionately represented among the homeless, when whānau in Tāmaki-makau-rau are facing a 90 percent rise in homelessness, and when even those battling serious illness are being turned away from emergency housing, is his Government not only cutting the number of State homes being built but refusing to act on Chris Bishop’s admission that you could make it easier for people to get a roof over their heads?
statement: As the member is aware, we are very committed to supporting Māori-led housing delivery across places as far, far away as Utakura in the Hokianga Harbour, where, I understand, the member has some whakapapa connections—or, indeed, Te Kao, where other members of this House have some whakapapa connections—and also futureproofing and cost-proofing the transitional housing costs that we inhaled from the previous administration that were not cost-proof. These are the things that we do knowing that many, many Māori live in transitional housing that this Government has taken decisions on to ensure that those Māori in genuine need for housing support get it in a timely manner.

explanation: Asked what recent reports he has seen on mental health workforce growth. He names the source (Health New Zealand payroll data) and its finding (almost 10 percent growth since the election). Squarely answered; only the surrounding framing sentences are padding.
question: What recent reports has he seen on growth in the mental health workforce?
statement: This Government is focused on faster access to timely mental health and addiction support. Health New Zealand payroll data shows there has been an almost 10 percent growth in the number of front-line mental health and addiction workers since this Government was elected. When Kiwis, their loved ones, friends, or family members make the brave step of reaching out for help, this Government is committed to ensuring we have the right support in place.

explanation: Asked where significant growth has occurred. He enumerates the specific workforce categories — mental health nurses, nursing support workers, clinical psychologists and drug/alcohol workers, psychiatry SMOs — with figures for each. Directly and completely on the question.
question: Where has there been significant growth in the mental health workforce?
statement: As the Minister for Mental Health, one of my top priorities is to grow the mental health and addiction workforce. Health New Zealand data shows there’s been a significant growth in front-line staff—registered mental health nurses, up by 21 percent; nursing support workers, up 20 percent; clinical psychologists and drug and alcohol workers, up 6 percent; psychiatry senior medical officers, up 9.5 percent. Workforce should never be a barrier to accessing timely mental health and addiction support, and this Government is working hard to make sure it isn’t.

explanation: Asked what the result of the workforce growth has been. He states the results: vacancy rate down, front-line staff up, resignation rates lower, more people getting support. Engages the question directly after a brief framing preamble.
question: What has been the result of the significant growth in the mental health workforce?
statement: In my view, one of the biggest barriers to timely mental health and addiction support in New Zealand is too many workforce vacancies. Since coming into office, the mental health workforce vacancy rate is down, total number of front-line mental health staff are up, and resignation rates are lower. Behind every one of these new front-line workers are hundreds of Kiwis now getting the support they need.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has received on the increased front-line workforce. He supplies feedback — the college of psychiatrists' statement and a quote from its chair. The Auditor-General/previous-government material at the end drifts, but the core question is answered.
question: What feedback has he received on the increased front-line workforce?
statement: We’re starting to turn the corner on mental health. Our plan is delivering decreased wait times and an increased workforce. The New Zealand college of psychiatrists said last week New Zealand was turning a corner on workforce shortages. Dr Hiran Thabrew, the chair of the college, said, “the Government had demonstrated a genuine commitment to listening to those working at the coalface of the mental health system.” The Auditor-General called for a specific mental health workforce plan in response to wait times and workforce shortages increasing under the previous Government. As a result, this is a priority of this Government, which we delivered in our first year: a dedicated mental health and addiction workforce plan that is delivering results.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement and, if so, why. He says 'Yes' and gives a reason (focus on growing the economy to create job opportunities). Both limbs of the question are met.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “We absolutely have endeavours to get Pasifika people into employment”; if so, why?
statement: Yes, and I acknowledge the current high rates of unemployment, particularly for Pasifika, which is the unfortunate after-effect of a historic period of out-of-control inflation, rapidly rising interest rates, and stagnant growth. That’s why our Government is relentlessly focused on growing the economy to support Pasifika and all New Zealanders with better job opportunities, higher wages, and a brighter future.

explanation: A narrow factual yes/no: is Pasifika unemployment double its end-2023 level? He confirms it and supplies both figures (around 12 percent now, around 6 percent then). Complete.
question: Is it correct that the current unemployment rate for Pasifika peoples is double what it was at the end of 2023 when his Government came into office?
statement: The current rate of unemployment for Pasifika is around 12 percent, and it is correct that when we first came into Government it was around 6 percent.

explanation: Asked why he cut $22 million from Tupu Aotearoa. He gives a reason — consolidating with MSD's similar programmes to get better delivery. The 'at a time when unemployment is twice the national average' framing is ignored, but the core 'why' is answered.
question: Why did he cut $22 million out of the Tupu Aotearoa Pacific employment and training programme at a time when Pasifika unemployment is more than twice the national average?
statement: What we’re wanting to do with Tupu Aotearoa is collaborate with the Ministry of Social Development (MSD), who have similar programmes, and we wanted to enhance the benefits we saw from Tupu Aotearoa in the last financial year, that delivered 2,551 outcomes. We believe we can do a better job in collaboration with MSD.

explanation: A two-part specific question: is the $22 million now being spent by MSD on targeted Pasifika programmes, and if so which ones? He neither confirms nor denies the reallocation and names no programme, restating the collaboration in general terms ('a more fine-tuned, focused delivery mechanism'). The core of a narrow question is avoided.
question: Is he saying that the $22 million previously allocated to Tupu Aotearoa is now being used by MSD for targeted Pasifika programmes, and, if so, what are they?
statement: What I’m saying is that the collaboration between what the Ministry for Pacific Peoples (MPP) does with Tupu Aotearoa and with what MSD was also doing with young people not in education, employment, or training is giving us a more fine-tuned, focused delivery mechanism.

explanation: Asked why he ignored officials' advice that targeted programmes are critical. He answers with a 'because' — reliance on other MPP programmes such as the Pacific Business Trust. He does not concede or contest that the advice was ignored, but a reason for the choice is squarely given.
question: Why, when officials advised him that “targeted programmes such as Tupu Aotearoa with defined interventions are critical to moving Pacific peoples into employment, education, or training.”, did he ignore the advice?
statement: Because we’re able to focus on other MPP-delivered programmes such as the Pacific Business Trust, which supports Pacific businesses to be successful and thrive and which delivered 320 jobs in the last financial year.

explanation: Asked why he shut down the Tauola Business Fund. He gives a direct causal answer: the Pacific Business Trust is already delivering, plus MBIE programmes like Alo Vaka. The question's 'why' is met head-on.
question: Why, at a time of rising unemployment, did he shut down the Tauola Business Fund, which supported Pacific businesses to foster growth and create employment opportunities?
statement: Because the Pacific Business Trust, as I’ve described, is already delivering effective and efficient services, plus there are other programmes such as those run by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment—such as Alo Vaka, which is supporting Pacific workers into higher-quality, better-paid jobs with some success.

explanation: Asked why he would cut back a specific employment programme for Pasifika given the unemployment gap. Reti never mentions the programme or the reason for the cut; he lists other government activity (infrastructure, construction pipeline, hospitality, tourism) that bears on Pasifika employment generally. It gestures at the topic — employment for Pasifika — without touching the 'why cut this' core.
question: Why would he make things worse for Pasifika families, when more are struggling to pay the bills and meet the rising cost of living, by cutting back a programme that helped more than 1,300 people into work in the last year alone, given that Pasifika unemployment is more than twice the national average?
statement: We’re looking to a range of endeavours for employment for Pasifika people, which include broader endeavours such as backing infrastructure, backing construction—we’ve announced the $6 billion pipeline for projects before the end of the year. We’re also backing hospitality and tourism. So as a wider suite of all-of-Government endeavours, we’re looking to improve employment for Pasifika.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees Netanyahu has 'lost the plot', and if so why. McClay answers the agree/disagree part squarely — 'Yes, in the context that the comment was made' — which is the crux of the question. The 'why' is only gestured at, with a list of government actions on Gaza rather than a reason for the agreement. Core answered, follow-up limb largely not.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has “lost the plot”; if so, why?
statement: Yes, in the context that the comment was made. The Prime Minister and I, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs, talk often on matters of foreign affairs that are important to New Zealand. That's why the Government has committed more than $37 million of humanitarian assistance to Gaza. We've also called for Israel and Hamas to implement a ceasefire, called for Hamas to release hostages, and for all parties to allow for the safe, rapid, and unimpeded flow of humanitarian aid. We have also declared Hamas a terrorist organisation.

explanation: Two limbs: does he agree with Seymour's characterisation, and why the month-long delay. He declines the first limb by saying he didn't see the comments and offering a charitable reading of what Seymour may have meant — an engagement, though not a yes/no. The second limb he does address directly: the Government will take an appropriate amount of time. Half answered, half sidestepped via non-sighting.
question: Does he agree with David Seymour that recognising Palestinian statehood as it currently exists would mean making friends with terrorists; if so, why is the Government spending the next month deciding whether they will make friends with terrorists or not?
statement: I didn't see the comments that the Deputy Prime Minister made, and they may well have been as leader of the ACT Party. But very clearly, what Mr Seymour may have been commenting on is the role that Hamas plays, who are a terrorist organisation who are active in harming people in that area. The member is right: the Government is going to take an appropriate amount of time to make a decision that is not only right but right for New Zealand.

explanation: A loaded question presupposing that ACT resistance is undermining NZ's credibility. McClay's first words reject the premise outright — 'No, that absolutely is not correct, and I refute it' — which is a direct response to what was put to him. The remainder is talking points about not grandstanding, but the question itself was engaged and answered in the negative.
question: Why is the Government allowing the resistance of ACT Party Ministers to undermine New Zealand international credibility and reputation, just as they did in the Deputy Prime Minister’s letter to the United Nations Rapporteur on Indigenous Rights?
statement: No, that absolutely is not correct, and I refute it. What the Government won't be doing is grandstanding in this Parliament on an issue that is so important merely for the theatrics of politics. We will be making a decision that's in the best interest for New Zealand and is the right decision, but we're going to ensure we consider all parts of this decision before we rush to any conclusion.

explanation: Two questions: does he agree NZ has long been friends with Israel, and is NZ still a friend of Israel now. The first is effectively answered ('a very long history with Israel'). The second — the one with the sting, about the present relationship after two years of Israeli actions — is left untouched, replaced by a pivot to decision-making process and a complaint about political grandstanding.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that we have been friends with Israel for a long period of time, and is New Zealand still a friend of Israel, following their actions over the last two years?
statement: New Zealand has a very long history with Israel, as we have many former Israeli citizens that live in this country. However, we are going to consider what is in the best interest of New Zealand and what is the right decision. And I say, again, to all leaders of parties in this House: political grandstanding for the theatrics of getting on television is not in the best interest of New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether words will convince Netanyahu and, if not, why he won't take further action such as sanctions. McClay answers neither limb: he recharacterises the question as 'what actions has NZ taken' and enumerates statements and UN interventions. Sanctions are never mentioned and the efficacy question is never addressed — he answers a different question than the one asked.
question: Does he think words on the international stage will convince the leader who has “lost the plot”; if not, why won't he take further actions, such as sanctioning Israel?
statement: It's interesting he asked what actions New Zealand has taken. New Zealand has issued eight ministerial statements since October 2023 and delivered 29 statements at the UN. In these, we have been clear in our condemnation of Hamas and our calls for hostages to be released; for humanitarian access into Gaza; for all parties, including Israel, to abide by international law; and for a ceasefire in this conflict to be enacted.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on COVID-19 and the economy. Bishop names a specific report — Treasury's long-term insights briefing — which is exactly what was requested. Flippant in form and offering nothing about the report's contents, but a report is identified, so the question is answered.
question: What reports has she seen on COVID-19 and the economy?
statement: Oh, I haven’t been able to stop reading Treasury’s long-term insights briefing.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen about people taking responsibility for the COVID-19 spend. He identifies a report seen yesterday about decision-makers declining to appear at the royal commission's phase two hearings, and adds the consequence. Directly responsive to what was asked.
question: What reports has she seen about people taking responsibility for the COVID19 spend?
statement: I did see a report yesterday that key decision makers during the COVID-19 have refused an invitation to participate in public hearings on phase two of the royal commission of inquiry into COVID-19. Sadly, the COVID-19 inquiry has cancelled its second week of public hearings, which I think will be upsetting for some New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether other countries have held public hearings with decision makers. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, and it completely resolves the closed question put to him.
question: Have other countries held public hearings with decision makers?
statement: Yes.

explanation: A narrow factual question — how many social houses funded in the 2024 and 2025 Budgets have been built. Bishop gives the number: forty-five. No evasion whatsoever; the exact figure requested is supplied.
question: How many social houses funded in the 2024 and 2025 Budgets have been built?
statement: Forty-five.

explanation: Asked how the 45 houses measure up against the 1,000-a-year Auckland pledge. Bishop engages the comparison head-on by arguing the two figures are not the same measure (Budget-funded builds vs the Auckland commitment) and then states the pledge is 'making good progress'. He addresses the question's core — the relationship between the numbers — but never actually measures performance against the pledge, so it stops short of a complete answer.
question: How does that measure up to Nicola Willis’ signed pledge to a net increase of 1,000 social houses in Auckland every year?
statement: Well, they’re completely different numbers, in the sense that—the question was, “How many social houses that were funded in Budget 2024 and 2025 have been built so far?”. That funding starts on 1 July 2025, which has just been, it’s about eight weeks ago. Forty-five of those houses have been built, but the funding goes until 30 June 2027, so there’s a couple of years. The question the member just asked is about the commitment to build 1,000 homes in Auckland per year over a three-year period, which we’re making good progress on.

explanation: Asked how 45 houses constitutes good progress on a 1,000-a-year pledge. He offers two reasons — time remaining until November 2026, and that many houses have been built in Auckland — which is a genuine attempt at justifying the 'good progress' claim rather than a pivot. But it never connects to the pledge's annual target, so the core of the challenge is only half met.
question: How is 45 houses good progress on the signed pledge to build a net increase of 1,000 social houses in Auckland a year?
statement: Well, firstly, there’s a long way to go until November 2026, for starters, and the second point is that many houses have been built in Auckland over the last 18 to 19 months.

explanation: Asked how he can credibly dismiss construction-sector leaders linking cancelled Kāinga Ora projects to 18,000 job losses. He gives a direct reason: Kāinga Ora and community housing are only 5–7 percent of the construction market, so they are marginal to the sector, while conceding it makes some difference. That squarely answers 'how can you dismiss it'. The trailing build-programme figures are supporting material, not a pivot.
question: How can he credibly dismiss leaders in the construction sector who link the Government cancelling Kāinga Ora projects and insufficient funding for social houses to the 18,000 jobs lost in construction since this Government took office?
statement: Well, Kāinga Ora, and the community housing sector more broadly, is about 5 to 7 percent of the construction market, so it’s on the margins of the construction sector. I’m not denying it makes a difference, but 93 percent of the residential construction market is the private sector—it’s not the community housing sector and Kāinga Ora. Kāinga Ora has built around 2,500 net new homes over the last year. They’ve got a build programme over the next couple of years of around 2,000 gross homes, and, of course, you’ve got around 2,000 community houses on top of that—and that’s not even counting Māori housing, which there is quite a lot of additional support going into, which my good colleague the Hon Tama Potaka has made announcements about, and many of those projects will be starting construction in the next year or so as well.

explanation: Asked how he can deny making things worse given job losses, 45 houses and rising homelessness. He re-explains the 45 figure and repeats the 5–7 percent market-share argument, which does address the denial. But he then moves to inflation, interest rates and an unrelated build-to-rent announcement, leaving the homelessness and job-loss elements of the charge untouched. Half engaged, half deflected.
question: How can he deny making things worse when 18,000 construction jobs have been lost, the Government has only contributed 45 new social houses, and homelessness in parts of the country has increased by over 90 percent.
statement: Well, there’s 45 new social houses built from the Budget 2024 funding that the member asked about, but the actual funding is 2,000 over the next two years, additional community housing funded programmes, on top of Kāinga Ora’s existing build programme.
