That is a genuine 'why' answer, though it partly re-frames the question by disputing the assumed knowledge.
question: Why did she not correct the record when she knew as early as 11 June that employment discussions had occurred because there was a disagreement about the level of funding between the Governor, the board, and the Government?
statement: Well, the member is making a number of assumptions about what I knew. You need to remember, at the time, I was not aware of the specific concerns the bank had raised with Mr Orr. I was not aware of how Mr Orr had responded to those concerns. I was not aware of the details of the agreement the bank had entered into with Mr Orr. I didn’t want to create legal or financial risk to taxpayers, and I did not want to be doing or saying anything that could be seen as politicising a sensitive employment process. I relied on the judgment of the Reserve Bank chair that he was saying as much as he could say. As has been traversed, it is my view that he should have dealt with that matter better.

explanation: Asked whether she no longer stands by her 18 June select committee statements. She answers directly — 'I stand by my statements' — with the single noted exception of a date corrected by personal explanation. Yes/no delivered plus the qualification.
question: Therefore, does she no longer stand by her statements made to the Finance and Expenditure Committee on 18 June?
statement: I stand by my statements, although the member will be aware that I made a personal explanation in this House last night correcting a date which I shared at that committee. I made that personal explanation as soon as that error was made known to me.

explanation: Asked whether New Zealanders can trust her and whether she drove Orr to resign. She neither addresses trust nor answers the causal claim; instead she characterises Edmonds as 'the great defender of Adrian Orr' and asserts her own good judgement in not politicising the exit. A pivot to the questioner plus a self-credit line.
question: Does she really believe that New Zealanders can trust her when she has withheld information, had to correct statements, also was on the possibility of receiving advice to allow for the removal of Adrian Orr, or, really, is the real reason why Adrian Orr resigned because she drove him to it?
statement: If Barbara Edmonds wishes to be the great defender of Adrian Orr, then that is for her. I have chosen not to politicise his exit from the Reserve Bank, which I think shows good judgment.

explanation: Two-part: was she aware of BlackSky–Israeli Defence Ministry links at approval, and if so did she raise concerns. Peters answers the awareness half squarely — MBIE advised of previous contracts but no evidence of a current one — but the 'did you raise concerns' half is never reached, and the 2021 Labour reference is padding.
question: Was she aware of the links between intelligence company BlackSky and the Israeli Defence Ministry when she approved payload launch permits, and, if so, did she raise any concerns?
statement: When I took this decision in December 2023, I was advised by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) that while there had been previous contracts between BlackSky and the Israeli defence ministry, there was no evidence of a current contract. We’d also like to note that the first BlackSky payload was approved by the previous Labour Government in 2021. The Minister for Space makes decisions on payload permits, based on MBIE recommendation, to protect New Zealand’s national interest.

explanation: Asked for an assurance that BlackSky payloads are not being used by the Israeli defence ministry in Gaza. The reply is entirely mockery of the Greens ('lost in space', 'one giant leap') and the observation that the satellite is already in orbit. No assurance is given, none is refused — the question is simply never engaged.
question: Can the Minister assure Kiwis that payloads launched from New Zealand on behalf of BlackSky are not being used by the Israeli defence ministry, in any form, to wage war in Gaza?
statement: Can I just say, very clearly, that the satellite is in the sky. What would the Greens have us do? Bring it back? I mean, the Greens might be lost in space, but the satellite is up there. The simple statement may be one small step for the Greens, but it’s one giant leap for the truth.

explanation: Asked whether it is in New Zealand's national interest to allow such launches. He answers by restating the MBIE advice about no current contract — a denial of the premise rather than a position on the national-interest question. It touches the topic but never reaches what was asked.
question: Is it in New Zealand’s national interest to allow intelligence companies to launch payloads from our shores that may be supporting Israel to wage their illegal war in Gaza?
statement: Again, MBIE advised in December 2023 that BlackSky had previously worked with the Israeli defence ministry. There is no evidence of a current contract.

explanation: Asked whether he views such launches as consistent with international obligations and in the national interest. He quibbles over the word 'link', then defends remote-sensing satellites' civilian uses and notes permit conditions barring data sales to sanctioned/designated entities — an implicit affirmative with justification, but he never states a view on the international-obligations limb directly.
question: Is it the Minister’s view that allowing launches of intelligence satellites for companies that have links to foreign militaries and that may be used to wage illegal wars is consistent with our international obligations and in New Zealand’s national interest?
statement: Well, first of all, when the term “link” is used in the question, a link is like a chain; it’s not a broken chain, and this is what’s being asked by way of a question here. Remote sensing satellites are general purpose satellites used for a wide range of purposes. For example, they help farmers manage crops, scientists monitor climate change, and emergency services respond to floods and fires. Do they suggest we should sacrifice all of that on the basis of suspicion? They are used for a range of security purposes. The Minister also imposes standard conditions on remote sensing payload permits prohibiting the sale of data to any individual or entity that is on New Zealand’s designated terrorist list or subject to sanctions and regulations. Those are the facts.

explanation: Asked why he cannot confirm whether the satellites are complicit in events in Gaza. His 'without one shred of evidence' brushes at an answer, but the bulk is an attack on the member and a demand about where his colleagues were in 2021. The question of why confirmation is unavailable is left unanswered.
question: Why can the Minister not confirm if satellites being launched from New Zealand are complicit in the unfolding genocide in Gaza?
statement: That member got all the way to that question, by way of conclusion, without one shred of evidence. The next question is: where were his colleagues in 2021? Where were you in 2021? I know. They were shouting out and making no sense, just like now.

explanation: Asked what announcements she has made on learning support. She names the announcement — learning support coordinators allocated to every school with year 1–8 students over three years — and what those staff will do. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What announcements has she made about strengthening learning support?
statement: Budget 2025 delivered the largest boost to learning support in a generation. Last week, I announced the allocation of learning support coordinators (LSCs) to every school with year 1 to 8 students over the next three years, so 101,000 additional year 1 to 8 students and their teachers will benefit from the skills and support of a learning support coordinator working in their school next year. These dedicated staff members will be trained in structured literacy, structured maths, and to screen for common neurodiverse needs like dyslexia and put strategies in place to give parents confidence and reassurance their child’s needs are being met. We’re working to raise achievement and provide support on the front line. Parents, teachers, and principals have been crying out for this support, and we’ve listened and delivered.

explanation: Asked when schools can expect to benefit. She gives the roll-out dates directly: 60 percent by 2026, 80 percent in 2027, 100 percent by 2028. Complete answer to the 'when'.
question: When can schools expect to benefit from a learning support coordinator?
statement: When learning support coordinator roles were previously announced in 2019, only a single tranche of funding was provided. This left significant inequities whereby some regions only had 18 percent coverage of their students supported by a learning support coordinator. Our fully funded roll-out will span three years. By 2026, we’ll reach at least 60 percent of all students across the country, rising to 80 percent in 2027, reaching 100 percent by 2028. In total, nearly 300,000 students in 1,131 schools will benefit from these changes. Parents can be confident that we are aspirational for their kids and are delivering more support to put their child’s needs at the centre of the education system.

explanation: Asked how the announcement is tailored to small, rural and isolated schools. She answers with the tailoring mechanism — combining part-time staffing entitlements across intervention and LSC roles, work with the rural and isolated schools association, guidance for boards and families. Some drift into general roll-out material at the end.
question: How has this announcement been tailored to support small, rural, and isolated schools?
statement: We’ve thought very carefully about flexible support for rural and smaller schools, where staffing challenges have persisted for too long, working with the rural and isolated schools association. Schools will be able to choose to combine their part-time staffing entitlements across intervention and LSC roles, making it easier to recruit and manage resources in their communities. School boards and principals will receive information that will include operational guidance, where to find employment support and advisory services, and time lines of roll-outs and phases and key dates. Guidance for families will also be available so everyone knows what to expect from this expanded support. Planning is also under way to deliver professional learning and development in literacy and numeracy, as well as that dyslexia screening. This is a Government that backs our rural and small schools.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has received. She states it has been overwhelmingly positive and quotes three principals/education leaders. Exactly the question that was asked.
question: What feedback has she received on these announcements?
statement: It’s been overwhelmingly positive. A number of principals have reached out to express their support. I note one who said, “Thank you, Erica, for consistently investing in on-the-ground support.” Another principal said, “Great initiative; 100 percent agree with this approach.” Another education leader emailed me to say, “I’m really excited to see this issue finally being addressed. It’s been a bit of a festering sore for many years, and it’s great to see the allocation being done in a way to account for those small, isolated rural schools that are often disadvantaged.”

explanation: Two-part question: does he agree, and if so why. The answer states plainly that he supports the Prime Minister — the first part is answered directly and unambiguously — but the 'why' is left entirely unaddressed.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister, who claimed, in reference to emergency housing, that “we’ve fixed it”; if so, why?
statement: E te Māngai o te Whare, āna, tautoko au i te Pirīmia.

explanation: Asked whether emergency housing is fixed given providers' 'worst in living memory' claim. The reply offers a comparative statistic about the housing register, which gestures at the topic and implies improvement, but never answers 'is it fixed' and never engages the providers' evidence.
question: Is emergency housing fixed when front-line providers are telling the Government that homelessness is now “The worst it’s been in living memory.”?
statement: What I can say is this: when we came into office, there were more people on the housing register in cars than there were last month.

explanation: Asked whether it is fixed given the City Missioner's attribution of rising numbers to emergency housing policy. The answer squarely contests that attribution, citing the Homelessness Insights Report on multiple causes — it engages the core premise — but never reaches the actual yes/no of whether the problem is fixed.
question: Is emergency housing fixed, when Auckland City Missioner Helen Robinson said, “I am very, very clear that the current emergency housing policies have a direct impact on these numbers going up.”?
statement: We might recall in this House the Homelessness Insights Report, which members opposite have relied on for the last four weeks, and, in that report, it states officially that attributing any increase in the number of people living without shelter to gateway changes for emergency housing is inappropriate because there are a lot of contributors, fathers and mothers, to people living without shelter—whether or not that’s meth use, drug or alcohol use, economic and social contexts, or, indeed, broken relationships. We’re not about that, and that’s why we support stronger whānau and stronger communities, not herding people like sheep into Ulster Street.

explanation: Asked whether it is fixed given a provider's statement that MSD housing support is not in fact available. The reply attacks the questioner for selective quoting and lists other providers who praise the Government; the specific claim that support is unavailable is never addressed, nor is the question answered.
question: Is emergency housing fixed, when Jill Hawkey from Christchurch Methodist Mission said, “Chris Bishop said in an interview that if people are homeless they could go to the Ministry of Social Development and housing support would be available to them. We know that’s not true.”?
statement: The selective use of quotes by the member opposite reveals his palpable anxiety around the success that this Government has delivered around emergency housing. We know that people like Murray Eldridge from the Wellington City Mission, or Paul Gilberd and my whanaunga Ali Hamlin-Paenga from the community housing associations, or Julie Nelson from The People’s Project, or, indeed, Barbara Brown from Kāhui Tū Kaha have all said that the recent decisions made by Minister Bishop and myself around taking action to address some of those living without shelter are very good. The best decision that we made was getting all those kids out of hotels.

explanation: Asked about more Auckland applications declined than approved. The answer directly disputes that factual premise — most applicants are granted, most declines receive some support — which engages the substance head-on, though it closes with a jab and never states whether the system is 'fixed'.
question: Is emergency housing fixed, when, earlier this year, there were more emergency applications declined in Auckland than there were approved?
statement: The stats and the data reveal that most people who apply for emergency housing are granted emergency housing, and most of the declines are actually granted some sort of support. But I’m sure that members opposite would like to elide around the data and truth.

explanation: Asked how much evidence it would take for him to admit his policies caused the increase. The reply pivots to hearsay-versus-facts framing and a target-achievement boast; it amounts to an implicit refusal to concede, but never engages the question of what evidence would change his position.
question: How much evidence from front-line providers will it take for the Minister to finally admit that it’s his policies that have led to an unprecedented increase of people sleeping on the street?
statement: There are members in this House that rely on hearsay, and there are others that actually go and find out the facts. We are absolutely energised and enthused by reaching the target that was set—target No. 8—to reduce the number of households in emergency housing by 75 percent in six years and achieving that in 12 months. Whilst others rely on outbursts, we rely on outcomes. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what announcement he had made about Watts Peninsula. He states the announcement directly: a reserve on the northern tip, via a 72-hectare LINZ-to-DOC transfer. Complete.
question: What announcement has he made, if any, about the future of Watts Peninsula—Mātai Moana?
statement: In 2011, the then Government announced that Watts Peninsula would be protected as a public reserve for the people of Wellington and all New Zealanders. Today, I was pleased to announce, alongside my good friend and colleague Mr Tama Potaka as Minister of Conservation, that a reserve will finally be created on the northern tip of the Miramar Peninsula. This will be made possible by the transfer of 72 hectares of land from Land Information New Zealand to the Department of Conservation (DOC) and through the joint efforts of Wellington City Council and Taranaki Whānui.

explanation: Asked why the reserve is being established. The answer gives the reasons — cultural and military heritage significance, public advocacy — squarely responsive.
question: Why is the Government establishing a reserve of Watts Peninsula?
statement: Watts Peninsula holds deep significance for Taranaki Whānui, iwi Māori, and many Pākehā New Zealanders as well. It’s home to important pā sites; wāhi tapu; and military heritage from the 1880s through to World War II and beyond, including Fort Ballance. The public has clearly voiced that it values protecting this special whenua, and I thank everyone who advocated for today’s outcome, including members in this House, former mayors of Wellington—including extensively Mr Andy Foster—and the local member of Parliament.

explanation: Asked how the reserve will be managed. Answered directly: a charitable trust with trustees from the council, Taranaki Whānui and DOC, funded by the council and the settlement trust.
question: How will the Watts Peninsula reserve be managed?
statement: The reserve will be managed by a charitable trust, with trustees appointed by Wellington City Council, Taranaki Whānui, and the Department of Conservation. I again acknowledge DOC and the responsible Minister, Mr Potaka, as Land Information passes the baton for this important work to progress. Funding for the reserve’s ongoing care and maintenance will come from Wellington City Council and Taranaki Whānui through the Port Nicholson Block Settlement Trust. Creating the reserve will generate a great opportunity to preserve and enhance and protect this important piece of land.

explanation: Asked what the benefit of establishing the reserve is. The answer names benefits — access for New Zealanders and visitors, protection of flora and fauna, ecological/historical/cultural preservation — with some celebratory padding, but the question is engaged.
question: What is the benefit of establishing Watts Peninsula reserve?
statement: The benefit will be felt by all New Zealanders and overseas visitors while protecting our beautiful indigenous flora and fauna. The trust will have an important role to preserve and promote the reserve as an ecological, historical, and cultural place of importance for everyone to access. I know that I speak for myself as well as the Minister of Conservation when I say how excited we are to celebrate the official opening of the reserve once it’s ready for public access. The decision announced today will safeguard a treasured part of Wellington and its rich history for future generations to enjoy.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the expectation, and what is he doing on cost of living. He answers the first with an unambiguous yes and then lists actions (tax relief, threshold changes, in-work tax credit). The second part drifts to general government policy rather than his own portfolio actions, but both parts are engaged.
question: Does he stand by his expectation of “prioritisation and utilisation of the Commission’s full regulatory and enforcement tool kit to achieve real impacts for consumers”; if so, what is he doing to make the cost of living more affordable for New Zealand consumers?
statement: Yes, I stand by my expectation. On this side of the House, we are absolutely committed to reducing the cost of living for New Zealand consumers. We’re doing that with a range of things including, for instance, tax relief that benefited millions of New Zealand households, changes to the income tax thresholds, the in-work tax credit, and other measures that made around 1.9 million New Zealand households better off.

explanation: Asked what specific steps he had taken on misleading pricing and fake specials. He points to three bills before the Finance and Expenditure Committee — a concrete, on-point action — though he does not identify them or connect them to the pricing issue, and adds an invitation to support them.
question: What specific steps has he taken to stop misleading pricing and fake specials that would deliver real cost of living relief to Kiwi consumers, especially the staggering 62 percent of New Zealanders who have noticed pricing inaccuracies recently?
statement: There are currently three pieces of legislation I have before the Finance and Expenditure Committee. I invite the member and her party to support those pieces of legislation.

explanation: Asked for specific steps on food prices; answer refers back to the primary answer and offers only "a range of things"/"a range of measures, including legislative steps" plus a jab inviting Labour to support them. It gestures at the topic but never names a step, which is precisely what was asked for.
question: What specific steps has he taken to help Kiwi consumers who are paying $10,000 more in a year to feed a family of four here than in Australia?
statement: As I said in the answer to the primary question, there are a range of things that this Government is doing. The portfolio that I have responsibility for is taking a range of measures, including legislative steps that the member’s party is most welcome to support if they choose.

explanation: Asked what specific steps he has taken on insurance costs; he names a forthcoming action — amendments to the Commerce Act coming to the House. That engages the question with an identified measure, though it answers about a future step rather than steps already taken and gives no link to insurance pricing.
question: What specific steps has he taken to help Kiwi consumers with the cost of insurance when house insurance prices are up 9.1 percent and contents insurance prices have risen 10.3 percent?
statement: The member doesn’t have to wait too long before some amendments to the Commerce Act come into this House for debate and consideration. I know that she will be looking forward to them as much as I am.

explanation: Asked what specific steps he has taken for a consumer facing 10% power and 20% insurance rises; the reply is entirely about an interjection on the oil and gas ban. The question is never engaged at any level.
question: What specific steps has he taken to help the Kiwi consumer, a mother, who said, “When I compared my power bills from May to July this year with last year, they’d gone up about 10 percent and my insurance renewal was around 20 percent higher across my policies”?
statement: I hear an interjection about repealing the oil and gas ban—

explanation: Asked whether tax cuts for landlords, tobacco and tech firms are the real reason for the cost of living; answered "No" — a direct, complete response to a yes/no question. The added invitation to reflect on her party's record is a rider, not a substitute for the answer.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Is the real reason the cost of living in New Zealand is so unaffordable is because this Government prioritised a $3 billion tax cut for landlords, a $300 million tax cut for tobacco companies, and half a billion dollars in tax rates for multi-national tech companies like Google and Facebook, rather than taking any action for Kiwi consumers who are falling behind?
statement: No, and I invite the member to reflect upon the role that her party had over the last six years.

explanation: Asked whether Cabinet has considered the Frontier Economics review and, if so, whether the response involves intervention; answered "No" to the antecedent, which disposes of the conditional second limb, and stated a response will come in due course. Direct on the question actually posed.
question: Has Cabinet considered the recommendations of the Frontier Economics review of the electricity market; if so, will the recommendations involve Government intervention in the electricity market?
statement: No. The Government will make announcements on the Frontier report and the Government’s response to it when it has been fully considered, and in due course.

explanation: Asked which of two ministers was right; he picks — "Both are, obviously, right" — and reconciles them by explaining the surgical-intervention framing. The paramedic quip is decoration on an answer already given.
question: Who was right: the Associate Minister for Energy, who said, in relation to the energy sector, that “Now is the time for urgency and bold ideas.”; or the Minister for Energy, who said, “small, surgical interventions will make a big difference and drive real results for Kiwi households and businesses”?
statement: Both are, obviously, right. The context which I noted was that we would be looking to make surgical interventions into the energy market. What I failed to note is I’m also a registered paramedic.

explanation: Asked for a commitment that reform will lower bills, and if not, why not. He neither commits nor explains why not; he defers to a future announcement and restates security and affordability as priorities. That touches the subject matter of the commitment without ever giving or refusing it.
question: Can he commit that any reform of the electricity market will deliver lower energy bills for households, businesses, and industry; and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, as I noted in the response to my primary answer, the Government will announce its response to the energy market review in due course. However, my main priority as Minister for Energy is to ensure that we have both energy security and energy affordability, and I expect the recommendations that we will be making will deal with both of those aspects.

explanation: Asked whether he will consider renationalising the gentailers or sides with the Deputy PM; he tells the member to be patient and repeats that the response comes in due course. It is a deferral rather than an answer or an explicit refusal to answer — neither limb of the alternative is addressed.
question: Will he consider the renationalisation of the gentailers, as proposed by his associate energy Minister; or does he agree with the Deputy Prime Minister, who said this would damage investor confidence?
statement: The member is just going to need to be patient. As I said, the Government will announce its response to the energy market review in due course.

explanation: Asked whether public disagreement among ministers gives the sector confidence; he rejects the premise, which is a real engagement (an implicit denial that they are at odds), but then moves to commitments and blame for prior Governments without answering the confidence question itself.
question: Does he think that it gives the energy sector confidence when the energy Minister, the Deputy Prime Minister, and the associate energy Minister all appear to be publicly at odds over the best way to move forward on electricity market reform?
statement: I don’t agree with the premise of that question. What is clear is that, on this side of the House, we are committed to ensuring New Zealand has energy security and we have affordable energy for New Zealanders. The reality of what we are dealing with is a result of decisions made by prior Governments that have put us in this position, and we will not stand by and not take the necessary action to get us back on track.

explanation: Asked whether the Government will implement sanctions per UN resolution 10/24; answered "We already have" and set out exactly which sanctions — travel bans on two Ministers and 35 settlers. Squarely and completely responsive.
question: Will the Government implement sanctions against Israel for its unlawful occupation of the Palestinian Territory as called for by UN resolution 10/24, which New Zealand voted for?
statement: We already have. The resolution called on States to implement sanctions, including travel bans, against people engaged in illegal and violent settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territory. That is precisely what we have done. Over the past 18 months, the New Zealand Government has imposed travel bans on two Israeli Ministers as well as 35 extremist settlers. We’ve made it clear that these people are not welcome in New Zealand, because they have actively undermined the two-State solution by illegally settling in the West Bank, perpetrated or advocated violence, and displaced Palestinian civilians from their homes.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts the ICJ finding on apartheid; he replies that this is a misinterpretation of the Court's finding, which directly engages and effectively answers in the negative. Slightly short of an explicit accept/not-accept, but the core is met head-on rather than sidestepped.
question: Does he accept the International Court of Justice finding that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank is in breach of the provision on apartheid in the convention on the elimination of racial discrimination?
statement: That is a misinterpretation of the International Court’s finding.

explanation: Asked why NZ has not yet recognised Palestine. Peters does supply a reason — the Government decides carefully after hearing all evidence, and will have that chance in New York — so the 'why' is engaged, but much of the answer is a comparative boast about NZ democracy versus Australia's rather than the substantive reason for the delay. Core reached, partially.
question: Why is New Zealand yet to join Australia, our only formal international ally, in recognising Palestine as a State?
statement: Because we are a very proud democracy with advances in the democratic system way beyond Australia’s, going back two centuries, and we make our own decisions carefully and quietly after we have heard all the evidence, which we will have the best chance to have when we get to New York. Only fools test the water with both feet.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the UN that Palestinians have an inalienable right to self-determination. He says it is a pronouncement the Government has always agreed with — an unambiguous yes to exactly what was asked.
question: Does he agree with the United Nations that Palestinian people have a right to self-determination—an inalienable right that cannot be subject to conditions of the occupying powers?
statement: That is a pronouncement from the United Nations that we have always agreed with.

explanation: Asked what his message to the Harbour Bridge marchers is. He gives one: the march would be a wasted blockage of transport and time. The trailing swipe about 'virtue signalling' is extra, but the message asked for was actually delivered.
question: What is his message to the thousands of people expected to march across the Auckland Harbour Bridge on Saturday in protest of this Government’s unwillingness to speak out against the unfolding genocide in Gaza?
statement: Well, that’d be a totally wasted blockage of people’s transport and time on Saturday, if that is what the purpose of the march is. However, I know they have a penchant for display rather than any hard, serious work, whereas this Government has found enormous amounts of funds for the Palestinian people and made every effort we can to help through other organisations as well, like the Red Cross, rather than just all talk and virtue signalling.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made on supermarket competition. She names the announcement — removing barriers to entry, creating an express lane for new supermarkets. Directly responsive.
question: What recent announcements has she made on supermarket competition?
statement: I recently announced steps to remove barriers that prevent competitor supermarkets from launching or expanding here. Among these changes is the creation of an express lane for new supermarkets, to boost competition and deliver better deals for Kiwi shoppers. This is just one of many things the Government is doing to address the lack of competition in our grocery market. This is good news for Kiwi shoppers, who are paying higher prices and have less choice than they would have if there was more competition.

explanation: Asked what the express lane is. She explains what it consists of: Fast-track Approvals Act amendment, a single building consent authority, MultiProof plans. The question is answered completely.
question: What is the express lane for new supermarkets?
statement: The express lane addresses widespread frustration with restrictive zoning, slow consenting, and cumbersome regulations that prevent potential competitors from opening the doors of a new supermarket. As part of the express lane, legislation will soon be introduced to amend the Fast-track Approvals Act, to make it clear that new supermarkets that would improve grocery competition will qualify as fast-track referrable projects, and I urge members of this House who want a better deal for shoppers to support that legislation. Building consenting processes for new supermarkets will also be streamlined by selecting a single building consent authority to standardise decisions for grocery developments, and Building Act regulations will be amended to allow pre-approved, MultiProof building plans for multiple grocery developments.

explanation: Asked what else the Government is doing. She lists further workstreams — Overseas Investment Act, guidance, Commerce Act predatory pricing, food importation options. Squarely on the question.
question: What else is the Government doing for supermarket competition?
statement: The Government’s focus is on regulatory, enforcement, and structural areas. The Overseas Investment Act is being improved, and new guidance has been published to support grocery investments. The Commerce Act will be amended to better combat predatory pricing, and we are actively looking at options around the importation of food into the country. The Government is determined to enable stronger competition in the supermarket sector. Potential competitors have told us that the changes we are making will help them to do that. For example, Costco has confirmed that the express lane will assist with their future expansion plans, which is great news for shoppers.

explanation: Asked what structural work is under way. She answers: a commissioned cost-benefit analysis on options for restructuring the duopoly, plus openness to market-led solutions. The specific structural work is named.
question: What structural work is under way?
statement: Some responses to our request for information argued that the only way to truly improve supermarket competition is for the Government to forcibly break up Foodstuffs and/or Woolworths, because they hold entrenched market positions and market power. That would be a significant intervention, with costs and risks that need to be rigorously weighed against the potential benefits to shoppers. The Government has commissioned a cost-benefit analysis on specific options for restructuring the duopoly. We also remain open to potential market-led solutions that may be put forward by the major incumbents.

explanation: Asked whether he was involved in the collective agreement negotiations and if so how. Answers 'no, I have not been involved', then volunteers the related letters he wrote. Both limbs addressed.
question: Has he been involved in collective agreement negotiations with doctors and nurses; if so, how?
statement: on behalf of the Minister of Health: On behalf of the Minister of Health—and a very good guy he is—no, I have not been involved. However, I have written to two of the parties in the senior doctors’ negotiations after they had had meditation—sorry, mediation; although meditation might help at this point—facilitated bargaining, and an Employment Relations Authority recommendation, suggesting that they might like to go to binding arbitration.

explanation: Two-part question: why he intervened, and whether it delayed a settlement. He gives a reason (prior processes had failed, patients missing procedures, so he proposed arbitration) and answers the second limb explicitly: 'No, I don't believe it has.' Both parts reached.
question: Why did he directly intervene in senior doctors’ bargaining to argue for binding arbitration, and has his intervention delayed a settlement?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question: as I just said, mediation, facilitated bargaining, and a recommendation by the Employment Relation Authority and still no agreement and still patients missing out on procedures that they desperately need. In that circumstance, I decided to propose a better solution so that they could get back in the operating theatres and back in the clinics and the hospitals to serve the patients. Has that delayed the progress? No, I don’t believe it has.

explanation: Asked why he agreed to the Order in Council changing employer responsibilities and the bargaining team, and whether that could have delayed settlement. The 'why' is answered only at the level of generic motivation ('improve outcomes for patients', '$2 billion more'), never touching the Order in Council itself, and the delay limb is not addressed at all. Mostly a pivot to spending talking points.
question: Why did he agree to an Order in Council changing employer responsibilities and the bargaining team during the New Zealand Nurses Organisation bargaining, and could this action have delayed a settlement?
statement: First of all, I did it because my underlying driver—this is on behalf of the Minister of Health—in everything I do is to improve outcomes for patients, because, for too long, too much money has been poured in for the results that we’ve got. We need to ensure that when we put more taxpayer money into healthcare—as this Government has: $2 billion more than when we were elected to now; $2 billion more—we need to make sure we’re getting results for that. I responded to the circumstances, motivated by care for the patients.

explanation: Asked whether he or his office directed Health NZ to withhold information. He states plainly that he is not in a position to answer, explaining that only the substantive Minister would know, and adds his belief that it is unlikely. A stated inability to answer, given directly, is engagement rather than a dodge — but the question itself is left unresolved.
question: Did he or his office direct Health New Zealand to withhold official information related to safe staffing levels sought by the nurse’s union in relation to their pay claim?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, I am not in a position to address that question. That is a question about a specific action that would only be known by the Minister. However, based on everything that I know of Simeon Brown, that sounds very unlikely.

explanation: Two-part question: why the sign was displayed, and whether he accepts it made settlement less likely. He contests 'provocative', offers a rationale (alerting people to patient welfare is the Minister's core job), and rejects the delay proposition as 'absurd' — effectively a no. Both limbs are engaged, though the second is answered by ridicule of the premise rather than reasoning.
question: Why did he display a provocative sign in his parliamentary office to striking nurses, and does he accept that that behaviour would make a settlement less likely?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, it is the member’s characterisation that it was provocative. However, I would say that alerting people to the welfare of patients is actually the core job of the Minister of Health. When I hear that that could somehow delay a settlement, let’s just consider for a moment what this Labour member is suggesting. They’re suggesting that because the Minister of Health put a sign advocating for the rights of patients on his own electorate office door, nurses would strike for longer and deny patients more care. I mean, I think the public can make up their mind for themselves. That’s an absurd proposition from the Labour Party.

explanation: Asked what recent announcement she made on the secondary school curriculum; she states directly that she announced the senior secondary subject list today and describes its scope. Squarely on the question.
question: What recent announcement has she made on the secondary school curriculum?
statement: Today, I announced the senior secondary subject list, for years 11 to 13 students, in both the New Zealand Curriculum and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa. We have introduced dynamic, innovative new subjects that will engage and inspire learners as part of what we are continuing to focus on, which is raising achievement and closing the equity gap. These new subjects will be phased in from 2028, starting with year 11, to create a modern curriculum which recognises the growing importance of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) subjects, as well as other relevant learning areas. To give students more choice, we’re also introducing new strengthened, industry-led subjects which will be tertiary aligned so students are best prepared for future study, training, and employment.

explanation: Asked what some of the new subjects are; she names a list of them across both curricula. Direct and complete.
question: What are some of the new subjects?
statement: Well, we’re introducing a range of exciting new subjects across the curriculum. In the area of STEM, students will be able to take subjects like further maths, statistics and data science, and electronics and mechatronics. We’re also introducing music technology; civics, politics, and philosophy; media, journalism, and communications; Pacific studies; and te mātai i te ao Māori. In Te Marautanga, we’ve created nine new subject areas, including tātai arorangi, te ao Māori, and te ao whakairo, as well as—for the first time ever—curriculum provision in te reo Māori at years 12 and 13, right across the subject areas, which should have been done much earlier. Thank you to Rawiri Wright, from Te Rūnanga Nui, for advocating for the inclusion of te ao Māori.

explanation: Asked what some of the new industry-led subjects are; she enumerates them (primary industry, automotive engineering, building and construction, etc.). Directly answered.
question: What are some of the new industry-led subjects?
statement: Well, to engage students through more choice, we’re also introducing new strengthened, industry-led subjects. Whether a young person wants to be a master builder, an automotive engineer, a teacher, or a lawyer, the curriculum should set them up for success, not split them into separate lanes. These subjects include primary industry, health and wellbeing services, outdoor education, automotive engineering, building and construction, infrastructure engineering, mechanical engineering, tourism and hospitality, and more. We are proposing an integrated system where all subjects, whether they’re ministry-led or industry-led, are equal in status, and these subjects will be industry-led and tertiary aligned. Excitingly, students taking these industry-led subjects will likely exit high school with both a secondary qualification and a tertiary qualification at level 2 or 3.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has seen; she reports a teacher's remark and a BusinessNZ comment. Answers the question, with a short pivot back to messaging at the end.
question: What feedback has she seen on the announcement?
statement: One teacher remarked that it’s great to see philosophy as a subject, stating that, previously, they had to piece together unrelated standards from other subjects to try and offer it. BusinessNZ CEO, Katherine Rich, said the inclusion of future-focused subject areas in NCEA reform is a positive step forward, preparing New Zealanders for a rapidly changing world of work. We want our students to have access to innovative, dynamic subjects that give every student the skills and confidence to thrive in their chosen field.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her comments and why; she says she stands by them and gives her reasoning (merit-based appointments, respect for independence, balance of experience). Both limbs engaged, with a mild qualifier about clarity.
question: Does she stand by her comments about the new appointments to the Employment Relations Authority; if so, why?
statement: I stand by my comments, in the context in which they were made—though I accept that my statements could have been clearer—that I make my appointments based on merit and I respect the independence of the authority. In particular, I stand by my comment that I’m really pleased with the progress we’re making to better balance a mix of public and private experience among members to better reflect New Zealand’s employment landscape.

explanation: Asked whether it is appropriate for a Minister to influence the judiciary; answered 'No.' One word, complete.
question: Does she think it is appropriate for a Government Minister to try and influence the judiciary?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether businesses' bottom lines matter more than working people's right to awards; answered 'No.' Direct.
question: Does she believe that businesses’ bottom lines matter more than working people’s right to awards?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether she was warned prior to her BusinessDesk comments; answered 'No.' A flat factual answer to a narrow factual question.
question: Was she warned, prior to making her comments to BusinessDesk, that they could be seen as politicising the judiciary?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether she accepted the Auditor-General's advice and, if so, whether she will desist. She responds to the premise by saying she does not believe the Auditor-General has reached out to her, which engages the first limb by denial but leaves the conditional undertaking unaddressed.
question: Has she accepted the advice from the Auditor-General of the need for “careful use of language when speaking of the judiciary”; and, if so, will she desist from similar comments in the future?
statement: I don’t believe the Auditor-General has reached out to me.

explanation: Standard 'does she stand by all her statements and actions'; answered 'Yes', with the usual context qualifier. Direct.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context they were given.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by a specific quoted statement; she says yes and restates her involvement in the process. Directly answered.
question: Does she stand by her statement from Tuesday, 9 September, in response to whether she sees her role in the fast-track process as advocating for the environment, that “Yes, I do get opportunity; I do bring environmental matters in my comments to the Minister,”?
statement: Yes, there is a legal process, and I am involved in that legal process in giving comments—yes.

explanation: Two limbs asked: why her only public comments say she is declining to comment, and whether she regards that as advocating for the environment. She explains the first via publication timing and asserts she has made comments, but never addresses whether this constitutes environmental advocacy.
question: Why, then, do her only publicly available comments on fast-track applications state that she is choosing not to provide any comment; and does she consider this as advocating for the environment?
statement: The timing of the information that goes up will dictate when my comments are put on to the application, but I can assure the member that I have made comments.

explanation: Asked what her comments were on the Waihi North fast-track application given DOC's warning. She does not state any comments but explains her practice — she does not re-comment where other entities (DOC, local authorities) have already commented — which functions as an implicit 'I made none, and here is why'. It engages the question's core without ever stating plainly that she made no comment, so partial rather than complete.
question: What were her comments, then, on Waihi North’s silver and gold mining open-pit and underground mine extension from OceanaGold, where the Department of Conservation warned in their comments that the project could cause “irreversible harm to high-value conservation areas and species.”?
statement: Well, as I’ve said, the comments come up as the application is made public, and where comments are being made by other entities such as local authorities, the Department of Conservation, or other departments, I don’t go and re-comment the sorts of comments they are making.

explanation: Asked how New Zealanders can be assured the fast-track process won't let developers sidestep environmental protections. The answer only restates that she comments 'where comments are necessary' — a rebuttal of the premise of silence, not any account of assurance. The question asked is never reached.
question: How, then, can New Zealanders be assured that the fast-track process won’t see developers sidestepping critical environmental protections, when she chooses to be silent on even her basic responsibility as the Minister for the Environment to advocate for the environment?
statement: As I have said, where comments are necessary from me, I make comments that are relevant to those applications.

explanation: A direct yes/no commitment question about advocating for the 16 water conservation orders. The answer neither commits nor declines: it says work is under way in the RMA replacement context and no decisions have been made. It gestures at the subject matter but explicitly leaves the commitment unanswered.
question: Will she commit to advocating for the 16 water conservation orders that protect the outstanding and intrinsic values of some of our most valued water bodies—places like the Te Waikoropupū aquifer—so that they might have a chance at retaining some level of protection from fast-track projects?
statement: As the member knows, we are working through water conservation orders and other freshwater matters in the context of what is a very comprehensive replacement regime for the Resource Management Act. No decisions have been made yet, but we are certainly working through these processes.

explanation: Asked what recent reports on tourism she has seen; she names the July international travel statistics released yesterday and cites the arrivals figure. Squarely responsive to what was asked.
question: What recent reports has she seen on tourism in New Zealand?
statement: Yesterday, international travel statistics were released for July. They showed 126,700 overseas visitor arrivals from Australia. This is the highest record month of arrivals of visitors from Australia. These visitors show our “Everyone Must Go” campaign targeting Australians was a huge success. These additional visitors help support local businesses, create more jobs, and strengthen our economy. Tourism is a crucial part of our Government’s Going For Growth agenda.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements will benefit tourism; she identifies the Qantas/Jetstar expansion and its seat numbers. Directly on the question.
question: What recent announcements has she seen that will benefit tourism across New Zealand?
statement: Yesterday, I was delighted to see Qantas and Jetstar announce their biggest expansion plans for their New Zealand and trans-Tasman services. This will add a total of 660,000 seats a year and will bring more supply, which generally means lower prices for flights, and will encourage more Australians to cross the Ditch. This announcement, alongside July’s highest visitor levels of Australians, will be extremely beneficial to achieving our goal to double the value of tourism exports by 2034. This positive announcement shows that creating the right environment and conditions for business to invest in leads to economic growth. I want all airlines to know that they are being welcomed by our Government and we are very open to having more airline capacity into New Zealand.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made in the hunting and fishing portfolio; he names the family fishing licence change and its effect. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has the Minister made in his hunting and fishing portfolio?
statement: During the recess, I was very pleased to announce that from the 2025-26 angling season, which opens on 1 October, both adults on a family fishing licence will be able to now fish independently and have voting rights in Fish & Game elections. This is a common-sense change to modernise a historical anomaly which prevented the second adult on a licence—more often than not a woman—from fishing on their own. This is a really good announcement to encourage more women into fly-fishing. I’d like to thank groups like Women on The Fly New Zealand for advocating for this change for many years, as well as Fish & Game patron Dame Lynda Topp for giving me a few fly-fishing tips on the beautiful mid-Canterbury Rakaia River.

explanation: Asked what other changes anglers can expect for the 2025-26 season; he answers with the confirmed freeze on angling licence prices. Directly responsive.
question: What other changes can anglers expect for the 2025-26 season?
statement: More good news: alongside these common-sense changes to the family licence, I am pleased to officially confirm that there will be no price increases to Fish & Game angling licences for the first time in five seasons. Kiwis are doing it tough, and the last thing they need is another financial burden hitting their wallets when all they’re trying to do is put food on the table for their families.

explanation: Asked how else New Zealanders can get involved in hunting and fishing; he points to the National Wild Goat Hunting Competition as a way to participate. Answers the question, with some padding at the end.
question: How else can New Zealanders get involved in hunting and fishing?
statement: As the House will have heard me say many times before, hunters are one of our best conservation assets. Currently under way is the National Wild Goat Hunting Competition, which is a partnership between the Department of Conservation and the New Zealand Deerstalkers Association. This is a great way for hunters and landowners to reduce the numbers of wild goats, which do serious damage to farms and the natural environment. I’m very pleased to inform the House that I myself have done my part, having taken out three wild goats already, and I’m sure all my fellow conservationists across the House will be taking out a few more old goats before the end of November.

explanation: Asked what immediate action she is taking on 4,000 tamariki held in police cells. She answers the action question head-on — no immediate action was needed because she was already aware — and describes the existing inter-agency process. The 'what are you doing' core is engaged, though the response drifts into justification of the status quo.
question: What immediate action, if any, is she taking in response to reports that there were 4,000 cases of tamariki and young people being held in police cells in the past 12 months, some for up to eight nights?
statement: I’ve not had to take any immediate action based on media reports, because this is something that I was already aware of. Police and Oranga Tamariki and the courts are working closely together to address this. The reality is that when a young person commits a serious crime, they do get arrested and taken into police custody, and then every effort is made to get them in front of the Youth Court so they can be moved to an alternative placement. Just the other week, the Minister visited Counties Manukau Police Station to see for herself where young people are held when they are in custody, and I want to take this opportunity to thank the staff there for their professionalism and their dedication to these young people. I do also think it is important to acknowledge that the safety of the community and of victims must also be of highest priority.

explanation: A narrow factual request for how many of those held over one night were Māori. No number is given, but the reply conveys that ethnicity/whakapapa data of that kind is not compiled by Oranga Tamariki, which is a reason for not confirming rather than a pivot elsewhere. Partial: it addresses why the figure isn't forthcoming without answering the count.
question: Can the Minister confirm how many of those tamariki and young people held in police cells for longer than one night were Māori?
statement: Oranga Tamariki don’t do ancestry.com to figure out exactly what bloodlines people are. What they do do is take those children that have committed crimes and try to keep them in a safe space, and the priority is to make sure that they are kept safe.

explanation: Asked how the Minister is working with Oranga Tamariki to urgently increase viable placement capacity. The answer cites the $33m Budget 2025 investment in youth justice residence facilities and transitional support, and claims it will cut time in police custody — responsive to the capacity element, but it does not address the working-with-Oranga-Tamariki or urgency framing.
question: How is the Minister working with Oranga Tamariki to urgently increase capacity in viable placements, given that the number of cases of tamariki kept in police cells overnight has increased in two years from 42 to 418?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, Budget 2025 saw a $33 million investment in safety and quality improvements to the facilities at youth justice residences, as well as greater investment in transitional support for young serious offenders. I believe this investment will reduce the number of young people being held in police custody for extended periods of time.

explanation: A yes/no question with a stated fallback ('if not, why not') on supporting the Children's Commissioner's call to end detaining tamariki in police cells. The answer reports having discussed it and being 'on the same page' that no one wants young people in custody longer than needed — neither endorsing nor rejecting the call, and giving no reason for declining. The core is left unanswered.
question: Does the Minister support the Children’s Commissioner’s call to end the practice of detaining tamariki in police cells; and, if not, why not?
statement: On behalf of the Minister for Children, I have discussed this matter with the Children’s Commissioner in our regular meetings and on a number of occasions. We are both on the same page, which is that no one wants to see young people spend more time in custody than they need to.

explanation: Asked for specific measures to stop placement shortages being used to justify cells. The answer offers no measure at all — it reframes to children having committed crime and asserts safety is paramount. The core ask (what, specifically, is being done) is never reached.
question: What specific measures, if any, is the Minister taking to prevent placement shortages becoming an excuse for locking children in cells?
statement: On behalf of the Minister for Children, it’s unfortunate that the Government, through their agencies, is having to pick up the pieces when children have gone out there and committed crime. At the end of the day, we want to make sure that they are safe, and that means that when they do go into police custody, it’s because they have committed a serious crime. Their safety will always be paramount when it comes to this Government and their actions with children.

explanation: Asked whether the Minister is committed to introducing safer alternatives including community-based and iwi initiatives. The answer describes existing custody arrangements (daily OT checks, separation from adults, ~48-hour average) and never states a position on alternatives or on the Children's Commissioner's warning. It is adjacent to the topic but does not answer the yes/no commitment asked for.
question: Is the Minister committed to introducing safer alternatives, including community-based and iwi initiatives, to adequately care for these tamariki, following warnings from the Children’s Commissioner that these cells expose tamariki to self-harm risk?
statement: I think what’s really important for everybody to know is that when our children are detained, they are being looked upon. We have Oranga Tamariki go into the cells at least once a day to check on the children and make sure that they’re OK. They are not kept with adults. There is a lot of work that’s being done to ensure the safety of these children. They are in cells because they have committed a crime, and the moment we get a placement for them, they are moved. I believe that it’s around 48 hours that children, on average, are kept—I need to be corrected on that if I’ve got that slightly wrong, on behalf of the Minister. However, what we do know is that in order to keep the children safe and in order to keep victims of our community safe, we will do the best we can by these children and make sure that they are cared for when they are detained.

explanation: A straight 'does she stand by' question answered 'Yes' with a restatement of the position. Complete.
question: Does she stand by her statement that there is “more concern that we need to be focused on around the actual completions of apprentices”?
statement: Yes, it is absolutely important that as many apprentices as possible are completing their apprenticeships.

explanation: Two-part question: has completion decreased since 2023, and by how much. She says 'Yes' to the decrease, so half the question is squarely answered, but the figures supplied run 2019–2022 and no since-2023 magnitude is given. The 'by how much' is left unanswered.
question: Has the completion of apprenticeships decreased again since 2023 under her watch; if so, by how much?
statement: Yes, what has occurred is that there had been a very large intake of apprentices over the 2021-22 period, when Apprenticeship Boost was in full swing. During that time, many of those additional learners withdrew, and we saw a significant decline in credit achievements during that time, going down from 85 percent credit achievements in 2019 to 77 percent in 2020, to 67 percent in 2021, and to 69 percent in 2022. Those large numbers brought about reductions in the completion-of-credit rates, and that is, of course, flowing through.

explanation: Asked whether her cuts made completion rates worse. She does engage the causal question — attributing the decline to the large 2021-22 intake and withdrawals — which functions as an implicit denial, but she never confirms or denies the role of her cuts. Answers the causation question while stepping around the part about her own decisions.
question: Is it correct that her cuts to the vocational education sector have made apprenticeship completion rates worse?
statement: What has impacted on the apprenticeship completion rate—recognising that most apprentices take around three to five years. What is showing the impact is the additional numbers taken in that did not complete sufficient credits, many of whom withdrew.

explanation: Asked what advice she has received on rising NEETs. She confirms advice on NEETs has come 'across a range of areas' — that engages the question — but the content of that advice is replaced with a pivot to youth guarantee places and foundation education. Half-engaged.
question: What advice, if any, has she received on the increased number of young people not engaged in education, employment, or training since 2023?
statement: Across a range of areas, there has been advice on the increase in NEETs—those people under 25 not in employment, education, or training. That is why we are so focused on ensuring that we have additional youth guarantee places which pick up on young people under 25 who have had low prior achievement. It is why we are focused on ensuring that foundation education is available and accessible to those young people.

explanation: Asked how the three declining indicators contribute to securing the workforce New Zealand needs. The answer asserts focus on training and blames the inherited economy for unemployment; it never addresses how the cited declines contribute to workforce needs. A pivot to talking points.
question: How do more young people not in education, employment, or training; fewer enrolments in apprenticeships; and fewer apprenticeship completions contribute to ensuring that New Zealand has the workforce it needs?
statement: We are very focused on ensuring that our young people have access to further training so that they are well prepared to be able to go into employment. There is no doubt that the current financial situation, which we inherited from the previous Government, left us in a situation where we were having to battle high inflation and high interest rates, which has resulted in higher unemployment than any of us would like, but it is equally important that we have sufficient education and training available to ensure those young people are well skilled and well able to enter the workforce as the economy improves.

explanation: Standard 'does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions' answered 'Yes.' One word, complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked what his Government is doing to support the Te Wiki o te Reo theme. He names actions — $142 million to the four Māori language entities and funding te reo teaching resources. That is a direct response to 'what actions'; it slightly under-connects to the specific 'Āke Āke Āke' theme.
question: He aha ngā mahi a tōna Kāwanatanga hei tautoko i te kaupapa o tēnei Wiki o te Reo, “Āke Āke Āke”, kia manawaroa ai, kia arotau ai, kia toitū ai te reo Māori?
statement: Well, I mean, firstly, this is a Government that is spending a huge amount of money—$142 million—with the four Māori language entities. It’s a Government that I am very proud of spending money on teaching resources in te reo, and I’m very proud of that.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned by Te Taura Whiri's warning and, if not, why not. He answers the concern question plainly — 'I totally disagree' — and supplies a reason (spending on bilingual resources). Both limbs are engaged, though he does not address the Education Act warning itself.
question: E māharahara ana ia i te whakatūpato a Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori ki ngā panonitanga a tōna Kāwanatanga o te Ture Mātauranga, arā ka “Undermine the status of te reo Māori as a taonga and as an official language of Aotearoa”, ā, ki te kore, he aha e kore ai?
statement: Well, I totally disagree. This is a Government that is spending money on resources to make sure that they are available in te reo and English.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Te Taura Whiri that elevating English over te reo for non-Māori public entities reduces the language's visibility and everyday use. He never states agreement or disagreement, instead explaining the navigability rationale and census first-language figures. Implicit disagreement at best; the agree/disagree core is skirted.
question: E whakaae ana ia ki tā Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori, arā ko te hāpainga ake o te reo Ingarihi ki runga ake i te reo Māori hei reo kawe kōrero matua mō ngā hinonga tūmatanui ehara i te hinonga Māori, he whakawhāiti kē i te kitea o te reo, he whakawhāiti hoki i te whai wāhi ōna hei reo o ia rā?
statement: If I understand the question correctly, we want to be able to make sure that our Government agencies are navigable by all New Zealanders, and, as a result, having their names in both English and te reo. If you’re a fluent English speaker—of which 95 percent of New Zealanders is their first language in the last census—they can navigate their Government in English; and if you’re a fluent te reo speaker, you can navigate your Government in te reo.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned that the proposed funding cuts to 174 te reo/literacy resource-teacher positions will narrow capacity to teach and support te reo. He answers 'No' outright, which squarely disposes of the question, then adds his reasons; he does not address the 174 positions specifically.
question: Kei te māharahara rānei ia ka whāiti kē atu te āheinga ki te whakaako, ki te tautoko hoki i te reo Māori nā runga i ngā poronga pūtea e marohitia nei, he pūtea mā ngā kaiako rauemi o te reo matatini me te reo Māori mā te 174 tūranga mahi?
statement: No, I’m very proud of the resources being made available in te reo and English, as I’ve said before. I’m more proud of the fact that we’re teaching our kids structured literacy, structured numeracy, encouraging them to get to school so they actually have a greater future—Māori or non-Māori.

explanation: Davidson asks whether he considers the Government's introduction of the Treaty Principles Bill — and its misreading of te reo — to have supported te reo Māori/Māori rights. Luxon replies only that the bill 'has been discussed and resolved', which addresses the bill's procedural status, not the question of whether it supported te reo or Māori rights. A near-total non-answer, though it at least names the bill.
question: I whakaaro rānei ia he hāpai tāna mahi i te reo Māori i te whakaurunga a tōna Kāwanatanga i te Pire Mātāpono Tiriti o Waitangi—me te whakaari anō i tētahi whakamārama hē o te reo Māori hei whakaiwikore i ā te iwi Māori mōtika?
statement: The Treaty principles bill has been discussed and resolved.

explanation: Closed question ('Does he stand by all of his Government's statements and actions?') answered with an unqualified 'Yes.' Complete.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked why he claims cost of living is under control when administered inflation hit 10.8 percent. He does engage the administered component partially — citing rates at 12.5 percent and a rate cap — but never addresses the 10.8 percent figure or justifies the 'under control' claim, substituting headline inflation for the specific measure asked about.
question: Why does he claim to have the cost of living under control, when administered inflation—the component of inflation that Government can most directly influence—hit 10.8 percent last month, the steepest rise in at least 35 years?
statement: Well, I’m very proud of this Government’s focus on reducing inflation. This is a Government that has put inflation back under 3 percent again. There are items like rates running at 12.5 percent. That’s why we support a rate cap, and I encourage that member to support it too.

explanation: Asked to accept that transmission charges, disaster levies and aviation levies are Government decisions driving costs. He explicitly answers only 'the first part' — rebutting on energy by blaming the oil and gas ban — and leaves insurance, airfares and the overall proposition untouched. Partial engagement with one limb of a multi-limb question.
question: Does he accept that the Government’s decision to increase transmission charges is driving up power bills, its decision to increase natural disaster levies is driving up insurance premiums, its decision to hike civil aviation levies is driving up the price of airfares, and that increased Government charges are now one of the biggest contributors to the cost of living pressure that Kiwi families are facing?
statement: In light of the first part of that question, I’d say to the member that the energy prices are a function of his administration’s banning of oil and gas and the fact that we do not have a supply of gas in this country, which has led to elevated electricity prices. Again, I would say to that member: think about the position, and support reversing the oil and gas ban.

explanation: A binary question — did the public transport funding cut increase or decrease cost of living pressure? He never says either; he pivots entirely to FamilyBoost, tax relief and rental stability. The word 'transport' does not appear in the reply.
question: Did his Government’s decision to cut funding for public transport, forcing some commuters and families to pay up to 50 percent more just to get to work or school, increase or decrease the cost of living pressure that Kiwi families currently face?
statement: Well, I can say to the member: what is helping those families deal with the cost of living is our expanded role for FamilyBoost. What is helping and supporting those families in a cost of living crisis is the tax relief that we have offered them. What is supporting them is, actually, rental stability—that is a good thing—and also making sure that we give people tax, inflation, and interest rate relief, which is what this Government is delivering.

explanation: Asked whether he has found one single family receiving the full $250 a fortnight. He thanks the questioner and describes expanded thresholds and 22,000 more families, but never says whether any family has received the full amount — the specific fact requested is simply never approached.
question: Speaking of FamilyBoost, has he found one single family that has received the full $250 a fortnight that he promised Kiwi families with kids during the last election campaign?
statement: Well, look, I want to thank the member for his question, because I really do appreciate answering this and bringing the attention of all New Zealanders who may be watching this to the fact that FamilyBoost rebates have been expanded, the thresholds have been extended, and, as a result, there is even more money. Actually, for the last 13 weeks, you can now access and get more support from this Government, which is absolutely fantastic. We think, actually, another 22,000 families will receive some support, and isn’t that a great thing?

explanation: Another explicit increase-or-decrease question, this time on the $50 registration fee rise. The answer never mentions registration fees at all and recites comparative inflation, interest rate and rent talking points. A clean dodge of a narrow question.
question: Did his Government’s decision to increase car registration fees by $50 increase or decrease the cost of living pressure that Kiwi families are currently facing?
statement: Well, again, I’d just say to the member that we are proud of the fact that we have lowered inflation. In this Government, yes, we have food inflation running at 5 percent, but that’s a lot lower than 12.5 percent under his Government. You know, 2.7 percent inflation is lower than 7.5 percent under his Government. Interest rates have been cut multiple times. Rents are stable. This is a Government that is focused on economic growth. Why? So that we can get New Zealanders getting more money in their back pocket, and that’s how they get ahead.

explanation: Asked why food prices keep rising if inflation is under control. He does supply an answer to the 'why': elevated red meat and dairy prices driven by global commodity prices, plus food inflation now at 5 percent, and points to fast-tracking supermarket entrants. The comparative jabs are padding, but the core question is engaged with a reason.
question: If his Government has inflation under control, as he is now claiming, why is the price of food continuing to increase, with statistics released today showing butter is up 32 percent, milk is up by almost $1, and the price of mince is now $22 a kilo, all under his leadership?
statement: Well, I’d just remind the member that when he was Prime Minister, food inflation hit 12.5 percent. It is 5 percent today. Yes, we have elevated prices for red meat and for dairy products. That’s due to global commodity prices, and that’s why our farmers are having record years and record levels of farmer confidence in this country. This is a Government that is focused on lowering inflation, and I’d just say to the member that that’s why you’ve seen us fast track supermarket entrants so that we can actually do everything we can to make it as easy as possible to open up the supermarket sector. But, again, the answer is not to increase the inflation target and increase prices for Kiwis, as his finance spokesperson has suggested.

explanation: Asked whether the Government plans a 12c petrol tax rise. He answers directly — no discussions about increasing fuel taxes at this time — before pivoting to inflation and growth lines. The qualifier 'at this time' is hedging at the margin, but the question is squarely met.
question: Does the Government plan to increase petrol taxes by 12c a litre?
statement: The Government has had no discussions about increasing fuel taxes at this time, but what we are very focused on is lowering inflation and making sure we lower interest rates, we get our economy growing, and we lower unemployment.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen regarding the West Coast. He recounts his Reefton visit, the mining history and the opening of new worker accommodation. It reports on the West Coast rather than citing a report as such, but it responds on the subject asked about.
question: What reports has he seen regarding the West Coast?
statement: Last Friday, I had the privilege of being in Reefton, down on the West Coast—otherwise known as “Mining-opolis”—where, previously, there were over 59 mines. I had the pleasure, along with the district council and the local development corporation, of opening new accommodation to cope with the flood of employees that are coming to the West Coast to fulfil a famous saying of this party that I belong to: “Dig, baby, dig.”

explanation: Asked what else he can say about West Coast economic development. He answers with mining driving the region, rising investment confidence, money flowing and a pipeline of production projects. The closing swipe at opponents is a tail-end digression, but the substance responds.
question: What else can he tell us about economic development on the West Coast?
statement: So much and so little time. We are rekindling the golden age of the coast. Mining is now driving the coast. Not only are people expressing more confidence to invest there but money is flowing. There is a pipeline of production projects. It will stimulate the economy for many years to come. It’s only disappointing that it has taken this long—in particular, with those who derive their heritage from such industries abandoning, demonising, and tainting such an industry, and I’m glad to be rid of them.
