statement: Well, yes, I do agree with the Infrastructure Commission, which is one of the reasons why I’m so proud to sit next to Minister Simeon Brown, who, on becoming the Minister of Transport, kicked off the pothole remediation plan, necessary due to the lack of road maintenance that occurred on her watch.

explanation: Asked how she will explain to provincial New Zealand the prioritisation of $3.8b on a short stretch of Wellington road over thousands of kilometres elsewhere. She does supply an explanation — it is 'both, not either/or', and points to a nationwide resilience programme — which is responsive to the 'how will she explain it' framing. She does not engage the comparative scale the question rested on, so it is answered but around the sharp edge of it.
question: How will she explain to provincial New Zealand that her Government is prioritising $3.8 billion on less than 2 kilometres of one car lane in each direction in our capital city when we could be improving thousands of kilometres—
statement: Well, it’s not a case of either/or; it’s a case of both. I would point out to New Zealanders who share my concern about the resilience of our transport network that NZTA has a multi-hundred-million-dollar programme of resilience works under way across the country to improve the resilience of our roads to increasing climatic events, including flooding and landslides. That work is vital, it must continue, and our Government will continue to ensure there is the funding available to support it.

explanation: A patsy question asking what reports she has seen on the economy. She names a specific report (yesterday's Monetary Policy Statement) and describes its content. Squarely and completely answered.
question: What reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: Yesterday, the Reserve Bank released its latest Monetary Policy Statement. This included the bank’s decision to keep the official cash rate (OCR) at 2.25 percent. The Reserve Bank’s forward track implies that this is likely to be the bottom of the easing cycle in terms of OCR reductions, but it also indicated that monetary policy is likely to remain accommodative for some time, with low interest rates continuing to provide stimulus to the economy.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government is taking on rental costs; Seymour names three concrete actions (spending restraint/mortgage rates, interest deductibility, RTA simplification). Squarely on the question asked.
question: What actions is the Government taking to take the pressure off rental costs?
statement: Well, many things. I mentioned earlier that we have been careful with our own spending so that mortgage rates can fall. They’ve halved under this Government. That means that we now see less pressure on rent because many landlords are trying to service mortgages. We’ve also made mortgage interest a deductible expense for people renting out homes, and that has put downward pressure on rents, which have fallen in many cases. We’ve also simplified the Residential Tenancies Act so that a landlord can take a chance on a tenant and offer them a place to live, knowing they can get out of the relationship if it goes wrong. Those three changes have made it better to be a tenant in this country, and we’re very proud of what we’ve done to make renting more affordable as a Government.

explanation: Asked what announcement he made about 12-month prescriptions; he states the announcement — from 1 February, up to 12-month prescriptions for stable long-term conditions. Directly responsive.
question: What recent announcements has he made about enabling 12-month prescriptions for patients?
statement: Our Government is focused on making a real difference for patients. That’s why, from 1 February this year, New Zealanders with stable, long-term conditions can now receive prescriptions for up to 12 months. This common-sense solution will help patients with conditions such as asthma, diabetes, epilepsy, and high blood pressure by reducing their need to renew prescriptions every three months. This change reduces costs for patients that need repeat prescriptions, improves access to medicines, and frees up valuable GP time for those who need appointments.

explanation: Asked how the change benefits patients with long-term conditions; answer gives exactly that — fewer doctor visits, fewer prescription charges, up to $120/year saved. Complete engagement with the question.
question: How will this change benefit patients with long-term conditions?
statement: We are making the system work better for the patients it serves. For those managing stable, ongoing conditions, this change will mean fewer trips to the doctor just to renew a routine prescription and fewer prescription charges over the year. Patients will continue to collect their repeats from the pharmacy as usual but will no longer need to return to their doctor each time for a new script. This is expected to save patients up to $120 per year, for those who receive 12-month prescriptions. This is a practical, patient-focused change.

explanation: Asked about benefits for access to primary care; answer addresses precisely that — reduced GP burden from repeat scripts, appointments freed up for complex needs. On point.
question: What benefits will this have for access to primary care?
statement: This is a win-win for both patients and health professionals. This gives doctors and prescribers the ability to prescribe for up to 12 months for stable, ongoing conditions, reducing the burden on GPs and other prescribers, who currently spend time issuing repeat prescriptions every three months. This initiative will free up appointments for patients with more immediate or complex needs. This policy isn’t just about expanding prescription lengths; it’s also about using our health workforce more efficiently to improve timely access to care and ensure patients can see a clinician when they need to.

explanation: Asked what other steps improve access to medicines; answer lists other steps (expanded nurse practitioner prescribing, pharmacy ownership restriction removal). Directly answers the 'what else' asked.
question: What other steps has the Government taken to improve access to medicines?
statement: In addition to 12-month prescriptions, we’ve also increased prescribing rights for health professionals such as nurse practitioners, enabling them to prescribe a wider range of medicines within their area of practice, and we’ve progressed practical changes to strengthen the pharmacy workforce by removing ownership restrictions that limited pharmacist prescribers from prescribing if they owned or held an interest in a pharmacy. Together, these patient-focused changes will ensure New Zealanders have quicker, easier, and more affordable access to the care and medicines they need. It’s all part of our plan to fix the basics and build the future for a more patient-focused health system.

explanation: Asked if she is confident FENZ is ensuring a fair deal, and why. She answers 'Yes' and gives the why (offer compliant with the Workforce Policy Statement, union claim 3x higher, ERA facilitated bargaining). The refusal to comment further on an independent process is itself a plain answer, not a dodge.
question: Is she confident that Fire and Emergency New Zealand is doing everything it can to ensure firefighters are receiving a fair deal; if so, why?
statement: Yes. I understand the leadership of Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) have sought an agreement with the New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union (NZPFU) that complies with the Government’s Workforce Policy Statement, is affordable, and doesn’t increase cost of living for Kiwis. I’m advised that the NZPFU’s most recent settlement proposal was more than three times higher than Fire and Emergency’s last offer, which they believe was fair, sustainable, and reasonable, and in line with other settlements across the Public Service. Facilitated bargaining with the Employment Relations Authority (ERA) is under way at the request of Fire and Emergency, as they believe the ERA gives them the best chance of coming to a positive, sustainable outcome and introducing some realism into discussions. That process continues and, as it is an independent process, it is not appropriate that I comment too much further.

explanation: Asked how she can be confident when firefighters are striking twice weekly. She never addresses the confidence question head-on, pivoting to condemning industrial action, but does offer an implicit basis (FENZ at the table for 583 days). Partial engagement — the core 'how can you be confident given the strikes' is talked around.
question: How can she be confident when firefighters are striking twice a week?
statement: Industrial action that puts the community at risk doesn’t help to get trucks fixed or build new ones or make any settlements. Fire and Emergency have been in bargaining with the NZPFU for 583 days. They have been willing to be at the table. Striking doesn’t help settle any faster.

explanation: Asked what announcement she made on school property; she names the announcement — the opening of Te Kura Rau Iti, with capacity, timeline and cost. Squarely responsive.
question: What announcement has she made regarding school property?
statement: Last week, I attended the opening of a brand new primary school in Takanini. Te Kura Rau Iti has the capacity for 700 students to support roll growth in the fast-growing suburb of Flat Bush. The school was built in under 18 months and came in below budget following our inquiry into school property and a subsequent value-for-money exercise. It cost $41 million—almost half the previous build cost, estimated to be $76.5 million projected in 2023. Not only did we build the school for $41 million, saving $35 million; we also delivered an extra 100 student places for that price—no open-plan classrooms, no expensive, unnecessary bespoke designs; just getting on with the job and delivering warm, safe, dry classrooms for our kids.

explanation: Asked how the Government delivered this; answer gives the how — property inquiry, ministerial advisory group, off-site manufacturing with standardised designs. Directly on the question.
question: How has the Government been able to deliver this?
statement: The delivery of this school on time and under budget proves that our Government’s approach to school property delivery is working. We undertook an inquiry into school property and appointed a ministerial advisory group to bring commercial oversight to school property. We’ve driven a focus in the ministry on moving away from bespoke, expensive, architecturally designed buildings. We’re using off-site manufacturing with standardised, repeatable, quality designs and layouts. Through these changes, we’ve been able to halve the cost of building a classroom so that we can deliver more classrooms faster and at a lower cost—and that’s what delivery looks like.

explanation: Asked what else she has announced on school property; answer supplies further announcements (two specialist day schools, satellite classrooms, redevelopments). Complete answer to the 'what else' asked.
question: What else has she announced on school property?
statement: For the first time in 50 years, we’re building two new specialist day schools to support children with high and complex additional learning needs. One is in Palmerston North, where there is no provision for 72 kilometres, and the other is in South Auckland where the wait-lists are just not keeping up. Over the last two Budgets, we’ve ring-fenced money for specialist education and property, including funding 50 new specialist satellite classrooms and the redevelopment of four specialist schools. Learning support is a huge priority for this Government, and that includes empowering parents to make the choice that is best for their children.

explanation: Asked how schools have been supported with maintenance; answer addresses maintenance support directly — depreciation uplift, $58m summer package, Five Year Agreement increase, rural schools work.
question: How have schools been supported with their maintenance work?
statement: As well as building more classrooms than ever before, this Government is focused on maintaining the schools and classrooms that we have. Budget 2024 uplift of $780 million in depreciation funding for school property maintenance was almost double that of the previous six years. We helped to get maintenance work under way over the summer break, with a $58 million package for schools to help their painting, repairs, and other minor fixes. We increased the Five Year Agreement funding for schools by 50 percent for the first time since 2010 to help schools with planned upgrades, modernisation, and replacement of existing school buildings. We’re completing work to support improvements in school property for 934 isolated small and rural schools. This work also means more jobs for our tradies, which is all contributing to economic growth.

explanation: Asked whether current student loan levels are sufficient for students to focus on study, and why. The answer never says sufficient or not — it restates the cost-sharing policy position and notes annual inflation adjustments, which gestures at a justification without ever reaching the yes/no at the core of the question.
question: Does he think that the current student loan levels are sufficient to allow students to focus on their studies; if so, why?
statement: The Government expects the costs of study to be shared between learners—for example, through part-time work or summer jobs—their families, and the Government, and this has been a long-held position. Since 2005, there has been an inflationary adjustment every year, through multiple Governments, designed to account for annual inflationary changes.

explanation: Asked how students can get by given living-cost indexation (2.2%) lagging food (4.6%) and energy (18%). Stanford defends the *methodology* of the annual calculation (unchanged since 2005) — tangentially relevant — then pivots to 2022 comparisons and general cost-of-living talking points. The question of how students manage the gap is never engaged.
question: How can students get by when the student loan living costs increased by 2.2 percent but the cost of food is up 4.6 percent in the last year and energy is up 18 percent since the election?
statement: As I have already outlined, the annual calculation to those increases has been almost exactly the same since 2005. There have been a couple of adjustments, but, for the most part, they have been the same. I would like to point out that in 2022, when the Consumers Price Index was running at 7.22 percent and food inflation was running at over 12 percent, it was really tough for students, but this Government has driven down the cost of living, we’ve got inflation under control, rents are flat to falling, and if that member was so concerned about the calculations—

explanation: Asked in what ways the Government has driven down the cost of living for students. She names a concrete way — rents, previously rising, now flat to falling, notably in Auckland and Wellington. That is an answer in the form requested (a 'way'), even if only one and not student-specific. Squarely engaged.
question: In what ways has this Government driven down the cost of living for university students?
statement: As I’ve just mentioned, if you compared the stats to a few years ago, they’re much better than they were. One example, of course, is rents: driven up under the previous Government by $150, they’re now flat to falling, and in places like Auckland and Wellington, significantly falling.

explanation: Asked whether he considers eating, rent and electricity optional luxuries for students. No yes/no, and the loaded framing is left untouched; but she does engage the underlying subject by setting out her position on who bears student costs (students, families, Government) and how students are expected to meet them. Gestures at the question without reaching its core.
question: Does he think eating, paying rent, and having electricity are optional luxuries for students?
statement: As I said in my primary question, the costs for students fall on three parties; it has been a long-held position. They fall on students, their families, and on the Government, and it’s up to students to make sure they’re making use of the student loan scheme as well as looking after some of their costs through part-time work, either during term time or during their summer jobs, and also with support from their families.

explanation: Two-part question: why is work the solution, and what about the Government making jobs harder to find. She contests the jobs premise directly (Treasury outlook worse than reality, investment, cost of borrowing, better outlook than a few years ago), which is genuine engagement with half the question, but never addresses why part-time work is the offered answer.
question: Why is his solution just for students to work on top of their studies when his Government has also made it harder for students to even find a job?
statement: The outlook, according to Treasury, was much worse than it actually has been. This Government has been working really hard to make sure that there are opportunities available for New Zealanders. We have been working hard to make sure that we’re driving investment into this country. We’re making sure that we are driving down the cost of borrowing so that companies can expand and create more jobs. The outlook for students, compared to just a few years ago, is a lot better than it was.

explanation: Asked what recent progress she has seen on tourism and major events. She answers with arrival figures, the 3.5 million threshold, and Australian and Chinese arrival growth. Directly and completely responsive to what was asked.
question: What recent progress has she seen on tourism and major events in New Zealand?
statement: New data released by Stats NZ last week showed international visitor arrivals reached 3.51 million in the year to December 2025, putting us at 90 percent of pre-COVID levels. This is the first annual period to exceed 3.5 million overseas visitor arrivals since the March 2020 year, meaning tourism levels are now at their highest since December 2019. Visitor arrivals from Australia reached 1.52 million in the year to December 2025—an increase of 10 percent on the previous year—while arrivals from China were up 29 percent over the same period. Growing tourism is a key part of our plan to fix the basics and build the future. This progress shows that our plan is working.

explanation: Asked about progress in the business events sector. Answers with the NZICC opening, projected visitors and spend, the $925m conference contribution, and 120 confirmed 2026 events. Fully on the question asked.
question: What progress has she seen in the business events sector?
statement: Last week, the New Zealand International Convention Centre (NZICC) was officially opened. This world-class venue is estimated to bring in 33,000 international conference visitors who would not otherwise come to New Zealand, contributing $90 million of new spending annually. New research from Business Events Industry Aotearoa also shows that multi-day conferences delivered $925 million in economic and productivity contribution in 2025. This was before the opening of the NZICC last week, so I’m really excited to see where we go from here. With more than 120 events having already been confirmed for NZICC in 2026, the strong pipeline of events means more visitors to New Zealand, more economic activity, more jobs, and more opportunities for Kiwis.

explanation: Asked how visa changes are affecting visitor numbers. Answers with the NZeTA pathway, 36,000 additional Chinese arrivals, estimated spend, and survey evidence on the decision to travel. Direct match to the question.
question: How are recent visa changes impacting visitor numbers?
statement: Changes that allow eligible visitors from China and the Pacific to travel to New Zealand from Australia with a New Zealand Electronic Travel Authority, or an NZeTA, rather than a visa are also making a difference. To date, we’ve seen over 36,000 additional arrivals from China travelling through this pathway. With an average visitor spend of $5,800 for Chinese visitors, that amounts to an estimated economic injection of $210 million for Kiwi businesses for those visitors. A new survey following these changes shows that being able to travel with an NZeTA was a deciding factor in people’s decisions to visit New Zealand. Eighty-five percent of respondents have said they travelled to New Zealand specifically because of the NZeTA option becoming available. I’m proud to have worked with my colleague the Hon Erica Stanford on this.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has seen on tourism and major events progress. She relays two named industry quotes (Tourism Industry Aotearoa, Hotel Council Aotearoa). That is exactly the thing asked for; the closing self-praise doesn't displace the answer.
question: What feedback has she seen on the progress on tourism and major events?
statement: We’ve received a range of positive feedback on our progress to date. Tourism Industry Aotearoa chief executive Rebecca Ingram says, “Forward bookings are looking positive, and the industry has real momentum.” She attributed that to the Government’s tourism focus and investments, targeted marketing from Tourism New Zealand, changes in visa settings, and new and exciting changes on the horizon. James Doolan from Hotel Council Aotearoa said, “Central government’s increased investment in event attraction and destination marketing have allowed private businesses to invest in their assets.” Tourism is critical to our economy, and our investments will help to deliver lasting benefits for communities and businesses from one end of New Zealand to the other.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Prime Minister's statement about iwi and marae in emergency management. 'Yeah, I definitely agree with that statement' — an unambiguous, complete answer to a yes/no question.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that “Iwi and marae are very good at emergency management. They don’t just stand up for iwi, they stand up for the entire community”?
statement: Yeah, I definitely agree with that statement from the Prime Minister. That has, without a doubt, been my experience since I’ve been Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the decision to cut $23m from the Climate Emergency Response Fund. He states plainly that it is not his portfolio — a direct response to the ask, though not the answer sought — then pivots to investment in marae in Tairāwhiti and Hawke's Bay and meetings with iwi leaders. The stand-by question itself goes unanswered.
question: Does he stand by the Government’s decision to cut $23 million from the Climate Emergency Response Fund that was intended to help hapori Māori deal with climate change adaptation and resilience?
statement: Well, that’s not my portfolio area, but what I would say in terms of our readiness, our response, and our recovery as a country is that we’ve made hundreds of millions of dollars of investment, particularly into marae in Tairāwhiti and the Hawke’s Bay. We continue to have conversations with iwi leaders. We just had a very good session and meetings up at Waitangi on how we continue to (1) make sure that marae are in the right place and are not exposed to flooding, and (2) make sure they are supported and ready to be able to respond to these weather events.

explanation: Asked whether the $1 million marae fund will be enough for increasing climate-related emergencies. He explains where the money went, why it was allocated, and the red-tape reduction on replenishment, but never says whether it is or is not sufficient — the adequacy question, which was the whole point, is left open.
question: Will the $1 million marae emergency response fund be enough to cope with the increased frequency of climate-related distresses in Aotearoa?
statement: Well, it’s money that we put immediately into Te Puni Kōkiri because, especially over the last couple of months, you will have seen that we’ve had lots of events to deal with. Local Māori and iwi have stood up, marae have been opened, and what happens is that they will have a stockpile of goods there to support the broader, wider community, but then they have to go through a big bureaucratic sort of process to replenish that. What we’ve done is, with meetings with the Prime Minister, getting around the country, we have tried to remove some of that red tape to make it much easier for marae to replenish those stocks, and we also put an additional $1 million in there, which has actually gone out to most of the marae now that they’ve been providing that support.

explanation: Asked whether he will commit to ongoing funding for marae emergency response and Māori climate adaptation. Opens with 'Yes' and then elaborates on mitigation work, the emergency management legislation and codified Māori representation on the coordinating executive group. The commitment asked for is given outright.
question: Will he commit to ongoing funding to support marae in responding to emergencies and to improve climate change adaptation and resilience for hapori Māori?
statement: Yes. Iwi are an extremely important partner for the Government, in readiness, response, and recovery and also in the reduction and the mitigation work. I could get into a lot of detail around that, because there’s a significant amount of money and work being done around the country with local iwi on mitigation work. Of course, we’ve got the emergency management legislation in front of the select committee. I want to acknowledge all the members in this House, from every party, who’ve worked really hard to get that into good shape, because it’s important for us as a country to have that as a launching pad in terms of how we deal with these emergencies. As part of that I actually codified and made sure that Māori have now got a seat at what we called our coordinating executive group, and that is the senior executive group that works together to make plans, and to be fully involved in how we respond to these weather events.

explanation: Asked whether Middle East conflict will impact the NZ economy. Willis answers directly — yes, as a trading nation significant global events do impact the economy — and addresses the magnitude question (depends on duration/escalation, historically short-term volatility). Core question engaged; slight hedging on size, but that is inherent to the question.
question: Will conflict in the Middle East have an impact on the New Zealand economy?
statement: New Zealand is a trading nation, and so significant global events do impact on the economy; the question in this case is how big that impact will be. A lot will depend on how long the conflict continues and whether it escalates. Recent history suggests that global conflict tends to cause short-term volatility in markets but that, over time, they settle back close to previous levels.

explanation: Asked how markets have reacted. The answer is squarely on point: muted reaction, crude oil up 7 percent to under US$78, compared with US$128 in March 2022, equities stable. Exactly the question asked.
question: How have markets reacted to the conflict?
statement: To date, financial market reaction has been relatively muted, so far. The price of crude oil has risen this week, but to nothing like the levels seen when Russia invaded Ukraine. When US markets closed at 10 a.m. today, it was up 7 percent on last Friday’s close, at just under US$78 a barrel. That compares with the price of US$128 a barrel on 8 March 2022. Global equity markets have remained stable; the Standard & Poor’s index actually rose fractionally overnight. But the duration and extent of this conflict remains unclear, and Treasury and the Reserve Bank will continue to monitor market developments closely.

explanation: Asked about the impact on NZ exports. She addresses it — Middle East is 3 percent of exports ($3.3b), Strait of Hormuz disruption will present challenges — before pivoting to government trade-diversification talking points and the US tariff comparison. The core is reached, then padded with unasked material.
question: What could be the impact of the conflict on New Zealand exports?
statement: The Middle East is a relatively small market for New Zealand, but one that is growing in importance. Total exports to the region last year were $3.3 billion, representing 3 percent of New Zealand’s total exports. The conflict, which is disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, will undoubtedly present some challenges. However, New Zealand’s exporters have shown themselves to be extremely resilient and adaptable in recent years, and they are taking advantage of the work the Government is doing to open doors by negotiating rules, removing non-tariff barriers, and diversifying markets to build resilience. It is notable that despite the imposition of tariffs on exports to the US last year, exports to the United States actually increased, as did our overall exports.

explanation: Asked about impact on fuel supplies and prices. Both halves answered: no domestic shortages anticipated short or medium term (reserve requirements, stock in transit), and price impact depends on duration/escalation. The price half is hedged but the hedge is itself a responsive answer.
question: How could the conflict impact on fuel supplies and prices?
statement: Recently introduced regulations require fuel importers to  maintain at least 28 days of petrol and 21 days of diesel reserves, with the Government having acted to increase that requirement. The petrol companies have all reported that healthy stock and additional supplies are already in transit, and so domestic fuel shortages are not anticipated in the short or medium term. The impact on price will depend on how long the conflict continues and whether it escalates.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, complete, no evasion.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether the NZ Government supports the US and Israeli air strikes on Iran. He states general support for action stopping Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon, then stresses NZ was not party to and had no warning of these strikes. That establishes non-involvement but never states whether the Government supports them — the yes/no core is circled, not answered.
question: Does the New Zealand Government support the US and Israel’s air strikes against Iran?
statement: Well, as I’ve said yesterday, we have long supported action that stops Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon that sponsors State terrorism around the world and also brutally represses its people. But these are independent actions by the US and Israel. We are not party to them, we have not had advance warning, and we have not had a subsequent briefing.

explanation: Asked whether the Government believes the strikes accord with the UN Charter. He does eventually give a responsive position — NZ cannot jump to conclusions either way and it is for the US and Israel to assert legality, i.e. the Government takes no view. A declared non-position is a real answer, but a chunk of the reply is spent on the questioner's lack of standing to judge rather than on the Government's own belief.
question: Does the New Zealand Government believe the US and Israel’s air strikes against Iran are in accordance with the United Nations Charter?
statement: Well, again, I’ve noted the member’s comments and his remarks today in the House and I’d just say that I’m unsure as to how he would possibly make the assessment that they are illegal or legal, and that is because the member—or any of the members—does not have access to the information. New Zealand cannot jump to conclusions either way, because, actually, at the end of the day, we have not been party to the information or intelligence around these strikes. We can make assumptions about that, but, as Prime Minister, I have to deal with the facts and the evidence that I have before me, and, as a result, that is why it is up to the US and it is up to Israel to assert the legality of these strikes.

explanation: A narrow question: is the UN Secretary-General wrong? He never addresses the Secretary-General's assessment at all, restating instead that the US invoked article 51 and that NZ is not in a position to determine legality. 'We won't judge' is partially responsive, but the specific proposition put to him — whether the SG is wrong — is left untouched.
question: Is the Secretary-General of the United Nations wrong when he said that the air strikes violated international law and breached core principles of the UN Charter?
statement: Well, as the member has read—as I have, as well—the US has invoked the right to self-defence under article 51 of the UN Charter. It is up for them to provide the legal evidence and the justification for these strikes, but sitting here in New Zealand with people jumping to assumptions based on what they’ve read in media reports, without the knowledge or the information, is not actually what we need to do. We need to be factual and evidence-based, and, as a result, we’re not in a position to determine whether they are legal or illegal. That is up to the Americans and the Israelis to assert.

explanation: Asked why he said any action stopping Iran getting nuclear weapons is a good thing, and whether that implied support for unlawful action. Reply: 'I clarified those remarks this morning.' It acknowledges the remarks but supplies no reason and does not repeat or summarise the clarification — the 'why' is never reached.
question: Why did he say that “any actions that stop Iran from getting [nuclear weapons] is a good thing.”, suggesting he’d support any actions, even if they’re contrary to international law?
statement: Well, I clarified those remarks this morning.

explanation: Asked why he repeatedly refused to condemn the bombing of schoolchildren. He calls civilian casualties a tragedy, which touches the subject matter, but gives no reason for the refusal and moves to wanting a quick resolution and Iran resuming negotiations. The 'why' at the centre of the question is not answered.
question: Why did he repeatedly refuse to condemn the bombing of schoolchildren?
statement: The bombing of schoolchildren, and, actually, any civilian casualties in a war is a total tragedy, and it is terrible what has happened there. But, as you’ve seen, and as I said yesterday, the Americans and the Israelis are commenting on that. This is why we want to see a very quick resolution to this. It’s why we want to see Iran and their leadership resume negotiations very, very quickly.

explanation: A two-part question. First part answered explicitly ('absolutely', he stands by the statement); second part answered with a stated reason for not taking a position — the Government lacks the information and intelligence behind the strikes. Both halves engaged, though it leans on the earlier reasoning and adds a jab about the member also lacking information.
question: Does he stand by his own statement that “We need to stand up for the international rules based system that has actually served New Zealand incredibly well … When it is under threat, you’ve actually got to call it out, and you’ve got to stand up and make your contribution.”; if so, why won’t he take a position on whether the US’ and Israel’s air strikes are consistent with that international rules-based system, particularly given that the Secretary-General of the United Nations has said they are not?
statement: In answer to the first part, absolutely, but, as I have just explained to the member, we don’t have the information or intelligence by which these independent actions by the US and Israel were launched, and the member doesn’t, either.

explanation: Asked what progress the Government has made toward its violent crime reduction target. Answered directly: 'excellent progress', with the specific figure of 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime in the year to October 2025. Squarely on the question.
question: What progress has the Government made towards its violent crime reduction target?
statement: Excellent progress. We’ve seen a significant drop in the number of victims of violent crime since this Government was elected, with the latest New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey showing there were 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime in the year to October 2025 than in the two years previous. This follows a focus on restoring real consequences for crime and placing victims at the centre of the justice system. There is still much work to do, but Kiwis can be proud of the progress that we’ve made together.

explanation: Asked for the original violent-crime victim target. He gives the baseline (185,000), the target (165,000), the reduction (20,000) and the date (2029). Complete and direct.
question: What was the original target that the Government had set to reduce the number of victims of violent crime?
statement: When we came into Government in October 2023, there were 185,000 victims of violent crime, and the Government set a target of reducing that figure to 165,000—a reduction of 20,000 victims—by 2029.

explanation: Asked why reducing victims matters. He answers it — victims, their families and communities are affected — before drifting into a contrast with the previous Government's prison-population focus. The core is reached, with padding around it.
question: Why is it important that the number of victims of violent crime reduces?
statement: This Government is committed to restoring the basics in law and order, and building a future where New Zealanders feel safe in the community, and it’s not just the victims of violent crime who are affected, of course; it is their families and their communities, as well. The previous Government, in its wisdom, had a focus on reducing the number of people in prison, and we’ve shifted that focus to focusing solely on reducing the number of victims of violent crime. That has been our focus and it will always be our focus.

explanation: Asked what is next on the agenda. He names three specific items: trespass law legislation, CBD disorder powers for police, and the Crime Amendment Bill. Squarely answered.
question: What is next on the Government’s agenda to further reduce the number of victims of violent crime?
statement: We’ve made tremendous progress, but there’s still more work to do. Very shortly, we’ll be introducing legislation to strengthen trespass laws in New Zealand, followed by legislation to provide the police with the power to deal with antisocial, disorderly behaviour in our CBDs, and our Crime Amendment Bill is making its way through the House. I’m proud of the work that the law and order team across Government are doing, which is making a real difference to the lives of New Zealanders, and we know right here that there is much more work to do.

explanation: Asked why she called Kiwis impatient given a July 2024 promise. She answers the 'why' directly ('Because they, like me, are impatient') and addresses the July 2024 clause by asserting relief was delivered then. Long, but both halves of the question are engaged.
question: Why did she say Kiwis are being impatient for cost of living relief, when she promised it in July 2024?
statement: Because they, like me, are impatient. We all want a stronger economy sooner, and I share their frustration. These are New Zealanders who as recently as 2022 endured annual price increases of 6.9 percent, 7.3 percent, 7.2 percent, and 7.2 percent in successive quarters, and I’d note that in July 2024, the Government did provide promised cost of living relief through tax changes that benefited around 1.9 million New Zealand households by an average of $60 extra a fortnight in their hand—$60 a fortnight, I take it, that the member would want to take back. This, of course, has been joined by other measures, including FamilyBoost, scrapping the Auckland fuel and ute tax, extending Working for Families, rates rebates for SuperGold card holders—I could go on. Most importantly, however, since 2023, inflation has come down markedly. I too am impatient for the economy to grow, with higher wages and higher employment, and inflation settled within the target band. That takes time, however, and international events, as we have seen, mean the recovery is not necessarily a smooth road.

explanation: A narrow numerical question — how many of 21,000 families received the $250. She declines outright, directing the member to a question on notice, which is a direct refusal, but then moves into FamilyBoost advocacy and disputes the premise rather than sticking to the decline. Half credit: the refusal is plain, the number is never approached.
question: How many of the 21,000 families that she promised would receive a $250 tax cut have actually received it, or are they just being impatient?
statement: If the member wants specific data, she should put it in the question on notice. However, it is the case that in terms of the FamilyBoost tax credit, we made changes to that last year—which I note the member’s party supported, having earlier opposed—which mean that many families have now got more than $150 a fortnight in relief from that policy, which, combined with the impact of tax relief, means there are undoubtedly families who will have received tax relief through bracket changes, Working for Families changes, and FamilyBoost that amount to that $250. Most importantly, we were always clear that they would receive up to that amount; we never promised that was an average.

explanation: Asked whether she promised to reduce food prices and has done nothing. She engages one half by contesting the premise — the quote is a journalist's paraphrase and the alleged statement is not in the video — which is a genuine response to 'she promised'. The 'done nothing to help' half is never touched.
question: Are families impatient because she promised to “reduce food prices for Kiwis.” and has done nothing to help?
statement: Well, I have gone and reviewed documents which the member’s leader referred to in the House, and he will note that I have written to him about this because the article the member is referring to now is a paraphrase from a journalist. The video which Mr Hipkins has referred to previously in which he said that I made the statement that “National would make groceries cheaper”—that statement is not included in that video at any stage. I have provided the full transcript to Mr Hipkins; he has chosen not to correct his statement.

explanation: Same accusation with a dated quote. She does not concede or deny the promise directly but does answer the operative 'she's done nothing' charge with named actions (fast-track changes, building consent rules, competition in groceries). Engages the substance without addressing the promise framing.
question: Are people impatient because she promised, on 27 August 2025, action on “[reducing] food prices for Kiwis.” and she’s done nothing to help?
statement: Well, I’m with every New Zealander who would like to see groceries cheaper. The question for us is whether or not we can make groceries cheaper than would otherwise be the case. It is the case that when inflation is higher, grocery prices increase more rapidly, and with inflation under control, they have not risen as fast as could have been the case with a more profligate and high-spending Government. It is also the case that our Government has taken action to do what we can to support more competition in the grocery sector. Those actions include changes to the fast-track legislation and changes to building consent rules to enable new entrants to compete. The Commerce Commission have reported extensively on the margins which supermarket operators charge for their goods and those increasing margins, and I join with those New Zealanders who wish to see grocery prices cheaper. I am realistic about the role of Government in that.

explanation: Asked about a promise on energy prices versus introducing a gas tax. The gas tax — the pivot of the question — is never mentioned at all; she reframes onto dry-year supply security and wholesale futures pricing. Gestures at energy affordability but avoids the specific contradiction put to her.
question: Are people impatient because she promised action on energy prices, but she’s introducing a gas tax instead?
statement: There can be no affordability and security of electricity supply in New Zealand unless we, as policy makers, address the very real challenge of what happens to electricity supply on days when there isn’t enough water in the hydro lakes, the sun isn’t shining, and the wind isn’t blowing. If we do not address that challenge, electricity prices will only go up, and I note that future pricing for energy on the wholesale market has reflected risk reduction since the Government’s statements on LNG and Genesis Energy.

explanation: Asked whether what Kiwis want is for her to stop making false promises and focus on her job. She does not address her own conduct at all, instead redirecting 'false promise' onto the Opposition's policy positions and closing with an attack on the questioner's seriousness.
question: Is the only thing that Kiwis are actually impatient for is for that Minister to stop feeding them false promises, to stop being distracted, and to just focus on her actual job?
statement: The loudest false promise I have heard in recent times has been from those who out of one side of their mouth say that they care deeply about the cost of living and out the other side of their mouth say that they would change the inflation-targeting regime, would introduce new taxes on tenants, and at the same time would remove the Investment Boost tax policy, which is the very thing that Treasury says will drive future wage growth. I care deeply about the cost of living, but it is not enough to care; that member needs to come up with serious policies on the cost of living if she wants to be taken seriously.

explanation: Asked what recent MSD reports she has seen on the traffic light system. She identifies the report released today and cites a specific finding (90 percent). Directly answered.
question: What recent reports has she seen from the Ministry of Social Development on the traffic light system?
statement: Today, the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) released an excellent report which reinforces the success of the Government’s traffic light system. It shows that 90 percent of clients found the traffic light system has been helpful for understanding their obligations. These obligations include attending interviews and seminars, reporting to MSD, and being available for work. Our Government is committed to fixing the basics and building the future by supporting more New Zealanders off welfare and into work.

explanation: Asked for the report's key findings. She supplies findings — 99 percent obligation compliance, a 10.6 percent drop in sanctions between named quarters — with only a short closing flourish.
question: What were the key findings of the report?
statement: MSD also found that nearly 99 percent of clients are fulfilling their obligations and the number of sanctions has dropped by 10.6 percent between the September 2024 and September 2025 quarters. The changes we have made have increased client activity and engagement with MSD. This includes a focus on ensuring jobseeker support clients are meeting their obligations. Our Government will continue to support unemployed New Zealanders into work, and having a more proactive welfare system is a really important part of this.

explanation: Asked how the system helped people understand obligations. She answers the mechanism: it resets expectations, the colour-coded tool aids quick re-compliance, and it particularly helps those with literacy or language barriers. On point throughout.
question: How has the traffic light system helped people understand their obligations?
statement: The traffic light system was designed to reset the expectations for those on welfare so that they’re clear about both their rights and their responsibilities. It is helping job seekers to understand and navigate their obligations, helping them to be prepared and proactive and to seize work opportunities when they come along. The colour-coded communication tool is useful because it helps clients re-comply quickly. This has been especially helpful for clients with literacy challenges or language barriers. We know that economic times continue to be challenging, but we want people to be ready as the jobs come. The traffic light system reinforces that expectation.

explanation: Asked what other initiatives the Government is implementing to help people into work. Upston names them: MSD front-line investment, phone-based case management covering 10,000 more people, and improved MSD-business matching. Directly on the question asked.
question: What other initiatives is the Government implementing to help people into work?
statement: The traffic light system is just one part of our wider Welfare that Works programme. Our Government continues to support job seekers into work, with investment into MSD’s front line. We’ve also introduced phone-based case management, supporting 10,000 more people in case management at any time. We’ve also improved the way MSD works with businesses to provide opportunities for job seekers to gain employment. The changes that we have made ensure our welfare system proactively supports those who can work to get off welfare, and we know that work is one of the best ways to lift people out of hardship.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, complete, no evasion.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware of how many people, including children, have been made or kept homeless by his Government's decisions. He never addresses awareness of that figure or offers it; he pivots to favourable housing statistics (affordability, rents, wait-list, children out of emergency housing). Adjacent subject matter, but the core of the question — the count of people made homeless — is untouched.
question: Is the Prime Minister aware of how many people, including children, have been kept or made homeless as a result of his Government’s decisions to tighten access to emergency housing, implement benefit sanctions, and more?
statement: Well, as I’ve said to the member before, I’m very proud that we’ve made house purchasing more affordable. Rents have come down, I think 6,000 or 7,000 people have come off the social housing wait-list, and, when I last looked, 2,100 children had been moved out of emergency housing into proper, dry homes, and there’s big investment going in and support happening in homeless situations, as well.

explanation: A yes/no on whether he accepts data showing homelessness rose nationally and doubled in Auckland. He never says whether he accepts it; he opens with a comparison to the previous Government's record, then cites Auckland CBD rough-sleeper counts and Housing First tenancies, which gestures obliquely at the Auckland claim without conceding or disputing the data.
question: Does the Prime Minister then accept the data that shows that homelessness has increased across the country, and doubling in Auckland alone, since his Government made decisions to tighten access to emergency housing?
statement: Well, as I’ve said to the member before, our record on housing is much better than that member’s, when homelessness went up 37 percent and $1 billion was spent. What we see is housing affordability for people who can afford to buy a house, we see rents coming down, we’ve seen 6,000 people come off the social housing wait-list and 2,124 kids come out of squalid motels and into proper homes, we’ve seen rents that are actually stable to falling, and, importantly, at last count, Auckland Council, as I understand, is doing daily counts of rough sleepers. There are about 30 in the Auckland CBD, and the good news is that of the 300 Housing First places that we’ve made available, 203 have been tenanted and 13 have signed leases. So our action plan to make sure that we can support and deal with homelessness in the Auckland CBD, in particular, is making good progress.

explanation: Asked where those denied emergency housing support are expected to go if issued move-on orders. After a spending preamble and a swipe at the questioner's record, he does reach a partial answer: police are connected to social service agencies and 'will plug people into them as need be'. The destination question is engaged, though only glancingly and without addressing those already denied support.
question: Where does he expect those experiencing homelessness who have been denied support because of his Government’s decisions to tighten the criteria on emergency housing—as in their having contributed to their own homelessness—to go if they end up being issued with his intended move-on orders, other than to the next shop front, the next park, or the next cemetery?
statement: Well, in answer to the first part of the question, this is a Government that spends $515 million a year with different agencies and organisations supporting homeless folk; it’s a Government that spends $5 billion a year on total housing support. But, again, with respect to the move-on orders—and as the member would have found in the difficulty of leading homelessness and having a 37 percent increase when they were in Government—I’d just say that every situation is different and they’re complex situations. Our police now have tools around the move-on orders. They also are well aware of the social service agencies and are well-connected and will plug people into them as need be. But we trust our police, they’ve developed outstanding operational guidelines on gang patches, and we expect similar here.

explanation: Asked whether he will take expert advice on move-on orders given he ignored it on emergency housing. He gives no answer either way — the entire reply is a comparison with the Labour-Greens record and pride in his own. The question of future acceptance of advice is never reached.
question: If he ignored advice and concerns from social service providers and experts that reducing access to emergency housing would result in more homelessness and then went ahead with it anyway and we saw more homelessness, will he then take the advice of social service providers and experts that his move-on orders will only exacerbate the problems associated with homelessness?
statement: As I’ve said to the member, I would put this Government’s record up against the Labour-Greens Government’s record, when there was a 37 percent increase in homelessness and $1 billion being spent on emergency housing. I’m proud of the progress that we’ve made, and I’m proud of the fact that our homeless action plan is starting to pay a benefit.

explanation: Two-part question: has he received advice, and what did it recommend. He confirms receipt explicitly and characterises the content (benefits to household bills, significant grid investment required), then links it to specific regulatory changes. Slightly short of stating the recommendations as such, but both limbs are engaged.
question: Has he received advice on the impact of high levels of rooftop solar and household batteries on wholesale markets and distribution network costs; if so, what were the recommendations in that advice?
statement: Yes, I have received advice on the impacts of high levels of rooftop solar and household batteries on wholesale markets and distribution costs. It identified potential benefits to household bills, while also requiring significant investment in the grid. That is why the Government is making a number of regulatory changes to make it easier to install rooftop solar and batteries. This includes removing building consent requirements for installing rooftop solar and batteries, and mandating retailers to pay fair price for electricity sold back into the grid from 1 July, along with a number of other regulatory changes to make it easier and cheaper to install rooftop solar and batteries.

explanation: Asked squarely whether he agrees with MBIE's regulatory impact statement that the incentive effect is unclear and minor. He neither agrees nor disagrees, and instead switches subject entirely to dry-year fuel security and the option-selection process for thermal/LNG. The solar incentive finding is never addressed.
question: Does he agree with Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment official advice in the regulatory impact statement on incentivising residential solar generation and sustainable buildings, which said of the changes that he has just outlined that “the incentive effect is not clear and [is] expected to be minor.”?
statement: It would be fair to acknowledge that we considered a long list of options, including renewables, demand response, and new thermal plant. The challenge that we have as a country is that in a dry year, we do not have sufficient fuel to make power, and we need a solution to deal with that problem. The solution which we have landed on took into account cost, time to deliver, flexibility, and the spillover effects to the other parts of the economy, and that is why we landed on the decision that we have made and not other options.

explanation: Asked whether he sought advice this week comparing LNG imports with distributed solar, and if not, why not. He never says whether such advice was sought. His account of LNG as a dry-year backup functions as an implied rationale for why the comparison was not made, which is a thin partial engagement with the 'why not' limb only.
question: Has he sought advice this week on the relative impacts on wholesale electricity prices of importing LNG compared with increasing the uptake on distributed solar generation; if not, why not?
statement: Well, the reality is—and I’m happy to provide a little bit more context for the member—that this Government isn’t intending to import LNG to replace natural gas, or for it to be imported regularly enough to see it set the gas price overall. LNG is simply a backup option to be imported during dry years. The alternative is that we have no fuel to make electricity, and that was the policy which we inherited, which drove power prices in 2024 to over $800 per megawatt hour and put New Zealand businesses and New Zealanders out of business.

explanation: Asked whether exposing New Zealanders to a volatile gas market is responsible. He reframes to what he considers irresponsible (blackouts) but in doing so does defend the exposure as a justified insurance policy and claims falling forward prices — an implicit 'yes, it is responsible'. Half-answered: the judgement is conveyed by inversion rather than stated.
question: Does he think it’s responsible to expose New Zealanders to a volatile gas market where in the last few hours, European LNG prices have jumped more than 50 percent, with projections of 130 percent spikes to come?
statement: Well, what I think is irresponsible is to pursue energy policy which incurs blackouts for New Zealanders because we do not have fuel to make electricity in a dry year, and that is the situation which we inherited as a Government. We have taken decisive action to import fuel for those dry years as an insurance policy, and as a result we’ve seen that future energy prices in this country, subsequent to our announcements, have a downward trajectory, which is positive.

explanation: A narrow factual question: has he or his office shared officials' solar advice or costings with the National Party or its policy writers. He answers a different question — the future release of advice under active consideration — and never confirms or denies the sharing. A specific yes/no left entirely unaddressed.
question: Has he or anyone in his office shared advice or costings prepared by his officials on solar options with the National Party and/or anyone involved in writing National Party policy?
statement: We have a range of advice regarding solar and batteries that is under active consideration, and when it is no longer under active consideration, then that will be released.

explanation: Asked what recent youth justice reports she has seen. She names the February 2026 Youth Justice Indicators Summary Report and an Oranga Tamariki briefing, with their findings. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent reports has she seen regarding youth justice?
statement: I have seen the Youth Justice Indicators Summary Report from February 2026, which shows a reduction in youth involved in the justice system. We are seeing fewer young people enter the justice system for the first time. I have also seen a briefing from Oranga Tamariki with more recent data that shows that Government Target 3 for reducing child and youth offending has decreased by 22 percent. This is against a target of 15 percent by 2030. I want to thank Oranga Tamariki staff for the lead they have taken in achieving this result, alongside their colleagues at Police and other agencies, to ensure there are timely, coordinated, and proper responses to youth offending.

explanation: Asked for the overall trend in child and youth offending. The answer states the trend directly — a third consecutive quarterly drop, consistent downward trend, with regional breakdown. Squarely on the question.
question: What is the overall trend for child and youth offending under her leadership?
statement: This is the third consecutive drop from the previous quarters, and it shows a consistent downward trend in serious and persistent youth offending by children and young people. The downward trend remains positive and continues to exceed expectations. It is also consistent across the majority of the country, with drops of 20 percent or more in eight of the 12 police districts.

explanation: Asked whether she is satisfied now the target is met early. Answer opens 'Absolutely not' and explains why the work continues. A direct, complete yes/no.
question: Is the Minister satisfied now that the target has been met ahead of schedule?
statement: Absolutely not. Just because we have achieved the target well ahead of expectations, it doesn’t mean we stop now. Every young person deserves the opportunity to be the best version of themselves. The great thing about collecting this data and reporting on it regularly means that we can see where we need to focus our resources and efforts to continue achieving success. For example, when the data indicates some parts of the country aren’t doing as well as others, Oranga Tamariki is able to respond quickly and work alongside police at a regional level to respond.

explanation: Asked what she puts the success down to. The answer begins 'There are a number of initiatives that have contributed' and stops — it points at the right category but never names a single cause, so the question is gestured at rather than reached.
question: What does the Minister put this success down to?
statement: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success—

explanation: Asked whether she stands by a specific quoted statement. Answer: 'Yes,' followed by supporting material. Direct and complete.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “for every New Zealander who is unemployed and wishes to have a job: our Government is on your side”?
statement: Yes. This Government is on the side of New Zealanders who want to work and get ahead. That is why we have been focused on restoring the economic conditions needed for job creation. That is also why we have supported the fast-tracking of job-rich projects, why we have supported the Investment Boost tax relief, and why we have taken action to reduce red tape and restore confidence across a range of industries from farming through to the film sector and through to tourism.

explanation: Asked whether she is on the side of Wellingtonians facing 10,000 fewer jobs. The answer disputes the provenance of the figure (attributing it to Labour's spokesperson) and never says whether she is on their side. It engages the premise but answers a different question — whose number is it, not where does she stand.
question: Is she on the side of the nearly 10,000 Wellingtonians who face 10,000 fewer jobs under her economic plan?
statement: I think the number that the member is referring to relies on an analysis by Craig Renney, the shadow finance spokesperson for the Labour Party—

explanation: Asked whether she is on the side of construction workers on jobseeker support. Answer: 'I am absolutely on the side of those in the construction sector,' with reasons. The stance question is answered outright.
question: Is she on the side of the 39,570 construction workers now on jobseeker support?
statement: I am absolutely on the side of those in the construction sector who wish to see more employment. That is why, unlike that member, I supported the fast track bill to ensure that job-rich construction projects can happen sooner so that people can have shovels in the ground rather than be swapping papers in court, that is why we have been on the side of replacing the Resource Management Act so that more construction can happen in future, that is why we have invested in job-rich public infrastructure projects, and it is why I stand by the Reserve Bank’s mandate, which has ensured that not only has inflation come down but interest rates have dropped considerably, meaning that construction projects that might have stayed on the shelf have been dusted off and are turning into action. That’s where construction jobs come from.

explanation: Two-part question: is she on their side, and why did she call them impatient. The first half is answered plainly ('I absolutely stand on the side of anyone who wants to work hard'); the 'impatient' half — the sharper part — is never touched, replaced with employment statistics.
question: Is she on the side of the 165,000 New Zealanders who want a job and can’t get one; if so, why did she call them impatient?
statement: Well, I absolutely stand on the side of anyone who wants to work hard and get ahead, and, as I’ve said in my answer to the primary question, that’s why we, as a Government, have worked so hard on restoring the economic conditions needed for job creation. I hope the member joins me in welcoming the fact that the latest statistics show that in the December quarter, 15,000 more New Zealanders were employed. I hope the member also joins me in celebrating today’s news from the tourism sector that thousands more jobs have been created in that sector over the past year alone.

explanation: A loaded 'how can she' question resting on four asserted premises. 'Multiple statements in that question were wrong' rejects the premises head-on rather than pivoting elsewhere, which is a real response, but it neither identifies which premises nor answers the 'how' — half engagement.
question: How can she be on the side of unemployed New Zealanders when she is destroying jobs, pushing people on to jobseeker support, dismissing them as being impatient, and driving them offshore to other countries for a better wage?
statement: Multiple statements in that question were wrong.

explanation: Asked how cutting 134 jobs fuels economic growth. The answer partly engages — efficiency and removing duplication are offered as the route to contributing to growth — but then moves to process (voluntary redundancies, board's operational call), leaving the causal question about growth only glancingly addressed.
question: How does the Bioeconomy Science Institute cutting 134 jobs, including 86 science roles, less than a year after it was formed fuel economic growth?
statement: The Bioeconomy Science Institute performs an important role in supporting the growth and development of New Zealand’s biological sector, but it will only be effective if it’s operating on a financially sustainable footing. I’m advised that the Bioeconomy Science Institute carefully assessed every application to ensure the institute retains the capability, expertise, and continuity needed to deliver impactful science and contribute to economic growth. The Bioeconomy Science Institute brought together four Crown research institutes with subsequently identified areas of overlap and duplication. I note this has been a voluntary redundancy round, and operational decisions about staffing sit with the Bioeconomy Science Institute board.

explanation: Asked whether the cuts are consistent with addressing the underinvestment his own advisory group identified. The answer asserts consistency with a different standard entirely — productivity, efficiency, sustainability, value — and never mentions underinvestment or the advisory group. It answers an adjacent question.
question: Are these job cuts consistent with addressing the long-term underinvestment identified by his Science System Advisory Group?
statement: These steps are consistent with requiring our science system to be productive, to be efficient, to be sustainable, and to generate real value for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether he takes responsibility for the cuts on the grounds of underfunding. The answer begins 'No' — a direct response to the question put — before giving countervailing material on scientist numbers and new funding.
question: Does he then take responsibility for these job cuts occurring because he has left the science sector underfunded?
statement: No, I’m encouraged by the last Stats NZ report, which actually showed that there are more scientists than we’ve had previously, and also new opportunities for science through the new emerging technologies with the Institute for Advanced Technology through artificial intelligence, through quantum, and through magnetic materials; through the Robinson Research Institute; and the $42 million Biodiscovery Platform.

explanation: Asked where the next round of science-sector job losses will fall. Reti rejects the premise and recites criteria the science system must meet (productive, efficient, financially sustainable). No location, agency or answer of any kind about future job losses — a pivot to talking points.
question: When he cut Callaghan Innovation, ransacked the Marsden Fund, and is now cutting 134 jobs from the new science institute, where can New Zealanders expect the next round of job losses to come from?
statement: I reject that member’s assertions, but, again, I return to the fact that the science system will need to be productive, efficient, financially sustainable, and generate real value for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether the Parliamentary Commissioner's warning has been proven right. Reti engages the question directly by saying it is too early — that analysis belongs at the end of the reforms — and adds that he is encouraged so far, which leans against the Commissioner. He declines to give the yes/no but states plainly why, so it is a partial rather than an evasion.
question: Has the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment been proven right when he warned that it is seldom worth such upheavals due to the “loss in productivity and morale”?
statement: Considering we’re still progressing through the science reforms, that’s a decision and an analysis to be had at the end of the reforms, but I have high expectations and I’m encouraged by the reforms to date.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes.' Complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he thinks New Zealanders are comfortable with 12-14 percent of children in poverty. 'No New Zealander wants to see children living in poverty' is a direct answer to the comfort question (no), before pivoting to the economy. The core was reached, then left.
question: Does he think New Zealanders are comfortable with the 12 to 14 percent of our children—roughly, the population of Tauranga—living in poverty?
statement: No New Zealander wants to see children living in poverty; again, that is why this Government is doing everything it can to grow the economy.

explanation: Asked to explain the kinds of trade-offs families in hardship face (doctor vs food, heating vs school supplies). Luxon concedes times have been tough and moves immediately to running the economy and blaming inflation. He never describes a single choice families face — the substance asked for is untouched.
question: Can he explain to the House what kinds of choices whānau in hardship face, such as whether to go visit the doctor or buy fresh veggies, or whether to turn the heating on or buy school supplies?
statement: It has no doubt been a very difficult and tough time for many New Zealanders, and that is why, if you care about low and middle income working New Zealanders, you run the economy, and you don’t create high inflation and put an economy into recession.

explanation: Asked which policy choices his Government faces in meeting the hardship-halving promise, with options named. 'I reject the characterisation of that question' dismisses the framing but is not a stated refusal to answer nor an answer — no choice, option or alternative framing is offered. Closes the question off without engaging it.
question: Can he explain to the House what kinds of choices his Government faces in trying to meet National’s election promise to halve hardship rates by 2028, such as increasing the minimum wage in line with inflation or restricting access to benefits, or supporting better access to public and emergency housing or criminalising homelessness?
statement: I reject the characterisation of that question.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Children's Commissioner that children cannot wait for the economy, and if not why not. 'That's why this Government is working incredibly hard to control spending...' implicitly claims alignment while substituting the economic programme for an answer; the agree/disagree is never stated and the 'why not' limb is unaddressed. Gestures at the question without reaching it.
question: Does he agree with the Children’s Commissioner that “Children cannot wait for our economy to improve. Children get one chance at childhood, and we’ve got to act and get this right now.”, and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, that’s why this Government is working incredibly hard to control spending so that we lower inflation, lower interest rates, get the economy growing, and get people into work.

explanation: A narrow question: have any Government policies or actions contributed to increased child material hardship? The reply lists inflation, interest rate and growth comparisons and concedes work to do on unemployment, but never addresses whether any of his own policies contributed. Answers a different question — how the economy is tracking.
question: Have any of his Government’s policies or actions contributed to an increase in child material hardship?
statement: Well, again, this Government’s actions to control spending and lower inflation are incredibly helpful for Kiwis that have been doing it tough: 3.1 percent inflation is better than 7.3 percent; nine interest rate falls are better than 12 interest rate rises; economic growth in the last quarter of 1.1 percent is better than a shrinking economy; and, certainly, we know we’ve got work to do as we want to see more people come out of unemployment and into work.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes.' Complete.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the LNG import facility decision in light of the price spike. He answers squarely — prices rise and fall, you don't change strategy for that, 'this has actually been a good move' — which is an unambiguous yes with reasons. Padded with attacks on the previous government, but the question is answered.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s decision to build a multibillion-dollar liquefied natural gas (LNG) import facility, at a cost of billions of dollars, which every Kiwi household will pay through his Government’s new proposed gas tax, in light of the 50 percent spike in LNG prices just this week, following the recent drone strikes in the Middle East?
statement: Well, international commodity prices rise and fall. That’s inevitable. You don’t change your approach or strategy just because of that. What I can say is that banning oil and gas put a chilling effect on this country. The Lake Onslow project, at $17 billion—to be delivered in 2037 at $8,000 a household—and $800 megawatt per hour wholesale electricity prices means that we have a failed energy policy. We have dry-year risk, and, as a result, this has actually been a good move, because it has lowered the forward electricity prices by about $25 since we made that announcement. [ Interruption ]

explanation: A narrow factual question: did the Government assess supply/price disruption risk before committing? He rejects the characterisation and switches to the $50 power-bill claim and dry-year backup. Whether any assessment was done is never addressed.
question: Did the Government assess the risk of a major supply or price disruption before committing New Zealand households to pay for an LNG import facility?
statement: I reject the characterisation of that question, because this is about lowering power bills by about $50 for every single household in this country. This is a backup source of energy, so that we don’t end up in the situation that the member and his Government created last time.

explanation: The same yes/no put again with the alternatives spelled out ('did it assess, or did it not assess'). He talks about commodity prices moving and asserts the policy is still the right answer. The binary asked for is squarely avoided a second time.
question: Did the Government assess, or did it not assess, the risk of a major supply or price disruption?
statement: It’s a natural thing that LNG prices go up and down as a global commodity price, but, irrespective of that, it is still the right answer to make sure we have a backup option to deliver dry-year risk, so we take the risk premium down—

explanation: Asked whether the Government's own Infrastructure Plan is wrong on LNG and electricity prices. Luxon opens by refusing to take 'lectures' from the questioner, recounts Indonesian coal under the previous Government, and cites a $25 futures-price fall. The plan's finding is never confirmed or contradicted; the price point only glances at the question sideways.
question: Is the National Infrastructure Plan released by his Government wrong when it says it isn’t clear that importing LNG would lower average electricity prices?
statement: Look, no disrespect, but I’m not taking lectures from that member on energy policy. I saw some wonderful comments that we should be more independent and have an independent energy policy. Well, actually, the actions of that member’s Government created an importation of Indonesian coal and didn’t actually create the independent energy policy that we are creating through an “and, and, and” approach of lots of initiatives.
