Chhour does not respond to the substance but states plainly that she must take it away and verify the claim before answering, and gives a reason (the prior question was incorrect). That is a direct, stated deferral rather than a pivot to talking points — it engages the question's status squarely but withholds the answer itself, so it lands mid-scale.
question: What does she say to the caregiver who stated, “We got told about her disability but got limited information around how to work with her needs. It was really rushed, especially not knowing anything or given any information”?
statement: I think that, because the first question was incorrect, I would have to take away and verify what that member is saying before I can answer it.

explanation: Asked how placing tamariki with complex needs alongside untrained caregivers fits her stated priorities of child safety and caregiver support. Chhour answers a narrower, different question — whether the ICM report mentions untrained staff in motels — which contests the premise but never touches the 'how does this fit your priorities' core. Premise-denial is partial engagement, not an answer.
question: How does placing tamariki with complex needs in the care of untrained caregivers and insufficiently trained caregivers, like security guards, fit with the key priorities she has set, including ensuring the safety of children and young people and supporting caregivers?
statement: I have read the ICM report very closely, and there is no mention in that report of untrained staff being used to look after children in motels.

explanation: Asked on what dates he or anyone on his behalf discussed TVNZ news coverage with board members or the CEO. Goldsmith gives the dates directly (Sunday 1 March, Tuesday evening, yesterday twice) and characterises each contact. Squarely responsive to exactly what was asked.
question: On what dates has he, or any person acting on his behalf, discussed TVNZ news coverage with any member of the TVNZ Board (including the Chair of TVNZ, Andrew Barclay) or the chief executive of TVNZ?
statement: On Sunday, 1 March, I received a text message from the chair of TVNZ asking for a call. We spoke about a range of matters including TVNZ financials and board appointments, and he observed, as I recall, that TVNZ had been in the news that week over a law and order story and that he was taking an interest in it in the context of the board’s interests in improving trust in TVNZ. I didn’t engage further in the discussion on that matter. Also, on Tuesday evening, I spoke at the 60th anniversary of Country Calendar , hosted by TVNZ, and spoke with three board members and the chief executive. To the best of my knowledge, TVNZ news coverage did not come up in those conversations. The primary point of discussion was the history of Country Calendar . Yesterday, I spoke to the chair, informing him that I had been questioned about our phone call on the way out of the House, as a courtesy, and I rang him again at 6.30 yesterday evening, after the coverage over the afternoon, to check on his welfare, as he is a new chair.

explanation: Asked whether he sought an assurance from the TVNZ chair, and if not why not. Goldsmith asks for the question to be repeated, saying it had too many legs to follow. Not procedural in the point-of-order sense but nothing in the question is engaged; the substance is left entirely untouched at this exchange.
question: Has he sought an assurance from TVNZ chair Andrew Barclay in any of those conversations that he hasn’t discussed or directed the Minister’s or his ministerial colleagues’ concerns around TVNZ coverage of crime numbers on 26 February 2026 with any staff member of TVNZ, and, if not, why not?
statement: Sorry, can I ask him to repeat that? It had so many legs, I couldn’t understand it.

explanation: Asked whether he sought an assurance from the chair, and if not why not. He answers the first half flatly — 'No, I haven't sought that assurance directly' — and then addresses the 'why not' obliquely by setting out what he expects of the board. The core yes/no is met head-on; the reason is reached only by implication.
question: Has he sought an assurance from TVNZ chair Andrew Barclay that he hasn’t discussed or directed the Minister’s or his ministerial colleagues’ concerns around TVNZ coverage of crime numbers on 26 February 2026 with any staff member of TVNZ, and, if not, why not?
statement: No, I haven’t sought that assurance directly. What is my expectation of the board? The primary Government interest in TVNZ is, one, that it maintains its financial stability; two, that it’s growing its audiences and producing great quality local content; and the third thing that has been raised in my letter of expectation is building or improving levels of trust. I expect the board to have an interest in all of those topics.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee to the public that the chair has not sought to influence editorial discussions. Goldsmith says what he would expect of the board rather than guaranteeing anything, never affirming or denying that it happened. He stays on the topic but hedges around the specific thing demanded — a guarantee.
question: Is he then guaranteeing to the New Zealand public that the TVNZ chair, Andrew Barclay, has not sought to influence editorial discussions at TVNZ?
statement: Well, I wouldn’t expect the board to be interfering in editorial decisions at TVNZ. I would expect the board to have an interest in the broader issue of improving trust, as I do with the Radio New Zealand board, and that’s absolutely appropriate.

explanation: Asked whether he has regular scheduled phone calls with the TVNZ chair. Answer opens 'No, I don't' and then explains the actual pattern (formal quarterly meetings, ad hoc calls with chairs generally). Direct and complete on the point asked.
question: Does he have regular scheduled phone calls with the chair of the TVNZ board, Andrew Barclay?
statement: No, I don’t. I meet the board formally every quarter, but I’m in the habit, quite often, of speaking with chairs of entities that I’m responsible for, at all hours. That member may not be aware, but being a Minister is a busy role, and we talk to people at all hours on all sorts of topics.

explanation: Asked what notes or record he made of the 1 March phone call. Answer: 'None.' One word, and it fully resolves the question.
question: What notes or record of the phone call on Sunday, 1 March did the Minister make?
statement: None.

explanation: Asked what he said when the chair raised One News crime-numbers coverage. He states he didn't engage further and may possibly have grunted. That is a direct account of what he said (effectively nothing), addressing the question rather than deflecting it.
question: What did the Minister say when the subject of One News coverage of crime numbers was raised by TVNZ chair Andrew Barclay?
statement: As I said in answer to the first one, I didn’t engage further in the discussion on that matter. I may possibly have grunted, but I’m not sure.

explanation: Asked whether it is appropriate for a Minister to complain about TVNZ news coverage in a public forum. Goldsmith never says appropriate or inappropriate — he observes that it happens, suggests previous Labour Ministers did it too, and closes with an aphorism about farmers and the weather. The normative question posed is left unanswered.
question: Is it appropriate for a Minister to complain about TVNZ news coverage in a public forum?
statement: Well, I’m afraid that does happen from time to time, and it seems to me it’s quite possible that the previous Labour Government Ministers may have done that from time to time as well. But I’ve often made the observation that a politician complaining about the media is like a farmer complaining about the weather: you may be right, but it makes no difference, and so you’ve got to figure out how to succeed in any respect. [ Interruption ]

explanation: Asked what he has done about ministerial colleagues complaining about TVNZ coverage. He conveys, obliquely, that he does nothing about it (he'd have no time left), and adds that no Minister may direct TVNZ and 'we certainly haven't done that'. The core — what action was taken — is answered as effectively 'none', but it arrives sideways and part of the reply drifts to the legislative rule rather than his own conduct toward colleagues.
question: What, if anything, has the Minister done about other Ministers in Government complaining about news coverage at TVNZ?
statement: Well, my concern is that I might find that I have no time left to do anything else if I was bothering myself. It is unfortunately something that happens from time to time. Now, whether that’s fair or not is inappropriate. But what I am clear about is the legislative requirement that no Minister, including myself, should seek to direct TVNZ in relation to their coverage of news items, and we certainly haven’t done that. [ Interruption ]

explanation: A two-part factual question: did Mitchell raise the 26 February One News item, and when. He answers the first part squarely — 'yes, I think he did raise it with me' — and gestures at the timing ('we were together'), but never gives the 'when'. Direct on the substance, incomplete on the second limb.
question: Did Minister Mark Mitchell, or anyone on his behalf, raise One News coverage of 26 February 2026 on rising gang numbers with him or any member of his office, and if so, when?
statement: Well, yes, I think he did raise it with me. We were together and we weren’t happy with the coverage, but that happens on a regular basis. We’re quite often not happy with particular coverage, but that’s neither here nor there. Sometimes we’re right; sometimes we’re wrong. [ Interruption ]

explanation: Asked for the level the service will be scaled to in the coming year. The reply speaks only of working with and accepting more providers 'in time', never reaching any level, target or figure, and is trailing into a further point when cut off. It gestures at the topic without engaging the question asked.
question: What level can New Zealanders expect the service to be scaled to in the coming year?
statement: We are working with providers, and we will accept more providers in time. But I’d just like—

explanation: A yes/no question about whether 100,000 users would be a tenth of originally promised volumes. 'I refute that question. It was never—' is a plain rejection of the proposition, so the question is answered in the negative; the supporting clause is cut off, but the answer to what was asked is given.
question: Is it correct that, even if the service hits 100,000 users this year, it will only be operating at a 10th of the volumes that were originally promised?
statement: I refute that question. It was never—

explanation: Asked to rule out military support and, if not, to say why not. She neither rules it out nor says she won't; instead she says no request has been received and that any decision would be for joint Ministers or Cabinet. That supplies a reason bearing on the 'if not, why not' limb, but the direct ask — rule it out, yes or no — is left unanswered.
question: Will she rule out sending any military support to the USA and Israel for their military strikes on Iran, which have led to the reported deaths of 1,097 civilians, including 181 children under the age of 10; if not, why not?
statement: We have not received any requests to contribute to the US and Israel’s military action. New Zealand is not central to the issues in the Middle East. Any decision would be one for joint Ministers or Cabinet, not for the Minister of Defence alone.

explanation: Asked why she refuses to categorically rule out support. She declines to add anything new but does restate a responsive reason: no request has been received and the decision is not hers alone as Minister of Defence. That engages the 'why' asked, though by repetition and without addressing the UN-authorisation framing.
question: Why is the Minister refusing to categorically rule out supporting the illegal invasion of Iran when these strikes were not authorised by the UN Security Council and there was no evidence of an imminent threat to the USA?
statement: I’m not going to repeat the answer I’ve just given; obviously, the member hasn’t taken that into account. We have not received any request to contribute to the US and Israel’s military action. New Zealand is not central to the issues in the Middle East. Any decision would be one for joint Ministers or Cabinet. I may be the Minister of Defence, but I’m neither joint Ministers nor Cabinet.

explanation: Asked how New Zealanders can trust the Government to keep out of the invasion given National's 2003 Iraq position. 'Because we're a really sensible Government and not stupid' is structurally a direct answer to the 'how can we trust' question (contentlessness is a Specificity matter), but the Iraq premise the question rested on is entirely ignored.
question: How can Aotearoa trust that this Government will stick to their word and keep Aotearoa out of this invasion when it was the National Party who advocated for New Zealand to support the invasion of Iraq in 2003?
statement: Because we’re a really sensible Government and not stupid.

explanation: Two limbs: does she agree with the PM about the rules-based order, and how would military support bolster it. She never states agreement with the PM, but she does directly contest the second limb's premise — no military support is being sent for that purpose, only consular evacuation flights. Rejecting the premise engages the question; the first limb goes unanswered.
question: Does she agree with the Prime Minister that we have a responsibility to do everything we can to bolster the existing rules-based international order; if so, how will sending military support to aid this illegal invasion bolster the existing rules-based international order?
statement: I’m not sure that the member has any understanding that I’ve just answered the question multiple times. We are not sending military support to deal with bolstering anything. What we are doing is sending military support with Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade consular people to be able to get those New Zealanders and those from Pacific nations out of the Middle East, and our other Commonwealth friends as well, who want to come back to New Zealand. I would have thought that was pretty clear. It’s not quite the same. I can tell the member we don’t have the sort of equipment that’s being used in the Middle East.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all the Government's statements and actions. 'Yes' — direct and complete, with an illustration appended.
question: Does he stand by all of the Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes—in particular, today, our Government’s various efforts to get money into the country by making overseas investment easier and, indeed, welcoming it. We’ve seen the time taken to consent an overseas investment application drop by 60 percent, from 71 days down to 28.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by removing the Reserve Bank's dual mandate. 'Yes, absolutely', followed by the rationale. Squarely answered.
question: Does he stand by removing the dual mandate of the Reserve Bank?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, yes, absolutely. Our Government has told the Reserve Bank to focus exclusively on controlling inflation, and the reason we have done that is that we saw the pain that was caused when the Reserve Bank let go of its focus on inflation. Inflation hit 7.3 percent and it hit the poorest people, who depend on living week to week, the hardest. It was OK for people with lots of assets—their assets appreciate when the Government takes its eye off inflation, but we care about the opportunities of everyone in New Zealand to get ahead, and to do that you need a stable currency, so a dollar in your pocket today will be worth as close as possible to a dollar this time next year.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by reforming interest deductibility for landlords. 'I absolutely stand by our policy' — the yes is unambiguous, with defence of the policy attached. Fully responsive.
question: Does he stand by reforming interest deductibility for landlords?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I absolutely stand by our policy of treating people in the property business exactly the same as every other business in the country. If you have an interest expense in any business, that is a legitimate expense to deduct from your income tax liability. None of this is complicated, but all of it is important. It’s not just that we want to be consistent in principles in our tax policy; it’s also that it has had real effects for those people who are trying to buy a home. A former Prime Minister said that we were removing interest deductibility from residential property to tilt the market towards first-home buyers. You know what happened? Rents went through the roof and first-home buyers had less to save a deposit. We actually have helped first-home buyers, who are now buying homes at record levels—I think at 28 percent of new purchases—because we’ve got rents going down in many regions and flat in others after we reduced unfair taxes on renting out residential property.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the pay equity changes. 'Absolutely', then an account of what remains in place and what was removed. The question put is answered directly.
question: Does he stand by changes to pay equity?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, absolutely. The Equal Pay Act 1972 remains in place. It is still possible to take an appeal if you suffer from sex-based discrimination, and that is something that our Government remains committed to. All three parties believe that all people should be treated with equal rights and free from discrimination. But what we don’t support is a bureaucratic, Byzantine set of rules that are overly complicated, overly expensive, and amount to setting wages by judges using crazy formulae in order to distribute money to places that it wouldn’t have otherwise gone. And I say to the people on the other side: if they don’t like it and they’re going to bring pay equity back, show us the money.

explanation: Asked whether he has seen reports of anyone wanting those three policy reversals. He answers the literal question head-on — "I have not seen any such reports" (and adds he has no such intention) — before the joke about the Edmonds cookbook. The partisan padding follows the answer rather than substituting for it, so it is engaged, not dodged.
question: Has he seen reports of anyone wanting to return the Reserve Bank to a dual mandate, remove interest deductibility from landlords, and/or turn the clock back on pay equity claims?
statement: Mr Speaker, I have no such intention. I have not seen any such reports. If I did, I would assume that it was simply a bad dream—a nightmare never to be repeated—and that it couldn’t possibly happen in a country as pure and innocent as New Zealand. But just in case there was a small or remote possibility, we will be campaigning hard to make sure that the book on people’s shelves is the Edmonds Cookery Book , not “Barbara Edmonds’ Book Cookery ” .

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made about NZDF assistance in the Middle East. She states the announcement directly: agreement with the Foreign Minister to pre-deploy consular staff and two C130Js for possible civilian evacuations. Squarely on the question.
question: What recent announcements has she made about the New Zealand Defence Force providing assistance to New Zealanders in the Middle East?
statement: Overnight, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and I agreed to pre-deploy New Zealand consular staff and two C130Js to the region to be ready, when conditions allow, for any civilian evacuations. We cannot be sure when and how civilian evacuations might be possible, but we want to be ready if and when the conditions on the ground make them possible. Our New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) and Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) staff are playing a vital role in the situation, stepping up to assist New Zealanders in distress overseas. There are limits on how much we can say publicly for reasons of operational security.

explanation: Asked how the assistance demonstrates the need for high readiness. She gives the connecting reasoning — crises emerge suddenly, 3,000+ registered New Zealanders, moving people quickly depends on having C130Js and trained personnel ready. Directly responsive to the 'how' asked.
question: How does this assistance demonstrate the need for the New Zealand Defence Force to maintain a high level of readiness to help in situations like this?
statement: This situation illustrates that crises can emerge suddenly and in places where thousands of New Zealanders may require assistance. With over 3,000 New Zealanders already registered in the region and potentially thousands more unregistered, the ability to move many people quickly to safety relies on having aircraft like the C130J and skilled personnel ready to deploy.

explanation: Asked how this demonstrates the need to invest in defence capability. She does make the link — the situation shows the requirement for kit and training — though a good share of the answer is a recital of the Defence Capability Plan. The core of the question is reached, with some drift into promotion of the plan.
question: How does this demonstrate the need for New Zealand to invest in its defence capabilities?
statement: The Defence Capability Plan 2025 is the Government’s multibillion-dollar plan for a modern, combat-capable New Zealand Defence Force that pulls its weight internationally and domestically. Situations such as the one we are seeing unfold in the Middle East demonstrate first hand the requirement for our Defence Force to be both equipped with the kit they need and trained to be able to use it. The Government’s approach to defence, outlined in the plan, deliberately focuses on what we can and must do to rebuild the NZDF. We must invest very wisely in critical capability to ensure our personnel are combat-capable, interoperable, and ready to be of use to New Zealand wherever they are needed.

explanation: Asked how NZDF's contribution complements other agencies. She answers exactly that: NZDF airlift complements MFAT's consular leadership within a whole-of-government effort. The added advice to New Zealanders is extra, not evasion.
question: How does the New Zealand Defence Force’s contribution complement the work being led by other agencies?
statement: The deployment is part of the whole-of-Government effort. The NZDF’s airlift capabilities complement the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s consular leadership, with pre-deployed diplomatic staff and military air crew to prepare options for all contingencies. Our advice to New Zealanders is to leave only if it is safe and possible for them to do so. Where it is not safe to leave, shelter in place and call MFAT’s 24/7 consular call centre for support and advice.

explanation: A two-part question: does he stand by the 7,000 figure, and how many were funded in Budgets 2024 and 2025. He answers both without qualification — "Yes" and "308". Complete on both limbs; the greeting to the gallery is irrelevant to scoring.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “there are 7,000 more social houses in the country”; if so, how many of these additional houses were funded in Budgets 2024 and 2025?
statement: Yes. Since this Government came into office, over 7,000 net new social houses have been delivered. Of those, 308 were funded in Budgets 2024 and 2025, and, of course, we’ve funded lots more social and affordable homes that are under way. Finally, because Nicola Willis forgot to do it, can I say hello to Mr and Mrs Willis in the gallery.

explanation: Asked how agencies are to house people given only 308 social houses in two years. He contests the premise but then does supply an answer to the underlying 'how': Housing First places may rent from the private market, which function as social houses with subsidy. That is a responsive mechanism, though he never engages the adequacy of 308 itself.
question: How are the front-line agencies supposed to find homes for what they claim are unprecedented levels of homeless people when his Government has only delivered 308 social houses in two years?
statement: I think the member is conflating two different issues. If the member is referring to Housing First places, then we have made an explicit direction that they can look at renting homes from the private market, which essentially become social houses because they attract the extra subsidy required for that. It is not the case that the Housing First places we have funded most recently—and, indeed, that successive Governments have funded in the past—are required to be new social-housing builds. We made that decision because, as I hope the member will appreciate, we wanted to get people who were sleeping rough into homes as soon as we could.

explanation: Asked how he expects to house a growing homeless population given an 83% fall in the construction pipeline. The answer on record begins with 'future Budgets to come' and is cut off mid-sentence. What exists gestures at a response without addressing the pipeline drop or the housing expectation; on the text available it barely reaches the question.
question: How can he expect to house the growing number of homeless when the pipeline of houses contracted or under construction has dropped from 8,863 in 2023 to just 1,513 today, a drop of 83 percent in just two years?
statement: Well, a couple of points to be made in relation to that. Firstly, there are future Budgets to come, and the Government’s—

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement about the social housing register, and why he then used it. He says 'Of course' to the first and explains the second — it is the measure we have, consistent across governments, so it enables comparison. Both limbs engaged.
question: Does the Minister stand by his statement that the social housing register is not an accurate measure of need and should not be referred to as a measure of success or otherwise, and, if so, why did he just do so in response to one of my colleagues?
statement: Of course. I’ve made that point many times. But it is the measure we have, and it’s also a measure the previous Government used to work out as a proxy of need for people in need of social housing. It is not perfect, but it is the measure we have. It has been consistent across multiple Governments around the eligibility to get on to the measure; therefore, it enables comparison between different periods of time. Is it perfect? No. Is it what we have? Yes. Could it be improved? Absolutely. The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet did a report under the previous Government recommending a series of improvements to it, some of which have been actioned, some of which are part of a longer-term programme. It’s not perfect, but it’s what we’ve got.

explanation: Asked what recent ACC announcements he has made. He names it directly: last week he announced ACC's strongest rehabilitation performance in more than a decade. Framing follows, but the question is answered up front.
question: What recent announcements has he made regarding the Accident Compensation Corporation?
statement: Last week, I announced that the Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) is delivering its strongest rehabilitation performance in more than a decade. Supporting injured New Zealanders to recover and return to work and independence is a core purpose of ACC. For too long, too many New Zealanders have been left waiting for the support they needed to recover and get back to doing what they love. That is simply not acceptable. That’s why, alongside the Minister of Finance, I directed ACC to lift its performance and put rehabilitation back at the centre of everything it does.

explanation: Asked what this means for New Zealanders needing ACC support. He answers the question asked — people get the right help at the right time and better recovery outcomes — while conceding more is to be done. The answer is thin on particulars, but thinness is specificity, not evasion; it addresses the question put.
question: What does this mean for New Zealanders who need ACC support?
statement: Well, by making rehabilitation the foremost priority, ACC will be better supporting people to get the right help at the right time. It’s not complicated: when the focus is on recovery, people get better outcomes, and we are already starting to see that flow through. I want to be clear: there is a lot more yet to do but, after years of decline, it’s encouraging to see some real progress being made.

explanation: Asked what direction he gave ACC. He answers with the direction itself: the letter of expectation setting three named priorities. Directly and completely on the question.
question: What direction has he given ACC to enable these results?
statement: My direction to ACC has been clear and very deliberate. In the recent letter of expectation sent to ACC, I set out three priorities: (1) putting clients first by providing care that supports lasting recovery; (2) helping New Zealanders return to work and independence, which is a fundamental purpose of the scheme; and (3) resetting ACC by getting the organisation back to basics, with a clear focus on delivery and outcomes. When ACC is aligned to those priorities, it delivers better results for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what recent trends in performance he has seen. He names the trend directly (long-term claims pool doubled since 2017, growth exceeding 14 percent, now reduced to below 1 percent). The closing lines drift into slogan territory, but the trend was stated squarely before that.
question: What recent trends has he seen in performance?
statement: The long-term claims pool represents around 25,000 New Zealanders who have been on ACC for more than 12 months. Since 2017, this pool has grown dramatically; in fact, it has doubled, with growth exceeding 14 percent. Now, that growth reflected a system that was failing far too many people. Under this Government, that trend has been turned around, and, as of this week, growth has been reduced to below 1 percent. That’s very significant. It’s a significant shift, and it matters because behind every number is a real person. On this side of the House, we’re focused on fixing the basics and building the future; ensuring that ACC does its job properly is a key part of that.

explanation: Asked what progress has been made toward repealing and replacing the Holidays Act. She names the concrete progress: the Employment Leave Bill was introduced to Parliament this week. Directly on the question.
question: What progress has she made toward repealing and replacing the Holidays Act 2003?
statement: This week, the Government reached a huge milestone in addressing one of the most vexing issues faced by business and workers across the country. This week, the Employment Leave Bill was introduced to Parliament. It will bring simplicity and logic to the way employment leave is calculated, which prevents many headaches for both employers and employees from getting payments wrong. The Holidays Act is complex, confusing, and it has led to huge remediation costs. I am pleased we’re one step closer to getting rid of it.

explanation: Asked how the new bill differs from the current Act. She states the difference: a switch from weeks-based entitlement to hours-based accrual for annual and sick leave, plus removal of the six/twelve-month stand-downs. Complete engagement with the question asked.
question: How is the Employment Leave Bill different from the current Holidays Act?
statement: The biggest change in the Employment Leave Bill is a switch from a weeks-based entitlement system to an hours-based accrual system for both annual leave and sick leave. There will be no more wrestling with the definition of “weeks” and “days”, adjusting balances when hours of work change, or trying to define what constitutes a “working week” for staff with variable schedules. It also means no more waiting for six months to access sick leave or 12 months to access annual leave. For most people, leave entitlements will stay the same but what will change is how it is calculated.

explanation: Asked how long previous Ministers have worked on fixing the legislation. She supplies the timeline — task force set up in 2018, still no complete draft by the 2023 election — which answers the question in substance, though she never states a duration outright and closes on her own record.
question: How long have previous workplace relations and safety Ministers worked on fixing the Holidays Act legislation?
statement: When I came into this job as workplace relations and safety Minister, I was well aware of the history of Holidays Act reform, and it has been plagued by multiple delays and a growing sense of frustration from the public that the Government can’t just get the job done. The previous Government set up the Holidays Act task force in 2018, but by the 2023 election, draft legislation still wasn’t complete and ready for introduction. I am proud of the significant progress made already, to have legislation ready and available for public feedback—a milestone that successive Ministers tried and failed to reach.

explanation: Asked what feedback she received on the consultation. She reports the feedback specifically: submitters preferring fundamental change, 70 percent of technical experts and 67 percent of employers, the Law Society's characterisation, a retail franchise owner's comment. Squarely answered.
question: What feedback did she receive when she consulted on draft legislation largely based on the previous Government’s decisions?
statement: This Government agreed to test whether the previous Government’s work was hitting the mark by going out for targeted consultation on the work that they had done to date, rather than having to start from scratch. Many submitters indicated that the general framework of that bill was not a significant improvement on the current Act, and that a fundamental change would better address longstanding issues. In fact, 70 percent of technical experts and 67 percent of employers expressed a preference for more significant change to the annual leave provisions. The Law Society, in particular, described that draft bill as “unnecessarily complex” and “difficult to follow”, with some provisions more complicated than what we have now. A large retail franchise owner told us that if a business of their size had challenges interpreting the proposed changes, then small to medium employers would have found it particularly challenging to navigate those changes.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on the bill. She lists them — EMA, Business Canterbury, Simpson Grierson — with what each said. Directly responsive.
question: What reports has she seen on the Employment Leave Bill?
statement: Since the bill has been introduced, I’ve seen that the Employers and Manufacturers Association has said “it’s good to see the reforms maintaining momentum as this overhaul has been needed for a very long time.” Business Canterbury has said that “businesses will be very pleased to see this bill enter Parliament, and congratulations must go to the Government and Minister van Velden for taking a piece of legislation that has been stuck in review for years and delivering changes that will make it clearer and more workable for both employers and employees.” Simpson Grierson have said that it has been “advocating for an overhaul of the Holidays Act for more than a decade, with a key focus on the need to move from a ‘days’ and ‘weeks’ based model to an hours-based framework”, which this bill does. [ Interruption ]

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. He says 'Yes' before appending a list of talking points. The yes/no was given plainly; the padding does not undo the answer.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and particularly our actions not to spend $66 billion on Government spending and wasting it; particularly our actions not to triple the debt and incur a $10 billion interest pay; and particularly our actions not to run up inflation and interest rates to record highs. [ Interruption ]

explanation: Asked how a specific list of cost increases (parking fines, insurance levies, registration, fuel tax) helps motorists with the cost of living. He does not address how any of them help; he attributes fees generally to rates and pivots to asking Labour to support the rates cap. It brushes the topic of costs without reaching the question.
question: How do increasing parking fines, more than doubling vehicle insurance levies, increasing the cost of registering a car, or his proposed 22-cents-a-litre hike in fuel tax help Kiwi motorists with the cost of living?
statement: Well, as the member would well understand, a lot of increases in fees and charges across New Zealand are linked to increases in rates. That’s why I would really ask the member and his party to consider supporting our rates cap work, which is a big, significant driver of the cost of living for New Zealanders and it’s running at four times that of inflation.

explanation: A narrow yes/no belief question about whether funding withdrawal affected rates rises. He gives no belief and no answer, instead urging support for a list of Government reforms. A specific question fully dodged.
question: Does he believe that the Government withdrawing funding from local government for things like roading and water infrastructure has had any impact on the rates increases that councils are imposing across the country?
statement: Well, again, I just would encourage the member to support the Government around the local government reforms, removing regional councils, Resource Management Act reforms, fast track legislation—it’s all designed to get things done for New Zealanders and to lower the cost of living.

explanation: Same question put again; this time he answers 'No' outright. The follow-on material about light shows and bike lanes is padding, but the yes/no the question sought was delivered.
question: I’ll ask it again: does he believe that the Government withdrawing funding from local councils for things like roading projects and water infrastructure has had any impact on the increase in rates that people are seeing across the country?
statement: No. As we’ve said from the very beginning, we want councils focused on what they can do. We don’t think light shows on public toilet blocks here in Wellington is a good use of public money. We don’t think putting bike lanes up Molesworth Street is actually a very good use of money; it would be better in three waters assets. No, councils need to get back to basics. We encourage the member and his party to actually support good, common-sense reform.

explanation: Asked how cutting public transport funding reduced cost of living pressures. Public transport is never mentioned; he substitutes a general account of spending control and a list of things the Opposition should support. Answers a different question entirely.
question: How did cutting public transport funding, forcing some commuters to pay up to 50 percent more to go to work or school, reduce cost of living pressures for New Zealanders?
statement: Well, I can tell you what is making the most difference to cost of living pressures for New Zealanders, and that is a Government that’s got control of spending. It isn’t spending $66 billion and half of it we don’t know what we’re getting for it. It doesn’t run up debt three times, and therefore we have high interest payments and high interest rates. I’d just say to the member, if he’s very, very serious about helping the Government lower the cost of living for New Zealanders across the system, he shouldn’t be progressing a Reserve Bank of New Zealand dual mandate, he should have supported the income tax thresholds increase that we had, he should be supporting RMA reforms and fast track.

explanation: The same question repeated. He refers back to his previous answer and repeats the spending line, then explicitly turns to public transport — but only to list cancelled projects (light rail, the walking bridge, Let's Get Wellington Moving), never addressing how commuters paying up to 50 percent more eased cost of living. It reaches the topic without reaching the question.
question: Thank you. How did cutting public transport funding, forcing some commuters to pay up to 50 percent more to get to work or school, reduce the cost of living pressures on New Zealand families?
statement: I just refer the member to my previous answer. The major driver of the costs of living challenges that New Zealanders have been experiencing is actually the Government spending out of control, driving up inflation, driving up interest rates, putting the economy into a difficult place, and people losing their jobs. I would just say, with respect to public transport—if I may, to address the question—this is a Government that has stopped Auckland Light Rail, because $300 million was wasted on that; $80 million on an Auckland walking bridge; and $110 million on Let’s Get Wellington Moving, which didn’t move at all.

explanation: Asked why the Government cut apprenticeship funding in critical infrastructure. The answer never mentions apprenticeships, training or the cut at all — it pivots to the 30-year infrastructure pipeline, inflation/interest rates and building-product reform. A different question is answered.
question: Why did his Government cut funding for apprenticeships in critical infrastructure areas, exacerbating skill shortages and depriving young Kiwis of future job opportunities?
statement: As I said to the member yesterday, I’m actually very pleased with the fact that this is a Government that’s put together a 30-year infrastructure pipeline to give the industry and sector great clarity about the projects that are coming. It’s also a Government that has made sure that we get inflation and interest rates down so the development sector, who do the building and construction in this country, can crack on with it. It’s also a Government that’s lowered the cost of building and construction by opening up the market to overseas building products and doing a lot of common-sense reforms that the previous administration didn’t tackle.

explanation: Asked whether specific cuts (schools, State houses, hospitals) contributed to a $5b fall in construction activity. The answer touches the same subject areas (Nelson/Dunedin hospitals, classrooms) and implicitly disputes the 'cut' framing, but never engages the causal claim or the construction collapse. Mostly a pivot to a record recitation.
question: Did cutting $2 billion from school-building funding, $1.5 billion from State house building, and funding from hospital rebuilds contribute to the $5 billion collapse in construction activity between when he became Prime Minister and last year?
statement: I’m actually very proud about the fact that we are investing in the Nelson Hospital rebuild, the Dunedin rebuild—that we got that project the right size after the hospital pass we literally got from the other side. I’m very proud of the work that we’re doing on education and building new classrooms for our schools across this country. It turns out you don’t need to pay $1.2 million a classroom; if you pay $600,000, you can get twice as many built, and that’s what we’re doing. It’s a fantastic record. [ Interruption ]

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on the long-term fiscal position. She names the Treasury statement on the long-term fiscal position released last September and describes what it says. Squarely answered.
question: What reports has she seen on New Zealand’s long-term fiscal position?
statement: Last September, the Treasury released its latest statement on the long-term fiscal position for New Zealand. These statements are prepared every four years, and they look at least 40 years into the future. The latest statement is not advice to one particular Government; rather, it describes the environment that successive Governments will face over the next few decades. The key factor, of course, is the ageing of our population. A greater proportion of the New Zealand population will be receiving superannuation and needing healthcare, and a shrinking proportion will be working and paying tax. As a result, successive Governments will face difficult choices around spending, revenue, and management of public assets and liabilities.

explanation: Asked what Treasury says about shorter-term actions. She quotes Treasury directly on creating fiscal space by returning to surplus and reducing debt. Directly responsive; the added COVID commission material is supplementary, not a pivot.
question: What does the Treasury say about shorter-term actions?
statement: What the books look like in the short term makes a big difference to how they evolve in the longer term. In the Long-term Fiscal Statement , Treasury says, “An important first step is to create fiscal space for future shocks and choices by returning to surplus and bringing debt down to more prudent levels”. That, of course, mirrors the COVID-19 royal commission statement that “There is a pressing need to reduce public debt to provide a buffer for future pandemics or other economic shocks.” The commission pointed out that the previous Government spent too much during COVID and for too long. This Government’s fiscal strategy is about returning to surplus and bending the debt curve over, from going up to going down.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing to get the books in order. After an opening jab about pay equity, she does answer: funding front-line investment by making savings elsewhere, aimed at surplus and lower debt. A sizeable chunk is spent attacking the Opposition's stance, so it engages the question but not cleanly.
question: What is the Government doing to get the books back in order?
statement: Well, for one, we haven’t committed to find $12.8 billion for an unaffordable pay equity approach without knowing where the money will come from. The Government is investing in front-line public services like healthcare, education, and law and order, and we’re funding those investments to a large degree by making savings elsewhere in Government. The Opposition has opposed every single one of those savings measures, and so let’s be clear about what that approach means. All else being equal, if Government spending in Budget 2024 and Budget 2025 had not been offset by our Government’s savings, this year’s operating balance before gains and losses, excluding ACC revenue and expenses deficit, would be $25 billion, and net core Crown debt would be on track to reach 59 percent of GDP by the end of the forecast period. That would be a terrible starting point for dealing with the challenges of an ageing population.

explanation: Asked what Treasury recommends about prudent debt. She gives the recommendation outright — a 50 percent of GDP ceiling as the maximum prudent level in normal times. Complete and on point.
question: What does the Treasury recommend about prudent debt?
statement: Well, in the Long-term Fiscal Statement , Treasury restates its advice from 2022 on a ceiling for net core Crown debt. It notes that New Zealand faces ongoing risks from natural hazards, including a 75 percent chance that the Alpine Fault in the South Island will rupture in the next 50 years, and it emphasises again that the maximum prudent level of debt for New Zealand in normal times is 50 percent of GDP. The latest Treasury forecasts show debt staying under 50 percent of GDP and the books returning to surplus. That will take work to achieve. Ongoing savings will be necessary, but this is the starting point that New Zealand needs when considering the long-term fiscal position and our resilience to future shocks.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. 'Yes.' One word, fully responsive.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts two specific propositions (higher sunshine hours than Germany; only 1 in 35 homes with rooftop solar). He neither accepts nor disputes either figure, saying instead that there is 'more for us to do' and that the Government is interested in rooftop solar. The topic is engaged, the accept/reject core is not.
question: Does the Prime Minister accept that Aotearoa has higher average sunshine hours than Germany, one of the world’s leading solar markets, yet only one in 35 New Zealand homes has rooftop solar?
statement: Well, there’s more for us to do, and we’re very interested in rooftop solar—we think it’s part of the solution, ultimately. That’s why this Government’s made some consenting changes to make it easier for people to do so. But what’s really exciting is the fact that we’ve got a renewables boom going on in this country, and that’s because of the great energy policy that we’re building.

explanation: Asked why an LNG terminal is prioritised over rooftop solar. He rejects the either/or framing and gives an actual reason for thermal firming — it enables renewable investment, gives market certainty and covers dry-year risk that raises power prices. That reaches the 'why', though it never addresses the prioritisation-over-solar comparison directly.
question: If that is the case, why is the Government prioritising an expensive LNG import terminal instead of putting cheaper, home-grown solar power on the roofs of New Zealand families?
statement: Well, actually good energy policy is “and, and, and”, and what we have done is made sure that by getting access to thermal firming energy, that actually enables more renewable investment to take place; gives more certainty to the market; and, importantly, covers off our dry year risk, which of course the member would understand drives into a risk premium, which leads to higher power bills.

explanation: A narrow quantitative question — how many households could be fitted with solar for $4b. No number, no estimate, no refusal to estimate; he dismisses the question as 'mixing her drinks' and recites the renewables-boom talking points. A specific ask squarely avoided.
question: How many households could be fitted for solar power systems for the $1 billion price tag of the liquefied natural gas—LNG—import terminal and the $3 billion price tag of the landlord tax cuts?
statement: Well, I think the member’s mixing her drinks in that question, but I just say that—as I said in my previous answer—it’s an “and, and, and”. This is a Government that’s incredibly proud that we actually have a renewables boom under way in this country. The settings that we have put in place through fast track, which none of the Opposition parties supported, has enabled that to happen. The work that we’re doing to reach out to investors overseas and here in New Zealand to expand solar, to expand wind, to expand geothermal is all very good. The fact that we have coal, the fact that we have gas—that’s all good because we need that for dry year risk, and that’s actually about lowering power bills.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware of specific Rewiring Aotearoa modelling (80% solar uptake ≈ 29 days of hydro storage). He never says whether he has seen it or engages the figure, only that the Government is 'very interested' in rooftop solar's role. The subject is acknowledged; the awareness question is left unanswered.
question: Is the Prime Minister aware that the modelling from Rewiring Aotearoa shows that if 80 percent of New Zealand homes had solar, it could provide the equivalent backup of up to 29 days of additional hydro storage?
statement: In answer to my earlier questions, that’s why this Government’s very interested in the role that rooftop solar can play in our total energy mix.

explanation: Asked why the Government chooses imported gas and landlords over home-grown solar. 'I reject the characterisation of that question' is a plain, direct response to the premise rather than a pivot — he is stating the choice as framed does not exist. But a 'why' question is left with no reason given, so it engages the question without fully resolving it.
question: Why is the Government choosing imported gas and the wellbeing of landlords over home-grown solar energy for whānau in Aotearoa?
statement: Well, I reject the characterisation of that question.

explanation: Asked a binary factual question — higher or lower than when she took office. The answer gives an inherited-baseline figure, blames trends starting in 2022, cites the COVID royal commission on Labour, and never states higher or lower. The 'worse before it gets better' line only gestures at the answer.
question: Is the number of people receiving jobseeker support benefit higher or lower now than it was when she took office?
statement: We inherited an economic downturn where close to 190,000 people were on the jobseeker benefit, and jobseeker numbers have been rising steadily since 2022, before we took office. Just yesterday, the COVID-19 royal commission inquiry found Labour’s increased spending drove up Government debt and inflation, which leads to higher unemployment. That’s why the forecast has always been due to get worse before it gets better. That’s why we’re fixing the basics—

explanation: A narrow arithmetic question — how many must come off to hit the 50,000 target. No number responsive to the target is given; instead a different number (83,000 exits into jobs) plus an invitation to celebrate. The core is untouched.
question: Can I ask the Minister how many people will have to come off the benefit for the Government to reach their target of 50,000 fewer people on a jobseeker support benefit?
statement: Well, as I’ve said in this House, we are absolutely focused on reducing the number of people on the jobseeker benefit, which is why I’m proud, despite still having the hangover of the previous Government’s excessive spending in the COVID years, we are seeing 83,000 New Zealanders exit benefit into jobs, which is great news, and I thought that member would celebrate with me.

explanation: Two legs: does she stand by the statement (answered squarely — 'absolutely, yes') and when does she expect a reduction (never answered; 'green shoots', filled jobs, participation rate, then inherited-legacy material). Half the question engaged.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. To the Minister, does she stand by her statement that “2026 will be the year that my progress towards the jobseeker target starts heading in the right direction.”, and, if so, when does she expect to see a reduction?
statement: Well, absolutely, yes, and what we are seeing are green shoots in terms of economic recovery if you look at the latest filled jobs data, showing the strongest annual growth in the hospitality sector. We’re also seeing confidence in the construction sector. We’re seeing the labour force participation rate increasing, which is one of the earliest indicators of labour market recovery. So, absolutely, I’m encouraged by what we are seeing. We are dealing with what we inherited from the previous Government, where Auckland was locked down for longer than it needed to be and the Government spent excessively, which led to higher unemployment.

explanation: Asked whether she commissioned officials to model long-term social and fiscal costs. The answer points to an unrelated Treasury COVID forecast being debated later and tells the questioner to look in the mirror. Never says whether such modelling was requested.
question: Has she asked officials to model the long-term social and fiscal costs of pushing more people into severe hardship because of her policies, or is she only interested in rhetoric rather than action?
statement: Well, just later in the day, we will be debating in this Parliament the Treasury long-term forecast or impact of what we saw during the COVID years that very much directly affected New Zealanders and the challenges they face today. So I suggest that member look in the mirror.

explanation: Asked whether she advised the PM his policies would raise jobseeker numbers, and if not why not. The answer restates inherited trends and lists a chambers-of-commerce partnership. Neither leg — did she advise, or why not — is addressed.
question: When the Prime Minister promised to fix the economy, did she advise him that his policies would instead lead to more than the population of Wellington city in terms of jobseeker benefits, and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, I said in my answer to the primary question: unfortunately, we inherited trends of rising numbers on the jobseeker benefit—unemployment has been increasing since 2021, and the jobseeker numbers going up since 2022. What we have done to fix the basics is create a far more active welfare system, including what we launched last week: an industry partnership with chambers of commerce up and down New Zealand, to support more New Zealanders into work.

explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should trust her to fix unemployment. She supplies an actual reason: the Government is addressing what it says are root causes (spending, inflation, interest rates) and driving growth, with a sector example. It engages the 'why trust' question rather than pivoting, though it ignores the specific record cited in the premise.
question: OK, I’ll go to my next supplementary, then, Mr Speaker. To the Minister: why should hard-working New Zealanders trust the Minister to fix unemployment and reduce job seekers when, under her watch, job seekers have increased every quarter, unemployment is at a 10-year high, and homelessness is out of control?
statement: Because it’s very simple: this is a Government that has been absolutely focused on reducing excessive Government spending which led to higher levels of inflation, higher interest rates, which leads to unemployment. So we are dealing with the root causes of what we have inherited. That’s why we have been focused on economic growth. We know that is what drives down the cost of living and supports more opportunities for New Zealanders being in work. If I look at one area we are focused on economic growth, it is tourism and hospitality—to the year to March 23, an extra 9,000 in employment, just in that one sector alone.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Two legs: standing by the quote (answered — yes) and committing to support victims of illegal aggression (explicitly set aside by answering only 'the first leg'). Transparent about what he is not answering, but the substantive second leg is left unengaged.
question: Does he stand by his statement: “As Prime Minister, I have a responsibility to do everything I can to bolster the existing rules-based order and to further strengthen New Zealand’s position offshore.”, and, if so, will he commit to supporting countries and peoples that are victims of illegal aggression?
statement: In answer to the first leg of the question, yes.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to material support for the displaced in Lebanon, and if not, why not. The answer discusses Israel's right to self-defence and calls the response heavy-handed, but never says whether support will be provided nor gives a reason for declining.
question: Will he commit to providing material support to the 700,000 people displaced from their homes in Lebanon by Israeli attacks, and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, Israel obviously has a right to self-defence against Hezbollah. You know, we would note that their response has been heavy-handed, it’s causing mass displacement, and it actually further destabilises what is already a very fragile region.

explanation: Asked what difference he sees between the two displaced populations. He does name a distinction — the Lebanon conflict involves Hezbollah, a terrorist organisation — after dismissing the comparison. Curt and largely unelaborated, but it reaches the question rather than sidestepping it.
question: What does he see as the difference between the people displaced by a war of aggression in Lebanon, whom he will not commit to providing aid to, and the people displaced by Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine, which he did provide aid to?
statement: Well, that comparison is embarrassing. Hezbollah is a terrorist organisation.

explanation: Asked for the criteria for a blanket visa extension. The answer describes the Iranian caseload, case-by-case handling by Immigration NZ, and the Minister's monitoring. No criteria are stated at any point.
question: What is the criteria for his Government to introduce a blanket visa extension for people in New Zealand whose countries are at war or under attack, as was done for Ukraine?
statement: I just would reassure the member that with respect to Iranians that are in New Zealand and need a visa extension—my advice that I’ve received is that there’s around about 130 whose visas might expire in the next two months—we have an excellent Immigration New Zealand response and a dedicated team that’s able to help them on a case-by-case basis. Of course, the Minister is monitoring the situation closely, and if she needs to change special directions in due course, she’ll give that some consideration.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the quoted constituent and whether he will push for a blanket extension. He restates the case-by-case approach and refers Muhammad to Immigration NZ, which implies a no without ever saying so; neither agreement nor the commitment question is directly answered.
question: Does he agree with Muhammad, an Iranian man with a 72-year-old mother on a visitor visa, who told The Post , “If they automatically extended the visas that would have been a great help from the Government and also peace of mind. They did that for Ukrainians … with a pathway to residency. So for us, it could be the same.”; if so, will he push for a blanket extension of visas for people affected by the war?
statement: As I said earlier, I just encourage Muhammad to reach out to Immigration New Zealand if his visa is expiring. The important thing is that Immigration New Zealand has set up dedicated resources and a team to actually respond to visa issues case by case.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on housing affordability. He names a specific report (Cotality) and recites its findings. The question is answered directly and completely.
question: What reports has he seen on housing affordability?
statement: Just this morning, I saw a report from Cotality showing that housing affordability in New Zealand has improved to its best level in almost a decade due to stable housing prices, rising wages, and falling mortgage rates. There are many measures of housing affordability, and all are looking good under this Government. Cotality says that in quarter four 2025, the house price to income ratio was 7.2, down from above 10 in 2021. The average years needed to save for a home deposit has also fallen from 13.4 years post-COVID to 9.6 years today. To top it all off, there’s been a huge improvement in mortgage payments as a percentage of household income, down from twin peaks of 56 percent in early 2022 and late 2023 to 42 percent now. This coalition Government doesn’t just talk about it; we deliver on housing affordability.

explanation: Asked what other evidence he has seen. He points to the HUD housing affordability indicator dashboard and its three indicators. Squarely responsive.
question: What other evidence has he seen on improved housing affordability in New Zealand?
statement: The Ministry of Housing and Urban Development has a housing affordability indicator dashboard on its website. It’s got three indicators—deposit affordability, mortgage serviceability, and rent affordability—and all three have improved since we came into Government. The rent affordability indicator shows that rents are the most affordable they have been since the series started in 2003, and over the last two years, with responsible fiscal management— mihi ana ki a koe e te Minita Pūtea Willis —an improvement of economic conditions. We have created the environment for low inflation and low interest rates, and since December 2023, the mortgage serviceability indicator has improved by 60 percent.

explanation: Asked what more affordable housing means for Kiwis. He answers on its own terms — more money in hand, more accessible homeownership, first-home buyer share. The 'Go the Chiefs' flourish is off-topic but the question was reached.
question: What does more affordable housing mean for Kiwis?
statement: Improved housing affordability means more pūtea in the hand for Kiwis. It means that our whānau can go to the movies now and again, or nanny can buy—especially in Hamilton West—rugby boots for her mokopuna for the season. It also makes homeownership more accessible. We’re starting to see more affordable housing bear fruit for whānau. In the December 2025 quarter, first-home buyers dominated New Zealand’s housing market and accounted for 28.4 percent of property purchases—the highest level ever recorded by Cotality. Go the Chiefs.

explanation: A closed question — has he seen evidence of rents up 10 percent? He answers 'no' explicitly and states what the measures he relies on show. Complete.
question: Has he seen any evidence of average rent prices going up 10 percent in the last year?
statement: Unlike some members of this House have asserted, no. I’m advised that the credible measures of rent price changes show that rents are flat. For instance, the stock measure, Stats New Zealand’s rent price index measure, shows rents up 1.2 percent in the year to January 2026—lower than inflation. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Development’s measure shows rents up 0.4 percent in the year to January 2026.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about counselling costs and six-month waits. He never says whether he is concerned, and cost is untouched, but the access-time and workforce statistics do engage the waiting-times half of the premise. Partial.
question: Is he concerned that unaffordable counselling costs and waiting times of up to six months for funded services are preventing many New Zealanders from accessing mental health care?
statement: Our mental health plan is working. We’re delivering faster access to support and more front-line workers: 83 percent of Kiwis are now accessing primary mental health support within one week; 82 percent of Kiwis are now accessing specialist mental health support within three weeks. The front-line mental health workforce has grown by 11 percent since coming into Government. The child and adolescent mental health workforce has grown by 19 percent. Last week’s Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission report found an extra 35,000 adults were seen last year due to 557 more specialist front-line staff.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned that funding, not counsellor capacity, is the binding constraint. He responds about growth in numbers served, which is adjacent and implies 'no', but never engages the funding-constraint claim itself.
question: Is he concerned that counsellors report that they could see more clients yet people remain stuck on waiting lists because funding is not available to them?
statement: I’m happy to announce to the House that when you look at primary counselling support, when we came into office, that was sitting at 200,000 Kiwis a year; we’ve now grown that to 250,000 Kiwis a year.

explanation: Two-part question: is he concerned about one in five counsellors leaving, and what impact on waiting lists? He answers neither part, offering instead an accreditation pathway that adds counsellors. Related to workforce supply, but the attrition concern and the waiting-list impact are both left unaddressed.
question: Is he concerned that around one in five counsellors say they are considering reducing hours, retiring, or leaving the profession within two years, and what impact will that have on already long waiting lists?
statement: Well, I’ve got a deal for them. Last year, we opened up the accreditation pathway so a further 330 counsellors can now be registered—when previously they couldn’t have been—to work for Health New Zealand publicly funded roles.

explanation: Asked why the private-pay patient gets faster help than the publicly funded one. He does not justify the disparity but directly contests the premise, saying the report showed private costs rising and private delays. Challenging the premise head-on is engagement, not evasion, though the underlying 'why' is left unanswered.
question: Why should someone who can afford private counselling be able to get help quickly while someone relying on funded support can be left waiting months?
statement: Ah, she’s bit confused there, because the premise of the report was, actually, that for private counsellors, the cost was going up, resulting in delays for people going private, which is quite contrary to that question.

explanation: Asked whether mental health care shouldn't be available on need rather than ability to pay. He never addresses the principle, pivoting to the questioner's party and Gumboot Friday funding. A pivot to attack and talking points.
question: Shouldn’t mental health care be available for people who need help, not just those who can afford it?
statement: The irony here is that we are talking about counsellors, and that member and her team rallied when this Government committed $24 million directly to fund 800 more counsellors on Gumboot Friday to deliver to 15,000 young people more access and support. We’re delivering for counsellors too.

explanation: Asked what actions he has taken on fuel market fairness. He lists them: a letter to the Commerce Commission setting monitoring expectations and a joint letter to fuel companies. Directly answered.
question: What actions has he taken, if any, to ensure fuel markets continue to operate fairly and transparently for New Zealanders?
statement: In a time of global uncertainty affecting international oil markets, it’s important that expectations are clear and oversight is strong. So, to that end, I’ve written to the Commerce Commission to clearly set my expectation that it closely monitor wholesale and retail fuel prices, as well as importer margins, to ensure motorists continue to receive a fair deal at the pump. At the same time, the Minister for Energy and I have also written directly to fuel companies to reinforce those expectations and encourage open and constructive engagement. When global conditions are uncertain, it is right for Government to set clear expectations and work with industry to safeguard fair outcomes for New Zealanders.

explanation: Two-part question — why he wrote and what expectations he set. He gives the reason (the Commission's monitoring role) and states the expectations (increased monitoring frequency, engagement on questionable behaviour). Both parts covered.
question: Why did the Minister write to the Commerce Commission, and what expectations has he set for his role during this period?
statement: The Commerce Commission plays a central role in supporting confidence in the fuel market. They do this by monitoring prices, margins, and engaging, where necessary, to ensure pricing reflects market conditions. In my letter, I asked the Commerce Commission to increase the frequency of its fuel price monitoring to closely watch pricing behaviour and margins and to engage with industry and consumers if any questionable behaviour emerges. The expectation is straightforward: it’s about giving households and businesses confidence that fuel prices are fair and reflect real market conditions.

explanation: Asked why they wrote directly to fuel companies. He gives the reason — transparency about government steps and reinforcing fair pricing expectations during volatility. Directly on point.
question: Why did the Minster and the Minister for Energy also write directly to fuel companies?
statement: The Minister for Energy and I wrote to fuel companies to be transparent about the steps the Government is taking and to emphasise the importance of fair pricing and clear communications during a period of volatility. This was not about making accusations, but about setting expectations and reinforcing the value of open constructive engagement between Government and industry. Fuel companies have an important role in maintaining public confidence, especially when global conditions are uncertain as they are currently.

explanation: Asked how the steps protect households/businesses while keeping the market competitive. Simpson names the mechanism (strengthened monitoring, open communication channels so price movements reflect genuine global pressures rather than unjustifiable increases) and explicitly addresses the balance between consumer protection and a well-functioning market. Trails into general government framing at the end, but the core of the question is engaged.
question: How do these steps help protect households and businesses while still supporting a competitive fuel market?
statement: New Zealanders, rightly, expect a competitive fuel market and the confidence that they are being treated fairly. By strengthening monitoring and keeping communication channels open, we are helping to ensure price movements reflect genuine global pressures, not unjustifiable increases. I also want to acknowledge the fuel sector’s ongoing contribution through the Fuel Sector Coordinating Entity, which is especially valuable at times like this. The balance between strong consumer protection and a well-functioning market is central to this Government’s work on fixing the basics and building for the future.

explanation: Asked whether he has concerns about LNG price volatility wiping out forecast savings, and if not, why not. Answer gives the direct 'no I am not' and then the 'why not' (forward electricity prices down ~13% / $20/MWh since the announcement, showing market confidence). Both limbs answered.
question: Does he have concerns about the volatility of international liquefied natural gas prices eliminating the forecast cost savings from the proposed liquefied natural gas import terminal; if not, why not?
statement: As I answered in the House last week, when the member asked this question, no I am not. Forward prices for electricity have declined about 13 percent, or $20 a megawatt hour since the Government’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) announcement. This clearly shows that despite international events, the market is confident that LNG will work as an insurance for the sector during a dry year.

explanation: Asked why electricity users rather than gas users are being levied. One-line answer: 'Because LNG is an insurance policy for the electricity sector' — a direct causal answer to the 'why'. It does not engage the questioner's premise about gas users being the primary beneficiaries, but the question asked for his reason and his reason was given.
question: Why did he decide that electricity users should be the ones levied for an LNG import terminal, when gas users will be the primary beneficiary of LNG by having an alternative to dwindling domestic supplies?
statement: Because LNG is an insurance policy for the electricity sector.

explanation: Asked whether a terminal would be commercially viable without the levy, and if not whether that shows electricity market failure. Neither limb is answered — no statement on commercial viability, nothing on market failure. Instead it restates the dry-year risk-premium rationale and pivots to blaming the previous Government for stopping gas exploration.
question: Would a liquefied natural gas terminal be commercially viable as a dry-year solution without the Government intervention to levy electricity users; if not, does this indicate that the electricity market has failed to deliver a solution for the dry-year problem?
statement: As I have noted previously, there is a risk premium built into power bills for households and businesses as a result of a lack of dry-year cover when we have insufficient rain, wind, and solar, and hence the solution required is to ensure that we have cover in a dry year, which is produced by both coal and gas. The challenge is that the last Government stopped gas exploration and, as a result, we have no gas. So we are looking to import that.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts that (a) the savings are estimates only and (b) the only guarantee is extra levied costs on electricity users. He implicitly contests (a) by pointing to actually-traded futures prices rather than estimates, which touches the first limb, but never addresses the second limb about guaranteed extra costs and never says whether he accepts the characterisation. Partial engagement.
question: Does he accept that any cost savings from an LNG terminal are estimates only, and that the only thing guaranteed about an LNG terminal is that there will be extra costs levied on electricity users in New Zealand households?
statement: As I answered in my primary answer, the member only needs to look at the future prices of electricity, which are traded on the Australian Stock Exchange and other exchanges, to see the numbers I have quoted. The pricing for 2027, 2028, and 2029 are all below or exceeding $20 per megawatt hour. Again, that is a reflection that the market has confidence that the solution which this Government is going to undertake deals with the challenge and the problem which we have, which is lack of cover in a dry year.

explanation: Asked whether she is confident $50m/year of cuts won't affect firefighter and public safety, and why. She disputes the premise (not cuts, cost efficiencies) and then answers the safety limb directly — $84.7m of investment in trucks, property and equipment that will improve working conditions and safety. Disputing a premise while still asserting a safety position engages the question.
question: Is she confident that Fire and Emergency New Zealand’s cuts of $50 million a year will not impact the safety of firefighters and the public; if so, why?
statement: Fire and Emergency New Zealand is not making cuts of $50 million per year; they are looking for cost efficiencies, something I support. In fact, I’m advised that in this financial year alone, they are planning to invest $84.7 million in new fire trucks, property, and equipment, all of which will contribute to improved working conditions as well as the safety of firefighters and of the public.

explanation: Asked whether cancelling recruit courses keeps the public and firefighters safe. She responds squarely to the question put — says she is not aware of any cancellation and will take it back to her office. That is a plain, non-evasive response addressing the premise head-on, though it leaves the underlying safety question unanswered because she disclaims knowledge.
question: Will cancelling recruit courses for professional firefighters keep the public and firefighters safe?
statement: I’m not aware of cancelling of recruitment, so I will take that one back to my office.

explanation: Asked whether cutting fire prevention, wildfire and support roles keeps people safe.
