explanation: Asked what the maths policy means for parents; the answer speaks directly to parents and enumerates what they can expect (curriculum, hour a day, workbooks, assessment, reporting, acceleration support). Squarely on the question asked.
question: What does this mean for parents?
statement: Parents can feel confident that we are delivering a cohesive approach to mathematics education: a clear, consistent, structured curriculum; an hour a day of maths; workbooks in the hands of every primary child; consistent nationwide assessment of progress, alongside clear reporting to parents; and effective, targeted acceleration supports for students who need it. We are committed to raising achievement and we’re not just talking about it; we’re doing it.

explanation: Standard 'does she stand by all her statements and actions' — answered 'In context, yes.' A direct yes with a qualifier; the core is engaged, not dodged.
question: Vinaka vakalevu, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: In context, yes.

explanation: Narrow question of whether the economy is shrinking. The reply says only that she is unaware of the context or quote — it never engages the substantive claim, which stands on its own regardless of the quote's provenance. A clear deflection of a specific factual question.
question: Is the Prime Minister correct that under her Government, New Zealand’s economy is shrinking?
statement: I’m not aware of the context or quote that the member is referring to.

explanation: Asked whether Stats NZ is wrong on real GDP per quarter being smaller. The reply concedes Stats NZ generally gets it right (an implicit 'no, they're not wrong') but immediately pivots to nominal GDP rather than confirming or denying the real per-quarter figure. Half-answered, with the core skirted.
question: Is Stats New Zealand wrong when it shows that real GDP per quarter is smaller now than when she took office?
statement: In general, Stats NZ gets it right, and they also show that nominal GDP is larger.

explanation: Asked whether she thinks the 52 percent of pessimistic Kiwis are practising 'glass half-empty economics'. Answered 'No, not at all,' with her own account of why they feel that way. The closing jab at the questioner is a Civility/Focus matter, not evasion — the question itself was answered outright.
question: Does she think that 52 percent of Kiwis that are now pessimistic about the state of our economy under her leadership are in the habit of “glass half-empty economics”?
statement: No, not at all. I think they’re living in the real world, where there’s a huge conflict in the Middle East and where we are experiencing the largest oil shock in history. New Zealanders are alive to the fact that those events have implications back at home, and it makes them feel somewhat pessimistic about the state of the world and realistic about the fact that New Zealand will be impacted by that. That member may be living in a delusion where she thinks that events in the Middle East don’t have an impact here, but New Zealanders are not.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees only full-time working families count as working families. Answered 'no', disputed the premise about what the PM said, and explained the actual in-work tax credit criteria. Direct.
question: Does she agree with the Prime Minister that only full-time working families are a working family?
statement: Well, no, and that’s not what the Prime Minister said. The in-work tax credit is available to families where they are not dependent on a benefit. It is often the case that Working for Families recipients have one parent working and another parent working part-time; the point is they are not dependent on the Government for benefit support.

explanation: Asked whether Bishop's remark reflects on her performance as Minister of Finance. Answered 'No' plainly; the follow-on line about attempts to divide them is commentary on the questioner's motive but does not displace the answer already given.
question: When Chris Bishop, on her behalf, said that the economy should be doing better, is that a reflection of how she is performing as Minister of Finance?
statement: No. Attempts to divide Chris Bishop and I will always fail.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has received on granny flats. Characterises the feedback as extremely positive and gives a concrete instance (New Plymouth builders). Answers what was asked.
question: What feedback, if any, has he received on granny flats?
statement: The feedback on granny flats has been extremely positive. Where Kiwis used to look at their backyards and see red tape, high costs, and long delays, now they see endless possibilities, or at least up to 70 square metres’ worth. Just recently in New Plymouth, with my colleague and friend David MacLeod MP, a group of builders told us that after decades in the industry, it is finally good to see rules becoming easier and not harder for a change, and there is more where that came from.

explanation: Asked how much interest there has been; gives quantities directly — 94,000 page views and 52,000 downloads. Exactly the question asked.
question: How much interest has there been in the granny flat changes?
statement: There’s been significant interest in granny flats, which shows that the public supports the Government’s plans to make it easier, faster, and more affordable to build. Officials have told me that there have been some 94,000 views of the granny flat guidance web page and 52,000 downloads of the supporting resources. This indicates strong demand by homeowners, tradies, and, of course, businesses.

explanation: Asked whether the Government is making changes to the granny flat rules. Answers 'Yes' and then states what the changes are. Complete.
question: Is the Government making any changes to the granny flat rules?
statement: Yes, and, in fact, today the Government announced, through Mr Jones, Mr Bishop, and me, that we are making changes to the rules to make the regime even easier than we had first said that it would be to use. These include specifically allowing for off-site construction to begin before a project information memorandum, or PIM, is issued by the local council. This will be a game-changer for the off-site manufacturing of minor dwellings. In addition, we are making changes to allow for more products to be used to construct granny flats, such as structural insulated panels with a CodeMark certificate.

explanation: Asked for the benefits of granny flats; begins on point with more choice about how and where families live, but the answer is cut off mid-sentence. What was delivered addresses the question; the truncation limits completeness.
question: What are the benefits of granny flats?
statement: Granny flats give Kiwi families more choice about how and where they want to live. They allow—

explanation: Asked whether he supports all of his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes.' One word, and complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about exposure to imported inflation. He describes efforts to minimise fuel-crisis impacts on inflation and a 'balanced approach', which engages the inflation topic and implies concern, but never states whether he is concerned about *imported* inflation specifically. Partial.
question: Is the Prime Minister concerned about our country’s exposure to imported inflation?
statement: We are working very hard to minimise the impacts of the fuel crisis on both inflation and growth, and that’s why we’re taking a very balanced approach to make sure we don’t repeat the mistakes of COVID—causing high levels of inflation and interest rates—while also trying to support vulnerable New Zealanders.

explanation: A narrow definitional question — what does he understand imported inflation to be. He asserts that he understands inflation and offers no definition at all. The core of the question is entirely unaddressed.
question: What does the Prime Minister understand imported inflation to be?
statement: I understand inflation, rest assured. To the member, I understand inflation.

explanation: Two parts: has he read the Moody's/Fitch reports, and what exactly is the Government doing to reduce exposure. He acknowledges the negative outlooks (glancing at part one) but gives no reading answer and no government action; instead pivots to attacking the questioner's borrowing and tax policy.
question: Has the Prime Minister read reports from Moody’s and Fitch downgrading our country’s credit rating outlook for reasons including our exposure to imported inflation, and, if so, what exactly is his Government doing to reduce our exposure to imported inflation?
statement: Well, look, I want to thank the member for raising the issue of the credit ratings because we have a negative outlook from both Moody’s and from Fitch. What’s quite obvious is that they are saying, very clearly, spend more, tax more, borrow more is not the way forward to manage our fiscal track. I’d just say to that member, if she took those warnings seriously, she’d backtrack from her policy of, actually, borrowing another $44 billion and increasing taxes by another $90 billion.

explanation: Asked a binary — has the LNG import facility increased or decreased exposure to imported inflation. He does not touch the LNG decision or the direction of exposure, pivoting entirely to blaming the questioner's party for the oil and gas ban.
question: Has his Government increased or decreased our exposure to imported inflation as a result of his $1 billion decision to invest in a new liquefied natural gas import facility?
statement: Well, I’d just say the single biggest thing that that member needs to take accountability for is the oil and gas ban. That is what has created a huge disfunction within our energy policy in this country. That’s what this Government’s fixing up.

explanation: Asked to name one action reducing exposure to imported inflation. He names one: fast-track consenting of renewable projects, with examples. That is squarely the thing asked for, whatever its merits.
question: Can the Prime Minister name just one action of his Government to reduce our country’s exposure to imported inflation?
statement: I would just point to the work of fast track, which is now rapidly consenting renewable projects up and down this country, including, just in the last week, where a housing development with renewable energy was supported; including projects in the South Island that were cancelled or not progressed under the previous administration and that power up 100,000 homes with renewable energy. That’s a good thing.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes' — direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Two direct asks: does he agree the Treaty clause review achieves the same effect as the Treaty principles bill, and will he vote against resulting legislation. Neither is answered; he describes the aim of removing uncertainty in generic Treaty clauses instead.
question: Does the Prime Minister agree that the Treaty clause review will achieve the same effect as the Treaty principles bill, and, if so, will he be voting against any resulting legislation, just as he voted against the Treaty principles bill?
statement: Well, what we’re doing is we’re making sure that there isn’t any uncertainty and that everybody’s clear with their obligations under legislation. Open ended, generic Treaty clauses cause confusion and don’t give clarity. We want them to be specific.

explanation: Asked to name a single piece of legislation where Te Tiriti protections were strengthened. No legislation is named and no acknowledgement that he cannot; he restates the problem his own policy addresses. The specific item requested is never supplied.
question: Can he name a single piece of legislation where Te Tiriti o Waitangi protections have been strengthened under this Government?
statement: Well, again, I’d just say the problem that we’re trying to address with this legislation are generic Treaty principle clauses that variously say, “give effect to” and “take account of” the principles. What we want is consistency so that everybody has clarity about the obligations they have to each other.

explanation: Asked whether Treaty clauses are being removed to avoid honouring Te Tiriti. Answers 'No' and rejects the characterisation — an unambiguous, complete response to the yes/no put to him.
question: Is his Government removing Treaty clauses from legislation so that they can avoid honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi in practice?
statement: No, and I reject the characterisation of that question.

explanation: Asked whether he denies this is a systemic roll-back. He responds 'No' followed by a rebuttal of the roll-back framing; the intent (rejecting the characterisation) is clear and engaged, though the literal 'No' to 'do you deny' leaves a small ambiguity about which way he answered.
question: Does he deny that this is a systemic roll-back of Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: No, this is about making sure that everyone understands their specific roles and obligation to each other by having specific clauses that are relevant to the legislation.

explanation: A narrow factual question about forecast spending on the Treaty clause review. No figure, no range, no refusal to give one — just a comparative jab at the questioner's party's tax policy.
question: How much money is forecasted to be spend on the Treaty clause review in addition to the millions of dollars that have already been wasted on the failed Treaty principles bill?
statement: I can tell you, a lot less than Te Pāti Māori’s taxation policy.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Bishop's statement on homelessness. Answers 'Yes' explicitly, then extends it. Directly and completely responsive.
question: Does he agree with the Hon Chris Bishop’s statement, “Homelessness is complex and there are no easy answers, but we’re determined to take meaningful actions”?
statement: Āna. Yes, and particularly the full statement and comment that was made by my erudite colleague, Minister Bishop: “Homelessness is complex and there are no easy answers, but we’re determined to take meaningful actions—like our Priority One policy which has seen more than 2,100 children and their families moved from emergency housing motels into homes.” May I add that that number is now nearly 2,400 children out of emergency housing into social housing, in addition to an extra circa 1,000 children that have come out of emergency housing and contracted emergency housing since this Government took office.

explanation: Asked how a $2,000 fine on rough sleepers constitutes meaningful action. The Minister says he is 'not across the $2,000 matter' — a brief acknowledgement — then pivots entirely to unrelated praise from housing providers about Housing First places. The core question (how the fine is meaningful) is never engaged, and the disclaimer is used as a springboard away from it rather than as a complete answer.
question: How is fining rough sleepers $2,000, as enabled under the Government’s move-on powers, a meaningful action?
statement: I’m not across the $2,000 matter, but what I am across are the walks that I go on with community housing providers and councils throughout the country, who have said that the actions that this Government have taken, particularly since the announcement of the Housing First 300 places, funded in September 2025, have made a considerable and material impact on the lives of many Kiwis and many New Zealanders and their whānau.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: is Lt Col Hutson wrong that move-on powers just shift homelessness? The answer redirects to another Minister's portfolio (a partial, legitimate deflection) but then supplies a long unrelated passage about nightshelter visits and provider support, never saying whether Hutson is right or wrong. The pivot dominates; the yes/no is left untouched.
question: Is the Salvation Army’s Lieutenant Colonel Ian Hutson wrong when he said, “Move-on powers don’t solve homelessness. They just shift it somewhere else.”?
statement: Matters to do with the move-on orders should be directed to the Minister responsible for that, but what I would say is this: the various community housing providers and transitional housing providers, including the Hamilton Christian Nightshelter, which the member of Parliament Ryan Hamilton and I have visited recently, have become far more aware of the intent of that proposed legislation and are absolutely supportive of this Government to continue to work closely with community housing providers and others to support Kiwis in need.

explanation: Asked whether Paul Gilberd is wrong that move-on powers don't work. The reply gestures at the question by claiming Gilberd and others are 'enthusiastic' about the Government's approach — an implicit contradiction — but never addresses the move-on powers claim itself, and expands into houses in Ohakune, Going for Growth and granny flats. It brushes past the question rather than reaching it.
question: Is Community Housing Aotearoa CEO Paul Gilberd wrong when he said, “Move-on powers do nothing to address the causes of homelessness … [they] don’t work. They haven’t anywhere in the world.”?
statement: I regularly catch up with Paul and others who are involved in the community housing space, and they have been absolutely enthusiastic and energised by the way this Government has actually attacked the challenges that come with rough sleeping and a wide range of homelessness, whether or not that is building more houses up and down the country, in places like Ohakune—I was there last Sunday, actually, supporting Ngāti Rangi to open more houses—or, indeed, supporting community housing providers, like the Salvation Army and like many of the entities that Community Housing Aotearoa actually represents, with community finance and the support that we’ve given them around their ability to lend funds to those that are building in this space. There are questions around how fast we can accelerate some of this building, but that’s why we’ve got the Going for Growth platform that Minister Bishop has been diligently leading over the many years, and, of course, the granny flats kaupapa alongside the papakāinga, which are going to see a range of housing typologies built around the country.

explanation: Asked whether Ali Hamlin-Paenga is wrong that move-on powers create an illusion of action. The Minister objects to the framing of the previous questions, then pivots to emergency housing exits and spending under the previous government. The named claim is never assessed; this is a procedural complaint plus talking points in place of an answer.
question: Is the CEO of the national Māori housing body Te Matapihi, Ali Hamlin-Paenga, wrong when she said, “Move-on powers create the illusion of action while leaving the underlying crisis untouched.”?
statement: We’ve had three questions conflating the issue of the move-on orders with homelessness and with rough sleeping. What I can assure this House is that to see the amount of people, whānau, who have left emergency housing, that moral, fiscal, social, and cultural disaster that was fomented between 2017 and 2023—we have taken responsibility, and we’re not going to stand by and continue to spend $1.1 million a day on emergency housing.

explanation: Asked how he can stand by move-on powers when his own ministry advised against them. The answer does engage one half — it argues advice is often wrong, citing prior advice about emergency housing gateway tightening that he says was proven wrong — which is a real (if oblique) response to the 'your officials said no' premise. But it never confirms he stands by the move-on powers or addresses the ministry's specific advice, and closes on an unrelated oil-and-gas jab. Partial engagement.
question: How can he stand by the move-on powers when his own ministry said they don’t work, that they won’t do anything meaningful to improve homelessness, and explicitly advised him not to proceed with them?
statement: There are a range of opinions that are proffered in relation to the steps that we have taken in order to address the root causes of homelessness. I had several opinions offered to me that our work around priority one and tightening the gateway for emergency housing would not work. However, as we have heard today from me, Auckland Council staffers have assured me that the work that we have done has been very successful, alongside community housing providers and people like Barbara Browne, who runs Kāhui Tū Kaha, who I’d invite members opposite to engage with. Finally, some people say and advise of things that would work. Well, guess what? The oil and gas ban didn’t work, and you thought it would.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on faster access to mental health support. He names the announcement directly — two new crisis recovery cafes in Christchurch and Dunedin — and describes what they do. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What recent announcements has the Minister made about faster access to mental health support?
statement: Our mental health plan is delivering results, faster access to support, more front-line workers, and a better crisis response. Recently, I opened two new crisis recovery cafes in Christchurch and Dunedin. This means more New Zealanders will have faster access to mental health support. I’ve heard loud and clear from people that emergency departments can be incredibly overwhelming and not the best environment. With these new services opening, there is a calm, non-clinical space where people can receive support from those with lived experience. Crisis recovery cafes connect people with community services, wraparound support, and can help refer people to long-term support. To deliver a better crisis response, we want to ensure there is someone to call, someone to respond, and somewhere to go.

explanation: Asked why the Government is expanding peer support workers in EDs. The answer gives the reason: improving crisis response as part of the mental health plan, with people who have lived experience able to sit alongside those in crisis. The 'why' is answered before he moves to rollout locations.
question: Why is the Government expanding peer support workers in emergency departments?
statement: Improving our crisis response is a key part of our mental health plan. That’s why we’re expanding peer support workers in emergency departments. These are people with lived experience of recovery who understand what it is like to be in crisis; and can sit alongside someone, help them feel heard, and support them through the process. I recently announced that Whangārei, Hutt Valley, and Hawke’s Bay are the latest hospitals to get peer support workers in their emergency department. They will join the roll-out of peer support specialists already working in eight emergency departments around the country since coming into office. No matter where you live, this Government is committed to ensuring that the right support is there.

explanation: Asked what progress is being made on faster access for young people. He points to the new dedicated child mental health service in Counties Manukau and its multidisciplinary team, plus reduced wait times. Directly responsive to the progress question.
question: What progress is being made to ensure young people get faster access to mental health support?
statement: More good news for mental health: we’re reducing wait times and we’re growing the front-line workforce. Last month, I opened a new dedicated child mental health service in Counties Manukau. The service has been established to support young people, up to intermediate age, along with their families who are experiencing, or are at risk of developing, moderate to severe mental health challenges. The multidisciplinary team will provide wraparound support and include psychiatry, nursing, clinical psychology, and social workers to work with young people and their families. Behind every one of these new services are hundreds of Kiwis now getting the support they need.

explanation: Asked what recognition he has given to organisations delivering support into communities. He names the recognition precisely — Speed Freaks as Volunteers of the Year — and describes the organisation. Complete answer to the question posed.
question: What recognition has the Minister given to organisations that help deliver faster access to support into communities?
statement: I was pleased to announce Speed Freaks as the winners of this year’s Mental Health and Addiction Service Volunteers of the Year. Speed Freaks have 130 volunteer coaches and peer volunteers who are committed to supporting people recovering from addiction or mental health distress, through running. With networks across Christchurch, Auckland, Taranaki, Whangārei, and the West Coast, they’ve created an effective and welcoming community for those seeking support. I want to thank every volunteer who contributes to our health system: your commitment has a lasting impact on individuals, families, and communities across New Zealand.

explanation: Asked what recent reports he has seen on school attendance. He identifies the report (term 1 2026 attendance data) and its content, including the 68.6 percent regular-attendance figure. Direct and on point.
question: What recent reports has he seen on school attendance?
statement: I’ve seen the term 1 2026 attendance data that showed school attendance rates were higher over that period than any term 1 since 2022. A student is considered to be attending school regularly if they are at school for more than 90 percent of a term. In term 1 this year, 68.6 percent of students attended school regularly, up 2.7 percentage points than the previous year. It’s also worth noting that many students will be only just below the 90 percent attendance figure and there will always be cases of non-attendance that can’t be helped, through illness or other circumstances, which, for the most part, are communicated to school leadership accordingly. This Government is focused on fixing what matters, and few things matter more to the future of our country than the number of children that get to school each day.

explanation: Asked how significant the attendance increase has been. He quantifies significance directly — 46.5 percent in term 1 2022 versus now, 176,000 more students attending regularly, plus a term 2 comparison. A brief aside about Middle East cost-of-living pressures does not displace the answer.
question: How significant has this increase in school attendance been?
statement: In term 1, 2022, only 46.5 percent of students were attending school regularly. That means, in the term just gone, 176,000 more students attended school regularly than in the same corresponding term 1 four years ago. I’m pleased to report that, despite the cost of living pressures being delivered by conflict in the Middle East, term 2 has started promisingly. In the first week of this term, the national average for attendance was 90 percent. That is compared with 88.4 percent for the same week last year—that is, the first week of term 2, 2025. I think what that shows is that the Government taking attendance seriously, has been followed by schools, parents, and students themselves taking it seriously, and it’s important that we continue to drive this change in order that we get continued gains in the number of students attending school regularly.

explanation: Asked how the Government intends to build on the attendance momentum. He answers with the intended means: $140 million from Budget 2025, the attendance management framework, mandatory school attendance plans, new case management software and a recontracted attendance service. Squarely responsive.
question: How does the Government intend to build on this positive momentum in school attendance?
statement: While much of the work is being done by simply reinforcing expectations by the school community, by parents, and by students themselves, Budget 2025 provided $140 million of additional funding to improve school attendance over the next four years. This has allowed us to implement a school attendance management framework that will continue that momentum. Every school in New Zealand is now required to have an attendance management plan, which allows schools and front-line attendance services to better manage cases of absenteeism. There is new case management software that allows all schools, attendance service providers, and the Ministry of Education to communicate and monitor attendance data in real time, so that issues can be addressed and resolved more quickly, and we have completely retooled and recontracted the attendance service to get better value for that money.

explanation: Asked how schools deal with absenteeism under the new regime. Answer lays out the escalation framework step by step (5 days, 10 days, 15 days, prosecution). Squarely the question asked.
question: How do schools deal with cases of absenteeism under the new regime?
statement: Schools each have an attendance management plan, as I mentioned, and that provides an escalating framework for responding to a student who is not attending. For example, if a child is absent for five days, school leadership will communicate with parents or guardians to determine the reason for unexplained absence and to set expectations for attending more regularly. After 10 days of absence, school leadership will meet with the parents, and at 15 days, the matter will be escalated further to an attendance service provider. If the absence escalates beyond this point, or for cases of non-enrolment, prosecution of parents becomes a possibility.

explanation: Asked whether the prosecution threat has been effective at getting students re-enrolled. Answer opens with 'Yes' and describes 17 of 34 referred students returning. Direct and complete.
question: Has the threat of prosecution been effective at getting students re-enrolled at school?
statement: Yes. For a long time, there was, really, a blind eye being turned to the possibility of prosecution, there having been none for six years. In the last year, 34 different students have been referred to the Ministry of Education for prosecution. Of those, 17 have decided they would rather go back to attending school. That has been quite effective as a deterrent. However, of the remaining 17, they are in various stages of the prosecutorial process. There was one where a case was to be heard just the other day, but, sadly, the parents in the case did not attend the court hearing, so that has had to be put back to another time. None the less, we do not give up, because we think that attendance is so important to the future of this country.

explanation: Two-part question: does she stand by the statement, and how do employment numbers compare to when the Government took office. Both parts engaged — 'Yes' plus a quarterly figure and a concession that the total is 'slightly lower' than the December 2023 quarter. The comparison is softened but it is made.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “There will be more job opportunities in this country”; if so, how do the numbers of people employed compare to when the Government took office?
statement: Yes, and there will be, as the economy recovers after a protracted downturn. The December quarter of last year saw 15,000 more people in work, compared to the quarter before, so the trend has been going in the right direction. The total was slightly lower than in the December quarter of 2023, but Treasury forecasts are for employment to rise by 60,000 this year and 240,000 by the end of the forecast period. The next Treasury forecasts will be released alongside the Budget.

explanation: A narrow factual yes/no: are there 32,000 fewer jobs than two years ago. The answer never confirms or denies, substituting a counterfactual ('more jobs than there would have been without our policies') repeated three times. The core of a specific factual question is entirely avoided.
question: Is it the case that there are 32,000 fewer jobs compared to two years ago, when she promised that “There will be more job opportunities in this country”?
statement: It is the case that there are more job opportunities in this country today than there would have been in the absence of sensible policies like fast-track legislation to support new developments, housing developments, quarries, and energy developments. There are more jobs in this country than would have been the case without the introduction of the Investment Boost policy, which has supported businesses to make investments in their growth. There are more jobs in this country than would have been the case without a number of the policies that this Government has put forward.

explanation: Asked what increased opportunities exist in regional New Zealand such as Hawke's Bay. The answer stays on the region and its agricultural sector but describes government posture toward farmers rather than naming any increased opportunity; it gestures at the question without reaching it.
question: What increased opportunities are there for people in regional New Zealand, such as Hawke’s Bay, where there are 9,400 fewer jobs?
statement: If you were to visit Hawke’s Bay and speak to those people who are working in the agricultural industry, they would tell you that being part of a country where the Government supports farmers and gets red tape out of the way, promotes their wool products, promotes their dairy products, and seeks out new markets for them rather than abusing them makes it a lot easier to create jobs and incomes.

explanation: Asked what increased opportunities exist in manufacturing. Roughly half the answer relitigates the previous Government's gas decision, but it does then name a specific source of opportunity in the sector (Investment Boost tax relief on new machinery) before turning to a challenge to the questioner. Partial engagement.
question: What increased opportunities are there for people who work in manufacturing now that there are 10,000 fewer manufacturing jobs in the past two years?
statement: It is the case that some manufacturers have been particularly challenged by the last Government’s decision to ban the exploration of oil and gas, which has meant an acute shortage in the amount of gas available and therefore spiking electricity prices, which has been a significant challenge for manufacturers. It is also the case that there has been opportunity created in the manufacturing sector as a direct result of the Investment Boost policy, which has reduced the tax paid by those firms who have invested in new machinery. I challenge the member to commit to the Investment Boost policy if she wants to stay on the right side of manufacturers.

explanation: Asked what increased opportunities exist for graduates. The answer acknowledges the premise (young people are hit hardest when unemployment rises) but offers only 'a range of opportunities depending on qualification' before pivoting to school-level literacy and numeracy — a different question. It touches the topic without answering what the opportunities are.
question: What increased opportunities are there for graduates, when careers expert Craig McAlpine reports, “50 percent of employers are saying that they have either stopped or slowed graduate intakes”?
statement: It is the case that for new graduates, there are a range of opportunities depending on their qualification, skills, and background—but I fully acknowledge that when unemployment is higher, it is often young people who are particularly impacted, and this can be very challenging for them. As we look to the future, it is really important that we have a school system that delivers people the reading, writing, and maths skills, and the comparable international qualifications, that allow them to seek and obtain good jobs.

explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should trust her on jobs given the track record. The answer does supply a 'because' — the comparative policy choice and claimed delivery of lower inflation and interest rates — so it responds to the 'why trust' framing, but it swerves past the track-record premise the question was built on and spends much of its length on the opposition's platform.
question: Why should New Zealanders trust her at all on jobs when her Government’s track record shows that job opportunities were going backwards way before the fuel crisis even began?
statement: Because politics is about a choice, and the choice that that member’s party is offering is more tax, more borrowing, more red tape, fewer fast-tracked projects, less focus on improving the conditions for businesses, and more taxes swallowing those businesses. The choice that our party is offering has been one that has delivered lower inflation, lower interest rates, and fewer taxes. Those are the conditions needed for job and income creation.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all the statements and actions of his Government. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Two-part question: does he agree with the UNESCO definition, and if so why is mining appropriate in such places. He answers the first part with 'yes' and explicitly confines himself to it, leaving the substantive second half — the 'why' — untouched. Half the question, and the lesser half, was engaged.
question: Does he agree with the definition of a UNESCO World Heritage Site that “World Heritage Sites are places recognised as having ‘outstanding universal value’. They are … deemed significant for their historical, artistic, or scientific importance.”; if so, why is it appropriate to mine in these places?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes.

explanation: Asked how he justifies granting a prospecting permit in a World Heritage Site specifically. The answer offers a general justification for mining and critical minerals but never addresses the World Heritage location that was the whole point of the question.
question: How does he justify granting a prospecting permit in one of only three of New Zealand’s UNESCO World Heritage Sites?
statement: Well, we are very interested in developing more mining in this country because we need critical minerals to make the clean, green transition. That’s what we’ve got in this country. We’re going to continue to explore them and develop all our natural resources.

explanation: Asked whether he thinks New Zealanders are OK with trading a place of outstanding universal value for short-term private profit. He inverts the frame to what New Zealanders are 'not OK about' — jobs and Kiwis leaving for Australia — and never states a view on the trade-off put to him.
question: OK. Does he think New Zealanders are OK with his Government trading off a place with outstanding universal value for short-term, private profits?
statement: Well, what I know New Zealanders are not OK about is not having high-paying jobs in regional New Zealand and actually banning oil and gas and mining projects that ends up having Kiwis leave New Zealand to go to Australia to access those jobs in those sectors. We are going to make this country wealthier and more prosperous for everybody, and that means using our resources.

explanation: Asked squarely whether the Government has departed from the 2012 no-mining-in-World-Heritage-areas commitment. The answer never says yes or no, offering 'we will find the balance' and pivoting to economic growth talking points about jobs and the economy. A narrow yes/no question left entirely unanswered.
question: Has his Government departed from the commitment of previous Governments first made under Sir John Key in 2012 that there would be no mining in World Heritage areas like the spectacular Te Wāhipounamu?
statement: Again, we will find the balance, but we are prioritising economic growth in this country. We are going to get things done, we’re going to get this economy moving, and we’re going to offer high-paying jobs to people in regional New Zealand. That’s a good thing.

explanation: Asked whether any supposedly protected land in Aotearoa is not open to mining. The reply doesn't name a category or give a clear boundary, but it does gesture at one: national parks of high environmental quality 'we'll continue to protect'. That is a partial answer to the core of the question rather than a full pivot away from it.
question: If he accepts that mining is appropriate in a globally recognised World Heritage area, is there any piece of supposedly protected land in Aotearoa that is not open to mining?
statement: Just remember, 30 percent of this country is in the Department of Conservation estate. We have very important national parks of very high environmental quality, and we’ll continue to protect those, obviously.

explanation: A standard 'does he stand by all statements and actions' question, answered 'Yes' with an added example. Direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and particularly our income tax relief, raising thresholds for working New Zealanders.

explanation: Two-part question: the dollar amount of the average weekly grocery shop, and whether it is more or less than at the start of his term. The figure is never given; the food-inflation comparison (3.4% vs 12.5%) engages the second half only obliquely — a positive inflation rate implies 'more', but he never says so. Engages the topic without reaching the question.
question: How much does the average New Zealand family spend in their weekly grocery shop right now, and is that more or less than when he became the Prime Minister?
statement: Well, actually, food inflation’s up 3.4 percent from memory; it was up 12.5 percent under his Government. So food price inflation exists, and as I said to him yesterday, deflation is not good for an economy, but food price inflation—there’s more to do, but at 3.4 percent it’s better than 12.5 percent, which he delivered.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the July 2024 'food prices are falling really quickly' claim and, if so, which prices fell. Neither limb is answered: no affirmation or repudiation of the statement, and no food price named. He restates the same inflation comparison used in the previous answer.
question: Well, does he stand by his statement in July 2024 that “food prices are falling really quickly”; if so, which food prices have fallen really quickly in the time he’s been Prime Minister?
statement: Well, as I said, the general point about food inflation is it went up to 12.5 percent under his leadership; under our Government, it’s up over the last year 3.4 percent. That’s a good outcome for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked for the average monthly power bill and whether it is higher or lower than when he became PM. The response gives no figure and no direction, pivoting immediately to the oil and gas ban repeal and fast-track legislation, then challenging the questioner to declare what he stands for.
question: How much does the average New Zealand family spend on their monthly power bill right now, and is that more or less than when he became Prime Minister?
statement: Well, again, that’s why I would say to the member, get in behind repealing the oil and gas ban, get in behind the fast-track legislation that’s generating an increase in renewables in this country. [ Interruption ] You know, you can cry crocodile tears, but actually back some stuff and actually come out and declare what you stand for.

explanation: Asked for the average monthly household insurance cost and the direction of change. The entire answer is a series of counter-questions aimed at the questioner about policies he should support. The question asked is not touched at all.
question: How much does the average New Zealand family spend on home, contents, and car insurance each month, and is that more or less than when he became the Prime Minister?
statement: Well, again, I’ll just say to the member, if he actually cares about the impact of the cost of living on New Zealanders, why doesn’t he propose some policy to actually come to the table with? Why doesn’t he support the rates cap? Because that’s a very big driver of the cost of living for New Zealanders. Why doesn’t he support fast track? Why doesn’t he repeal the oil and gas ban with us? And why doesn’t he actually just support extending prescriptions, saving healthcare costs for regular New Zealanders? There’s a lot that you could be doing, but you’re not.

explanation: Asked what a tradie spends filling up a ute now versus at the start of his term. No figure is given and no comparison to the actual starting point; he offers a counterfactual instead ('a lot less than it would have been if he'd stayed in power') before pivoting to the rates cap. The fuel-cost counterfactual is adjacent to the question but substitutes a different comparison for the one asked.
question: How much does the average tradie or sole trader spend filling up their ute right now, and is that more or less than when he became the Prime Minister?
statement: Well, the good news is that we abolished the ute tax. Remember that one? That was a special. We abolished the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax, if you remember that one, so it’s a lot less than it would have been if he’d stayed in power. We’ve actually cancelled Labour’s fuel excise hikes that were planned. We’ve kept that in place frozen, but we’re progressing a rates cap—get on board with that. Why don’t you support that very simple thought and idea.

explanation: A precise numerical question — how many more people are unemployed now than when he became PM. No number is given. The answer is a causal account of the previous government's spending and interest rates, closing with unquantified 'thousands of new jobs' last quarter, which is a different measure than the one asked for.
question: How many more people are unemployed now compared to when he became the Prime Minister?
statement: Well, as I’ve explained to the member before, the rule of economics is that if you increase Government spending by 84 percent, you drive inflation up to a 32-year high, you have 13 interest rate rises, you put the economy into slow down, if not recession, and people lose their jobs. But in the last quarter, we are pleased to see that we’ve created thousands of new jobs for New Zealanders. That’s good, but we’re going to get the economy growing and that’s how we get people back into work.

explanation: A pointed (if loaded) either/or question: doesn't know the answers, or doesn't care. The reply, though cut off, begins on a record-defence talking point ('we have done more to support working—') and selects neither limb. Scored as a genuine question rather than a point of order.
question: Is the reason he can’t answer a single one of those questions about the day-to-day reality New Zealand families face under his Government and instead resorts to blame and excuses, that he doesn’t know the answers or that he just doesn’t care?
statement: Yeah, well, I’ll tell you, we have done more to support working—

explanation: A patsy question asking what recent economic reports she has seen. The answer names a specific report (Moody's latest review) and sets out its contents. Squarely responsive.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: Last week, Moody’s Ratings released its latest review of New Zealand. It confirmed that New Zealand’s sovereign credit rating would remain at triple A—the highest possible rating—but it revised the outlook from stable to negative. Moody’s highlights that current global economic uncertainty presents downside risks to growth in New Zealand while inflation pressures persist. It says these factors may delay the Government’s fiscal consolidation—that is, getting the Government’s books back to surplus and bending the debt curve from going up to going down. This comes after Fitch Ratings also changed its outlook for New Zealand to negative.

explanation: Asked what the recent outlook changes indicate. The answer states directly that they indicate a risk to both ratings and explains what the agencies will be watching and the resolution timeframe. Directly on the question asked.
question: What do these recent changes in outlook indicate?
statement: What these changes indicate is a risk to both ratings. Moody’s and Fitch will be watching developments closely to determine whether to move New Zealand’s ratings one notch lower, or to maintain the rating and revise our outlook back to stable. I’m advised that Moody’s typically shifts to a negative outlook when they see at least a one-in-three chance that a downgrade could occur and that an outlook is generally resolved over 12 to 18 months. This gives time to monitor how the fiscal position is evolving. Budget 2026 will be released on 28 May, and members will see the latest Treasury forecasts then.

explanation: Asked what the ratings reviews mean for the Government's fiscal approach; she states directly what they mean — they support the strategy of spending restraint, surplus and debt control, and the negative outlook is a warning to stay the course. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What do these ratings reviews mean for the Government’s fiscal approach?
statement: These reviews support the Government’s fiscal strategy of keeping a tight rein on spending, getting the operating balance back in surplus, and getting debt under control, all within the next few years. Being on negative outlook is, however, a warning that we need to stay on this course and demonstrate progress, even when global events make it more challenging, and it’s a warning to others who might want to spend more and borrow more that ratings agencies are watching carefully. The interest cost on Government debt is already around $9 billion a year. A credit rating downgrade would increase this interest bill further if debt increased, and even more so if New Zealand faced higher interest rates from being considered a riskier country.

explanation: Asked how fiscal consolidation can be achieved; she names the two available routes (revenue vs expenditure restraint) and says which one the Government uses, citing savings made. The closing jab at opponents is an add-on, not a substitute for the answer.
question: How can fiscal consolidation be achieved?
statement: There are two possible fiscal strategies available for consolidation, as the member Chlöe Swarbrick points out. The parties opposite me prefer tax. Our approach is to keep a lid on spending, rather than increase taxes. Fitch makes this point explicitly in its review, saying that there is broad-based consensus across the political spectrum towards fiscal consolidation, although the consolidation strategy may vary. It says that the current Government focuses on expenditure constraint, and that is true. Over the last two Budgets, the Government has made a total of $44 billion worth of savings and reprioritisation. On the other hand, Fitch says that others would emphasise revenue measures to reduce the deficit—that means increasing taxes. People who have those plans should tell the country which taxes they’ll be increasing.

explanation: Asked what assurances he can give that RMA reform won't affect Waitākere protections. He engages the mechanism — the 2008 Act, the fact consequential amendments were omitted at introduction and will be needed to maintain its intent, with the committee considering it. That addresses the substance but stops short of giving the assurance itself, leaving it to the select committee.
question: What assurances, if any, can he give to the people of Tāmaki Makaurau that his RMA reforms will not impact the protection of the Waitākere Ranges?
statement: There is special legislation in place for the Waitākere Ranges—the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act 2008. The Act requires Auckland Council to give effect to its purpose and objectives when making plans under the Resource Management Act (RMA) that affect the area and to have particular regard to that purpose and objectives when making resource consent decisions in the area. The Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill, which will replace the RMA, are currently before the Environment Committee for consideration. When those bills were introduced, it was acknowledged that not all consequential amendments to other Acts were included, and the committee, as I understand it, has been made aware of that fact. To maintain the intent of the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act under the new planning system, consequential amendments will be needed, and the Environment Committee will be considering that as part of its scrutiny of the bills.

explanation: Asked how he justifies overriding the 2008 Act's protections and what specific safeguards will remain. He rejects the premise ('that's not what I'm doing') and tells her to read Hansard. Premise rejection is some engagement with the first half, but the direct question about which safeguards remain is never touched.
question: How can the Minister justify advancing planning legislation that effectively overrides the protections of the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act 2008, and what specific safeguards, if any, will remain to prevent irreversible environmental degradation in the Waitākere Ranges?
statement: I suggest the member, at the end of the night, goes back and reads the Hansard , because if she was listening, she would find out that that’s not what I’m doing.

explanation: Two-part question: what weight he gave community and mana whenua opposition, and why it isn't reflected in the bills. He answers the second part obliquely (about 100 Acts need consequential amendments, the committee will consider them) and notes submissions have been made, but never says what weight he gave the opposition.
question: What weight has the Minister given to the strong opposition from local communities and mana whenua who are concerned that his RMA reform will undermine the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act 2008, and why are these concerns not currently reflected in the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill?
statement: Again, I gave a pretty comprehensive answer to the primary question, which was that there are a range of consequential amendments required—there’s around 100. It’s not just about the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act, it’s about 100 other pieces of legislation that require consequential amendments, which the select committee will be considering. In relation to the first part of the question, my understanding is that there has been a range of submissions in that regard to the Environment Committee. The bill is in the hands of the committee.

explanation: Asked whether he will accept responsibility for irreversible damage if protections are weakened. He answers a different question entirely — a list of the good outcomes he will take responsibility for. The responsibility-for-damage question is never engaged, yes or no.
question: Should the protections be weakened in any way, shape, or form, will the Minister accept responsibility for any irreversible damage to the Waitākere Ranges?
statement: If the Government’s planning reforms work as intended, I will take responsibility for the abundant development opportunities that will land in this country. I will take responsibility for the renewable energy that will be far easier to build—the windfarms that don’t take six years to build. I will take responsibility for infrastructure projects not tied up in endless red tape to build transmission and roads and rail projects. I will take responsibility for the prosperity that we have been denied as a country because of the straightjacket of the RMA.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made; he lists them — the 100 million litre tank recommissioning and diesel, a planned hydrogen road map event, plus geothermal, fusion and oil and gas. Directly responsive.
question: What recent announcements has he made?
statement: Obviously, we have already announced the recommissioning of the 100 million litre tank and the diesel that will go into that tank, but we are also pursuing a strategy with a suitable, legislatively speaking, and a high-quality large event to lay out a road map and a strategy for hydrogen. That is something that will join the host of other announcements I’ve made in terms of geothermal, nuclear fusion, and oil and gas. We are going, in our regions, to ensure that we have the supply of energy by using our regional resources, including hydrogen.

explanation: Asked whether New Zealand has potential for hydrogen as a fuel of choice. He implies yes by saying it is important to explore hydrogen's role in fuel and energy resilience, but never states a view on the potential itself before pivoting to a grievance about prospecting permits and anti-mining opponents.
question: Does New Zealand have potential for hydrogen being a fuel of choice?
statement: Being very interested in clean, green outcomes, I think it’s very important that we join with the different stakeholders in our community and explore the role that hydrogen can play boosting our fuel resilience, our energy resilience, coming off the afflictions associated with the Persian Gulf military conflict. It is important, however, that when people apply for innocuous prospecting permits, they are not pilloried, they are not cancelled, and they are not harassed by opponents to mining when they are legally entitled to go and get an innocuous permit to learn about the potential of hydrogen and other minerals on the Department of Conservation estate—and watch this space.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions; she says yes (in context), and volunteers the Fitch discussions specifically. Direct and complete.
question: Vinaka vakalevu, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: In context, yes, including those statements I made in my discussions with the Fitch Ratings agency. I can assure members that I said the same thing to them in private as I say to New Zealanders in public.

explanation: A narrow factual question — was she in the room for the Fitch meeting. She answers 'No' immediately, then adds commentary about what the agency reported. The added attack does not displace the answer.
question: Was she in the room when Barbara Edmonds met with Fitch?
statement: No, but I wish I’d been a fly on that wall, because what it led the ratings agency to report was that the Opposition intends to achieve fiscal consolidation through additional revenue measures. I was surprised to read this because, of course, the capital gains tax which the Labour Party have announced, they’ve already said all of that money has been stitched up for doctors appointments.

explanation: Asked whether New Zealanders are currently experiencing a cost of living crisis. She says 'Yes' outright and then discusses causes. A direct answer to a question ministers often duck.
question: Are New Zealanders currently experiencing a cost of living crisis?
statement: Yes, and events in the Middle East are playing a very significant role. We have seen the price of diesel almost double since that conflict began. Diesel is a fuel that powers not only vehicles but freight and a number of inputs into our economy, and it is correct to say that that will have an effect on the cost of living for New Zealanders. On the other hand, the effect of the events in the Middle East has shown that in the past couple of weeks we’ve seen that diesel price come down about 55c, which demonstrates that it is in all of our interests to see the conflict in the Middle East resolved as soon as possible.

explanation: Asked for a count of families receiving the full $250. Willis re-frames the promise as 'up to $250', gives a different number (10,000+ on FamilyBoost), and closes on an attack. The specific count asked for is never given, though adjacent figures are offered.
question: How many families have actually received the full $250 that she promised them?
statement: Well, as I’ve set out to that member several times—and I hope this time she’ll listen—National committed that the sum of our tax policies would deliver up to $250 a fortnight to families. We delivered on every single one of the commitments that underpin that $250. Up to $150 of that would be delivered by the FamilyBoost payment—and I have been advised that more than 10,000 families have received that payment in a fortnight—and up to $100 of that would be contributed through our changes to personal income tax thresholds and changes to Working for Families credits. Now, that member opposed those tax reductions and opposed that additional income for New Zealanders. I’m proud that we delivered them actual cash into their bank accounts to help with the cost of living.

explanation: A yes/no 'does she stand by' question, answered 'Yes' in the first word. The trailing jab about secret taxes is irrelevant but does not undo the direct answer; only slight deduction for not engaging the 70-percent premise at all.
question: Does she stand by her statement that “This Government has got your back.” when 70 percent of workers didn’t get a pay rise above inflation in the last year?
statement: Yes, because I’m not cooking up any secret taxes.

explanation: Asked whether the listed cost increases square with 'having New Zealanders' back'. She addresses one item (rates, via a cap bill), ignores the gas tax, registration, prescription fees and line charges, never answers the yes/no, and pivots to attacking the questioner.
question: Is it having New Zealanders’ back in a cost of living crisis when her Government is increasing the everyday costs through her gas tax, increases to car registration, the reinstatement of prescription fees, increases in line charges, and increases in council rates?
statement: To pick one, we are introducing legislation to this House to cap rates increases, unlike that member who, again, opposes yet another practical measure to help with the cost of living. You see, the problem is that that member has an opinion on everything and a policy on nothing.

explanation: Asked what announcement was made about the India FTA; McClay states the signing, the date, the place and the tariff terms. Squarely and completely on the question.
question: What recent announcement has the Government made regarding the free-trade agreement with India?
statement: On Monday, New Zealand signed a free-trade agreement (FTA) with India in New Delhi. This marks a major step forward in opening up one of the world’s fastest-growing markets for Kiwi exporters to their 1.4 billion consumers. Ninety-five percent of New Zealand’s exports face tariff elimination or reduction, almost the highest of any India FTA, and almost 57 percent of our exports will be duty free on day one, increasing to 82 percent when fully implemented. The New Zealand - India free-trade agreement gives unprecedented access to India for Kiwi goods and services. This means our businesses will be able to sell more and employ more people, thus setting our businesses up to succeed and helping New Zealand with its goal of doubling the value of exports over 10 years.

explanation: Asked whether he supports the TPK role cuts and why. He answers a different question — whose legal responsibility staffing is — which implicitly declines to state a position but never says whether he supports it or gives the 'why'.
question: Does he support the proposal to cut roles from Te Puni Kōkiri, on top of earlier reductions; if so, why?
statement: Kia ora. Decisions around staffing levels at Te Puni Kōkiri (TPK) are operational matters and are the responsibility of the Secretary for Māori Development, as chief executive. The member will be—well, at least should be—aware of section 54 of the Public Service Act 2020, passed when he was a Minister of the Crown, which provides that there is a duty on the CE of agencies like Te Puni Kōkiri to act independently on employment matters.

explanation: A narrow numerical question answered with a number: a net reduction of 25.4 FTE since June 2024. Direct and complete on its face.
question: Since taking office, how many people have lost their jobs at Te Puni Kōkiri?
statement: I am advised that since around June 2024, there has been a net reduction of 25.4 fulltime-equivalent staff at Te Puni Kōkiri.

explanation: Asked how he defends cuts given TPK's new functions. He opens with a partisan contrast, but does eventually offer a defence — quality of advice over quantity of roles. The new monitoring functions raised in the question are never addressed.
question: How can he defend further job cuts when Te Puni Kōkiri has just taken on new monitoring and Māori-Crown relations functions and is supposed to be holding other agencies to account for their performance for Māori?
statement: You see, this is partly a question that can help me explore the differences between the member, whose modus operandi and party believe in massive big government and spraying the cash bazooka, and the fiscal prudence that exists on this side of the House. We are not about the quantity of roles through Government but, actually, the quality of advice, and I’m very confident about the quality of the advice that the Ministry of Māori Development—Te Puni Kōkiri—is providing me.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with his own prior quote and how cuts serve that aim. He responds with a joke about himself in the third person and an invitation to the bar; neither limb of the question is engaged.
question: Does he agree with Tama Potaka that “Anything less than an increase in power for Māori would signal yet another failure in respecting the Treaty”, and, if so, how does cutting jobs at TPK achieve this objective?
statement: Again, the member confuses the citation of that great and diligent man Tama Potaka with the number of staff at a single agency, and I recommend that the member talk with Tama Potaka—great guy—at Copperfields after this debate.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Seymour's view and whether it explains the cuts. He disclaims responsibility for Seymour's views and disputes that the quote is accurate — engaging the premise but never stating agreement or disagreement, nor addressing the cuts.
question: Does he agree with David Seymour that population ministries like TPK slow down the business of Government, and, if so, is this the reason why he is slowly cutting staff, to prepare for TPK to be cut altogether?
statement: I recall traversing this matter before; I’m not responsible for the views of David Seymour, and I recommend that the member actually check the record to ensure that that is consistent with what has actually been said by David Seymour.

explanation: A yes/no 'does he admit' question. The recorded response is a truncated three words ('Again, the member—') that reaches no part of the question.
question: Does he admit that the latest job cuts prove the Government’s negative Māori agenda is ramping up, and for all his rhetoric about thriving whānau, the only things thriving under National are more cuts and misery for Māori?
statement: Again, the member—

explanation: Asked what announcement supports farmers and growers; Butterick names the India FTA and ties it directly to market access for food and fibre producers. On point throughout.
question: What recent announcement has the Government made about supporting farmers and growers?
statement: On Monday, the Government signed a free-trade agreement (FTA) with India, in New Delhi. This agreement has been described as a once-in-a-lifetime deal, a landmark FTA, and historic. This agreement opens doors and offers further opportunities to our farmers and growers. These are opportunities that have not previously been available. We know that our food and fibre is world class. This agreement will allow these products entry into a new market without significant barriers. This agreement will help grow our export returns and allow our farmers and growers better access to a market of 1.4 billion customers.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees migrants are not disposable workers; she opens 'No person is disposable', which is agreement, then explains the visa policy. The proposition put to her is answered before the pivot to justification.
question: Does she agree with the Union Network of Migrants that “migrants are not disposable workers”; if not, why not?
statement: No person is disposable. However, our priority always must be job opportunities for New Zealanders, especially in times of economic challenge. I appreciate that there are some migrants who came to New Zealand for lower-skilled roles who are approaching the end of their visa and wish to remain here. However, it was clear when they came to New Zealand that these were temporary work visas, and it is important that New Zealanders who are seeking work have the opportunity to apply for these jobs when migrants reach the end of their maximum continuous stay.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees the stand-down period harms wages/conditions/productivity. Answer begins with a plain "No" before being cut off — the yes/no core is squarely answered, even if the supporting remarks are truncated.
question: Does she agree that the stand-down period, which prevents workers from being able to remain in a job for the long term, contributes to poorer wages, lower working conditions, and poor productivity as a result of employers not being able to retain them?
statement: No, but on this topic—

explanation: Same agree/disagree question. "No, I don't agree with that" answers it directly; the follow-on about prioritising New Zealanders for jobs is a pivot, but the question itself was engaged and resolved first.
question: Does she agree that the stand-down period, which prevents workers from being able to remain in a job in the long term, contributes to poorer wages, lower working conditions, and poor productivity due to employers not being able to retain these workers in the long term?
statement: No, I don’t agree with that, but what I do agree with is that it is very important for New Zealanders to be prioritised for jobs, and I’d like to acknowledge the hard work of the Minister for Social Development and Employment, Louise Upston, and the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) for contacting New Zealanders who need work and job opportunities when people who are coming towards the end of their maximum continuous stay are required to leave New Zealand, giving Kiwis access to these jobs.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with Paul Scott that IELTS band 6.5 is inappropriate for establishing ability to settle. "I do not" answers the question outright, followed by direct engagement with the settlement rationale.
question: Does she agree with Paul Scott who has been teaching English for speakers of other languages, including pre - International English Language Testing System (IELTS) preparation, in New Zealand for 30 years, that “IELTS, along with many other similar testing systems, especially requiring band 6.5”—this is the case for migrant bus drivers—“are completely inappropriate for establishing the ability to settle in the country.”?
statement: I do not. This is a standard of English that has been in place since the early 2000s, across multiple Governments, and it does ensure that migrants are able to settle well in New Zealand. I would also make the point that it’s only the primary applicant that has to have that level of English. Their partner and their children do not and it is very important for that person to be able to live and integrate well into New Zealand society, and that is why we have such good levels of settlement in this country.

explanation: Narrow factual question about whether she lifted the English requirements higher for undergraduate students. "No." is a complete, unhedged answer to the yes/no put to her.
question: Is it not correct that she lifted those very requirements to one that is even higher for undergraduate students trying to start at university?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether golden visa holders can buy homes, make large anonymous donations and vote without English tests. The response — "Those things—" — never reaches an answer; the specific factual proposition is left entirely unaddressed.
question: OK. Is it correct that golden visa holders are able to buy homes, maker larger anonymous political donations, and get the right to vote without sitting any English tests?
statement: Those things—

explanation: Asked whether he stands by a specific quoted statement. "Yes, I stand by my full statement" answers it completely, and he then quotes the fuller statement he stands by.
question: Does he stand by his statement regarding heavy vehicle weight limits that “there are sensible changes we can make that will lift productivity without compromising standards”?
statement: Yes, I stand by my full statement, which is “We need to balance that with safety and network impacts, but there are sensible changes we can make that will lift productivity without compromising standards.” The Government is exploring a range of temporary, targeted, and timely measures to support New Zealanders; this includes preparatory work to remove or suspend regulatory barriers that make it harder for businesses and communities to cope with global fuel shocks. Small increases in permitted loads for heavy vehicles could reduce the number of trips needed, saving time, lowering costs, and reducing fuel use.

explanation: Asked how he can claim no compromise to standards given his own acknowledgement roads will suffer. He restates the balancing formula and says no decisions have been made — this engages the tension obliquely and defers it rather than explaining how the claim holds, so it half-reaches the core.
question: How can he claim these changes will not compromise standards when he himself has acknowledged there is “no doubt” roads will suffer from heavier trucks, and such a change will put pressure on repairs and maintenance, and on former Minister of Transport Simeon Brown’s pothole patrol?
statement: I think the answer is in the answer to the primary question, which is that we need to balance that with safety and network impacts. We’re doing the work right now, and no decisions have been made.

explanation: Asked squarely whether a weight-limit proposal has the support of all three coalition parties. He answers a different question — that the Government has considered no formal advice — leaving the coalition-support question unanswered.
question: Does a proposal to lift heavy vehicle weight limits have the support of all three coalition parties, given that when asked whether he would veto changes to truck weight limits, one coalition partner has said, “Stand back and watch”, and, “We are not going to go down that pathway”?
statement: The Government hasn’t considered any formal advice on the matters the member is referring to.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Peters that weight limits exist for good reasons. "Yes, in a general sense" plus affirmation that heavy vehicles impact roads directly answers the agree/disagree question; only lightly hedged.
question: Does he agree with Winston Peters that weight limits “are put there for good reasons, because of potholes and bridge strength”?
statement: Yes, in a general sense. It is undoubtedly true that heavy vehicles have an impact on the road. We are considering that matter right now, and, as I say—

explanation: Asked whether he will accept responsibility if changes proceed and safety concerns are disregarded. He concedes the impact point and pivots to the fuel crisis rationale, never addressing whether he would accept responsibility.
question: Should weight limit changes proceed, will he accept responsibility for safety and other concerns having been disregarded—concerns that have been expressed by members of his own coalition Government?
statement: Well, as I say, the member makes a not unreasonable point that the impact of heavy vehicles has an impact on the roading network. We are considering that, and you’ve also got to balance it with the undoubted situation that we find ourselves in, or potentially find ourselves in. If the fuel crisis worsens, we might find ourselves in a situation in which it would make sense for trucks to do fewer trips, thus improving fuel economy—

explanation: Asked why he prioritises regulatory relief for trucking over motorists at the pump. He attacks Labour first, but does contest the premise by asserting he is prioritising regulatory relief for everyone — that engages the framing without answering the "why this rather than that" put to him.
question: Why is he prioritising regulatory relief for the trucking industry when ordinary New Zealanders are paying record prices at the pump just to get to work, drop their kids off at school, and put food on the table?
statement: Well, this is a classic of the Labour Party genre, which is a series of fallacious assertions backed up with no policy of their own. As Minister, I am prioritising regulatory relief—in fact, the whole Government is prioritising regulatory relief for everyone.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made about land transport rules. He names the WOF/COF inspection reform and sets out exactly what was announced — the question is fully and squarely answered.
question: What recent announcements has he made about land transport rules?
statement: Recently, Minister of Transport Chris Bishop and I announced that New Zealand’s warrant of fitness—with your indulgences, sir, I’ll refer to them as WOFs—and certificate of fitness A, which I’ll refer to as COFs, light vehicle inspection requirements will soon be significantly reformed, saving Kiwis valuable time and money. The changes mean that most light vehicles under 14 years old will move to two-yearly WOF inspections, up from yearly, and new vehicles will go to four years before needing their WOF. Older vehicles, motorcycles, and light rental vehicles will move from six-monthly to yearly inspections.

explanation: Asked how much the changes will save Kiwis a year. He gives a concrete savings figure ($2.6–4.1 billion in net benefits) with the sources of saving, so the core cost question is engaged — but over 30 years, not the per-year figure asked for, leaving the questioner to divide. Squarely on the question, slightly off on the unit.
question: How much will this save Kiwis a year?
statement: These are simple changes that will deliver massive benefits for Kiwis. The cost-benefit analysis done by officials shows that these changes are expected to deliver between $2.6 billion and $4.1 billion in net benefits to Kiwis over 30 years through reduced inspection fees, less time spent on compliance, and fewer unnecessary repairs. I know many people around the country, including people in this House, will welcome these changes, especially when many households are feeling pressure due to high fuel prices caused by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

explanation: Asked when the changes take effect. Answer opens with 'From 1 November' — a direct date. The added material about ongoing roadworthiness obligations is padding, not evasion.
question: When will these changes come into effect?
